en: The Buddha-treasury is profound, vast, and expansive; it has reached such a magnitude that its volumes fill the rafters and exhaust the oxen’s sweat, such that it can never be fully investigated.

How could it not be the wondrous truth of the Three Vehicles and the awakening conditions of the Five Aggregates? As for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it extensively expounds upon *prajñā* and reveals the *pāramitā*.
Since the translation during the Yao Qin dynasty, there have been the sub-commentary by Guifeng in the Tang and the record by Changshui in the Song.

Reaching down to the Ming monk Dayun, who compiled them into a topical outline (*kehui*), the words and meanings became perfectly clear; yet, as this was not widely circulated, it failed to serve as a broad bridge for those looking toward the distant goal.
Consequently, many virtuous people have always regretted that they were unable to see it in its entirety. [Friend...]
The person Jichuan Zhu has here brought forth an old manuscript of Yunqi that he obtained, making a vow to reprint it for universal distribution to the great assembly.

This shall expand the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom and develop the source of the teachings for requesting instruction, so that among the bhikṣus, those who see the finger may know where to return, as if by a staff or a shout.
Through this, they may transcend to awaken to the essence of Chan and penetrate the mirror of the mind; its subtlety and mystery are inconceivable.

The deliberation upon these merits is likewise inconceivable. At the beginning of this scripture, I have composed and distinguished this preface to certify those in the world who receive and uphold this sutra.
On the Buddha-Bath Day of the Renyin year of the Qianlong era, the Layman Canglang, Sun Xiaozeng, studies the Buddha-vehicle of the two wheels to save sentient beings.
Initially, his views of self and others had not yet been eliminated; subsequently, [his views of] self and dharmas...
Because their attachments still remained, they arose during the assembly at the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and asked the Tathāgata twice how they should abide.
The Tathāgata, with his adamantine wisdom of reality, repeatedly pointed out and shattered [their delusions], decisively severing all doubts.

He caused them to know that the essence of true emptiness does not involve the two extremes; it is the primary gateway for entering the Way and the ultimate realization of Buddhahood. This is the core teaching.
The various patriarchs of our school have taken this sutra as the seal of their minds, alongside the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other scriptures.
As for those among the monastic and lay communities who have recited and studied this sutra, there are miraculous responses recorded that are beyond counting.

Indeed, while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is the foremost of all sutras, this *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* is, in turn, the foremost among the eight divisions [of the Prajñāpāramitā]. Since the time of Bodhisattva Asaṅga...
There are eighteen dwellings (*vihāra*). Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s *Twenty-Seven Doubts* provides an interpretation based on the verses;

it is no different from having received the Buddha’s intent directly. Following this, there are various compositions such as those by Qinglong, Dayun, and Zhidu, each of which is vast and expansive in its phrasing, like a deep ocean.
Among these, the most prominent is the *Commentary on the Compendium of Essentials* by the Great Master Guifeng of the Tang Dynasty.

Based on the text and its expanded meanings, I have synthesized the various commentaries. Furthermore, having obtained the definitive edition by the Great Master Changshui, I have composed this record anew.

Although the sections are numerous and the reader may feel overwhelmed like one facing the vast ocean, the subtle words and great principles of this sutra are nonetheless fully contained herein. As for the Confucianists—

Regarding the *Xue* (Learning): there are thirteen classics with their commentaries and sub-commentaries (*zhùshū*). Although later generations have held the Song Confucians in high esteem, the words of Zheng Xuan and Kong Yingda have not been discarded for ages.
This present classic is perhaps similar; though the years since its publication have not been long, the woodblocks have already suffered damage and loss.

There was the Master Mìyún, a true dragon-elephant within the teachings, who once sought to raise funds to carve these blocks, yet his aspiration remained unfulfilled. Now, Lǎoxiū has completed this task.
The Master extensively cultivated roots of goodness and continued the aspirations of his predecessors. He requested the layman Mr. Sun Xiaocong, Mr.
Zhu Yuqing, and others to procure materials and assemble craftsmen; before long, it was completed. Once the work was finished and the carving was accomplished, he asked me for a preface.
I consider that in Vaiśālī the Buddha remained silent and in Magadha the room was closed; the gate of non-duality does not reside in language or written words. Nevertheless, in the final age...
Since the Dharma has long since departed from us, the study of its meaning is all the more precious. The survival or loss of the sutras determines where the teachings will be anchored.
Moreover, you gentlemen have, by means of this single sutra, realized your own minds, severed your doubts, and given rise to faith, thereby causing Prajñā to manifest before you.
This is the seed of all Buddhas. For those who abide as instructed, how could they be merely the meritorious ministers of the three previous masters? This sutra...

There have been seven translations in total; this [work] relies exclusively on the translation by [Kumārajīva] of the Qin dynasty. The textual divisions and syntheses each possess their own thematic gateways (arthamukha), which only the discerning reader can fully comprehend for themselves.
Written by the Layman Hequan Gu Guangda on an auspicious day in the fourth lunar month of the forty-seventh year of the Qing Qianlong era.
Commentary and Record on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Classified and Synthesized, Volume One.
Exegesis by the Great Master Guifeng of the Tang Dynasty;
Record by the Great Master Changshui of the Song Dynasty.
Compiled by the junior scholar, the Śramaṇa Daběn of Yunqi Monastery, with a topical outline and a record. [Record and Preface]:

The teaching of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* among the followers of the Buddha has been esteemed since ancient times. From the Qin dynasty until the present, how many hundreds of years have there been?

Carrying on this tradition, they chanted and recited it without distinction between the lowly and the noble; thus, spiritual resonance filled their scrolls and tablets, benefiting even the netherworld and reaching up to the divine spirits.
This is truly the broad path leading toward the Great [Vehicle] and the grand strategy for shattering the Small [Vehicle].

Therefore, the *Buchu-song* (Hymn of the Successor) serves as the foundation, while the two treatises provide the systematic exposition. Various commentaries offer mutual interpretations, some following the original intent and others deviating from it. As for Master Guishan:
I have selected the essence and discarded the superficial and false, titling this work *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium).

It draws upon the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean) and further extends the *Jilue* (Brief Records) for the purpose of facilitating study and transmission. Master Shibi subsequently compiled a *Guanyi* (Extended Commentary), which, while admirable, is often prolix in its phrasing;
consequently, many later students find it inconvenient to use. I have now revised and edited this work, pruning away what is redundant and chaotic.

This is so that [the teachings] may circulate without stagnation, and that students may study and reflect upon them for exposition; it is my hope that the Way will suffer no further peril of falling into oblivion.
This preface was written on the day of Jiazi in the final month of winter, the second year of the Tianzheng era of the Great Song.
[Commentary] *Jingang jing zuanyao kanding ji* (Record of the Collated Essentials of the Vajracchedikā Sūtra), compiled by the Śramaṇa Zixuan of Changshui.

The explanation of the *Jingang jing zuanyao shu* (Subcommentary on the Collated Essentials of the Vajracchedikā Sūtra) is divided into three parts: first, the title; second, the preface to the fundamental tenets;

and third, the exegesis of the main text. The first part, the title, is further divided into two sections: first, the title of the sūtra and its subcommentary; second, the honorary name of the author.
First, the title of the commentary on the sutra. [Commentary]:
*Jingang Banruo Jing Shu Lun Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium of the Commentary on the Diamond Prajñā Sūtra), together with the preface.
[Record]: The text of the commentary is divided into three parts. First, the title and heading. Second, the initial title of the sutra commentary.

[Commentary] Regarding the title *Jingang banruo jing shu lun zuanyao* (The Essential Compendium of the Commentary and Treatise on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), these nine characters proceed from the broad to the narrow and involve six layers of subject and object (*neng-so*).

First, the subject and object of explanation: the five characters "Jingang" (Diamond) and so forth are the object (*so*), while the four characters "shu lun" (commentary and treatise) and below belong to the subject (*neng*).
Second, the subject and object of what is expressed: the sūtra and commentary belong to the subject, while the four characters "Jingang" and so forth are the object.

Third, the distinction between subject and object has two parts: first, the distinction regarding the general; this means that while the *Sūtra* encompasses the temporal teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha's ministry, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is restricted solely to its own specific section.
Second, the distinction regarding the particular; this means that while the *Prajñāpāramitā* still extends across eight sections, the *Vajracchedikā* belongs exclusively to a single sūtra.

Fifth, the metaphors for the subject and object: "Vajra" is the subject, and "Prajñā" belongs to the object. Sixth, the compilation of the subject and object: the character "zuan" (compilation) belongs to the subject, referring to the author of the commentary;
the character "yao" (essential) is the object, referring to the correct meaning. If the two characters "bingxu" (with preface) are added, they also belong to the subject.

Furthermore, there is one additional layer. The two characters [“纂” and “述”] signify the agent (the subject), while all preceding elements are subsumed under the object. Nevertheless, these seven layers do not transcend the categories of teaching, practice, and principle.
Specifically, the five characters—“經” (sūtra), “疏” (commentary), “論” (treatise), and “并序” (together with the preface)—constitute the teaching;

that is, they represent that which expresses, explains, and introduces. The term “般若” (Prajñā) refers to the universal practice, meaning contemplative insight. The character “纂” (compiled) pertains to the person, namely the author of the commentary. “金” (Gold).

The character *yào* (essential) pertains to principle (*lǐ*). "Vajra" (*jīngāng*) is the true mark (*shíxiàng*), which is ultimate truth (*zhēnlǐ*). The character *yào* is the correct meaning (*zhèngyì*), which is the underlying logic (*dàolǐ*).

[Commentary] Having understood that this single title involves both the subject (*néng*) and object (*suǒ*) and thus removes attachments, one must further understand the depth and shallowness of the principles within the title. Vajra...
There are three meanings: namely, firmness, sharpness, and clarity. Prajñā also has three meanings: namely, the true mark (*dharmatā*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and words (*vyañjana*).
A sūtra has three meanings: namely, constant, pervasive, and inclusive. A commentary (*śāstra*) also has three meanings: namely, to resolve what is obscure, to spread out, and to explain.

"Treatise" (*lun*) means deliberation; it also has three meanings: namely, deliberating on principles, deliberating on wisdom, and deliberating on practice. The *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) also...
There are three meanings: namely, essential meaning, essential practice, and essential text.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the three meanings of "Vajra": because it cannot be destroyed by any phenomenon, yet can destroy all phenomena, and furthermore possesses the function of illumination, it may be used as a metaphor for the three kinds of *prajñā*.
"Firmness" is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the true nature of reality), because even though it passes through...

Throughout many kalpas, it has flowed and scattered through the six realms of existence, yet it has never been born or extinguished, and it has never been diminished or deficient; therefore, it is called "firm.
Thus, the Heart Sūtra says: "The mark of the emptiness of all these dharmas is that they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing," and so forth.

"Sharp" is a metaphor for the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*); this means that when this [wisdom] manifests, it illuminates the emptiness of all dharmas, and is thus called "sharp."

Therefore, the Heart Sutra says: "When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and distress. It continues by stating, "There is neither ignorance nor attainment," and so forth.

This clarifies the metaphorical correspondence with the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), for it is through words that one can explain, manifest, and illuminate the contemplative realization of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Because it causes [the nature] to manifest, and by virtue of these three meanings it resembles that vajra, the vajra is cited as a metaphor for *prajñā*.
However, this *prajñā* is possessed by all Buddhas and sentient beings alike; because it remains within the entanglements of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), it cannot be utilized.
If one can hear the teachings and attain realization through the power of internal and external cultivation, then one will be able to sever the afflictions and emerge [from them].
In birth and death, when principle and wisdom are in profound union, they can give rise to great function, no different from that of a Buddha.
It is like gold within ore: it cannot yet serve a purpose; however, once extracted from the ore, it will surely be able to form vessels and cut through objects.
Thus we know that this wisdom is not absent in anything; thus we know that this wisdom can establish the Great Meaning. What is now called *prajñā* (wisdom) is, in essence, the Great Wisdom.

This is its Sanskrit pronunciation. "Vajra" (Diamond) is the primary metaphor for Prajñā (Wisdom). Since both the dharma and the metaphor are manifested together, it is called the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
[Commentary] If one were to follow the full title of the sutra, it should read "Pāramitā," which praises the merit of wisdom. (Tang)

The expression “reaching the other shore” (pāra-gata) follows the custom of the Western Regions. If one were to conform to the usage of this region [China], it should be said “reaching the other shore from this shore.
As for “the other shore,” it is precisely nirvāṇa; because it is contrasted with “this shore” of birth and death (saṃsāra), nirvāṇa is designated as “the other.”
This clarifies that *prajñā* is the wisdom that reaches the other shore; this is the specific characteristic of wisdom. Now, this wisdom that reaches the other shore has, in brief, two aspects:
namely, the sudden (*tun*) and the gradual (*jian*). As for the sudden: when this wisdom manifests, in a single *kṣaṇa*, it illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena;
this is precisely reaching the other shore, and is therefore called the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Because— [text continues]

After passing through a long period of time, it is then called "sudden. As for the "gradual," although one may suddenly illuminate the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*), habitual tendencies still persist as innate dispositions, leading to spontaneous conceptual attachments.

Therefore, one must employ the wisdom of that sudden awakening to observe these deluded sentiments, diminishing them again and again until reaching the state of non-action (*wuwei*). This is the ultimate arrival at the other shore; it is also called "arrival."

The wisdom that reaches the other shore is called "gradual" because it spans a long period of time. Although gradual and sudden differ in their speed, both are equally termed "wisdom that reaches the other shore.
Therefore, in full, it should be called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Diamond Wisdom that Reaches the Other Shore);
here, it is abbreviated and not mentioned.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the explanation that the characters of the sūtra possess three meanings: according to the interpretations of various schools, there are many such meanings, namely "gushing spring," "origination," "measuring line," "garland," and so forth.
However, in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, only two meanings are taught: "pervasion" (*guàn*) and "gathering" (*shè*).
"Pervasion" refers to penetrating the meanings that ought to be explained; "gathering" refers to sustaining and holding the sentient beings to be converted. For now...

Since the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa more than two thousand years ago, those who have been able to hear the True Dharma while his lingering influence still persists have all realized the meaning of being threaded through by the Sūtras.
Sentient beings drift and wander, not knowing where to turn; yet now they have found the gateway to the Buddha’s teaching.
"That all return to the correct destination" refers to the meaning of being "subsumed" by the sūtra. Possessing these two meanings, it is called a "sūtra.
Now, adding the meaning of "permanence" to these two, they correspond to the three kinds of *prajñā*:

namely, the permanence of the *dharmatā* (real aspect), the continuity of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the subsumption of the written word (*vyañjana*). However, this particular sūtra was translated by Kumārajīva; its verses and phrases...
It is pure and refreshing, causing those who hear it to rejoice. To this day, from the young and old to the high and low, they fill the world;
there are none who do not uphold this sutra.
[Commentary] The *Shu lun zuanyao* (Essential Compilation of the Commentary) refers to this single fascicle of commentary. The commentary is that of Qinglong Dayun.

The commentaries (*śāstra*) include those by Zisheng, Chenwai, and others. A "commentary" (*shu*) refers to that which elucidates and penetrates the underlying principles, discerns the characteristics of the meanings, and arranges them into written words.
The "treatises" (*lun*) refer to those by Vasubandhu, Asaṅga, Nāgārjuna, Vajrasattva, Guṇaprabha, and others.

Within each of these treatises, the principles, wisdom, and practices are expounded with spontaneous ease. Question: Since there already exist commentaries and treatises that explain the sūtras, why...

Question: Why must this commentary be newly composed? Answer: It is for the purpose of compiling the essentials. That is to say, this commentary is formed by extracting the essential meanings from other commentaries and treatises.
Now, the establishment of such a compilation of essentials generally involves two intentions: first, to accord with the intent of the Sage above; second, to harmonize with the minds of people below.
The intention is to demonstrate that various [other] explanations may fail to accord with the Sage’s intent or harmonize with the minds of people.
Regarding the mind: first, as for the "intention," this very sutra belongs to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which does not maintain the existence of dharmas;

yet [this commentary] explains it by extensively enumerating the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). This does not accord with the Sage’s intent, as it loses the fundamental tenet. Therefore, the preface states:
Some incorporate [the teachings] into names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), which clings to phenomena and deviates from the fundamental tenet.

Others, upon hearing of this school of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*), interpret it as a single-flavored path of signlessness (*animitta*). This too does not accord with the Sage’s intent; for although the tenet is signless, its meanings are manifold.
To explain it as a single flavor is to be deluded regarding the secondary details. Thus the Preface says: "Or merely..."

Regarding the claim that "the One Truth" (Yun-yi-zhen) is like looking for the source while lost in the tributaries: the former fails to conform to the fundamental principle (*zong*) yet does not lose the lineage (*pai*);
the latter loses the lineage yet does not fail to conform to the fundamental principle. Each has its strengths and weaknesses; both lack complete and thorough realization.

Furthermore, there are those who, indulging in biased views, provide commentaries based on them, thereby losing both the fundamental principle and the lineage; these are not worth evaluating. Thus, the Preface states: "As for the rest—those discourses from the breast and commentaries from the imagination..."
This is sufficient for the treatise. However, although each of those various expositions has its own merits, they all contain errors and lack comprehensive clarity;

therefore, they were all judged to be inconsistent with the intent of the Sage. Now, I have composed this commentary (*śāstra*). I have not added further doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to avoid deviating from the fundamental school, and I have explained the text according to its words so as not to lose sight of the lineage.
Thus, free from the two aforementioned faults, it attains the middle way in a truly perfect manner. This, then, is transcendent.
This alone accords with the Sage’s intent. However, since the current commentary (*śāstra*) employs the Sage’s own words throughout, the preface states:
"Therefore, what is here described does not attack heterodox views. The commentary is the treatise itself; the milk is not within the city, let alone the two Bodhisattvas.

The Teacher is the Honored One who is to succeed [to Buddhahood]; the one to succeed is the Tathāgata; the Teacher is Śākyamuni Buddha. Thus, tracing back through successive stages, the Buddhas transmit it to one another, descending down to...
Asas and Vasubandhu have no further divergent explanations; therefore, it should be known that this commentary is indeed the word of the Buddha.

Those who slander this commentary are the same as those who slander the Buddha. Thus the preface says: "Furthermore, Vasubandhu and Asaṅga were the Honored Ones who served as the Vicars of the Buddha; how can later students harbor doubts?
Whether adding to or discarding [the text], [one must proceed] next in accordance with the minds of people. Furthermore, regarding the various commentaries and treatises currently extant:
The reasoning is not yet appropriate, and the text is so verbose that it causes students to rarely dare to apply their minds to it;

thus, those who merely recite the words are numerous, while those who achieve thorough understanding are rare. Therefore, the preface states: "This has led to oral recitations as thick as cow hair, while mental penetration is as rare as the horn of a unicorn.
Now, this commentary extracts the essential pivot points and directly elucidates the sūtra. Combining the sūtra and its commentary, they fill fifty sheets of paper.
Whether among monastic companions or worldly laypeople, one may apply one’s mind to this; it is not only those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties who can study it.
Because these two considerations are present, I have composed this work. This represents wisdom first followed by compassion, benefiting both oneself and others.
Therefore, it is titled *The Essential Compendium of the Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

[Commentary] Regarding "with the preface" (*bing xu*): "with" (*bing*) means together, inclusive, or including. "Preface" (*xu*) means to narrate; it refers to the narration of the meaning of the commentary on the sutra.
Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means a thread or beginning; it signifies that these few lines on half a sheet of paper serve as the introductory thread for the composition of this commentary.
△ Second, the author’s honorable title.
[Commentary] Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Daxingfu Temple in the Capital.
[Sub-commentary] Second, the author’s honorable title. "Capital" (Jīng) means the metropolis; it is great. It is the place where the commoners and gentry, the noble and the humble, all assemble.
This is a major location. However, it refers to the Western Capital (Xijing) and not the northeast; because there is the Daxingfu Temple located therein, "west" is not explicitly stated.

*Śramaṇa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "diligent cessation. It is the general title for the assembly of Śākyamuni’s followers, meaning that they diligently cultivate all practices and bring afflictions to rest.
The term "narrator" (*shu*) clarifies that this is not a formal composition, corresponding to the preceding term "compilation" (*zuan*).
The essential point is this: it merely recounts the intent of the former sages rather than being a separate composition of one's own. For example, the Master said:
"I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity, and I venture to compare myself to our Old Peng."
[Commentary] Revised and finalized by the Śramaṇa Zixuan of Changshui.

△ Second, the introduction to the fundamental tenets, in two parts: first, the introduction praising the intent of the sutra; second, the statement of the purpose for composing this commentary. First, the introduction praising the intent of the sutra, in two parts:
first, a general clarification of the conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, a specific clarification of the intent behind the preaching of the teaching. First, the general...

II. Clarifying the Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching. This has two parts: first, clarifying how delusion regarding the truth gives rise to falsehood; second, clarifying the circulation through the flow of habitual falsehood.
Regarding the first, clarifying how delusion regarding the truth gives rise to falsehood, there are two parts: first, true emptiness; second, false existence. Regarding the first, true emptiness:
[Commentary]: "The mirror-like mind is fundamentally pure; the reflected forms are originally empty. [Record]:

The second section concerns the fundamental tenets of the introduction. It has two parts: first, the introduction praising the purport of the sutra; second, a general clarification of the conditions for the arising of the teaching.
II. First, clarifying how delusion arises from the truth; second, first, true emptiness.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "mirror-like mind" and so forth: to state it briefly, the preceding clause refers to the true nature being free from conditions, while the following clause refers to conditions having no self-nature.
This is the general outline. For a detailed explanation, one should first provide a brief correspondence, which shall follow.
Broad Explanation.

[Commentary] Regarding the brief correlation: within these two phrases, the "mirror image" is the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), while "mind and form" (*citta-rūpa*) are the phenomena (*dharma*). Their fundamental purity and primordial emptiness apply to both the phenomena and the metaphor.
The mirror is used as a metaphor for the mind, and the image is used as a metaphor for form. The image is that of the mirror...
Regarding what is manifested: just as form is a manifestation of the mind, although a mirror manifests images, those images are fundamentally empty;
this reveals that the mirror is originally pure. Although the mind manifests forms, those forms are fundamentally empty; this reveals that the mind is originally pure.

What is called "original purity" (benjing) is precisely "intrinsic purity" (xingjing), for it pervades both cause and effect, as well as ordinary beings and sages. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is not consciousness..."
It is that which can be known, yet it is not the realm of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure, revealing itself to all living beings.
This is a brief indication of the correspondences.
[Commentary] To explain extensively: the "mirror" refers to the mirrors used by people in the world. However, if they are buried in dust, they become unfit for use.

Regarding "that which is used": there are those that, though pure, remain within a casket; and there are those that are pure and free from dust and grime, suspended high upon a platform where the myriad phenomena are all reflected therein.
Here, we take the latter as our metaphor. As for the "mind" (*citta*): the explanations of the two schools—the Nature (*svabhāva*) and the Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—differ.

According to the proponents of the School of Characteristics, some define the mind as that which "accumulates and gives rise to" (*saṃcita-utpādaka*), referring exclusively to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which accumulates all seeds.

"Son, it is because they arise as active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). Alternatively, taking that which perceives objects as 'mind' applies to all eight consciousnesses, as each is capable of perceiving its own respective object.
However, what has been described here refers only to conditioned phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; it is not what is being illustrated now.
As for those who speak according to the Nature School (*Xingzong*), it is the Tathāgatagarbha, the primordially pure mind of the original nature. Yet, what is clarified here is as follows:"

This is precisely this mind. As it is the root of both delusion and enlightenment, and that upon which all ordinary beings and sages alike depend, neither the mundane nor the supramundane exists apart from it.
Therefore, in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, it is established as the essence of the Mahāyāna.
Thus the treatise says: "The Mahāyāna consists of one dharma and two meanings. That which is called 'dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses [all things]."
All mundane and supramundane dharmas depend upon this mind; thus the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. Furthermore, it is said:
"Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates: first, the gate of the suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*);
second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). These two gates each comprehensively encompass all dharmas. What is the meaning of this? It is because...
These two gates are not separate from one another. Because the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the universal characteristic, it encompasses all things.
Although the gate of arising and ceasing is a particular characteristic, because this arising and ceasing is itself identical to True Suchness, it also encompasses all things.
Since these two gates both take the single mind as their source, one knows that the myriad phenomena do not transcend this mind. It is like a flower.
The "Strict" [teaching] is the perfectly consummate One Vehicle. It also takes this mind as the substance of the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, that commentary states: "To unify the four dharma-realms into the One True Dharma-realm means it is tranquil and vast, profound and expansive, encompassing all things;
it is precisely the One Mind. Its substance transcends existence and non-existence, and its characteristics are neither arising nor ceasing," and so forth.
It says: "The Buddhas realize this; their wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous, and they manifest the attainment of Bodhi to reveal it to all beings," and so forth.

Now, this single mind possesses both essence (*xing*) and appearance (*xiang*). As for appearance, there are distinctions such as ordinary person versus sage, delusion versus awakening, cause versus effect, and defilement versus purity.
The nature is luminous and never obscured; it is ever-knowing and clearly aware. Yet this nature and its manifestations are neither identical nor separate.

Because manifestations do not depart from the nature, they are different precisely within the state of sameness. Because the nature does not depart from manifestations, it is the same precisely within the state of difference.
Because the nature is not identical to manifestations, there has never been any differentiation. Because manifestations are not identical to the nature, they have never failed to be [the nature].
This is truly extraordinary. It is because the nature and its manifestations are of one flavor that both identity and difference coexist. This is like water, waves, and moisture;
through them, the identity and difference of nature and manifestation can be understood. Yet this numinous mind is fundamentally not any thing at all, yet it is capable of being all things.
The name "mind" is also established by virtue of this. What is now called "purity" refers solely to the meaning of ultimate emptiness;
it does not mean that purity is designated in contrast to defilement. Since there is only the single mind that penetrates both defilement and purity, Heze said:
"The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all wonders; all dharmas are established in dependence upon it. As this constitutes both gain and loss...
This secret treasury is the profound pivot of ascent and descent; it is called the Gate of Myriad Wonders and is truly ultimate.
What is now being discerned is precisely this mind. However, the two types previously described in the Dharma-character (lakṣaṇa) school are merely one gate of arising and ceasing within this mind.
To distinguish between their relative shallowness and depth, they must be carefully examined; yet when harmonized and integrated, they are fully subsumed [within this mind]. Thus:
Truly, there is nothing left out. Regarding "original purity," it can be understood through analogy. Within this Dharma, there are two meanings:
first, that this mind has been fundamentally empty in nature from the very beginning; second, that although it is currently entangled by afflictions, it remains undefiled.
This corresponds to the "Gate of True Suchness" (*tathatā-mukha*) in the *Awakening of Faith*. Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
"Good son, the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure.

Because the mind is fundamentally pure, the various fetters of affliction cannot defile it, just as empty space cannot be stained. The nature of the mind and emptiness are equal and without distinction.
○ 'Images' refers to the myriad images manifested within a mirror. ○ 'Form' refers to that which arises from the fundamentally pure mind."
All phenomena are manifested; however, these manifested phenomena do not transcend form and mind. Now, the reason why only "form" is mentioned and "mind" is not is threefold:
first, because the phrasing is concise; second, because [mind] is implied by its presence below; and third, because the initial term subsumes what follows.
The first two points are easily understood. As for the latter intention: all phenomena do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and among these, form is the first.
The character [“form,” *rūpa*] stands at the beginning of the five aggregates. When we now speak of “form,” we cite the first to encompass the subsequent ones.
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, whenever all phenomena are categorized, “form” is invariably placed first. As it says: “Subhūti, because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure;
because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) is pure,” and so forth. This is due to...
Although this passage mentions "form" (rūpa), its intent encompasses both form and mind. Once form and mind are manifested, the myriad dharmas are complete.
○ Regarding "original emptiness": it can be understood through analogy. Within the dharma, there are two meanings. First, that it is originally empty. As the Treatise states:
"All dharmas exist only in dependence upon deluded thought; if one is separated from mental thought, they do not exist."
Regarding the characteristics of all objective realms: secondly, because emptiness is directly perceived. All phenomena, such as form and so forth, are originally and inherently empty.
Deluded people do not know this and falsely cling to them as being existent. Although they cling to existence, they have never ceased to be empty. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"If all phenomena were not empty, there would be neither the Path nor its fruit. It further states: "Because the principle of emptiness exists..."
All phenomena are thus established. ○ However, this single phrase also serves to resolve doubts.

Fearing that people, upon hearing it said that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), and further seeing the treatise state that "this mind encompasses worldly phenomena and so forth," might conclude that it inherently possesses defilement and the like, and thus argue that it is improper to call it "pure," the following phrase provides the resolution: "The form of the image is originally empty. The meaning is that form...
If these [objects] were real, they would defile the pure mind. Since form and so forth are empty, by what means could the mind be defiled? It is like a mirror manifesting a foul image;

the foul image is fundamentally empty, appearing as if it exists while actually being non-existent. How, then, could there be defilement? Therefore, it is said that the mirror-like mind is fundamentally pure.
The forms and colors are fundamentally empty. The *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* states: "Purity has two meanings. First is natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which is its universal characteristic.
Second is purity through the removal of defilements (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*), which is its specific characteristic.
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, there are likewise two meanings: first, natural purity, which refers to liberation through intrinsic purity; second, purity through the removal of defilements.
"Purity" refers to liberation through the exhaustion of hindrances. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* translated during the Wei dynasty states: "The mind is of two kinds:
first, the associated mind, which refers to all afflictions, sensations, perceptions, mental formations, and so forth;
second, the dissociated mind, which refers to the ultimate truth—the eternally abiding, unchanging, and intrinsically pure mind. That which is elucidated here is [this latter].

This refers to the mind that is intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); therefore, it is called "originally pure. Furthermore, these two phrases mutually clarify one another:
by explaining the latter phrase through the former, the meaning of the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) is established;

by explaining the former phrase through the latter, the meaning of the purity of mind (*citta-viśuddhi*) is established. If form were not empty, the mind would not be pure; if the mind were not pure, form [would not be empty].
This is precisely non-emptiness. Because the mind is pure, form is empty; because form is empty, the mind is pure.
Since the two dharmas of form and mind are not mutually separated, one should know that it is only through the purity of the mind that form can manifest, just as it is when a mirror is pure.
Only then can it manifest images; if it is defiled, it cannot. Furthermore, because form is empty, it cannot defile the mind.

Just as an image, being empty, cannot soil a mirror, whereas a solid object would indeed soil it. Thus, the preceding and following phrases clarify the correspondence between the Dharma and the analogy, establishing them through mutual reinforcement;
hence, they are said to be "mutually explained."
△ Second, false existence.
[Commentary] The dream-consciousness has no beginning; external objects and environments constitute existence.

[Record] Regarding the "dream-consciousness" section of the Commentary: this second part clarifies false existence, which corresponds precisely to the "arising and ceasing of the mind" (*citta-utpāda-nirodha*) in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana*.

Section on the Gate. This also possesses both the dharma (the principle) and the metaphor. Consciousness is compared to a dream, and the objects appearing within the dream are compared to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

It is like a person who, after falling asleep and dreaming, perceives objects where there are no objects; this serves as a metaphor for how the mind, when deluded, becomes consciousness and perceives an objective realm where no realm exists.
Although objects appear based upon the dream, the dream-objects are all empty and false. Although the realm arises from...
Consciousness arises; yet both consciousness and its object are equally illusory.

[Commentary] As for "one who dreams": it is like an ordinary person covered by the shroud of sleep, whose mental consciousness becomes dim and obscured, such that in a state of daze, a dream is formed.
According to the *Qièyùn* (Cuts of Pronunciation), "dreaming" (*mèng*) refers to the state of mental confusion. It is also said that what one sees while asleep is called a dream;

this clarifies that when the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) becomes turbid and disordered, one perceives extraordinary phenomena, which is termed a "dream. As for "consciousness" (*shí*): it is the fundamentally pure single mind that suddenly fails to be aware.
This lack of awareness is delusion (*mṛṣā*), whereas the nature of the mind is reality (*satya*). The union of reality and delusion is designated as "consciousness."
This is precisely the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Depending upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth-and-death;
that is to say, the unborn and undying is conjoined with birth-and-death, being neither identical nor different, and is named the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Regarding "having no beginning": "beginning" (*ādi*) means "initial point. This intends to clarify that this consciousness has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
However, although the true mind and deluded consciousness differ in terms of being real or unreal, if one investigates their source, both lack a beginning.
There are two points to consider: first, as stated in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* (Foding jing), both afflictions and bodhi are beginningless;
that is to say, from the time this true mind has existed, this deluded consciousness has likewise existed—it does not mean that the true came first and the deluded followed later. Furthermore...

It is not that the false comes first and the true comes later. If one were to say that the true comes first and the false comes later, then it would follow that the Buddhas must further give rise to ignorance.
If one were to say that the false comes first and the true comes later, how could there be a false that exists independently, devoid of truth?
For this reason, we know that both are beginningless. This, then, makes the analogy of the dream inconsistent; rather, it is like gold and its ore. If one were to say...
The ore comes first and the gold follows; by smelting the discarded ore, one obtains the gold.
If it were said that the gold comes first and the ore follows, then pure gold vessels should be able to be regenerated from within the ore. Thus, both of these substances are without a beginning.
This can be understood from the Dharma. Question: As the treatise states, "Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth and death.
Since it says that the false depends upon the true, the false would be posterior and the true prior. How, then, can it be said that both are beginningless? Answer:
Not so. What is called "relying" clarifies that delusion has no self-substance and is established by relying on the True [Suchness].

This reveals the meaning of the fundamental and the derivative, not the meaning of priority and posteriority. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning.
If one were to say that there are sentient beings outside the triple world who first arise," [it would be a false view].
This is what is taught in the scriptures of the non-Buddhists. Second, it means that the substance of delusion is entirely empty, with no trace whatsoever of its arising;
therefore, it is said that delusion has no beginning. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic."
This is precisely that meaning. If one relies on this intention, the analogy of the dream is exactly appropriate, because when one dreams, no tracks are left behind.
Since there are these two points of meaning, it is said that delusion has no beginning. However, within the aforementioned two analogies of the dream and the ore—
Taking a small portion from each, we shall together illustrate the principle that a single consciousness has no beginning; only then will its true meaning be fully exhausted.

The dream serves as a metaphor for phenomena that have no beginning, while the ore serves as a metaphor for time that has no beginning. If one were to employ the metaphor of ore alone, it would imply that the deluded consciousness possesses substantial reality.
If one were to take only the analogy of a dream, then deluded consciousness would have a beginning.
Now that we have taken both the similarities and differences into account, the principle is fully established. "Objects" refers to the objects manifested within the dream.
"Realms" refers to the realms of the self and other phenomena transformed within consciousness. "To establish existence" means, for instance, as when one sees oneself in a dream.
Regarding other realms, upon awakening one reflects back and concludes that they were certainly non-existent; yet while in the dream, they were definitely existent.
If this were not so, how could there be such things as praise and joy, slander and anger, aversion and suffering, or delight and pleasure? Therefore, we know they exist.
As it is said in the *Zhuangzi*: "Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly, completely forgetting he was Zhuang Zhou."
When one awakens from sleep and the dream has vanished, where has the butterfly ever been? While he was Zhuang Zhou, he did not envy the butterfly;
while he was the butterfly, he likewise did not envy Zhuang Zhou. Each followed its own course, and they were unaware of one another.
However, according to that text, its intent is to demonstrate that birth and death are equal and level. The intent of what is cited here is to clarify the meaning of grasping at reality:

namely, that based upon deluded consciousness, the appearances of a self and other phenomena arise through transformation; yet, when one awakens and attains full realization, one truly knows them to be empty.
If one is in a state of genuine delusion, one certainly clings to them as being existent. Were it not so, how could there be greed and hatred?
Is it not the case that there are matters such as attachment, aversion, grasping, and discarding? Therefore, we know they exist. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Based on what is transformed by consciousness, one falsely perceives a self and dharmas, which are like illusions and dreams. By the power of these illusions and dreams, the mind manifests as various external objective appearances;
conditioned by these, one clings to them as being real external objects. ○ However, although one sees various things within a dream...
When one investigates the root of these phenomena, they are found to be nothing but the dreaming mind; when the dreaming mind ceases, all dream-objects likewise cease. It is the same with dharmas:
though objects are infinite, when one traces them to their root, they are found to be nothing but the consciousness-mind; when the consciousness-mind ceases, [all phenomena cease].
Objects of perception cease accordingly. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought.
If one is free from mental ideation, then there are no appearances of any objects. From this, one knows that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only;
how truly unfounded would it be to think otherwise! Consequently, all contaminated [dharmas] within the triple-worldly realm...
All defiled phenomena arise from deluded consciousness; therefore, this consciousness is named the "deluded root.
Now, regarding the sequence of the arising of all outflowing (sāsrava) defiled phenomena, there are generally two levels: first, the beginningless root; second, the successive branches and offshoots.
The successive branches and offshoots are those explained in the subsequent section on "Pursuing Delusion. The [beginningless root]...
It begins with the fundamental. This section precisely addresses this point. As for "fundamental," it refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
As for "ignorance," it means that there is no clarity of wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*). Speaking in terms of its general characteristics, it corresponds to this consciousness.
However, fundamental ignorance has two meanings, namely: being deluded regarding the Truth and clinging to the false. Regarding "being deluded regarding the Truth," it is...

The true mind is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; its virtuous attributes and karmic functions exceed the sands of the Ganges in measure. Yet, in daily life, one remains unaware of it, like one who is mad or intoxicated.
It is like a treasure trove within a poor woman’s house, or a bright pearl inside a destitute son’s garment—though present, it is as if non-existent, leading one to undergo suffering in vain.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To be ignorant of the primary truth is called ignorance (*avidyā*)."

"Grasping at the delusive" means that the delusive refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Both form and mind are like illusions and transformations; they have no substantial reality from the beginning.
Sentient beings recognize these as their own body and mind, reckoning the unreal to be real; therefore, it is called "grasping at the delusive. Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:

"They falsely recognize the four great elements as the characteristic of their own body, and the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristic of their own mind. This is...
The conclusion states: "Because of this delusion, there is the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). However, these two meanings mutually establish one another;
when one is mentioned, the other is implied by extension, for they never exist independently. If one clings to the delusory, one must be confused about the Real;
if one is confused about the Real, one must cling to the delusory. It is like a person who, being confused about the east, necessarily clings to the west."
They establish one another; this can be seen upon reflection.
△ Second, clarifying the circulation of habitual delusion.

[Commentary]: Because of this, afflictions and karma are repeatedly practiced, and retributions and responses revolve in cycles. Through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they cannot be blocked or severed.

[Commentary] From "By this" onwards, the second section clarifies the circulation through the cultivation of delusion; this corresponds to the second gate of the sequential development of the secondary branches of deluded phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "by this" (*youshi*): "by" (*you*) means cause; "this" (*shi*) refers to this very [delusion].
Because of this delusion regarding the Truth, consciousness is formed, and all worldly objects manifest. Taking these objects as conditions, one gives rise to afflictions and creates [karma].
Karma. The retribution received is inexhaustible. ○ Within this context, the four characters "delusion (惑), karma (業), retribution (報), and response (應)" constitute the three paths.
However, among the various teachings, these three dharmas are called the "three obstructions" (trīṇy āvaraṇāni) because they obstruct the Noble Path; alternatively, they are called the "three paths."
Because the mind is led in a gradual succession until it reaches karmic retribution, these are also termed the "three defilements" (*tri-saṃkleśa*), as their nature is not pure.

Furthermore, these three obstacles depend upon one another: from afflictions (*kleśa*) arises unwholesome karma; through the causal conditions of unwholesome karma, one obtains bitter fruits [of suffering].
Regarding the first term, "delusion" (*moha*), this refers to the afflictions themselves; its categories consist of the root [afflictions].
And as for the secondary [afflictions], there are six root [afflictions]: namely, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view. There are twenty secondary afflictions:
namely, anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, and so forth, up to distraction and lack of clear comprehension.
To state it briefly, they do not go beyond the three root [afflictions], namely greed, hatred, and delusion; these three alone are capable of establishing [the others].

Regarding the three realms of the world, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Due to greed, hatred, and delusion, one gives rise to actions of body, speech, and mind, thereby committing all manner of evil karmas—immeasurable and boundless.
These afflictions arise as causes; they originate from the preceding ignorance that is deluded regarding the principle of equality.

To falsely identify with the body and mind of the five aggregates—this very body and mind—is the root of all afflictions. Thus, Master Zhao said: "In relation to heaven and earth, there are high and low;
in relation to the sun and moon, there are east and west; in relation to the body, there are self and other; and in relation to the mind..."
This constitutes right and wrong. Laozi also said: "I have a great affliction: it is because I have a body. If I had no body, what affliction would I have?
Thus, one knows that this body is the root of all faults and afflictions. Having grasped at it as existing, one consequently distinguishes between self and other;
based upon this body and mind, one gives rise to various afflictions regarding all objects of favorable conditions.
First, attachment arises toward all objects of desire; second, aversion arises toward all disagreeable circumstances in order to protect oneself and establish one as a sovereign.
Within these two, not knowing them to be illusory and arising spontaneously is called delusion (*moha*).
When one investigates the cause of these afflictions, they all originate from fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Furthermore, as for what is called "karma": although karma is immeasurable, it is generally comprised of only three types—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable.
Due to the preceding intensity of greed and hatred, one incites body and speech to perform various unwholesome karmas;

these are the ten unwholesome paths of action, consisting of the three of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind. Alternatively, there are those who have some knowledge of cause and effect and, out of greed for prosperity in future lives, [perform such deeds].

Regarding the matter of pleasure: it consists of transforming evil into good by observing the five precepts, such as non-killing, or the eight, ten, or fifty-eight precepts; these constitute wholesome karma (*kuśala-karma*).

Alternatively, by wearying of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower realms, and rejoicing in the purity, subtlety, and detachment of the higher realms, one cultivates tainted meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*);
this is called immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*). Although these three types of karma differ in their relative superiority or inferiority, they are all produced by a deluded mind. All [are...]
They are subsumed under the tainted (*sāsrava*). Therefore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ārya-bhadracarī-praṇidhāna*) concludes its discussion of the three karmas by stating:
"Because they all constitute saṃsāra, they do not bring about the holy path. From this, one knows that the aforementioned three karmas are all produced based upon afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the term "retribution" (*vipāka*), "response" (*ying*) is itself "retribution" (*bao*). Once the seeds of karma exist and are stored within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), when the conditions and causes converge, [the result] will necessarily...

One must undergo retribution. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Neither in the void, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering between the rocks of the mountains—there is no place on earth where one may escape and not undergo retribution.
The *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*) says: "When Heaven sends down calamity, it may still be avoided; but when one creates calamity for oneself, it cannot be evaded.
From this, it follows that where there is karma, there must be its corresponding retribution. However, if one examines the essence and characteristics of these various karmas...

There is absolutely none. Yet, when the retribution is received, there has never been any discrepancy: evil causes result in bitter fruits, and wholesome causes result in pleasant fruits, like shadows and echoes, precisely without error.
However, speaking generally of karmic retribution, although the six realms differ, when categorized by their nature, they comprise only three types:
suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Due to the aforementioned evil karma as the cause, one experiences the three miserable realms.
The retribution of suffering refers to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
By taking prior wholesome karma as the cause, one experiences the retribution of pleasure in the human and celestial realms, namely the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm.

By taking prior immovable karma as the cause, one experiences the distinct retributions of the upper realms, namely the form and formless realms. However, within these three realms, that which is experienced...

The body of suffering and pleasure is the direct retribution (*vipāka*) of individual karma (*pratyeka-karma*). The superior or inferior vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) in which one dwells is the supporting retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*).
The direct retribution consists of birth, aging, sickness, and death; the supporting retribution consists of formation, subsistence, dissolution, and emptiness.

As the vessel-world empties and reforms, and sentient beings die and are reborn, this process has continued in an unbroken succession from beginningless time until now, as they remain deluded and attached.
Love is truly pitiable. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house.

Consequently, retribution arises from causes and karma is induced by it. Karma is formed through delusion (*moha*), and delusion is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance has no beginning; it is the false existence of a single thought-moment.
Thus we know that, when one investigates the origin of all sentient and insentient beings within the three realms and six paths, they are all due to a dream.

It exists through consciousness. Regarding the phrase "succession (*xi*) and habituation (*xí*), and the revolving wheel (*lún lún*"): "succession" refers to inheritance, which carries the meaning of continuity;

because afflictions give rise to karma, and karma is capable of summoning suffering, they proceed in successive continuity. "Habituation" refers to perfuming, which carries the meaning of mutual influence.
This clarifies that delusion and karma are learned and cultivated moment by moment; because they are perfumed moment by moment, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because it coexists with the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas and the habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), it is called 'habitual tendency' (*śīkṣā*). However, these two meanings necessarily support one another.

This means that because of continuity there is imitation, and because of imitation there is continuity; hence it is called "successive habituation" (*śikṣā*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"When the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has already been exhausted, another maturation arises again. It is like a person who practices the Confucian arts and literature.
Because one inherits the Confucian tradition, one is able to study the literary arts; and because one studies the literary arts, one is able to inherit the Confucian tradition.
Is the meaning of their mutual dependence not evident? "Lun" (綸) refers to the thread or continuity.
This means that although the karmic seeds of sentient beings are boundless, they do not all simultaneously receive retribution within the six realms of existence. As for "retribution" (報)...
Because there is a continuous sequence, it is called "thread" (*luǒnxù*). There are two meanings to this: first, like a person who owes a debt, the stronger [creditor] pulls them forward;
second, like a person planting seeds, that which is moistened grows first. "Wheel" (*lún*) refers to revolving;
it means that after being born one dies again, and after dying one is born again. Because birth and death do not cease, it is called "revolving. Or, one may die in the heavens...
Beings are born as humans; beings die as humans; beings are born as animals, and so forth. Thus, the *Anityatā-sūtra* says:
"Circulating within the three realms is like a waterwheel drawing from a well. Furthermore, these two meanings mutually support one another:
by means of the threads, there is rotation; by means of rotation, there are threads. It is just like unwinding silk from a cocoon: it proceeds by means of that thread-wheel.
And it does not stop. Thus, it causes the silk threads to arise without interruption; and because the silk threads arise without interruption, it causes the silk wheel to turn without ceasing.
Alternatively, "lun" (淪) may also be interpreted as "to sink," which carries the sense of being submerged.
This refers to being long submerged in the great river of birth and death; hence it is called "lun. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
If there are sentient beings who delight in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and engage in various karmic actions, such persons lose their way and become confused regarding the true and eternal.
This is called "emerging for a moment only to sink back down. In the commentary, the character "wheel" (*lun*) is used provisionally;

as previously explained, regarding delusion and karma, it refers to their successive accumulation (*xi-xi*), while regarding retribution and response, it refers to their revolving cycle (*lun-lun*). Nevertheless, these two pairs are contrasted and analyzed, yet they also mutually support one another.
This means that because afflictions and karma are habitually accumulated, retribution and response are spun out in a continuous cycle;

and because retribution and response are spun out in a continuous cycle, afflictions and karma are caused to be habitually accumulated. Thus, one rides upon causes to elicit effects, and relies upon effects to create causes; cause and effect mutually support one another.

By means of this, [the cycle] does not cease. This is precisely the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein each preceding factor serves as the cause and each succeeding factor serves as the effect.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "Due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two appropriations (*dvaya-graha*), once a previous maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again.
Someone may say: "In this way, one gives rise to delusions, creates karma, and undergoes retribution in a cycle..."
[It] turns. Does the duration of time and kalpas obstruct it? Therefore, it is said next: "For kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and grains of sand, it cannot be obstructed or cut off.
"Dust" refers to the minute particles of the ten directions' worlds when ground to powder; "sand" refers to the flour-like sand in the Ganges River.
This means that this river is forty *li* in circumference, and its sand is as fine as flour. *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "time-division" (*shifen*).
Whether it be a great *kalpa* or a small *kalpa*, a long duration or a short duration—despite their differences in extension or brevity—they are collectively termed "time-divisions.

"Unable to do so" (*mo zhi zhe*) means "incapable of. "To arrest and cut off" (*e jue zhe*) means "to cease and extinguish. The intended meaning is that sentient beings within the six realms of existence give rise to delusions.

Since beginningless time, as we have created karma and undergone the cycle of rebirth, if one were to take a single grain of sand to represent one kalpa, the grains of sand would be exhausted long before the kalpas;
if one were to take a single mote of dust to represent one kalpa, the motes of dust would be exhausted while the kalpas remain endless.
Sand and dust are finite, whereas kalpas are infinite. This continuity has persisted until now, unable to be halted or extinguished; hence it is said:
Nothing can obstruct or sever it.

[Commentary] Although these two sections contain many characters and phrases, if one discusses the actual reality, it does not exceed five words: namely, mind-consciousness, delusion, karma, and retribution.
All other passages are merely explanatory statements describing how truth and falsehood establish the cycle of saṃsāra. This is the intended meaning.
This means that what was originally the one mind, through non-awakening, becomes consciousness; it gives rise to delusions and creates karma, resulting in an endless cycle of birth and death.
For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests his body and expounds the teachings; thus, the major section refers to the "conditions for initiating the teaching."

△ Second, the specific explanation of the intent behind the teaching has two parts: first, the narration of the intent for teaching the Āgamas; second, the narration of the intent for teaching the Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the first (the narration of the intent for teaching the Āgamas), there are two parts: first, the formal narration; second, the concluding judgment. Regarding the first (the formal narration), there are two parts:
first, the manifestation of the body; second, the establishment of the teaching. Regarding the first (the manifestation of the body):
[Commentary] Therefore, I, whose pure awakening is fulfilled, manifest my appearance among human beings.
[Record] Regarding the section beginning with "Therefore, I," there are two parts that specifically clarify the intent behind preaching the teachings. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"With my Buddha-eye, I observe the sentient beings of the six realms; they are impoverished, lacking in merit and wisdom, and have entered the perilous path of birth and death. Their appearance...
The suffering continues without interruption. Even for the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to great compassion and so forth.
The text has two parts: first, explaining the intent of the *āgama*; second, the actual exposition. Regarding the first part, the initial two lines indicate the manifestation of the Buddha’s body.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) carries the sense of "the reason why. "I" refers to the Buddha himself. The term "fully pure" (*pariśuddha*) serves to distinguish him from those who are only partially [purified].
"Purity" [is so called] because the Buddha has eternally exhausted ignorance and reached the ultimate state of non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*). "Awakened" (*jue*) refers to awakening;
"the one" (*zhe*) refers to the person, meaning that the Buddha is the person who has awakened. If we speak of the Sanskrit *bodhi*, this is translated as "awakening," which refers to the dharma.
If we speak of the Sanskrit *buddha*, this means "the awakened one," which refers to the person. Here, the distinction is made with respect to the person.
Therefore, regarding the term "Awakening" (*jue*): the "full character" (*manzi*) serves as the general category, while "pure awakening" (*jing jue*) serves as the specific instance.

The character "one" (*zhe*) refers to the person; it clarifies that the Tathāgata is the one who possesses full purity and full awakening. This distinguishes him from other sages whose awakening and purity are not yet complete.
Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has exhausted all three obstructions and perfected all three types of awakening; thus, the Tathāgata is titled the One of Full Pure Awakening.

If one examines these two [aspects] in relation to sentient beings, those of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas, as well as their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), there are two kinds of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First: Sentient beings are impure; those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas are partially pure;

the Buddhas are fully pure; and the fundamental nature is simply pure. Second: Sentient beings are unawakened; those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas are partially awakened; the Buddhas are... [fully awakened].
The Buddha is fully awakened; his original nature is simply awakening. Now, within these two sets of four phrases, he corresponds to the third in each.
Regarding "manifesting signs": this refers to the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). "Among humans" refers to the place where he manifests.

He manifests signs only among humans because those in the heavens are attached to pleasure and have no means to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, while those in the three miserable realms suffer extreme agony and likewise lack the capacity.

It is in difficult circumstances that one encounters hardship; this occurs only among human beings, where suffering and pleasure coexist. It is precisely when confronted with suffering that one is able to resolve to attain enlightenment.
Therefore, when a Buddha appears in the world to transform beings, those in the heavens are like an illness that has not yet manifested—what need is there for acupuncture or moxibustion?

Those in the three miserable realms are like a terminal illness of the vital organs—they are beyond medical treatment. Only those among humans who are afflicted by a minor ailment can be given medicine. Thus, the Buddha...
[The Buddha] appears. However, there are four general types of manifestations of the Tathāgata:

namely, the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) for others' benefit, and various Transformation Bodies (nirmāṇakāya), including both great and small transformations according to the capacity of beings. What is explained here as this teaching refers specifically to the small transformation body.
Furthermore, it possesses eight phases: first, descending from Tuṣita Heaven; second, entering the womb; third, dwelling in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb.

1. Leaving home (at age nineteen). 2. Attaining enlightenment (at age twenty-five). 3. Turning the Wheel of Dharma (after fifty-five years had passed). 4. Entering Nirvana (at age eighty). This treatise manifests his physical presence;
it clarifies only the characteristics of his attainment of enlightenment. Next, it clarifies his preaching of the Dharma, which is the characteristic of turning the Wheel of Dharma.
As for the characteristics of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment: his body is sixteen feet tall, with a complexion like purple-polished gold, and his neck is adorned with...
He possessed a circular halo and the *svastika* mark upon his chest. He was endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Protected by the eight classes of supernatural beings and revered by the fourfold assembly, he stood majestic and towering, his radiance eclipsing the sun and moon. His virtuous attributes were so vast and manifold that they cannot be fully described.
This small transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is inferior and weak in appearance; compared to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it is as different as clouds from the earth.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that the elder removes his precious, noble robes and puts on tattered, soiled garments.

The precious, noble robes are used as a metaphor for the enjoyment body, while the tattered, soiled garments illustrate the body of purple-golden hue (*cāmīkaravarṇa*). This is because sentient beings are defiled.
It is grave [that they cannot see him]. Being unable to behold his supreme and wondrous body, they likewise hear nothing of it;

thus, they would derive no benefit whatsoever from sentient beings. Out of great compassion for those he seeks to reach, he manifests a minor transformation-body, just as is taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The impoverished son saw his father seated upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet; his wealth and nobility were extraordinary, and his majestic virtue was preeminent.
Upon seeing him, the impoverished son thought to himself in secret: "This must be a king, or one equal to a king; this is no place for me to earn goods through hired labor.
When the elder saw his son, he silently recognized him, and so on, until it says: "He immediately removed..."
Wearing necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments of adornment, he further put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes, holding a vessel for removing filth in his right hand.
By these expedient means, he was able to approach the impoverished son;
this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata concealing his superior body and manifesting inferior appearances.
△ Second, the establishment of the teaching.
[Commentary] First, he explains the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, so that [beings] may realize suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "First, he explains... in the commentary: this correctly clarifies the establishment of the teaching. For in this realm, the Buddha’s work relies upon vocal sounds. If...
If there is no verbal teaching, what benefit is there in manifesting signs? Regarding the teaching that first establishes the Small Vehicle and only later speaks of the Great Vehicle, some say:
"This clarifies Prajñā; why discuss the Small Vehicle? The answer is: although both are the Buddha’s words, they have depths and shallows.

If one does not engage in comparative discussion, how can one know their relative depth? Nevertheless, the Buddhist teachings of a single lifetime do not transcend the Great and Small Vehicles, and so forth.
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is also subsumed within the Mahāyāna. That which it takes as its fundamental principle is entirely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Although both [the Small and Great Vehicles] take dependent origination as their principle, there is a difference between them regarding depth and subtlety. The Small Vehicle concerns itself with dependent origination characterized by arising and ceasing, whereas the Mahāyāna concerns itself with dependent origination characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Regarding this dependent origination of the absence of intrinsic nature, as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Of those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare..."

This is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Emptiness is the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Now, to clarify the perspective of the Hīnayāna, it is said that there are causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.
As for these causes and conditions for arising and ceasing: when various phenomena (*dharma*) meet with conditions, they arise; when conditions depart, they cease.

Since they both arise and cease, one sufficiently knows them to be impermanent (*anitya*). Thus, it is not that the phenomena of arising and ceasing do not exist; this is because of the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). However, the Buddha...

Transcending the world, he first speaks of the "small" [teachings], because there are two types of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*). He speaks of arising and ceasing to counteract the attachment to a self held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
for "self" carries the meaning of being a sovereign master. Since he speaks of arising and ceasing, one knows there is no master. Where there is no master and no sovereign, there is no self.
He speaks of causes and conditions to counteract the non-Buddhist calculation of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). As for the non-Buddhists'...
[They] cling [to these views]. Because they largely cling to a *puruṣa* (self) that acts and experiences, they also cling to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Since it is said to be "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is neither a *puruṣa* nor spontaneous. To remedy these two [views], he first explained the causal conditions of arising and ceasing;
that is, immediately after the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way, beginning at the Deer Park, he delivered the five *bhadravargīya* monks, followed by Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Kātyāyana.
The teachings spoken by the three brothers, including Yaśas, over the course of twelve years are precisely the various *Āgama* sūtras and others.
Regarding "causing them to awaken," the Buddha’s intention in preaching this Dharma was to lead sentient beings to realize the Four Noble Truths.
This involves two kinds of cause and effect: namely, that "origination" (*samudaya*) is the cause of the world, and "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is the fruit of the world; while "the Path" (*mārga*)...

This is the cause for transcending the world; cessation (*nirodha*) is the fruit of transcending the world. Suffering (*duḥkha*) consists of the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.

The three sufferings are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*). The eight sufferings are birth, old age, sickness, death, not obtaining what one seeks, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), separation from the beloved, and association with the hated.
Accumulation (*samudaya*) refers to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), as explained in the section on "Pursuing Delusion. Cessation refers to *nirvāṇa* with remainder.
The two kinds of *nirvāṇa* without remainder can be seen in the sūtras. The Path (*mārga*) is the Eightfold Noble Path, namely:
