Śāriputra, why is it said that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause and condition?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so as to make them pure;
they appear in the world even unto the point of desiring to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Regarding the world, according to the *Tianchang Shuji* (Commentary by Tianchang), it is said: The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is "one" because it is neither three nor five;
it is "great" because it is vast and all-encompassing; it is a "matter" because the ritual protocols of all Buddhas speak of this birth through transformation (*nirmāṇa*);
it is a "cause" because sentient beings possess this capacity to evoke the Buddha; and it is a "condition" because the Buddha responds to them. Thus, it is that which...

In terms of its meaning: for this one great causal purpose, the Buddha appears in the world. Regarding these four phrases—"opening, showing, awakening, and entering"—they do not exceed two categories:
the first two phrases represent the transformer (the teacher), and the latter two phrases represent those being transformed (the disciples).

There are two aspects to the capacity for transformation (*nirmāṇa*): namely, "opening wide" and "showing by way of curvature. These belong to the Buddha. There are also two aspects to those who are transformed (*nirmeya*):

namely, "initial awakening" and "final entry. These belong to sentient beings. According to the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra), "opening" refers to the simultaneous opening of the two unsurpassed fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa;
"showing" refers to specifically indicating the dharmakāya to reveal that the three vehicles share the same essence.

"Awakening" (wu) means knowing the meaning; it specifically refers to the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know this, [the teaching] is spoken so that they may come to know it.

"Entering" (ru) has the sense of a cause, for by cultivating the cause, one accords with and enters [the truth]. The Master of the *Huayan* Commentary explains: "Opening" (kai) means removing the obstacles of delusion; "showing" (shi) means revealing the true principle;

"awakening" (wu) means awakening to the fact that delusion is fundamentally empty and realizing that the substance of the mind is quiescent. This is intended solely to bring about awakening to the above.
The Truth. "Entering" means merging with the essence of the mind. Shi Bi explains: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature" is the broad opening;
"pointing it out" means that within the mind, it is clearly and distinctly manifest as Buddha-nature, which is the detailed instruction.
To attain realization afresh and receive the seal of certainty without doubt is the initial awakening. All conceptual thoughts vanish entirely—this is the ultimate [realization].
[They] enter [this teaching]. The interpretations of various schools differ in their underlying intent; like white jade and gold, each is a supreme treasure.
△ Second, the specific revelation of this sutra has two parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration. First, the general heading.
[Commentary] The subsequent section separately elucidates this sutra in five parts.

[Record] Regarding "the subsequent section separately elucidates": this refers proximately to the single-fascicle *Vajracchedikā* and distantly to all sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as they share the same fundamental doctrine.
The intent is to clarify the underlying reasons for preaching this Sutra of Non-characteristics (*animitta-sūtra*). Within this, there are five segments, which fully...

Listed as in the commentary. △ Second, the specific enumeration has five parts: first, counteracting the two attachments to self and dharmas; second, severing the two types of doubt regarding seeds and manifestations;
third, transforming and extinguishing the two types of karma, light and heavy; fourth, revealing the two causes of merit and wisdom; fifth, elucidating the true and the responsive.
The second fruit. First, the antidote to the two attachments to self and dharmas. Part one: the heading; part two: the explanation; part three: the conclusion. First, the heading. [Commentary]:
First, it is for the purpose of counteracting the two attachments to self and dharmas.
[Commentary] This section has three parts. First is the heading. Regarding "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*): it is like prescribing medicine for an illness; the meaning is seen in the Preface.

Regarding "clinging to a self" (*ātma-grāha*), there are two types: first, the conceptualization of a self by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which is the grasping of the general characteristic of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a sovereign master.

Second, the "divine self" (*puruṣa-ātman*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which is either distinct from or not distinct from the aggregates, and is conceived as being either vast or minute, a mysterious spirit or a sacred deity.
All inconceivable movements and activities are reckoned as real; therefore, this is called "clinging to a self" (*ātma-grāha*).

To reckon all phenomena (*dharma*) as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called "clinging to phenomena" (*dharma-grāha*). Now, although the Buddha’s teaching of the *Hīnayāna* has already eliminated clinging to a self, the present teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* addresses this again because the profound necessarily encompasses the shallow.
Consequently, while primarily eliminating clinging to phenomena, it also clarifies [the elimination of clinging to a self].
The self is empty.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, a general indication that obstacles arise from clinging; second, a specific demonstration of the faults and afflictions of the two obstacles.
First, the general indication that obstacles arise from clinging.
[Commentary] Due to these two attachments, the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya*)—arise.

[Record] Regarding the section beginning with "Due to this," there are two explanations. First, a general indication that obstacles arise from attachment. ○ *Kleśa* refers to the root and secondary afflictions;
these arise based on the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), as explained previously in the section on "chasing after delusions. ○ *Jñeya* refers to the root...
This is fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "The meaning of ignorance is termed the obstruction of wisdom;
it is precisely the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This arises based upon the grasping at phenomena as real (*dharmagrāha*).

△ Second, the specific exposition of the faults and afflictions of the two obstacles, in two parts: first, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). First, the obstacle of afflictions. [Commentary]:
Because the obstacle of afflictions obstructs the mind, the mind does not attain liberation. Consequently, one creates karma and undergoes rebirth, transmigrating through the five destinies.
[Commentary] From "Due to afflictions" (*klesha*) downwards, there are two sections separately demonstrating the faults and calamities of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
First, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Regarding "the mind is not equal": the mind is fundamentally pure, sovereign, and its wondrous functions of merit exceed the sands of the Ganges.
Because it is obscured by this obstacle, these qualities cannot manifest; therefore, it is said that "the mind is not liberated. Liberation (*vimukti*) means sovereignty.
Not only does this prevent the mind from attaining liberation, it further enables one to create and nourish karma—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karma.
Because these karmic causes exist, they inevitably summon retributive fruits, which is to say, the process of taking birth.
The places where one takes birth are what are known as the five destinies. Being born and then dying again, going and then coming back, is why it is called "revolving" (saṃsāra).
The characteristics of cyclic existence have already been explained in the introduction regarding the meaning of the "spinning wheel" (lun-lun).
Tracing its source back, it is found to be self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*). Therefore, one should know that self-grasping is the root of all afflictions; thus, it must be eliminated.
△ Second, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

[Commentary]: Because the cognitive obscuration obstructs wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom does not attain liberation. One fails to understand one's own mind and does not penetrate the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Even if one transcends the three realms, one remains stalled at the level of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and cannot achieve Buddhahood; therefore, it is called an "obscuration."
[Commentary] "By virtue of the objects of knowledge" and so forth refers to the two types of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding "wisdom being unequal":

this refers specifically to the profound wisdom of the Mahāyāna, not the shallow wisdom of the Hīnayāna. If this wisdom were to arise, one would clearly perceive that the five aggregates are all empty and are nothing other than the nature of the mind;
apart from one's own mind, there are no separate phenomena. However, at present, it is obscured by ignorance and thus cannot be attained.
[This is] for the purpose of development. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "If one does not understand one's own mind, how can one know the right path?
Through inverted wisdom, one increases all evils. Regarding the phrase "not attaining [it]," etc.: however, the nature and characteristics of all dharmas have both specific and general aspects.
Specifically, it is like water, which has moisture as its nature and movement or stillness as its characteristics. Generally, all...

The Dharma is identical in taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its nature and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as its characteristic. Because of this "non-existence," wisdom is unable to comprehend it.
However, comprehending the mind is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while comprehending nature and characteristics is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

That these two wisdoms do not manifest is due to ignorance (*avidyā*). If ignorance is not eliminated, the Buddha-dharma will not be realized; hence it is said: "Even if one emerges from the three realms..."

They are likewise obstructed by the two vehicles and so forth; this means that although they have emerged from the burning house, they still halt at the conjured city and do not reach the treasure site.
If one traces this back to its root, it arises from attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); thus, one should know that attachment to phenomena is the fundamental source of all afflictions.
[Commentary] However, these two obstacles do not function as opposing forces; they both arise from a single mind. They differ only in their degree of subtle attachment:

the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is subtle, while the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is coarse. Although they differ in coarseness and subtlety, they possess no separate essence whatsoever.
It is like a single body of water: when stirred, it forms waves. Within this, there are also two meanings. As soon as it is stirred...

It cannot manifest its form; it is identical to that which is known [by it]. When it is fierce and intense, it capsizes boats and drowns people—how much more so in the case of the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
The correspondence between the dharma and the analogy is clearly visible.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding liberation through mind and wisdom, when distinguished according to persons, four permutations are established: 1. Liberation of mind but not liberation through wisdom:

this refers to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). 2. Non-liberation of mind but liberation through wisdom: this refers to Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion. 3. Liberation of both: this refers to the Buddhas.
4. Non-liberation of both: this refers to ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
△ Three Bonds.
[Commentary] If the two attachments are eliminated, the two obstacles will accordingly be severed. It is for the sake of eliminating these two attachments that this sutra is taught.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "the two attachments" in the commentary, there are three bonds. ○ This is because the previous analysis has thoroughly investigated the root of all faults and afflictions.
Regarding these two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*): if the two attachments are dispelled, the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) are eliminated;
if the two hindrances are eliminated, then all faults naturally cease. Since the source of these afflictions is precisely those two attachments, this sutra is expounded in order to eliminate them.
Thus, one should know that this sutra is a great panacea. Therefore, the *Heart Sūtra* says: "Prajñāpāramitā..."
It is a great mantra of power; it is a great mantra of illumination, and so forth, up to: "it can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
If one wishes to know how this sutra eliminates the two attachments, as the sutra says:

"there is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span"—this eliminates the attachment to self. It further states: "there is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas."
This is the elimination of the attachment to dharmas. Such examples are found throughout the sūtras.
△ Second, the refutation and severing of the two types of doubt regarding seeds and manifestations. Part one: the heading. Part two: the explanation. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Second: This is for the purpose of eliminating both the doubt regarding the seeds (*bīja*) and the manifest [defilements] (*samudācāra*).
[Record] Regarding the second point in the Commentary: "Second," the first part is the heading, which is self-evident.
△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of the sūtra. First, the direct explanation.
[Commentary]: This dispels doubts regarding seeds that have not yet arisen and cuts off doubts regarding active manifestations currently arising.
[Record]: There are two explanations. Regarding "doubt" (*vicikitsā*): it is a state of hesitation and indecision concerning principles or phenomena;

it is one of the categories within the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Furthermore, there are two types: first, seeds (*bīja*); second, active manifestations (*samudācāra*). "Seeds" refers to those that reside within...

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), when not yet manifested, is called "not yet arisen. Its active manifestation—meaning its movement within the mind or its expression through speech—is called "presently arisen.
To "restrain" it means to obstruct its seeds so as not to allow them to arise as active manifestations.
To sever it is to sever its active manifestation; that is, to eliminate its very root. This is like building an embankment to stop water, or pouring sand over a flame;
the meaning is clear from these analogies.
△ Section Two: The Sūtra on the Two Fingers.

[Commentary] This refers to the portion of the sūtra following the answers to the questions posed; it traces the sequence of the discourse to sever doubts section by section until the conclusion of the sūtra, consisting of twenty-seven segments.

[Commentary] "That is, the sutra below" refers to the sutra text. However, according to the sutra, after answering the three questions, [the Buddha] proceeds to sever [the doubts] through a continuous sequence;
thus it is said that "section by section, it reaches twenty-seven. Furthermore, the term "severing and cutting off" (zhedu) has two general meanings.
First, there is the passage in the sutra where Subhūti presents his doubts, which concerns active mental states (*samudācāra*). This is the first...
The second, eleventh, and nineteenth [categories]—the others lack interrogative phrasing—are all seeds (*bīja*).

These are, at that time, entirely manifest activities (*samudācāra*); yet, in relation to future generations, they are collectively termed "seeds. Thus, when manifest activity is severed, it is precisely the seed that is obstructed.
However, between these two interpretations, the latter is slightly more compelling; therefore, the twenty-seven doubts are all...
It speaks of "cessation" but not of "obstruction.
△ Third, the turning and extinguishing of the two types of karma, light and heavy, in two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the heading. [Commentary]:
Third, for the purpose of turning and extinguishing the two types of karma, light and heavy.
[Commentary] Among the three sections of the sub-commentary, there are two parts: first, the heading;
second, the explanation.
[Sub-commentary]: It transforms heavy karma so that it is experienced lightly, and extinguishes light karma so that it is not experienced at all.
[Commentary] There are two explanations. Generally speaking, there are three types of karma: wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable. There are three times for their fruition:

the present life, the next life, and subsequent lives. If one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds in this life and experiences pleasure or pain in this very life, it is called *karma with fruition in the present life* (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

If one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds in this life and experiences the results only in the immediately following birth, it is called *karma with fruition in the next life* (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*). If...

If one performs good or evil deeds in this life and only begins to experience their results from the third lifetime onward, continuing through hundreds or thousands of lifetimes before they are fully received, this is called "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" (*aparāpariya-vedanīya-karman*).
When people in this world perform good or evil deeds and receive no retribution immediately, they may then doubt the existence of cause and effect.
This is truly because they do not understand these three timings of retribution. Therefore, the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* states: "Practicing goodness..."
Those who practice it encounter adversity in all matters; those who commit evil find success in all things.
This causes the foolish people of the world to claim that good and evil cannot be distinguished. In my sutras, I have taught that there are three kinds of retribution, as described above.

Regarding what is now called "transformation and extinction": among the three [types of karma], it refers exclusively to the transformation of evil karma, as this contradicts reason; however, in terms of time, it applies to all three.
Now, concerning the retribution for this evil karma, according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna school, there are determinate and indeterminate types.

For example, the four grave offenses (pārājika) of the first category are termed determinate karma, while those from the saṃghāvaśeṣa downward are termed indeterminate karma. When these are correlated with time, it should be understood accordingly.
This forms four permutations: namely, karma with fixed time but indefinite retribution; karma with fixed retribution but indefinite time; both fixed; and both indefinite.
According to this sutra’s teaching, however, it is not so. For one who has not yet entered my Dharma, it is called "determined karma";
for one who has entered my Dharma, it is called "undetermined karma. As for what is called "indeterminate," it may be light or heavy, and it may be experienced [in this life] or...
"It is not received. Question: "If that is so, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* state: 'Except for those karmas of fixed retribution which must be experienced'?
Answer: "It merely transforms the heavy into the light; it does not cause them to not be experienced at all.
Therefore, there is no contradiction. As this sūtra says: 'If there is a person who upholds, recites, and studies this sūtra, yet is treated with contempt by others, such a person...'"
Karmic offenses from previous lives that would have caused one to fall into the evil realms are extinguished by being treated with contempt and disdain by people in the present life;
thus, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Regarding the phrase "previous lives," there are two meanings. First:
That which existed prior to one's previous life is called the "prior world" (pūrva-janman). Second, that which precedes the holding of this sutra is also called the "prior world.

Although both meanings apply, the latter sense is correct here. Now, by substituting the karma of the three miserable realms with the state of being despised, the timing of retribution is made indefinite;

thus, what would have been experienced in a future life is instead repaid in the present life, making the time of retribution indefinite. All of these methods serve to transform heavy karma into light. ○
As for the extinction of light [karma], it is not mentioned in the sutras. Although there is no textual passage in the sutras, the meaning logically implies its existence.

Furthermore, there are two interpretations. First, by using the heavy to illustrate the light: the intention is that if heavy karma can be transformed so as to become light, then light karma should naturally not be experienced at all.
Second, regarding those who have previously fallen into the three miserable realms (trāya), even when they emerge among humans, they still possess residual [karmic effects].
Karma refers to the various sufferings such as poverty and decline. Since one does not fall into the three miserable realms, other karmic results will necessarily be avoided;
this is also a case where both the time and the retribution are indeterminate.
△ Four: Manifesting the Two Causes of Merit and Wisdom. First, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. First, the heading:
[Commentary] Fourth, for the purpose of manifesting the two causes of merit and wisdom.
[Commentary] Regarding the four points in the sub-commentary, there are three [sections]. First, the heading.

Second, the explanation, which has two parts: first, that not having heard [this teaching] constitutes the fault of being an ordinary person or a follower of the Small Vehicle; second, that having already heard it constitutes attaining the cause for Buddhahood.
Initially, it was not stated that the fault consisted in being an ordinary person or a follower of the Lesser Vehicle.

[Commentary: Before the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment and had yet taught the *Prajñāpāramitā*, sentient beings, due to the absence of sublime wisdom, caused their practice of giving and so forth to abide in signs, whereby all became outflowing (*sāsrava*).
Alternatively, they became stalled at the level of the Two Vehicles.

[Commentary] There are two interpretations. First, the fault of not yet having taught [the Mahāyāna] is that it would be regarded as being for ordinary people or followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Regarding "The Buddha attained perfect enlightenment":

this refers to the manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment when, beneath the Bodhi tree, he severed the fetters through thirty-four moments of mind, and the fivefold Dharma-body was first perfected.

Regarding "Not yet having taught," etc.: this refers to the period from after his attainment of the Way until twelve years had passed, during which he taught only the teachings for human beings [and Śrāvakas].
The causes and effects of the heavens, as well as the Four Noble Truths and dependent origination, have been explained; however, the three kinds of emptiness and *prajñā* have not yet been taught.
Regarding the phrase "those who lack wondrous wisdom": "wondrous wisdom" refers to the signless and profound *prajñā*. This is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Because *prajñā* has not yet been taught, the emptiness of phenomena has not been revealed, and thus they lack this wisdom. Regarding the phrase "abiding in the marks of giving and so forth," "and so forth" [refers to...]
The four [virtues] beginning with precepts and patience abide in the marks of self, person, sentient being, and so forth, as well as in the marks of phenomena and non-phenomena.
Since they abide in such marks as self and phenomena, they constitute worldly cause and effect; therefore, they are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).

This refers to ordinary beings who rely on the teachings of humans and devas, or those who are stalled at the level of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), even if they have severed delusions and realized [attainments].
True. It is not that they lack weariness with suffering and delight in joy; yet, even if they transcend the three realms, they fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This refers to those who rely on the teachings of the Hīnayāna. If one were to judge them by the standards of ordinary beings, they would also lack coarse wisdom; however, this is stated according to their superior attainments.
Therefore, it is said that there is no "wondrous wisdom" [in the absence of this].

△ Second, having already explained that [wisdom] serves as the cause for becoming a Buddha, this section has two parts: first, an exegesis in accordance with the principle; second, a negative demonstration. First, the exegesis in accordance with the principle. [Commentary]:

Thus, by discussing *prajñā*, it is shown that wondrous wisdom is the cause of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the five perfections (*pañcapāramitā*) are the causes of the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "Therefore, it is discussed below" has two parts: first, it explains that [the preceding] has already been stated to be the cause for attaining Buddhahood; second, it provides a sequential explanation.
This refers to the period after twelve years, during which the teachings of the various *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras were expounded to elucidate sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
This sublime wisdom is precisely the sixth *prajñāpāramitā*. Since the *dharmakāya* is the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness), it is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; however—

When it is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. If sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) illuminates and pierces through the afflictions, the ultimate truth manifests and the Great Dharmakāya is realized;
therefore, it is said that sublime wisdom is the cause of the Dharmakāya. Regarding the "five perfections" (*pañca-pāramitā*) and so forth:
The five perfections are giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.

The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the physical form characterized by the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, with a complexion like purple-polished gold; this is that which is realized through the accumulation and practice of the five *pāramitās*.
Therefore, it is said that the five perfections are the causes for the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya).
△ Second, the negative demonstration.
[Commentary]: If there were no Prajñāpāramitā, then the five practices such as giving would not be "perfections" (pāramitā) and could not be called the causes of Buddhahood.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "If there were no... provides two forms of negative illustration (*pratiṣedha*). Regarding "not being a *pāramitā*," although one may practice giving and so forth, because they lack the guidance of wisdom, they all result in abiding in signs (*nimitta*).
Because they abide in signs, they become outflowing (*sāsrava*). Consequently, they merely constitute worldly causes for virtue and fruits of pleasure;
thus, they are not the cause for Buddhahood. Therefore, the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā* (or *Bodhisambhāra-śāstra*) states: "Giving, morality..."
Patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, as well as the remainder of these five, are all subsumed under the *pāramitās* by virtue of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
△ Third, the conclusion.
[Commentary]: Therefore, one must possess the two adornments of merit and wisdom before one can become a "Dvipadottama" (the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings).

[Commentary] Therefore, the sub-commentary below concludes with three points. First, merit and wisdom belong to the cause; that is, the five or six perfections (*pāramitā*), which serve as the adornments.
The two types of feet (the physical and the Dharma body) belong to the fruit; that is, the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which are the objects to be adorned.

Now, although the meritorious virtues of the Buddhas' fruition are immeasurable and boundless, to speak of them in essence, they do not exceed these two. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Just as..."
The Dharma thus attained is adorned by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom; by means of this, one delivers sentient beings and personally realizes the unsurpassed path.
The general meaning is that, due to the absence of prajñā, practices such as giving do not become pāramitās and fail to constitute the cause for Buddhahood.
Therefore, one must possess the two adornments of merit and wisdom to achieve the wondrous body of the "two feet.
However, the preceding five and the sixth mutually assist one another, for the two fruits of the True and the Responsive must both be complete; it is like glue, indigo, and pigments.
Colors do not adhere without glue; glue has no color without colors. The six [perfections] are not the five [aggregates], yet they lack characteristics;
the five are not the six, yet they lack causes. As the Sūtra says: "One should dwell nowhere"—this is the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Practicing giving"—this is the cultivation of merit (*puṇya*). Furthermore, by means of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span—this is the cultivation of...
This is wisdom (*prajñā*). To cultivate all that is wholesome is to cultivate merit (*puṇya*). There are many such examples.
△ Fifth, the clarification of the two fruits of the True and the Responsive, in three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Five. This is for the purpose of elucidating the two fruits of the Real (zhen) and the Responsive (ying).
[Record] Among the five points in the Commentary, three are presented; first is the heading. Regarding "the two fruits of the Real and the Responsive":

although various sutras and treatises all speak of the three bodies (*trikāya*), only two are clarified here because they already subsume them. As for the "three bodies," these are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Transformation [is explained] as taught in the provisional schools: the Dharma-body is principle (li), untainted and unconditioned;

the Reward-body is wisdom (jñāna), produced by the transformation of consciousness, conditioned and untainted. Although it realizes principle, this wisdom is not itself the principle, just as the sun occupies the sky.
Thus, wisdom and principle are divided into two. Since the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is a reflection, it is naturally different [from the other bodies].

It is for this reason that the Buddha is said to have three bodies (*trikāya*). What is now referred to as "two" is because the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) are unified;

since wisdom is identical to principle, it is like light being identical to the jewel. Therefore, they are spoken of together as the true body (*svabhāvakāya*). As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-body is without..."
Since it does not fall within any numerical categories, how could one say that the essence of retribution is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)? Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If a person says that the Tathāgata is identical to the conditioned, they shall fall into hell upon death.

For this reason, the three [bodies] are not mentioned here, but only two are spoken of. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha has two bodies: first, the true body (*dharmakāya*); second, the responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*)."

It is also said that both the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Question: The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body are all bodies of the Buddha.

Since the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are not distinct from one another, why is the essence of the Transformation-body explained separately? Answer: The Dharma-body and the Reward-body are both real.
Therefore, they are discussed together. Since the substance of transformation is purely empty, it is appropriate that they be distinguished.
△ Second, the explanation.
[Commentary]: Before hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one spoke only of physical forms as being the Buddha, not knowing that the manifested response (nirmāṇa) is nothing but the True.
The shadow [body]. One does not see the true body (dharmakāya) and the response body (nirmāṇakāya) as they truly are.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "I have never heard... and below, there are two explanations. ○ This refers to those of the Hīnayāna before the twelve years [of the Buddha's teaching of the Mahāyāna];
they took only the golden body with its thirty-two marks to be the true Buddha, not knowing that there was yet another true Buddha. Thus.
It is said that one merely speaks of the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "does not know" below:

because one has not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one does not know that these marks are merely images manifested within the True Body (*dharmakāya*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom..."
They are able to manifest and produce reflections of the bodies, lands, and wisdoms. Since it is said that these are reflections, one knows they are not real. Thus, Maitreya’s verse says:
"The response-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "not knowing, etc.":

if one knew that the true body is real and the response body is empty, and further understood that the characteristic is identical to the absence of characteristics—this is called the true body. There is no...
The identity of characteristics and their names is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. One who perceives in this manner is said to see according to reality (*yathābhūta*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"To see the real as real and the unreal as unreal—thus understanding the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa)—is what is called a Buddha.
If one does not do so, it is called seeing that is not according to reality."
△ Three Conclusions.
[Commentary] Therefore, this section elucidates the two fruits, so that one may know they are realized through the two preceding causes.
[Record] Regarding "Therefore, this section... and "Three Conclusions": ○ "Elucidating the two fruits" refers to what the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks..."
"That the thirty-two marks are non-marks" elucidates the True Body (*dharmakāya*). "This is called the thirty-two marks" elucidates the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Furthermore, it says, "Then it is not a complete physical body," which elucidates the True Body;
"this is called a complete physical body," which elucidates the Responsive Body. Other instances should be understood by analogy. II. The Causes.
"Et cetera" [means]: the True Body (*dharmakāya*) is realized through the aforementioned cause of wisdom; the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is realized through the aforementioned cause of merit.
In the preceding section, it was stated, "Therefore, one must cultivate the two adornments of merit and wisdom," which explains the causes with reference to the results.
Now, it is stated, "Therefore, this is revealed," which explains the results with reference to the causes. To speak in this manner is intended to lead the multitude...
[This] refers to the arising [of realization], the cultivation of two kinds of causes, and the verification of two kinds of fruits.

[Commentary: However, the preceding five gates follow one another in succession. That is to say, when explaining the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the primary purpose is to eliminate the two types of grasping; therefore, there is the first gate.
Although the two types of grasping have been dispelled, the two doubts still persist; therefore, there is the second gate. Even if one is free from doubt...
Yet, how could one help but acknowledge past karma? Thus there is the third [section]. Once evil karma has been extinguished, the cause of outflowlessness (anāsrava) is established;
thus there is the fourth. Since the cause is so manifest, how could the realization of the fruit be far off? Thus there is the fifth. By means of this, the general purport of the sutra is revealed.
This reaches the limit of these five layers.

△ Second, clarifying the essence and substance of the scripture, in two parts: first, the general indication followed by the specific opening; second, the detailed explanation according to the opening.
First, the general indication followed by the specific opening.
[Commentary] Second, the elucidation of the essence and substance of the sūtra.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the elucidation of the essence and substance of the sūtra in the commentary: "essence" (zōng) refers to that which is expressed (the signified), while "substance" (tǐ) refers to that which expresses (the signifier).
△ Second, the detailed explanation based on the opening [of the text] has two parts: first, clarifying the core tenet (śāstrārtha) of the sūtra; second, clarifying the essence (śarīra) of the sūtra.
Clarifying the core tenet of the sūtra has two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the heading.
[Commentary] First, the Thesis (*zong*). [Record] Now, first:
"Thesis" (*zong*) means honorable and weighty; it is that which the mind and speech esteem. Since speech arises from the mind, Master Zhao said:
"Those whose sentiments esteem emptiness encounter every word and find themselves guests of non-being. (The Preface to the *Mao Shi*)
It is said: "When the emotions are stirred within, they take form in speech. All other cases follow this principle. The text has two parts. Part Two:
Explaining [the Meaning]. This has two sections: First, a general clarification of all teachings; second, a specific revelation of the present sutra. First: A General Clarification of All Teachings.
[Commentary] Generally speaking, the Buddhist teachings take dependent origination as their primary tenet.
[Record] First, a general clarification of the various teachings. Now, throughout the ancient and modern periods of this land, there have been three types of teaching;
as their depths and shallownesses differ, their primary tenets also vary. The first is Confucianism. Its master is King Wenxuan, namely Kong Qiu (Confucius). It takes as its tenet...

The Five Constant Virtues are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity. Their purpose is to cultivate the self and exercise caution in conduct, thereby governing the state and the family, and leaving a reputation for future generations.
Second is the Daoist Teaching. Its progenitor is the August Emperor of Mysterious Origin, who is Lao Dan. It takes "spontaneity" as its fundamental principle;
spontaneity means dissolving the distinctions between right and wrong and equalizing life and death, ultimately returning to the void. Third is the Buddhist Teaching.

The Teacher is Śākyamuni himself. His school takes dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as its fundamental principle, intending to cause those with deluded consciousness to shatter their afflictions, realize the truth, and give rise to spiritual function.

Therefore, the Commentary states: "Dependent origination is the fundamental principle. Nevertheless, throughout the entirety of the Buddha’s teachings across his lifetime, dependent origination is universally taken as the fundamental principle.

Although there are differences in depth—such as the arising-and-ceasing of the Hīnayāna versus the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna—a general overview shows that they all [converge upon this].
This refers to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). However, there are two types: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane. The mundane has two: first, the internal;
second, the external. The external further has two: first, that which takes the seed as the cause and soil, water, man, time, and so forth as the conditions, whereby the sprout is produced;
and again, that which takes the lump of clay as the cause and the wheel, cord, potter, and so forth as the conditions, whereby [the jar is produced].

The vessel [world] is thus established. Second is the internal [world], which means that with ignorance as the cause and the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as the condition, the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as the two links of birth and old age and death, arise.
The former two constitute the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), while the latter one constitutes the sentient world (*sattva-loka*).
Thus, one knows that the formation of these three realms of the mundane world arises solely from the two characters "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*pratyaya*).

Second, regarding the supramundane, there are three types: first, intrinsic awakening (*prakṛtisthā-gotra*) acts as the internal cause, while the external influence of a teacher’s instruction acts as the condition;

thus, initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is produced. Second, initial awakening acts as the cause, while the five perfections (*pāramitās*), such as giving (*dāna*), act as the conditions; thus, the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished.
Third, great compassion is the cause and sentient beings are the condition, whereby the manifestation of transformation bodies arises.

Thus, one should know that all supramundane, pure, and wondrous phenomena do not transcend the two words "cause" and "condition. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions;
for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. And the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes..."
[It is] dependently originated. Furthermore, it is said: "I declare that this dependent origination can extinguish all conceptual proliferations.

However, if one comprehensively summarizes all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms—whether in terms of existence (*sat*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the conventional (*prajñapti*), or the middle way (*madhyama*)—though they differ in depth, they all fall within the scope of dependent origination.
To speak of "existence" means there is arising and ceasing; that is to say, all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions.
They arise; when conditions cease, they perish. As the bhikṣu Aśvajit spoke this verse for Śāriputra:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, phenomena perish. Such is their arising and such is their cessation—thus the śramaṇa has taught."

As for emptiness (*śūnyatā*): since it pertains to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one knows it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That lack of intrinsic nature is precisely the meaning of emptiness. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Of those phenomena produced through dependent origination, I say they are empty. As for the provisional (*prajñapti*), it is like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water;
although these are not real, they inevitably appear when conditions converge. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is like a shadow, arising from karma."

Regarding the "Middle" as dependent origination: because it is provisional, it is not empty; because it is empty, it is not provisional. That which is neither empty nor provisional, yet is both empty and provisional, is called the meaning of the Middle.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The teaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent;

all phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions. Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* fully elucidates the four meanings, such as existence, stating: "That which arises from causes and conditions..."
"Those dharmas that arise, I declare to be empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Thus, the meanings of emptiness, existence, and the provisional taught within the doctrines of the Three Vehicles do not transcend dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said that the fundamental principle of the Buddha's teachings is dependent origination.

△ Second, the specific exposition of the present sutra has three parts: first, the formal establishment according to the Dharma; second, the explanation through analogy; third, the concluding manifestation through practice.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "specific exposition" (*bie xian*) and so forth: this refers to the particularity within the general. In whichever sutra it may appear, the primary tenet of each is distinct.
They are distinct, such as the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, the One Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the inconceivable True Suchness and Buddha-nature of the *Vimalakīrti*.
The text has three parts; first, the formal establishment based on the Dharma.
△ First, the formal establishment based on the Dharma.

[Commentary] To specifically reveal this sutra: its central tenet consists of the fact that the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) and the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*) are neither identical nor distinct.
[Commentary] However, regarding the categories of *prajñā*, various explanations differ. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun), three types are taught:

first, the letter (*vyañjana*), which refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning]; second, contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*), which refers to the wisdom that contemplates; and third, the true nature (*dharmatā*), which refers to the object contemplated.
Later, Kumārajīva expanded these into five types by distinguishing the "retinue" from within contemplative illumination. That is to say:
The five aggregates that follow along with the roots of goodness such as "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth open up a sphere of objects within the true nature (*dharmatā*).

This is the sphere of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Among these five, only "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), while the others are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compounds). This is explained in the *Mahāmegha-ṭīkā*.
All five are "function-as-nature" (dharmatā-karma). This means that the nature of words and letters is emptiness, for it is precisely Prajñā.

Since its retinue and its object are identical to words and letters, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is itself the Dharmakāya. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Based upon this Dharmakāya, it is termed 'original enlightenment' (mūla-avabodha).
Although there are three and five [categories], the triad is the primary [classification]. Why? Because all that is illuminated by Prajñā is reality.

Because it is characterized by [marks], it is not merely *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "To illuminate that form and so forth are empty is called their true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This nature-emptiness is the ultimate principle; it is free from inversion because it is not false.

To see emptiness as empty is also called an inversion; to have no attachment to emptiness is the true dharma. Form and so forth are false and deceive the human faculty of sight; thus one knows that..."
In terms of being non-erroneous and free from falsehood, it constitutes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the two truths—ultimate and conventional—are taken together as a single true mark.
Since the attendants such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are associated and concomitant with it, for both observe and illuminate [the object] together.
Therefore, one should know that observation and illumination encompass the attendants. Consequently, although three [stages] are mentioned, they already include the five [path-factors].
Since this accords with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it must certainly coincide with the profound sūtras; thus, the "Three" (the Three Contemplations) are correct.

However, the various schools establish their tenets by focusing either exclusively on contemplation or exclusively on the true aspect (*dharmatā*). Both of these are incorrect. Furthermore, as for what this sūtra elucidates, every single thing is devoid of marks;
how could it be merely contemplation? Moreover, it teaches and transforms sentient beings, severing doubts and shattering attachments; how could it be merely the true aspect? For these reasons...
This is so. Now, this commentary takes both [aspects] together as its thesis. Regarding "neither one nor two": if one wishes to speak of them as one, the essence and its function are distinct;
if one wishes to speak of them as two, quiescence and illumination are always coexistent. Therefore, they are neither one nor two.
△ Second, the explanation by means of a simile. [Commentary]:
Because one uses the wisdom that is identical to principle (*tattva*) to contemplate all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), it is like a vajra, capable of severing everything.

[Commentary] The principle that is identical to wisdom is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is like a vajra—firm, solid, and difficult to destroy. [Sub-commentary] From "The principle that is identical to...
onwards, the two points are explained by means of a metaphor to establish the argument; this reveals that taking both [aspects] together is correct.

Furthermore, the original text cites a single vajra that is both firm and sharp as a metaphor for the two kinds of *prajñā*: the *prajñā* of contemplation and the *prajñā* of the true mark. If taken singly...
If one takes up contemplative observation alone, it lacks the meaning of solidity. If one takes up the true mark alone, it lacks the meaning of sharpness.

Furthermore, the repeated use of the term "immediately" (ji) explains the characteristic of non-duality; for while there is illumination, there is constant quiescence, and thus principle is not external to wisdom.

Because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, wisdom does not exist outside of principle. Since there is no wisdom apart from principle and no principle apart from wisdom, it is like a vajra—both firm and sharp.
△ Third, the conclusion by way of practice.
[Commentary]: Among the myriad practices, not a single one may obscure this. Therefore, these are combined to constitute the core tenet of the sutra.

[Commentary] Below the section on the "ten thousand practices," the third point summarizes and clarifies by way of practice. This means that within the bodhisattva path, one must necessarily possess both of these.

If one is ignorant of the true reality (*dharmatā*), it will be difficult to eliminate conceptual discrimination; one will then fall into abiding in signs (*nimitta*) and thus descend into the outflows (*āsrava*).

If one is ignorant of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), one lacks the function of wisdom (*prajñā-karman*); one will then stagnate in a partial emptiness and become identical to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Therefore, both matters are required.
Only by practicing both simultaneously does one accord with the Middle Way; this is precisely the meaning of the "proceeding according to the profound" mentioned above.

For this reason, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* explains calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) together; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* describes the adornment of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);

the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* clarifies the two matters of concentration and wisdom as that upon which Bodhisattvas rely; and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reveals that if concentration and wisdom are unequal, one will not perceive the Buddha-nature. Thus it is in all the teachings.

The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "Ignorance and false views arise from this. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Commentary says: "The myriad practices are cultivated simultaneously, forgetting both [subjective] illumination and [objective] objects;
sudden and gradual approaches are unimpeded as one enters both at once. All of these refer to this same principle.
△ Second, explaining the essence of the sūtra, in two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.
First, the heading. [Commentary]: Second, the essence.
△ Second, the explanation, in three parts: first, the establishment of the heading; second, the formal explanation; third, the summary conclusion. First, the establishment of the heading.
[Commentary]: The *prajñā* of words and letters is the very essence (*śarīra*) of the sutra.
[Record]: The two essences are divided into three parts. First, the initial heading and establishment; this may be understood.

△ Second, the formal explanation, which has two parts: first, clarifying that it possesses the four dharmas; second, clarifying the inclusion of the principle (*nīti*) to be expressed. First, clarifying...
"Endowed with four dharmas.
[Commentary] "Characters" (vyañjana) includes sound, name (nāman), phrase (pada), and syllable (vyañjana).

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the section beginning with "characters": this is the second part, the formal explanation. Some say that the "teaching-substance" (deśanā-dharma) identified by various schools all takes sound as its essence.
Regarding "name (nāman), phrase (pada), and syllable (vyañjana)": these may be taken collectively as referring to the dharmas they express. Why, then, are only the syllables (letters) taken here?
Because the *Śāstra* states: "Syllables include sound, name, phrase, and sentence. This clarifies that all four factors are present. Sound refers to vocal utterance;
the triad of name, phrase, and sentence is the modulating expression upon that sound. A "name" (nāman) expresses the intrinsic nature of various dharmas.
The *dharmatā* (nature). The phrase (*pada*) expresses the distinctions among all phenomena (*dharma*). The syllable (*vyañjana*) is the letter (*akṣara*), which serves as the basis for these two.
Question: Among the four factors, the syllable occupies the very last position. How can it encompass such factors as sound? Answer:
There are two reasons why it is able to encompass them. First, there are three locations where the syllable is manifested: namely, it is manifested upon the mind.

That which is manifested upon sound is the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). That which is manifested upon form is the object of the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), and that which is manifested upon color is the object of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Now, because we take the former [the mental consciousness], it is able to subsume them all. Second, there may be sound without necessarily having names, phrases, or syllables;

however, where there are syllables, there must necessarily be sound, names, and phrases. What precedes does not necessarily contain what follows, but what follows must necessarily contain what precedes it.
Just as a sprout must have roots, roots do not necessarily have sprouts. For this reason, sound and so forth are included [within the category of names].
△ Second, clarifying the inclusion of the principles that are signified.
[Commentary] The nature of letters is empty; this is precisely Prajñā. There is no separate essence of letters.
[Record] From "The nature of letters is empty" onwards, it clarifies the inclusion of the principle that is expressed (*vācya*). That is to say, based upon Prajñā, the letters are manifested.
Since letters are fundamentally empty, they are themselves Prajñā; there is no separate essence of letters. However, there are two [aspects].
First, its substance belongs to dependent origination because it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Second, there is no separate dharma that constitutes the substance of the syllables.
These points all intend to reveal that *prajñāpāramitā* is the substance of the syllables; it is like molten gold being cast into the form of an image.
The image is itself the gold.
△ Third, the general conclusion.
[Commentary: Therefore, all are inclusively subsumed; there is no principle that is not exhausted. Taken collectively, they constitute the essence of the teaching.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "Therefore, all... is the third section, the summary. Regarding the meaning of "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*): as clarified above, both the subject (the capacity to express) and the object (that which is expressed) are fully encompassed;
thus, it is said that "there is no principle not exhausted. Here, "words" (*vyañjana*) fully encompass the expressive capacity, while "Prajñā" fully encompasses that which is expressed.
Since both the expression and its intended meaning are complete, it is stated that they collectively constitute the essence of the teaching (*śāsana-tattva*).
△ Section Three: Distinguishing the Locations and Assembling the Two. First, a general heading followed by a detailed opening; second, an explanation based on that opening.
First, the general heading and detailed opening. [Commentary]:
The third section distinguishes the locations and assembles the two.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary (*shu*) analyzes the locations and assemblies of the text in two parts.
△ Second, the detailed explanation based on the opening [of the text] has two sections: first, a general clarification of the locations and assemblies where the Buddha preached this great collection;

second, a specific clarification of the masters who transmitted and translated this fascicle. First, the general clarification of the locations and assemblies where the Buddha preached this great collection has two parts: first, the heading; second, [the explanation].
Commentary. First, the heading.
[Sūtra-ṭīkā] First, a general explanation of the locations and assemblies of the Mahāvaipulya sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts: first, a general indication of the Mahāvaipulya sūtras; second, a specific manifestation of this particular sūtra.
[Commentary] This section has two parts. First, a general presentation of the entire collection; second, a specific exposition of this particular sutra.
Regarding the first, the general presentation of the entire collection, there are two sub-sections: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration. This is the general heading.
[Commentary] Six hundred fascicles. Taught in sixteen assemblies across four locations.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration.
[Commentary] First, seven assemblies at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha (four assemblies on the mountain and three assemblies on the summit). Second, seven assemblies at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.

There were four assemblies: first, one at the Maṇi-jewel Treasury Hall in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; second, one at the White Heron Pond in the Bamboo Grove Garden at Rājagṛha; third, [one at] the Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha;
and fourth, one at the side of the White Heron Pond in the Bamboo Grove Garden at Rājagṛha.
△ Second, specifically revealing this sutra.
[Commentary] This sutra is the fifth hundred and seventy-seventh fascicle of the ninth assembly in the two locations [of the canon].
[Record] The general meaning is thus understood.
△ Second, specifically clarifying the master who transmitted and translated this fascicle at that time, in two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Next, there is a separate clarification of the masters who transmitted and translated this fascicle.

△ This section has three parts: first, a formal explanation of the chronological sequence of the translations in the Eastern Land; second, an analysis based on the differences and similarities in Western exegesis;
third, a demonstration of the specific bases for the current structural analysis (*ko-p'an*). First, the formal explanation of the translations in the Eastern Land.
There are two parts: first, a general discussion of all translations; second, a specific indication of what has been transmitted.

[Commentary] Within the section explaining them individually, there are three parts. First, the actual explanation of the chronological sequence of translations in the Eastern Land (China). Second, [the general discussion of all translations]. First, a general discussion of all translations.
△ First, a general examination of the various translations, in two parts: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration. First, the general heading. [Commentary:
There are six translations in total, arranged chronologically.
△ Second, the specific enumeration, in two parts: first, the listing of individual titles; second, the manifestation of their common designation. First, the listing of individual titles.
[Commentary]: 1. Kumārajīva of the Later Qin; 2. Bodhiruci of the Later Wei; 3. Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty; 4.
Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty; 5. Xuanzang of the early Tang; 6. Yijing of the Great Zhou.
[Commentary]: As for Paramārtha (Liu-zhi), in the second year of the Tientian era, he translated it at Luoyang in fourteen sheets;
it was titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. ○ Paramārtha (Zhen-di), in the first year of the Taikang era, translated it at Jinling Commandery in fourteen sheets;
it was titled *Vajracchedikā*. ○ Dharmagupta (Ji-duo), in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, translated it at Luoyang in sixteen sheets.

It was titled *Vajracchedikā*. ○ Xuanzang, in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, translated it at Yuhua Palace into eighteen sheets of paper, titled *Nengduan Jingang* (The Diamond that Can Cut).
○ Yijing, in the second year of the Zhenxing era, translated it at Foshouji Monastery into twelve sheets of paper, titled *Nengduan Jingang* (The Diamond that Can Cut).
△ Second, revealing their common titles.
[Commentary]: The six individuals mentioned above are all masters of the Tripiṭaka.
△ Second, specifically indicating what was transmitted.
[Commentary] What is transmitted here was translated by Kumārajīva at Cángtáng Temple in Cháng’ān in the fourth year of the Hóngshǐ era.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the passage "What is transmitted here" and below: these two lines specifically indicate what has been transmitted.

△ Second, distinguishing the differences and agreements in the Western exegesis. This has two parts: first, clarifying the reception and transmission of the verses; second, clarifying the differences and agreements in the treatise.
Regarding the first, clarifying the reception and transmission of the verses, there are two sections: first, receiving them from Maitreya; second, transmitting them to Vasubandhu.
"Initially received from Maitreya.
[Commentary]: In India, there was the Bodhisattva Asanga. He entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi), ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, and personally visited Maitreya.
He received and transmitted the eighty-verse hymn.
[Commentary] The section beginning with "In India" below distinguishes the differences and similarities in the Western (Indian) commentaries.
△ Second, the transmission to Vasubandhu.
[Commentary] Furthermore, he transmitted this verse to Vasubandhu.

[Record] Regarding the transmission to Vasubandhu, some say: because Vasubandhu had long practiced the Hīnayāna and had recently turned toward the Mahāyāna teachings, [Asaṅga] transmitted it to him so that he might purify his emotional attachments.

△ Second, clarifying the differences and agreements between the treatises, in two parts: first, Vasubandhu’s elimination of doubts and attachments; second, Asaṅga’s elucidation of the stages of practice.
First, Vasubandhu’s elimination of doubts and attachments. [Commentary]:
Vasubandhu composed a prose commentary, forming a treatise of three fascicles. He explained it by way of eliminating doubts and attachments.
△ Second, the stage of manifest practice as elucidated by Asaṅga.
[Commentary] Asaṅga further composed a two-fascicle treatise, which explains [the stages] by way of the stage of manifest practice.
[Record] This correctly clarifies the stage of manifest practice by severing doubts and attachments; it may be seen within the main text of the treatise.
△ Third, showing the differences in the bases for the current structural analysis (*ko-p'an*) has two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the basis for the structural analysis and commentary;

second, the conclusion establishing the reason for the title. Regarding the first, the explicit explanation of the basis for the structural analysis and commentary, there are two [sub-points]: first, Vasubandhu and Asaṅga.
Regarding the second point, the various commentaries on other treatises: first, those by Vasubandhu and Asaṅga.
[Commentary]: Now, in the structural analysis of the sūtra, I rely solely on Vasubandhu; however, in explaining the meaning, I incorporate both Asaṅga as well.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary now divides the text below into three parts: first, it indicates the differences in the basis for the current structural analysis;

second, it explicitly clarifies the basis upon which the structural analysis and commentary rely. Regarding the phrase "including Asaṅga": this demonstrates that while this sub-commentary primarily relies on Vasubandhu, it also peripherally employs the works of Asaṅga.
△ Second, other treatises and various commentaries.
[Commentary: One also seeks out other treatises incidentally and collects various commentaries.
[Record: Regarding "other treatises and various commentaries," the meaning may be seen in the introductory section.

Because there is a distinction of superiority and inferiority in its function, it is divided into cause and effect; yet because its essence neither increases nor decreases, cause and effect are identical as one.

[Commentary] There are two meanings regarding "according to what a person requires. First, as with other things, they cannot adapt to one's needs;

[Commentary] This refers to the wisdom of original enlightenment that corresponds to the illumination of the emptiness of the five aggregates.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "This refers to the illumination...": this defines the essence by way of its function. The illumination of the emptiness of the aggregates is the function;

Perception is like a mirage; mental formations are like a plantain tree; consciousness is like a magical illusion. One who contemplates in this manner is said to "illuminate the emptiness of the aggregates.
Regarding the term "correspondence" (*xiangying*): fundamental awakening (*benjue*) is the Tathāgatagarbha, the intrinsically pure mind.
It is called "fundamental" because it is not newly produced; it is called "awakening" because it is not dull or dark. Wisdom is initial awakening (*shijue*). Function arises based upon the essence.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom. At its inception, it is identical to the fundamental source; thus, it is said to be "in correspondence" (*xiangying*).
Now, fundamental awakening (*benjue*) and wisdom are neither one nor two. Because they are not two, they are said to be in correspondence; because they are not one, they are called wisdom.
Therefore, Zisi said: "The deluded mind perceiving the conventional is called ignorance (*avidyā*); the awakened mind illuminating the ultimate is called *prajñā*.

While the conventional realm consists of the myriad existents and the perceiving mind necessarily differs [in its objects], the principle of true emptiness is one; thus, awakening is without deviation. This is the emptiness of the primary truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)."
Detachment from illumination is illogical; the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (*prakṛti-viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*) is itself both principle and illumination.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called wisdom.

These passages all testify to the meaning that essence and function are neither one nor two. ○ However, the "original" is the true reality (*dharmatā*), while the "initial" is contemplative illumination (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

It is said that all have reached the other shore. The meaning of "reaching" and "leaving" will be clarified next through the explanation of the text.

II. Exegesis according to the Meaning (in two parts): A. Explanation of the Meaning; B. Resolution of Difficulties. A. Explanation of the Meaning (in two parts): 1. Direct Explanation of the Meaning of Reaching and Leaving;
2. Clarification of the Meaning of the Other Shore. 1. Direct Explanation of the Meaning of Reaching and Leaving.
[Commentary] This means: leaving behind this shore of birth and death, crossing over the turbulent middle stream of afflictions, and reaching the further shore of nirvana.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "This means leaving behind" in the commentary: there are two parts, the first of which explains the meaning according to its significance. Within the first three phrases:

In each line, the preceding part provides the principle (*dharma*) and the following part provides the metaphor (*upamā*). The intent clarifies that afflictions (*kleśa*) are like a great river because they are difficult to cross;
saṃsāra is like this shore because sentient beings dwell upon it; and nirvāṇa is like the other shore because all Buddhas abide there.
Thus, wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which can abandon, cross, and reach [the goal], while saṃsāra and the like are that which is to be abandoned, crossed, and reached. If one wishes...
To depart from this shore and reach the other, one must necessarily cross the middle stream. This is explained in terms of the Four Noble Truths;
the principle is thus clear. Knowing suffering is departing from this shore; abandoning the origin and cultivating the path is crossing the middle stream;

realizing cessation is reaching the other shore. This is explained according to the meaning of the Hīnayāna. The subsequent scripture, however, directs one to enter the Mahāyāna nirvāṇa without remainder.

One must immediately depart from this shore of the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), board the raft of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), cross the middle current of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*),
and reach the further shore of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, an explanation of the meaning of the "further shore."
[Commentary]: *Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*) and also as "Extinction and Crossing Over" (*mièdù*). [Sub-commentary]:

Regarding terms such as *nirvāṇa*, since the translation of *pāramitā* (perfection) as "the other shore" (*bī'àn*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, the meaning of "the other shore" is explained here in terms of the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Now, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) refers to both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) types, while afflictions (*kleśa*) refer to...

This generally encompasses both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). ○ "Perfect Quiescence" (*parinirvāṇa*) is a semantic translation. It means that when virtues are complete as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is called "Perfect" (*yuan*);

when one is wondrously transcendent from the burdens of phenomenal marks, it is called "Quiescent" (*ji*). ○ "Extinction and Crossing Over" (*mie-du*)—Sengzhao says: "Nirvana is called 'unconditioned' (*wuwei*) in the Qin language, and is also called 'extinction and crossing over.
Sometimes it is simply called 'extinction' (*mie*). However, this 'extinction' differs from that of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), for the Lesser Vehicle takes the extinction of birth as its goal."
Death is cessation. In the Mahāyāna, however, quiescent extinction (*śānti*) is taken as cessation. Thus the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.
Here, "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers solely to the fruit, whereas "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) encompasses both cause and fruit; now, by means of the fruit, the cause is indicated.
Therefore, it is called "extinction and deliverance" (mie-du). Thus, in the sutras, the term *nirvāṇa* is used above and "extinction and deliverance" is used below;
this is likewise a simultaneous manifestation of both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms. The various categories of *nirvāṇa* will be explained in detail in the following section.
△ Second, resolving two difficulties. First, citing a sutra to raise a difficulty; second, explaining and resolving it based on the meaning. First, citing a sutra to raise a difficulty. [Commentary]:
All sentient beings are already the mark of quiescent extinction; they do not need to be extinguished again.
[Commentary] The section beginning with "All" below addresses two general objections. This is a passage from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, which states:
"If Maitreya were to receive a prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive a prediction. Why? Because all sentient beings are already in the state of quiescence;
they do not need to be extinguished further," and so forth. Now, this text is employed as the basis for the objection. It is an objection.

The intention [of this] is as follows: Since sentient beings are already identical with quiescent extinction (*śānti*), how could there be a departure from here to arrive at another place? Now, if one speaks of "arriving at that place," does this not contradict the sutras?
△ Second, explaining and resolving according to the meaning.
[Commentary: It is simply that when one is deluded and perceives birth and death through false views, one is said to be "on this shore.
If one awakens to the fact that birth and death are fundamentally empty and have always been perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*), one is said to have "reached the other shore."

[Commentary] From "But" (*dan*) onwards, the text provides an exegesis to resolve the difficulty. "Only by taking the overturning of delusion into enlightenment as the standard does one truly depart from this [shore] and arrive at that [shore].

Once this has been awakened to, the gradual elimination and gradual realization thereof is termed 'ultimate' (*niṣṭhā*). However, for the perfections (*pāramitā*) to be fully established, they must correspond with the seven types of supremacy (*saptavidha-sampat*), as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
△ 3. General Conclusion according to the Meaning.
[Sūtra Commentary] If one were to include *prajñā* (wisdom) and adjust the phrasing accordingly, it should read: "the wisdom that reaches the other shore.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "If one were to include... in the Sūtra Commentary: this is the general conclusion according to the meaning among the three [types of *pāramitā*], namely, the *śruta-pāramitā* (perfection of hearing) within the *pāramitās*.
This refers to the wisdom of reflection and cultivation.
△ Second, the explanation of the expressive terminology has two parts: first, the transliteration of the name; second, the explanation of the meaning. First, the transliteration of the name:
[Commentary] "Sūtra" is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*; its meaning is translated as "Scripture of Accordance."
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "The commentator on the sutra... and below, there are two parts explaining the capacity [of the term].
First, the translation of the name: *Sūtra*, sometimes called *Sūtru* or *Sūtrānta*; these are merely differences in the dialects of the Sanskrit language.
Regarding the translation of the meaning: *Sūtra* is correctly translated as "thread" (*sūtra*), because in India the single term *sūtra* was used [in this sense].
They summoned four types of "reals" (sūtras): namely, the sacred teachings (*āgama*), mats, ropes, and threads. There, they frequently offered flowers to the Buddha and placed them upon a table;

fearing that the wind might blow them away, they strung them together with thread. Furthermore, they observed that here in this land, the sacred teachings are able to uphold the Buddha’s words so that nothing is lost, just as flowers are threaded on a string.
For this reason, they designated [the scriptures] by the name "thread" (*sūtra*). Regarding that place:

It is called *sūtra*. According to this direct translation, it should properly be rendered as "thread" (*sūtra*). Because the term "thread" is not esteemed in this land [of China], it was translated as "scripture" (*jing*).
This thus implicitly accords with the "woven mats" (*sūtra*) of that region [India], while simultaneously conforming to the "classics" (*jing*) of the Confucian and Daoist traditions of this land.
Nevertheless, although it accords with and conforms to both, it cannot avoid being confused with them; for this reason, the character "agreement" (*qi*) was further added.
To distinguish it from others, one should further add the two characters *yùdǐ* (欲底) above the term *xiūduōluó* (修多羅), translating it as *qìjīng* (契經);
thus, both the Chinese and the Sanskrit terms will be complete.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has two parts: first, the explanation of the character *qiè* (契); second, the explanation of the character *jīng* (經). First, the explanation of the character *qiè*. [Commentary]:

"Qiè" means to express and manifest principles and meanings, thereby harmonizing with the minds of people; that is, to accord with the principle (*lǐ*) and to accord with the capacity (*jī*) of the audience.

[Commentary] "The term 'khi' (契)... and below provides two explanations of its meaning. "To express and represent... and below explains the character *khi*. To "express and represent" (*ch’üan-piao*) principles and meanings is to explain "conforming to principle" (*ch’i-li*).

This means that when explaining phenomena, they are explained as they truly are; when explaining principles, they are explained as they truly are (and so forth). To "conform to" (*ch’i*) the human mind is to explain "conforming to the mind" (*ch’i-hsin*).

"Releasing" (*śe*) explains "to accord with the capacity" (*qìjī*). This means causing people to attain realization and understanding, so that they joyfully accept and believe [the teaching], and so forth.

This, then, is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound meaning "a sūtra that accords with principle and accords with capacity. Although the wording is inverted, the intended sense is that the sūtra is that which accords.
△ Second, the explanation of the characters of the sūtra.
