[Commentary] Regarding "sūtra," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it can thread together and encompass, it is called a sūtra. This refers to the holy teachings of the Buddha.
It penetrates the meanings that ought to be explained and sustains those beings who are to be converted.
[Commentary] Regarding the word "sūtra" (*jing*) below: first, it is presented; then, from "by the Buddha" onwards, it is explained, as was clarified in the introduction.
Now, the reason we say only "sūtra" (*jing*) and not "scripture" (*qiè*) is to distinguish it from the *Prajñāpāramitā* [literature], thereby clarifying [its specific nature].
This is not a sūtra concerning non-morality and the like; therefore, it is not mentioned.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text has two parts: first, the structural division; second, the detailed commentary. First, the structural division.
[Commentary] The subsequent section explains the scriptural text. Following the standard threefold division: first, the Introduction; second, the Main Body; third, the Circulation.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "The subsequent section explains," there are two parts to the explanation of the scriptural text. First, the structural analysis. This follows the method of Dao’an.

The Master’s judgment is that all Buddhist scriptures, regardless of whether they are Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, are categorized into three parts. His intention is as follows: the *Nidāna* (Introduction) clarifies the causes and conditions for the preaching of the Dharma;
the *Saddharma* (Main Body) expounds the profound gate of the original intent; and the *Pariṇāmana* (Circulation) perpetuates the distant fragrance [of the teaching] for ten thousand ages.

This accords with the Western Regions in a hidden way and has been universally followed throughout antiquity and the present. In this sutra, from "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) up to "having spread his seat" (*niṣadya*).
And sat down. This is the introductory section (*nidāna*). From "At that time, the Elder" down to "should contemplate in this manner," is the main body of the teaching (*sūtra-śarīra*).
From "The Buddha spoke this sutra" down to "faithfully accept and practice," is the section on dissemination (*pariṇāmana*).
△ Second, the word-by-word commentary has three parts: first, the introduction; second, the main body; third, the dissemination section. The first, the introduction, has two parts:
first, the sequence for attaining faith; second, the sequence of the incitement.
[Commentary] The initial section has two parts: first, the *samyak-pratyaya-nidāna* (序 of Certification and Faith); second, the *utpatti-nidāna* (序 of Origination).

[Record] "Certification and Faith" refers to the six *niṣpatti* (成就, accomplishments). It clarifies the time, teacher, and place of the teaching, making each point distinct and clear, so as to certify that it is not erroneous and cause sentient beings to give rise to faith.
"Origination" refers to using specific events and characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) to represent and initiate [the teaching].
This is the meaning of the "Correct Main Text" (zhèngzōng). However, these two prefaces also have other names, namely the "General Preface" (tōngxù) and the "Specific Preface" (biéxù).

"General" means that it is common to all sūtras (and so forth); "specific" means that it is distinct for each sūtra (and so forth). They are also called the "Postscript to the Sūtra" (jīnghòuxù) and the "Preface to the Sūtra" (jīngqiánxù).
Regarding the Postscript to the Sūtra: it did not exist at the time the Buddha preached [the sūtra], but only came into being at the time of the compilation (saṃgīti).
Regarding the establishment [of the sūtra]: as for the "preface" (*nidāna*) at the beginning of the sūtra, it is because the Buddha first initiates [the discourse] before he speaks the sūtra.
The first [section], the *Śraddhā-nidāna* (Preface of Faith), has three parts: first, clarifying the cause of its establishment; second, clarifying the purpose of its establishment;
third, the formal explanation of the textual meaning. First, clarifying the cause of its establishment:

[Commentary] First, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the introductory section on authentication (*samyak-pratyaya-nidāna*) is explained in three parts. First, the cause for its establishment:

when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested instruction on four matters, and the Buddha answered each one in turn: (1) after my parinirvāṇa, abide in accordance with the four foundations of mindfulness;
(2) take the precepts as your teacher; (3) silence and exclude monks of evil character; and (4) [regard] all sūtras...
First: All [versions] state, "Thus have I heard at one time; the Buddha was at such-and-such a place, together with such-and-such an assembly of such-and-such number.
[Commentary: Of the three sections in the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), this is the first. (And so forth). ○ Regarding the "Establishment of the Causes" in the *Shu*:

the intent is to clarify on what basis the words "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth are established. ○ "The Buddha, approaching... means that as the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was filled with grief and distress. Ānanda...
Aniruddha addressed Ānanda, saying, "You are one who upholds the Dharma of the Buddha; you must exercise restraint for now. You should go there and inquire about future matters.
Ānanda asked, "What are these future matters? Aniruddha said, "While the World-Honored One was alive, we took the Buddha as our teacher.
After the World-Honored One has passed away, whom shall we take as our teacher? While the World-Honored One was alive..."
"While the World-Honored One was present, we relied upon him for our dwelling. After the World-Honored One has passed away, upon what shall we rely?

As for evil-natured bhikṣus, while the Buddha was alive, he himself subdued them; after his parinirvāṇa, how shall they be subdued? To benefit future generations for a long time, it is only right that we hold a council.
What words should be placed at the beginning of all the sūtras? Ānanda received these instructions and inquired about each point one by one. Now...
The *Suyǐng lüè* (Abridged Commentary on the Shadows) does not record the questions; it records only the answers. Regarding the "Four Foundations of Mindfulness" (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*):

"Four" refers to body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) here means mindfulness-wisdom (*smṛti-prajñā*). "Foundation" (*upasthāna*) means that the body and so forth are the places where mindfulness-wisdom abides.
Thus, mindfulness is the subject that abides, while the four foundations—body and so forth—are the objects wherein it abides. One should abide within these four foundations.
"Mindfulness and wisdom" is called "abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness"; this is an analysis based on apposition (*dvandva*). 1. Contemplating the impurity of the body:
This refers to the contaminated aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which possesses five kinds of impurity. First is impurity of the seed:
because it takes up the seeds of past karmic consciousness and gathers the semen and blood of the present parents to form the body. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body..."
It is like an illusion, arising from inversion. This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "The seed of this body is impure; it is not some other exquisite treasure. It does not grow from between flowers, but emerges only from the foul path.
Second, its dwelling place is impure: within the mother’s womb, it resides below the stomach and above the intestines, constantly undergoing suffering."

Because it is defiled by impurities. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "This body is like a foul object; it does not arise from among flowers, nor does it come from the *campaka*, nor does it emerge from a mountain of jewels.
Third, the impurity of its own substance: because it is composed of thirty-six constituent elements.
That is to say, externally there are ten [elements]: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eye-secretion, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, filth, and sweat; as well as excrement and urine.
Second: Next there are the twelve [parts] consisting of skin, blood, flesh, sinews, veins, bone, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes. Within these are the twelve internal organs:
the spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, red phlegm, white phlegm, the raw viscera (*āma-koṣṭha*), and the cooked viscera (*pakva-koṣṭha*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The substances of earth, water, fire, and wind are able to contain and receive impurities; even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body..."
1. It cannot be made fragrant and clean. 2. Its own characteristics are impure, because the nine orifices constantly discharge impure substances.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Various kinds of impure things fill the interior of the body, flowing out incessantly, like a leaking bag filled with objects.
3. It is ultimately impure; once life ends, it swells, decays, and becomes foul and loathsome.

Ji (the Record): Because one cannot bear to see [its decay], the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "This body is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, yet it must ultimately return to destruction.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Observe this body with discerning clarity: it will ultimately return to the place of death; it is difficult to restrain and shows no regard for the past."
"Being ungrateful like a small child. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also says: "Though one constantly provides for them, they harbor resentment and malice;
in the end, they abandon me, being unaware of my kindness. 2. Contemplating that feeling (*vedanā*) is suffering: Feeling is a mental factor (*caitta*), one of the five universal mental factors.

It further comprises three types: suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Suffering refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); pleasure refers to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

Suffering. Equanimity refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Question: If the pleasant sensation has not yet ceased, should it not be considered non-suffering? Answer:

Because pleasure is a cause of suffering, ordinary beings delusively reckon it as pleasure, whereas it is fundamentally suffering. Question: Since equanimity is neither painful nor pleasant, how can it be suffering? Answer:

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is subject to constant flux and oppression, and is thus perpetually suffering; however, this is merely obscured by the coarse characteristics of pain and pleasure.
Ordinary people do not realize that this is subtle suffering; therefore, these three factors are all termed "suffering.
Third, regarding the contemplation of the mind as impermanent: the mind refers to the mind of discursive thought and arising-and-ceasing.

This means that from moment to moment, one thought perishes and the next arises, continuing in an uninterrupted succession like the flow of a stream. Thus, it is said in the sutras that within a single thought-moment there are nine...

Ten *kṣaṇas* [constitute one moment], and within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred arisings and ceasings. ○ Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*):

"phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). This means that when one investigates each and every phenomenon among the five aggregates—both within the aggregates and apart from the aggregates—one finds that there is no self in either case.
○ Contemplating in this manner is able to counteract the four kinds of inversions of ordinary beings; that is to say, ordinary beings...
Through inversion, one creates karma and undergoes rebirth; conversely, by employing the mind in this way, one naturally incurs no fault.
Regarding those who take the precepts as their teacher, they follow their model and rely solely upon the Vinaya, making clear what is to be done and what is to be avoided.
Thus, the Preface to the Bodhisattva Precepts states: "The Prātimokṣa is your great teacher; while the Tathāgata was in the world, it was no different from this."

Regarding "silent censure" (*tūṣṇīmbhāva-parivāsa*) and so forth: The Buddha-dharma is characterized by compassion and thus possesses no corporal punishments. When a bhikṣu is of evil character, the only recourse is silent censure;

this is intended to cause him to reflect upon himself and recognize his shame, whereby he will naturally become disciplined. The explanation for the phrase "at the beginning of the sūtra" and so forth is found in the subsequent text.
However, among these four [methods], the primary intent lies in the fourth; the preceding ones are mentioned incidentally as a matter of convenience within the text.
Three. △ Second, clarifying the intent behind the establishment [of the teaching].
[Commentary]: Second, clarifying the intent behind the establishment. There are three aspects to this intent.
[Commentary] Regarding the intent behind establishing [the categories]: what is the purpose of establishing such statements as these?
There are three intents, as presented in the three sections of the commentary.

[Commentary: First, it is for the purpose of severing doubts. That is to say, at the time of the compilation [of the scriptures], when Ānanda ascended the seat, desiring to proclaim the Buddha-dharma, he manifested his own physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as being identical to those of the Buddha.
Consequently, the assembly gave rise to three doubts: first, the doubt that the Buddha had arisen once more to preach the Dharma;

second, the doubt that a Buddha from another direction had come; and third, the doubt that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood. Therefore, by speaking these words, the three doubts were instantaneously severed.
[Commentary] Regarding "the severing of doubts" and so forth: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various heavenly kings and others requested Kāśyapa, saying:
"The city of the Dharma is about to collapse; the banner of the Dharma is about to fall. You should, out of great compassion, establish the Buddha-dharma.
Having accepted this request, Kāśyapa went to the summit of Mount Sumeru and struck the great ghaṇṭā (bell). The noble disciples [thereupon] attained...
All those possessing supernormal powers gathered together. Kāśyapa addressed them, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is about to perish; sentient beings are to be pitied.
Wait until the compilation is finished, and then you may enter parinirvāṇa as you please. All the noble assembly who had come accepted his instruction and remained in the Piṇḍola Cave.
Kāśyapa entered meditative concentration and, observing with his divine eye, considered: "In this assembly now, who possesses afflictions that should be eliminated?"

As for those who departed, there was only Ānanda, whose afflictions were not yet exhausted. At that time, Kāśyapa arose from his meditative concentration and, in the midst of the great assembly, led Ānanda out, saying: "In this pure assembly, we are compiling the Dharma-treasury;
since your fetters are not yet exhausted, you should not remain here. Thereupon, Ānanda was filled with shame and wept bitterly, addressing Kāśyapa, saying: "I..."

"You possess the power to attain the Way after a long time. However, because you served the Buddha, and since an Arhat is not permitted to serve as an attendant, you have retained residual fetters and have not severed them completely. Kāśyapa said: "You have committed yet another transgression.
The Buddha’s intention was not to permit women to leave the household life; yet, through your earnest entreaties, you caused the Buddha’s True Dharma to decline by five hundred years."
[The Buddha’s] strength declined. This was your *duṣkṛta* offense. When the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa near Kuśinagara, he suffered from back pain;
he folded his *uttarāsaṅga* robe and spread it out to lie upon. He said to you, "I need water," yet you did not provide it.

This was your *duṣkṛta* offense. In the past, the Buddha asked you: "If there is someone who skillfully cultivates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they should be able to remain for the duration of a kalpa."
If there were none, one kalpa would have been reduced; because you did not respond to [the Buddha's summons], causing the Buddha to enter parinirvāṇa prematurely, this is your *duṣkṛta* offense.
At another time, you lay down with your *uttarāsaṅga* robe used as a pillow beneath your body; this is your *duṣkṛta* offense.
In the past, when folding the *saṃghāṭī* robe for the Buddha, you stepped upon it with your feet; this is your *duṣkṛta* offense.
[You committed] a *duṣkṛta* offense. To display the Buddha’s mark of the concealed organ (*kośagatavastiguhyatā*) to women after he had entered *nirvāṇa* was truly a cause for shame;
this is your *duṣkṛta* offense. Kāśyapa said, "You have these six kinds of *duṣkṛta* offenses;
you should repent before the Saṃgha. At that time, Ānanda removed his leather sandals, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms.
Having performed repentance for the six kinds of *duṣkṛta* offenses, Kāśyapa led Ānanda out and said to him, "Your outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted;
you may come [in]. Having finished speaking, he closed the cave door himself.

At that time, Ānanda wept with tears of grief, seeking to sever his fetters and delusions with the utmost sincerity. When the final watch of the night arrived, being utterly exhausted, he lay down to rest; before his head had even—
Upon reaching his pillow, Ānanda attained sudden enlightenment; he realized the three insights and the six supernormal powers, becoming a great arhat.
He returned to the entrance of the cave and knocked on the door, calling out. Kāśyapa asked, "Why have you come back? He replied, "My outflows are exhausted.
Kāśyapa said, "If your outflows are indeed exhausted, you may employ your supernormal powers to enter through the keyhole of the door. Ānanda then leaped through the air and entered.
He prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha. Kāśyapa placed his hand upon Ānanda’s head and said: "I wish to act for your sake so that you may attain the Way; do not harbor resentment.
This is like the case of Sūqín and Zhāngyí [who were merely pawns] (and so forth). However, to ascend to the fruits of sainthood, it depends entirely upon cultivating the mind.
If one does not practice what they preach, what benefit is there in serving the Buddha? To borrow the tiger's majesty like a fox—this must surely be brought to an end. Thus he spoke.
The meaning is most subtle. Examine it carefully and be on guard. At that time, the great assembly requested Ānanda to ascend the seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.
Once he had ascended the seat, before he had even spoken, his own physical marks and signs were miraculously transformed to resemble those of the Buddha.
At this, the great assembly gave rise to three doubts. Therefore, the text says below: "Since he said, 'I heard this from the Buddha,' one knows that he was not the Buddha."
He arose again. It was neither that a Buddha from another direction had come, nor that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that his three doubts were suddenly severed.
As this is explained extensively in that treatise, I have provided only a brief account for fear of being too prolix.

[Commentary]: Second, it is for the sake of quelling disputes. If one did not attribute [the teachings] to having heard them from the Buddha, but claimed they were composed by oneself, then disputes would arise.

[Record]: Regarding the phrase "quelling disputes" in the commentary: since they were all equally Arhats and their virtues and accomplishments were largely identical, if one had claimed [the teachings] were merely his own words, clamorous disputes would certainly have ensued.
[Commentary]: Third, because it differs from the heterodox. It is not like the beginning of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) sūtras, which say "A-yu" and so forth.
[Sub-commentary]: Regarding the phrase "differs from the heterodox" in the Commentary: "A" means non-existence; "yu" means existence.

The intention of the non-Buddhists is that although the myriad dharmas differ, they do not transcend existence and non-existence. They place this at the beginning of their sūtras to signify auspiciousness; because the beginning is auspicious.
It was auspicious even after midday; now it is not so. Therefore, it is said to be "different" (yi).
△ Third, the correct explanation of the textual meaning has two parts: first, the heading, enumeration, and statement of the intent; second, the explanation according to the topical outline.
First, the heading, enumeration, and statement of the intent.
[Commentary] Third, the correct explanation of the meaning of the text. It possesses six accomplishments, namely: faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly.
If these six conditions are not complete, the teaching will not arise; it must possess all six, hence they are called "accomplishments."
[Commentary] The sub-commentary (*śāstra*) correctly explains the following two points. First, the headings, enumeration, and statement of the intent. Regarding the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*):
this means that the six [perfections] are the agents of accomplishment, and the teaching is that which is accomplished.
△ Second, the explanation according to the topical outline has six parts: first, the accomplishment of faith; second, the accomplishment of hearing; third, the accomplishment of time;

fourth, the accomplishment of the principal [disciple]; fifth, the accomplishment of the place; sixth, the accomplishment of the assembly. Regarding the first, the accomplishment of faith, there are two sections:
first, the combined explanation; second, the individual explanation. First, the combined explanation.
[Commentary: First is faith. If "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) is interpreted in conjunction with "thus" (*evam*), it is a phrase pointing to the Dharma:
"Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha."
[Commentary] Regarding the first section, "Explanation according to the topical outline," there are six parts. Within the first [of these], there are two: first, the combined explanation.
This refers to the combined explanation of the current section together with the following one. This constitutes a distinct category and is not counted within the total of six.
△ Second, the single explanation of the three [sections]. First, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; second, citing Liu Qiū’s commentary; third, citing Emperor Wu of Liang’s explanation.
Regarding the first citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Regarding the first, the heading:
Thus it is.
[Commentary] Regarding the single explanation of "thus" (*evam*): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that it signifies the fulfillment of faith.
[Sub-commentary] "Single explanation" means the direct explanation of the meaning of the fulfillment of faith. The cited passage from the treatise contains both the heading and the explanation.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, answering the question; second, the formal exposition. First, answering the question:
[Commentary] "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom."
[Commentary] "The Buddha-dharma" below is the explanation. ○ Some say: Why is it that at the very beginning, faith (*śraddhā*) is clarified?

This is the explanation for that. ○ Regarding "faith is that which enables entry": although the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable, faith is its primary foundation. If one lacks the mind of faith, how could one ever be willing to practice?
For this reason, within the five stages (*pañca-vastu*), the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) is placed first; among the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), [it is likewise].

Among all [virtues], faith is called the foremost. Of the eleven wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), faith is likewise the precursor. Thus we know that prior to the mind of faith, there is no other wholesome dharma upon which to rely.
Only when this faith is fundamental can understanding and practice (*jñāna-caryā*) arise, leading even to realization and entry.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness and severs the net of doubt."

It emerges from the river of craving and reveals the unsurpassed path to Nirvana; it is now placed at the beginning of this scripture to signify that the mark of faith is the starting point for entering the Dharma.
Wisdom is that which enables crossing over; among the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva, nothing is accomplished without wisdom.

If one lacks wisdom, one will stagnate in attachment or cling to emptiness. By taking wisdom as the primary guide, one does not adhere to the two extremes and thus establishes the cause for the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) and attains the fruit of *bodhi*.
Therefore, the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā* (or *Bodhipathapradīpa*) states:

"Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and that which remains beyond these five—all are subsumed under the *pāramitās* by virtue of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
△ Second, the actual manifestation.
[Commentary] One who has faith says, "This matter is thus. One who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus.
[Sub-commentary] From "One who has faith" onwards, it is clearly shown that the two characters "thus" (rúshì) are terms of faith. All of the above is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
[This is] the explanation.
△ Second, citing Liu Qiū’s commentary: [The Commentary states:
Furthermore, when the Sage preaches the Dharma, he does so solely to reveal the *tathatā* (suchness). Since only *tathatā* is what is correct, it is called "Thus" (*evam*).
[Commentary] Furthermore, "The Sage... and below is the explanation from Liu Qiu’s commentary on the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

All that follows is explained in terms of the Dharma. To "reveal Suchness" means that because the suchness of sentient beings is obscured, they sink into the three realms; thus, one desires to sever [the bonds of] the three realms.
Because it manifests as suchness, it is said: "only for [the sake of] suchness. Because everything other than suchness is entirely false and illusory, it is said:
"only suchness is correct. The Treatise says: "Except for the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), all else is the work of Māra. It further states:
"From the initial attainment of the Way up to Nirvāṇa, there is nothing taught therein that does not accord with suchness."
△ Third, citing Emperor Wu of Liang’s interpretation, which has two parts: first, the simultaneous integration that reveals Suchness; second, the simultaneous negation that reveals Thisness.
First, the simultaneous integration that reveals Suchness.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, the non-duality of existence and non-existence constitutes Suchness.

[Commentary] Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover" is the interpretation of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. Its intent clarifies that because existence is itself non-existence, it is not existent;
because non-existence is itself existence, it is not non-existent. Since these aspects are simultaneous, they are called "non-dual. Non-duality is itself suchness (*tathatā*).
This explains suchness by means of their mutual integration.
△ Second, the dual negation to reveal what it is.
[Commentary] "As it is not that non-existence and existence are the *tathatā*.
[Record] Regarding "as it is not" below: fearing that upon hearing that non-duality of existence and non-existence is the *tathatā*, one might then claim that the essence of *tathatā* is existent.
There is none. Therefore, it is negated by saying, "it is like neither existence nor non-existence. The intent is to clarify that existence and non-existence are precisely what it is not;
thus, it is "neither existence nor non-existence.
[Commentary] Regarding these two preceding interpretations, the character *ru* (like) reveals the essence (*tǐ*). The character *shì* (is) means that there is no "not" (*wēi*).
△ Second, the accomplishment of hearing, which has two parts: first, the formal explanation of the meaning of "I heard" (evam mayā śrutam); second, an investigation of the Dharma heard.

Regarding the first, the formal explanation of the meaning of "I heard," there are two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of difficulties. Regarding the first, the formal explanation:

"I have heard. [Commentary] Regarding the second point, "hearing": "I" refers to Ānanda, a provisional designation for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Hearing" refers to the arising of consciousness through the faculty of the ear.
[Record] In the commentary on the second point, "hearing," there are two parts. First, the direct explanation of the meaning of "I have heard. Now, there are four kinds of "self."

First, the self-conceptualization of ordinary worldlings; second, the divine self (*ātman*) of non-Buddhists; third, the provisional self of the Three Vehicles; and fourth, the true self of the Dharmakāya.

Now, in order to exclude the others, it says "the provisional entity of the five aggregates. This refers to the third [category], which follows worldly convention and requires the distinction between host and guest;
thus, when one says "I, Ānanda," although one has already realized the emptiness of the self, in reality, no conceptual attachment is maintained.
Regarding the term "provisional": as for "hearing," various treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna distinguish different views on how hearing occurs.

Some say it is the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); some say it is the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); and others say it is the conjunction of the faculty and consciousness that hears. Here, it is stated that the ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness.

This refers to the latter [of the two] meanings. Since neither the sense organ nor consciousness alone can hear [the teaching], and so forth. However, while the sense organ and consciousness hear the sound, they do not hear the teaching;
if one follows the categories of name (*nāman*) and phrase (*pada*), it is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that hears it.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing is [a matter of] inference (*anumāna*). Nevertheless, because the ear-consciousness takes the object of sound as its condition, it hears simultaneously with the mental consciousness. However...
Regarding these two consciousnesses hearing sounds, names, and phrases, in reality they do not occur at different times, one preceding the other;
rather, because the sudden ear-consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness (manovijñāna) function together, they are able to hear. This is the case for all five sensory consciousnesses.
△ Second, resolving the objection. [Commentary]:
Setting aside the particular to follow the general, it says, "I have heard. [Sub-commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "setting aside the particular," some say: Since it is said that hearing occurs because consciousness is produced by the faculty of the ear, one should properly say "the ear hears. Why does it say "I hear"?

Why is it that in certain sūtras it is stated simply, "I heard"? This is the explanation: the ear is a specific part of the six sense faculties, whereas the "self" (ātman) is the totality of the body.
Here, the specific ear is set aside in favor of its totality, the self; therefore, it is said, "I heard."
△ Second, the comparative evaluation of the Dharma heard, in two parts: first, restating the words of the objection; second, the comprehensive explanation.
First, restating the words of the objection: [Commentary] The sūtras from twenty years ago that Ānanda did not hear.
[Commentary] "Ānanda" and below: the second section deliberates upon the Dharma he heard. The first two phrases cite the objection:
Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; he became an attendant only at the age of twenty.

Therefore, regarding the teachings the Buddha delivered during the twenty years prior to that, Ānanda had not heard them. How, then, could he state in the compilation of the various sūtras, "Thus have I heard"?

△ Second, a general explanation of the two [aspects]. First, provisionally relying on the power of the Buddha; second, provisionally relying on one's own power; third, directly tracing back to their source.
First, provisionally relying on the power of the Buddha.
[Commentary] Some say: "The Tathāgata repeated his teaching.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "Some say" below, this provides a general explanation containing three points. The first is that some say he taught it repeatedly.
When the Buddha first commanded Ānanda to be his attendant, Ānanda requested three vows from the Buddha; the first was not to wear the Buddha’s discarded robe.
Second, he did not follow the Buddha in accepting separate invitations. Third, he requested that the Buddha preach the Dharma he had not yet heard. The Buddha granted his wish;
therefore, he was able to hear it.
△ Second, briefly considering his own power:
[Commentary] Some say: "He attained the profound samādhi that governs all.
[Record] Regarding "attained the profound samādhi" and so forth, this is the second point. The *Vajrapuṣpa-ṛṣi-sūtra* states:
"Because Ānanda attained the power of the *dharmatā-bodhy-vaśitā-samādhi*, he was able to remember and uphold all the sūtras previously spoken, as if he had heard them anew."
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "The World-Honored One is most rare and extraordinary; he causes me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, just as I have heard them today."
△ Third, directly tracing back to the source.
[Commentary]: If one traces back to the source, Ānanda is a great *mahā-upāya* bodhisattva; what dharma is there that he does not penetrate?
[Commentary] If one traces it back, this is the third [category]. The *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas who manifested in the forms of śrāvakas and also came to sit in the assembly; their names were Śāriputra, up to Ānanda, and so forth.
This means that among these three, the first two are provisional teachings while the last one is the ultimate reality; therefore, it is said that one must trace back to the source.

...Also. △ Third, the accomplishment of the three times, in two parts: first, the explanation by means of selection and manifestation; second, the explanation by means of reconciling the dharmas. First, the explanation by means of selection and manifestation, in two parts:
first, the manifest explanation; second, the selective explanation. First, the manifest explanation.
"At one time. [Commentary] Regarding the "three times": when teacher and disciple assemble, the teaching and listening reach their conclusion; hence it is said, "at one time.
[Record] Regarding the section "Three times" in the commentary, there are two parts. First, the selection, clarification, and explanation. "Teacher and disciple assemble" refers to the speaker...
One who teaches others through morality is called a teacher (*śāstṛ*). "To receive" (*tsū*) means to take up; it refers to following the teacher’s instruction and taking it up for practice.

Because both the Buddha and the great assembly were fully engaged in speaking and listening, it is called a "gathering" (*saṃnipāta*). Since the speaking was completed and the listening was finished, it is called "concluded" (*niṣṭhita*).

The meaning is that the teaching was delivered without interruption from beginning to end, as if there were no different seats [for speaker and listener]; thus it is called "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*). — *Buddhabhūmi-vyākhyāna* (The Commentary on the Stage of the Buddha).
It is said: This refers to the continuity of moments without interruption, from the beginning of the teaching until its conclusion, which is collectively termed "at one time.
The phrase "at one time" is because the Buddha himself spoke it. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the past, at one time, the Buddha was in the Śīśumāragiri Forest. It also says: [and so forth].
"At one time, I was in the kingdom of Kāśī. This clearly explains that the capacity for hearing and all that is heard have been fully perfected.
△ Second, the selection and explanation.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the various directions and time periods": their durations differ in terms of extension and brevity; therefore, it simply says "one. [Sub-commentary]:
The section beginning with "Regarding the various directions" distinguishes [the nature of] time. There are two ways in which they differ: horizontally, they are irregular and unequal;

vertically, they differ in terms of extension and brevity. As for the difference in extension and brevity: for example, fifty years among humans [is equivalent to one day and night] for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
One day and night [is established] because each successive [continent] increases twofold. As for the discrepancies, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur simultaneously across the four continents. Given this, why do you definitively claim that the sun and moon rise at specific times such as the first, second, third, or fourth watches?
△ Second, the interpretation through the convergence of phenomena.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, at the time when the Dharma is preached and the Dharma is received, the mind and its objects vanish, and principle and wisdom merge. Ordinary beings and sages are as one; the beginning and the source converge.
At this moment, when all these dualistic phenomena are one, [the realization occurs].
[Commentary] Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Again it says" below explains the Dharma through two assemblies; this is the intention of Master Kuiji’s *Lengyan jing shu*.
"Speaking and receiving" refers to the relationship between teacher and disciple. Below, there are four pairs [of categories]. Regarding "the merging of mind and object":
at the time of hearing the Dharma, deluded thoughts do not arise. Since the mind does not arise, objects do not manifest. Because both mind and object are forgotten, they are said to "merge."

This means that one cannot use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to listen to the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*). This [critique] applies universally to all conceptual reckonings; therefore, all are extinguished.

Thus, the dyad of the defiled mind and conventional objects is resolved. Regarding the "fusion of principle and wisdom": at the moment of listening to the Dharma, subject and object are not differentiated.
Since the stirring of a thought immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma, both are equally real; hence, they are said to be fused.
Yet it does not speak of their merging. This refers to the pair of the pure mind and the true realm. Regarding the "sameness of ordinary beings and sages":
when the mind discriminates, one perceives sages and perceives ordinary beings; since the mind no longer arises, who is ordinary and who is a sage?

Since characteristics are fundamentally exhausted, they are said to be "as such" (*tathatā*). This refers to the pair of cause and effect. Regarding the "convergence of the original and the initial": deluded thoughts arise.
At that time, the distinction between the original and the emergent is severed; since thought no longer arises, the original and the emergent are naturally identical.
As all functions are gathered back into the essence, it is called "convergence. This constitutes the pair of essence and function. Question: How does this differ from the second [stage]? Answer:

The former wisdom is the fundamental wisdom within initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*); the former principle is the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within original awakening (*prakṛti-āśraya*). As for this [present] beginning and origin...
The fundamental [nature] penetrates both the ultimate and the conventional; since it contains both the initial and the subsequent, it is narrow at first and broad later.

The former refers to the defilement of form, speaking only of the purity of the ultimate realm and wisdom; this [latter] clarifies everything, and thus speaks of fundamental awakening and initial awakening.

Furthermore, the former is based on partial realization, hence it says "principle and wisdom are fused"; this is based on ultimate realization, hence it says "the fundamental and the initial meet. [Omission of various...]
The second point concerns the oneness of mind and object, principle and wisdom, ordinary beings and sages, and the original and the initial. Although these meanings differ, they are all termed "one.
Specifically: mind and object are one because they are dissolved; principle and wisdom are one because they are fused; ordinary beings and sages are one because they are as they are;
and the original and the initial are one because they are unified. Though their meanings vary, they are all designated as "one. Therefore...
It is said: "At one time.
△ Fourth, the accomplishment of the principal [subject] has two parts: first, the translation of the name; second, the explanation of the meaning. First, the translation of the name:
*Buddha*.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Four Lords": the full term is *Buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One.

[Sub-commentary] Under the section "The Four Lords," there are two parts. First, the translation of the name. The reason the Sūtra only designates "Buddha" is because the people of the Qin dynasty preferred brevity.
Furthermore, the Sanskrit sound is retained to avoid confusion with *bodhi* (enlightenment), for if it were translated as "Awakening," it would belong to that category.
Regarding the term *dharma*, it now refers to a person; thus it is called "Buddha" (*buddha*) to avoid the error of confusion. Therefore, it is not translated [directly].
If one were to explain its meaning, it requires the language of Tang (Chinese); hence, it is first translated as a counterpart. Now, "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to discernment and enlightenment.
Enlightenment is the illumination of the true reality that is inherently existent; discernment is the realization that delusion is inherently empty. To realize that delusion is inherently empty—
Thus, one does not pursue the delusive; by illuminating that the True is inherently present, one does not become confused about the True.

Once both the True and the delusive are clarified, one is able to shatter the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) and extinguish the continuous mind (*saṃtati-citta*), thereby manifesting the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and making wisdom purely immaculate.

At that time, the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual; there is only a single awakening (*bodhi*). Although the Bodhisattva likewise illuminates the True and understands the delusive, [he has not yet...]
Having attained the ultimate, they still retain the name "Sattva. Only the Buddha-Tathāgata has brought his task to completion; therefore, he alone is called the "Awakened One" (Buddha).

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts: first, the direct explanation by citing the treatise; second, the indirect explanation by citing the treatise. First, the direct explanation by citing the treatise...

The second section [of the commentary] has two parts: first, an explanation based on the essence (*tattva*) as being free from conceptual thought; second, an explanation by citing three meanings according to the stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the first, the explanation based on the essence as being free from conceptual thought, there are two sub-sections: first, citing the text; second, summarizing the meaning. First, citing the text:
[Commentary] The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called the meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body."
△ Second, the summary of the meaning.
[Commentary] Thus, non-thought is designated as "Buddha.
[Record] From the *Awakening of Faith* below, there are two explanations of the meaning. First, the explanation based on the essence being free from thought. Now, this treatise clarifies...

The essence of the mind as original enlightenment (prakṛtistha-gotra) is by nature free from all discursive thoughts. This present citation and explanation regarding the Buddha of the fruit [of Buddhahood] is because the essence of the Buddha of the fruit is itself original enlightenment, which is primordially free from thought.
Although cause and fruit are distinguished, their freedom from thought is no different.
Therefore, the freedom from thought of original enlightenment is itself the essence of the Buddha. Thus, a sutra says: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena."

And so forth. Therefore, while within the bonds of affliction it is called "original enlightenment" (mūla-avabodha), when free from these bonds it is called "ultimate enlightenment" (atyanta-avabodha).

From beginning to end, its essence is one; there is no other dharma. Thus the Treatise says: "This is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body. Based upon this Dharma-body, it is designated as 'original enlightenment.
The commentary below concludes that original enlightenment, being free from conceptual thought, is the very body of the Buddha.
△ Second, the explanation of the three meanings according to the stages has two parts: first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation.
First, the general indication. [Commentary]: Now, awakening (bodhi) has three meanings.
[Commentary] "However, regarding 'awakening' below," there are two [sections]: first, an explanation based on the three meanings according to the stages;
second, a detailed explanation of the three [aspects]. First, self-awakening; second, awakening others; third, the fulfillment of awakening. First, self-awakening.
[Commentary]: First, self-awakening. This refers to awakening to the knowledge that one’s own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
[Record]: "Without arising or ceasing" means that wisdom illuminates *tathatā* (suchness) by seeing it according to its true principle.

However, there are two meanings. The first is that within the mind there are no phenomena of arising or ceasing. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "As for true emptiness, from the very beginning..."
Come. Because all defiled dharmas are non-associated [with this mind], when thought arises, there is defilement;
now that thought is absent, they are non-associated. It is not that these two are nonexistent; it simply clarifies that this mind is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.
This is identical to what the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* says: "Because one is far removed from subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind; the mind is then eternally abiding. Constant.
To abide is precisely to be without arising or ceasing.
△ Second, awakening others:
[Commentary] Second, awakening others means awakening to the fact that all dharmas are none other than Suchness.

[Commentary] "Awakening others" refers here to *shijiao* (initial awakening). Realizing that phenomena are themselves the truth (*zhen*), one regards them from the perspective of one's own mind; thus, it is called "awakening others.
This is identical to what the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) states:

"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the marks of names and words, free from the marks of mental conditions, ultimately equal, without change, indestructible, and are solely the One Mind."
Therefore, it is named *tathatā* (Suchness).
△ Third, the fulfillment of awakening.
[Commentary]: Third, the fulfillment of awakening. The principle of the three types of awakening is perfect; thus it is called "fulfillment."
[Commentary]: Regarding "awakening is fulfilled": with respect to the two preceding types of awakening, there was both understanding and realization;

because there were distinctions of priority and inferiority, and because the characteristics of self and other still persisted, they could not yet be called "fulfilled. Now, this [awakening] is perfectly complete, and since it does not establish the distinction between self and other, it is called "fulfilled."
[Commentary] According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "awakening oneself" means awakening to the fact that one possesses Buddha-nature;

"awakening others" means awakening to the fact that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; and "fulfilling the awakening" means that there is no duality between the Buddha-nature of oneself and that of others.
[Commentary] Generally speaking, it is said that "self-awakening" distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); "awakening others" distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles;

and "fulfillment of awakening" distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas. However, what is stated here is that "self-awakening" already distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles and from Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings—not to mention ordinary beings alone.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The nature of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing. How marvelous is the Great Guide!"
The Master: "One who is self-awakened is able to awaken others.

△ Second, citing treatises to provide a counter-explanation, which has three parts: first, the counter-demonstration; second, the citation of evidence; third, the concluding summary. First, the counter-demonstration.
[Commentary] Therefore, one knows that where there is thought (*smṛti*), it is not called awakening (*bodhi*).

[Recorded Notes] Regarding the section beginning with "Therefore, one knows": this consists of two parts: first, citing a treatise to provide an inverse explanation; second, the initial inverse clarification. The intended meaning is:
because it is free from thought, it is called awakening; one should know, therefore, that where there is thought, it is not called awakening.
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence.

[Commentary]: The *Awakening of Faith* states: "All sentient beings are not called awakened because, from time immemorial, their thoughts have continued in succession without ever being free from discursive thought."
[Commentary] "The *Awakening of Faith*," etc. Second, citing evidence. Previously it was stated that "the substance of the mind is free from thought," which applies to both cause and fruit;
now it clarifies that sentient beings are not called "enlightened" (*jue*), thereby specifically revealing that only those at the stage of fruition are termed "enlightened."
△ Third, the Conforming Conclusion.

[Commentary] It further states: "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought (amanyana), they are thereby heading toward Buddha-wisdom. [Record] Regarding the section beginning with "It further states":
this is the third, the conforming conclusion. It correctly concludes that non-thought is the meaning of Buddhahood, because non-thought is...
The Buddha. Thus, one who is able to contemplate non-thought is one who is heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
△ Section Five: The Accomplishment of the Five Sites, Part Two. First, an explanation of Śrāvastī; second, an explanation of Jetavana. First, an explanation of Śrāvastī.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

[Commentary: There are five meanings for this location. Śrāvastī means "Hearing of Things" (聞物), because it is renowned throughout distant lands for its abundance of sensory objects (*kāmaguṇa*), wealth and treasures, extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), and liberation (*vimukti*).
Yi Jing translated it as "The Great City of Renown."
[Commentary] Below the fifth section of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), part two: first, an explanation of Śrāvastī. Śrāvastī is also called Śāvatthī; in the new [translation], it is called Śrāvastī.
These are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit (the "archaic" and the "modern"). This city is located in the kingdom of Kośala within Central India.
Because there is also a kingdom of Kośala in Southern India, [the author] uses [the term] to avoid confusion with that country. Therefore...
"City" is the name of the country. Regarding "famed objects": this refers to a reputation for superior virtue and rare, precious treasures, which are produced in great abundance in this country.
The phrase "that is to say, possessing... provides the explanation: "sensual objects" refers to beautiful women; "wealth and treasures" refers to rare and precious items;

"much learning" refers to being extensively versed in both internal and external scriptures; and "liberation" refers to those such as the rishis who possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
It means being far removed from desire. This is precisely the abundance of the four virtues of the kingdom; it is also translated as "abundant virtue. Regarding "widely heard" and so forth:
the four matters mentioned above are all that which is heard of and known by foreign lands. As for the passage concerning Yijing:
it merely serves to verify the meaning of "widely heard," for because one possesses a reputation, one's name is heard afar.
△ Second, the explanation of Jetavana, in two parts: first, a general indication; second, a detailed explanation. First, the general indication:
"The Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. [Commentary]:
Regarding "Jeta Grove" and so forth, this refers to the trees donated by Prince Jeta. As for "Anāthapiṇḍada," it refers to the Elder...
"Buying it in the garden.
[Commentary] "Under the Jeta tree. Regarding the two explanations of "Jeta’s Garden": first, a general indication.
King Prasenajit, the ruler of Śrāvastī, had a high minister named Sudatta. He went in person to Rājagṛha city to arrange a marriage for his son.
He was staying at the residence of the householder Sudatta. At midnight, the householder rose, adorned his home, and prepared a variety of delicacies.
Having heard this, Sudatta asked, "Great Being, do you wish to invite the king for a wedding feast?
He replied, "I invite the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King. Upon hearing this, the hairs on Sudatta’s body all stood on end.
"Vatsa," he asked again, "what is meant by the term 'Buddha'? The elder explained at length the virtues of the Buddha for him.
Sudatta said, "Excellent, Great Being! As for what is called a Buddha, his virtues are unsurpassed. Where is he now?
The elder replied, "He is at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, Sudatta focused his mind with single-minded devotion.
Suddenly, it became as bright as day; its radiance was so intense that it was like the midday sun. Seeking the source of the light, he arrived at the city gate.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the gate opened of its own accord. He proceeded along the road, and at that time, the Tathāgata had gone outside to walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*).
Upon seeing him, Sudatta was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; not knowing the proper etiquette, he spoke directly to the World-Honored One.
At that time, Śuddhāvāsadeva manifested as four men for the sake of the elder and went to where the World-Honored One was.

They prostrated at his feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground to pay their respects, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew to stand to one side. Having seen this, Sudatta followed their example and did likewise.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma to them according to their needs. Upon hearing it, the elder attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Later, he again invited the Buddha, saying, "I pray that you will deign to visit me and accept my humble offering upon arriving at the city of Śrāvastī.
The Buddha then asked, "In your kingdom of Śrāvastī, is there a vihāra capable of accommodating me?

Sudatta replied, "If you would indeed condescend to visit, I shall immediately prepare one. At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent. Then Sudatta turned back...
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Buddha instructed Śāriputra to go with him and direct the procedures for building the monastery.
Thereupon, Sudatta spread gold to purchase Prince Jeta’s grove; Prince Jeta then donated the trees and forests within the grove. The two men together constructed the vihāra.
Once it was completed, he took up an incense burner and, facing toward Rājagṛha, spoke these words from afar regarding what had been provided:

"It is prepared. We only pray that the Tathāgata will accept this dwelling place. At that time, the Buddha, knowing the householder's mind through his supernormal knowledge, set out from Rājagṛha with the great assembly;
in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the elder offered what he had prepared to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it and remained there;

the details are as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, and the *Records of the Western Regions*. Those who wish to consult these sources should go and examine them.
Now, as the Buddha preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at this location, it is said: "In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove."
It is also called the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden. However, Sudatta was the patron, while Jeta assisted in its completion.

The reason the tree is mentioned first and the garden second is that the Prince is the heir apparent, whereas Sudatta is a minister; this is done to distinguish between the noble and the humble according to protocol.
According to Paramārtha’s commentary, there are two types of dwellings: first, the "territorial dwelling," which is Śrāvastī itself, established for the purpose of transforming worldly beings.

Therefore, there are two bases of reliance, namely the Jeta Grove. This is because it serves as a unifying center for those who have left the household life. Furthermore, the *Samantapāsādikā* (Sifen lü shanfan buque xingshi chao) states:
"The city of Śrāvastī is mentioned so that those from afar may know [the location], and the Jeta Grove is mentioned so that those nearby may know [it]; thus, both are cited together."
△ Second, the detailed explanation is threefold: first, the explanation of Jeta; second, the explanation of Anāthapiṇḍada; third, the explanation of the character for "garden.
First, the explanation of Jeta. [Commentary]:
Jeta means "Victorious in Battle" (Saṃjaya). He was the crown prince of King Prasenajit. At the time of his birth, the King and his...
He won a victory in battle; it was for this reason that he took his name.
[Commentary] Regarding "Jeta" (秖陀) below: there are two parts to the specific explanation. First, the explanation of Jeta. As for "Victory in Battle" (戰勝), it is also called "Victory Grove" (勝林);
the rest is as explained in the sub-commentary.
△ Second, the explanation of "Anāthapiṇḍada.
[Commentary]: The Sanskrit name is Sudatta, which here means "Good Giver" (Śubhadāna). "Anāthapiṇḍada" is precisely "Good Giver," as he also constantly practiced giving.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage beginning with "In the Sanskrit language," there are two explanations for *Anāthapiṇḍada*. First, one who is young and without a father is called *gu* (orphan), and one who is old and without a son is called *du* (solitary).
To provide for those who are orphaned and solitary is termed "excellent giving" (*śubhadāna*).
Second, as for the phrase "likewise," although the orphaned and solitary are particularly objects of compassion, it is because, in reality, he does not fail to give to others as well.
△ Third, the explanation of the character for "garden" (yuan).
[Sūtra Commentary]: In the Western Regions, a monastery is called *saṃghārāma*; here it is translated as "Garden of the Assembly. [Sub-commentary]:
Regarding the section "In the Western Regions," etc., this is the third explanation of the character for "garden. The full Sanskrit term is *saṃghārāma*, which here is translated as...

Regarding "Jung-yuan" (Monastery Garden): the *saṃgha* refers to the community of those who dwell there, while *Lan-mo* refers to the garden where they dwell; this is merely a designation based on the relationship between the inhabitants and their residence.
As for "Si" (Temple): it means an office or a government residence. When the Buddha-dharma first arrived, it was housed in the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Si*).
Later, a monastic residence was established there, and thus the name "Si" was adopted for it.
△ Section Six: The Achievement of the Six Groups. Part One: Explaining the Designation of the Category. Part Two: Explaining the Enumeration. First, explaining the designation of the category:
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. [Commentary] "Six groups" (ṣaḍvargika).
"Together with" (sārdham) means "along with" or "and. "Great" (mahat) refers to those whose names and virtues are renowned. "Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term.

This term contains three meanings; therefore, the Sanskrit original is retained without translation: first, "Frightener of Māras" (bhikṣu); second, "Alms-seeker" (bhikṣu); and third, "One of Pure Precepts" (bhikṣu).
As for the "assembly" (saṃgha), it refers to both harmony in principle and harmony in practice.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "The six groups of monks" and below, the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the categories indicated by the titles. *Gao-ming* (high reputation) means that one’s fame is praised from afar and near.
*De-zhu* (manifest virtue) means that one’s conduct and practice are grand and flourishing. *Bumo* (frightening Māra) refers to the day of their initial renunciation;

when the flying yakṣas announced it, the news reached the palace of Māra, and thus he was frightened. This is because the renunciation of a single person leads to a successive transformation and deliverance of others.
Because it diminishes one's retinue. However, for those who have left the household life, there are three occasions from cause to fruit when they fear Māra:

namely, at the time of leaving home, at the time of generating the bodhicitta, and at the time of attaining perfect enlightenment. During the first two, they merely feel fear; only at the latter does he raise his weapons.
He is subdued by the Buddha; there is none who is not brought to submission. ○ As for the "mendicant" (bhikṣu):
this means that, above, he begs the Dharma from virtuous friends to refine his mind, and below, he begs food from donors to sustain his body. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"What is called a bhikṣu? A bhikṣu is called a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Because he maintains a pure livelihood, he is called a mendicant. As it is said in the sūtras:
Śāriputra was begging for alms; he turned toward a wall and ate. At that time, there was a daughter of a brahmin named Viśākhā who came and saw Śāriputra and asked, "Śramaṇa, is your food pure?
He replied, "The food is pure. Viśākhā asked, "Śramaṇa, do you eat with your head down? He replied, "No.
She continued to ask about eating with one's face up, facing the four directions, and so forth, and each time he replied, "No."
The daughter Viśuddhanetrī said: "There are four kinds of food. I questioned you about them, and you replied 'no' to all of them.

I do not understand what you have said. Śāriputra replied: "There are renunciants who earn their livelihood through impure means, such as compounding medicines, sowing grain, planting trees, and so forth;
this is called 'food obtained by downward-facing' (adhomukha-bhojana). There are those who observe the stars, the moon, the sun, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and so forth..."

To live by impure means is called "looking upward for food" (*ūrdhvamukha*). To live by impure means through crookedness, flattery, using one's influence with the powerful, and skillful speech to solicit much from the four quarters is called "looking toward the four directions for food" (*caturmukha*).

To live by impure means through various incantations and divining good or bad fortune is called "looking to the sides for food" (*tiryagmukha*). Sister, I do not fall into these four kinds of impure livelihoods.

In the middle [of this], I sustain my life by means of pure alms-seeking. Having heard this teaching on the food of the pure Dharma, Viśuddhanetra rejoiced with faith and understanding, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Because he sustains his life in this way through pure alms-seeking, he is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu).
Regarding "pure precepts," this refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus and the five hundred for bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*): there is the observance of the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the maintenance of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Maintaining the precepts in a state of purity is called "pure precepts" (*viśuddha-śīla*).

Some explain this through five meanings: namely, pure livelihood (*ājīva-viśuddhi*), and the destruction of evil (*pāpa-prahāṇa*). Now, the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is equivalent to pure livelihood, and the pure precepts are equivalent to the destruction of evil.
Therefore, there are only three. ○ Regarding "harmony in principle" (li-he): the Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "congregation in harmony.
This means that there is no contradiction in principle and no dispute in practice.
△ Second, the explanation of the enumeration:
"Accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
[Commentary] Regarding the one thousand two hundred and fifty: when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he converted the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, and subsequently...
He converted the three Kāśyapa brothers, totaling one thousand followers; next, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with one hundred followers;
and subsequently, he converted fifty people, including Yaśas, the son of a householder. These figures are cited as approximate totals.
Therefore, five persons were subtracted.
[Commentary] "One thousand two hundred," etc., provides two explanations for the number. "The Buddha’s first attainment of the Way" refers to the site beneath the Bodhi tree.

This indicates the manifestation of perfect enlightenment. Regarding Kauṇḍinya and the others—namely the remaining Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Pūrṇa, and Vatsa—it is stated in the *Sūtra on the Original Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) that when the Buddha first attained the Way, Brahmā, the King of Gods, and others requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Having accepted their request, the World-Honored One reflected: "Among all beings in the world, who should be the first..."
They have attained liberation. In the past, those five sages were of great benefit to me; they are capable of receiving my first turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
He further thought, "Where are those five sages now? With his purified divine eye, he beheld those five sages in the Deer Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded toward that grove and extensively [taught] for them.
As he preached the Dharma, the bodies and minds of the non-Buddhists were entirely subdued and extinguished. The robes they wore instantly became the three monastic garments (*tricīvara*);

the alms bowls appeared in their hands, and their hair and beards fell away of their own accord. After seven days had passed, their dignified deportment was fully perfected, like that of bhikṣus with a hundred years of seniority.
Eventually, for them he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths, and they attained the fruit of Arhatship. ○ As for the three elder brothers of Kāśyapa:

Regarding the phrase "the younger brothers," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: At that time, the eldest, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, was at the head of five hundred disciples in the Fire Dragon Cave, teaching them.
The second, Nadī-Kāśyapa, led three hundred disciples and practiced at Elephant Head Mountain (*Gajaśīrṣa*).
The third, Gayā-Kāśyapa, led two hundred disciples and was at [Mount] Hī... (text fragmentary).
Including those from the Hecuo (Hear-Curve) River, there were a total of one thousand people who were all subdued by the World-Honored One and sought to leave the household life.
Both teacher and disciples attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Regarding Śāriputra and the others, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in a village in Magadha there was a Brahmin named Dhanjaya who had eight sons; among them was one—
The son was named Upatisya, who is Śāriputra. There was also another Brahmin whose son was named Kolita, who is Maudgalyāyana.
These two youths became close friends and went forth as renunciants under the non-Buddhist teacher Sañjaya.
With one mind, the two made a vow: "If either of us should find someone superior to this [teacher]," [the other would follow him].
"The Teacher has taught us the supreme path of ambrosia; we shall surely attain realization through it.
At that time, the World-Honored One had a disciple named Aśvajit, whose deportment was dignified and orderly as he entered the city to beg for food, proceeding with measured and proper conduct.
Having seen him, Śāriputra went to where he was staying and addressed him, saying, "Venerable sir, are you the True Teacher, or are you a disciple?
Aśvajit replied, "There is another Great Teacher; I am his disciple. He asked again, "What Dharma does your Great Teacher teach?
He answered, "All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease from conditions. Thus it is.

"This is cessation and this is arising; thus has my teacher taught. When Śāriputra heard these words, he immediately, at that very spot, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. He returned to his lodging and spoke likewise to Maudgalyāyana.
The two of them together led their respective disciples and went to the place where the Buddha was, seeking to leave the household life.

The Buddha called out, "Welcome! and their hair and beards fell away of their own accord; the saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies and they held alms bowls, assuming the appearance of bhikṣus.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas, each attained the foremost rank in wisdom and supernormal powers. These were the two hundred members of his retinue.
They all attained the going-forth and immediately received full ordination, eventually achieving the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding Yaśas and the others, I have not yet verified [the source].
Da Bin respectfully examines the *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect), which states: There was the son of an elder named Yaśas, who possessed great eloquence.
Cai was intelligent and wise. During the middle watch of the night, he saw a radiance in the sky.

Following the light, he went to the Deer Park and beheld the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. He prostrated before the Buddha and said, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will rescue and deliver me.
The Buddha said, "Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
“I am [the Buddha]. Do you know me? He replied, “Indeed, I do. Upon hearing these words, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and became an Arhat.
He then expressed his wish to seek ordination. The Buddha said, “Welcome, Bhikṣu,” and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, fifty sons of elders who were friends of Yaśas heard that Yaśas had gone forth and together went to where the Buddha was.
He wished to seek ordination. The Buddha said, "Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
Do you understand this? Upon hearing this, his outflows were exhausted and his mind was liberated. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, there were fifty-six arhats in total. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You are capable of serving as the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. You should each travel to various regions to teach and transform others, delivering all sentient beings with a heart of compassion.
Furthermore, according to the *Record of the Tathāgata’s Manifestations*, he first delivered five people, and next [Yaśas].

He left fifty men behind, all of whom remained at Rṣipatana (the Deer Park). Next, he subdued the fire-dragon in a stone cave and converted the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their thousand followers.
Thereafter, he proceeded to Rājagṛha and accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra.
Residing at the Bamboo Grove, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to the Bamboo Grove, saw the Buddha, and attained liberation;
each had one hundred disciples, totaling one thousand two hundred and fifty people. This number is cited for the sake of a complete total; it does not mention five people.
[Commentary]: These are the "constant followers"; therefore, their number is specifically listed, though it does not mean there are no other assemblies;

the text merely emphasizes some over others. [Record]: Regarding these "constant followers" and so forth: these individuals previously all followed external paths, undergoing hardships for many kalpas without attaining anything.
Upon first encountering the Buddha, they immediately attained the supreme fruit (*agra-phala*). Because they were moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, they constantly follow him.

However, although there were the fourfold assembly as well as the nāgas, devas, and others, here only one is made manifest while the rest are concealed; this will be seen for oneself in the *parīndanā* (concluding) section.
[Commentary]: "Together" means at the same time and in the same place.
[Commentary] "Together" (俱) refers to what follows. The preceding section was a designation pointing toward the subject in relation to the assembly; thus it said "with" (與).
This [section], however, is a comprehensive conclusion concerning both the subject and the assembly taken together. When viewed from beginning to end, the matter remains no different.
△ Second, the Prologue of the Arousing [of the Resolve], in two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the detailed explanation. First, the statement of the intent. [Commentary]:
Second, regarding the Prologue of the Arousing, it refers to the deportment of begging for food and remaining free from wrong livelihood; this constitutes the upholding of the precepts.

Precepts can support meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, by means of precepts and concentration, one brings forth the primary teaching of *prajñā*.

[Commentary] Regarding the section "Second, Bringing Forth," there are two parts. First, the statement of the intent. Regarding "Precepts can... and so forth: the meaning of precepts is the prevention of what is improper and the cessation of evil;
the meaning of concentration is tranquility and immovability; the meaning of wisdom is luminous illumination and discernment. However, it is only through [precepts] that one can prevent...
No. When the mind is unmoving, wisdom becomes clear and distinct; there is no phenomenon, whether mundane or supramundane, that it does not reflect.
It is like the ocean wishing to manifest the myriad phenomena: it requires the water to be clear. To seek clear water, nothing surpasses stillness.
To achieve stillness, do not allow waves to arise. Cessation of the waves is like the precepts (*śīla*); the stillness of the water is like meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Water is clear like wisdom; the myriad images manifested therein are like all phenomena (*dharmas*).
In this analogy, if the water does not give rise to waves, the water is still; when the water is still, it is clear; when the water is clear, it manifests the myriad images.
In the Dharma, if the mind does not arise, the mind is quiescent; when the mind is quiescent, it illuminates and knows all phenomena. Within all phenomena, there is but the single mind.
In the analogy above, there is only water; when the phenomenon (dharma) and the analogy are contrasted, the meaning becomes clear.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "If śīla is not pure, samādhi will not manifest. This means that precepts serve as the support for concentration. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states:
"The unimpeded and pure wisdom of all Bodhisattvas is born entirely from dhyāna-samādhi. This means that concentration gives rise to wisdom.

△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, the precepts; second, meditative concentration. First, the precepts have two parts: first, the topical outline; second, the enumeration and explanation.
First, the topical outline: [Commentary] The text has two parts. First, the precepts, which are explained in seven sections.
[Commentary] The commentary on the precepts consists of seven sections, as detailed in the sub-commentary (shū).

II. Listing and explaining the seven [sections]: 1. Explaining the principal teacher of the transformation; 2. Explaining the time of the transformation; 3. Explaining the ritual of the transformation;

4. Explaining the place of the transformation; 5. Explaining the deeds of the transformation; 6. Explaining the equality of the transformation; 7. Explaining the conclusion of the transformation. First, explaining the principal teacher of the transformation.
At that time, the World-Honored One.
[Commentary] First, the Master of Transformation. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that he possesses the aforementioned nine titles;
because he is revered by sentient beings, he is called "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*), for he is honored alike by those in the heavens and those among humans.
[Commentary] First, the Principal of Transformation. Regarding "possessing the nine titles mentioned above":

since the Buddha has ten titles and the title "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) constitutes the tenth, it is said that he possesses the nine titles mentioned above. The ten titles are: 1. Tathāgata; 2. Arhat; 3.
Samyaksaṃbuddha; 4. Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna; 5. Sugata; 6. Lokavid; 7. Anuttara; 8. Puruṣadamyasārathi; 9. Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; 10. Bhagavān.
1. Lord (Bhartṛ), 2. Teacher of Gods and Men (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām), 3. Buddha (Buddha), 4. World-Honored One (Lokanātha).
△ Second, explaining the time of his manifestation:
at the time of eating.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the time for alms-gathering: it is during the *śukla-pakṣa* (the first watch of the day), when food is easily obtained and one does not cause distress to oneself or others.
Having finished begging, one returns to the monastery garden precisely at the *mādhyāhnika* (midday) hour, following the regular rules for the midday meal.
[Commentary] Second, the time of transformation. Regarding "at the first watch of the day": this means that the twelve periods of a single day and night are collectively divided into four parts.
