First is the first watch (*pūrvāhṇa*), comprising the hours of *yǐn*, *mǎo*, and *chén*; this is the mealtime for the devas. Second is the middle watch (*madhyāhṇa*), comprising the hours of *sì*, *wǔ*, and *wèi*; this is the mealtime for humans according to the human law.
Third is the afternoon watch (*sāyāhṇa*), comprising the hours of *shēn*, *yǒu*, and *xù*; this is the mealtime for spirits and ghosts. Fourth is the night watch (*rātri*).
That is to say, the hours of Hai, Zi, and Chou are the times when animals feed; what is now called the hour of Chen is the final limit of the first period of the day.
In the two translations by Tang and Zhou, both state it is the "initial period" of the day; this refers to the superior timing.
At this time, begging for food is not difficult, because it is hard to obtain [alms] if one is either too early or too late. If one were to beg for food at an improper time...

If one gives, there is nothing left; if one does not give, one feels ashamed and thus causes distress to others. If they beg and do not receive, they will lose their provisions and suffer from hunger.
This is to afflict oneself.
△ Third, explaining the ritual of transformation:
donning robes and holding an alms bowl.
[Commentary: Third, the ritual of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*). He wears the *saṃghāṭī* robe and holds the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding the "ritual of transformation" below: it means that the Buddha has three robes (*tricīvara*). First is the *antarvāsaka*, which consists of five strips;
it is called an inferior-grade robe (*kaniṣṭha-cīvara*), and is also known as the robe for walking, performing tasks, or as an undergarment. Second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, which consists of seven...
The seven-strip robe is called the middle-grade robe, and it is also called the robe for entering the assembly to preach the Dharma.

Three *saṃghāṭī* robes—ranging from nine strips to twenty-five—are called the superior-grade robe, and they are also called the field-of-merit robe (*puṇyakṣetra-vastra*), fashioned in the likeness of a rice paddy.
Because seeing [the robes] generates merit, he enters royal cities and villages wearing these very garments; he wears them now because he has entered the city to beg for alms.
○ Regarding the "Tianwang bowl" (King of Devas bowl): the Sanskrit term is *pātra*, which here means "measured vessel. This is the bowl of the past Buddha Vipaśyin.
After he entered *nirvāṇa*, a dragon king took it to his palace to offer worship. Śākyamuni... [text continues].
When the Kāśyapa attained enlightenment, the Dragon King escorted him to the surface of the sea. The Four Heavenly Kings wished to take [alms bowls] for him;

they manifested as four bowls, each receiving one bowl which they offered to the Tathāgata. Having accepted them, the Tathāgata stacked the four bowls together in his left hand and pressed them with his left hand so that they merged into a single bowl.
This is the bowl made of dark-blue lapis lazuli stone; he held it and used it for begging.
This is for the purpose of eating. ○ When the Buddha goes out to transform beings, he must wear robes and carry an alms bowl because he remains free from the two extremes of suffering and pleasure.
As for householders, they take pleasure in brocades, silks, and fine ornaments; their clothing and precious vessels increase their heedlessness.

Excessive attachment to the extreme of pleasure is seen in those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist outsiders and in the ascetic Nirgranthas, who go naked and receive food in their hands, thereby inviting reproach and ugliness.
Excessive attachment to the extreme of suffering is likewise seen; therefore, the Buddha dwells in the Middle Way, which is why he wears robes and carries an alms bowl.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the place of transformation.
He entered the great city of Śrāvastī.
[Commentary]: Fourth, the place of transformation. The park was five or six *li* to the southeast of the city. "Entering" refers to going from the outside toward the inside; this is the location.
The common saying that "a vast multitude is called 'great'" is as follows.
[Commentary] Regarding the "four sites of transformation": the garden (*ārāma*) is the place where he dwells, while the kingdom is the place where he transforms beings. "Zhi" (之) means "to go.

Because he is currently traveling to transform beings, he departs from Jetavana and enters Śrāvastī. As for the phrase "the site is vast and so forth," it accords with the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions).
The circumference of the kingdom is over sixty *li*. The inner city wall is twenty *li* in circumference; thus it is said that its territory is vast.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are nine hundred million households; thus it is said that the population is great.
△ Five: Explaining the Acts of Transformation (Vikurvaṇa-karman). Part Two. First, the direct explanation; second, resolving difficulties. First, the direct explanation.
Begging for food. [Commentary]:
Fifth, the acts of transformation. The Buddha, wishing to manifest the merits of *dhūta* (ascetic practices) and to cause those who are negligent to feel shame, [performs these acts].
[He practices] the integration through commonality; therefore, he personally begs for food.
[Commentary: Regarding the "five transformative acts," this explains the two characters "begging for food" in the sutra. Below the section on *dhūta* (ascetic practices), some say:
The Buddha is the Teacher; why then must he beg for food? This is what the commentary explains.
○ *Dhūta* means "shaking off" (*dousou*), for one shakes off afflictions (*kleśa*). There are twelve types of *dhūta* practices, namely:

always begging for food, dwelling in an *āraṇya*, and so forth, up to sitting at the foot of a tree, sitting in the open air, or sitting among graves. The present case refers to the first of these. If one practices this...

By performing these deeds, one attains great merit. The Buddha manifested this practice so that people might emulate it. Since the dhūta practitioner attains such merit, it is evident that negligence carries even greater fault.
If even the World-Honored One personally begs for food, how could others be justified in being indolent?
Out of shame, remorse, and trepidation, one will naturally practice it. This "gathering through common purpose" is one of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu). [End of section]
Furthermore, regarding the Buddha’s practice of begging for alms, the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* explains that there are ten purposes.
First, to cease suffering; that is, it enables the blind to see. Second, to obtain happiness; that is, a single glance or a single prostration generates immeasurable merit.

Third, to eliminate pride; that is, when sentient beings see him, they do not give rise to arrogance. Fourth, to fulfill the vow of the bowl; that is, even if one desires to give much, the bowl [is sufficient].
1. It was empty; though the poor offered little, the bowl became full because of the offerings of the five *yakṣas*.
2. Those with the six hindrances were able to see the Buddha; thus, the old, the sick, the poor, and the lowly all gained the sight of the Buddha.
3. To demonstrate the bowl offered by the heavenly kings. 4. To establish a model for imitation. 5. To eliminate slander. 6. To ensure that his disciples would not... [The text continues].
Because he stores the eight kinds of impure items, there are these ten reasons for which he begs for food himself.
△ Second, resolving objections.
[Commentary]: The *Yingluo jing* (Necklace Sutra) states that the body of a transformation Buddha is like a solid piece of diamond; it lacks both the raw and cooked internal organs.
That which is now being requested is for the sake of benefiting others. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "For the sake of non-eating, one should accept that food.

[Commentary] The section beginning with "The Girl Maṇimekhalā" below addresses the objection. The preceding section citing the sūtra presents the objection. The section beginning with "That which is now... provides the resolution.
Regarding the phrase "under the name of Purity": this merely serves to verify the meaning of begging for food and not eating [forbidden items] mentioned above.
△ Sixth, the explanation of the transformation [of the city], etc.:
Having finished begging in sequence throughout that city...

[Commentary] Sixth, regarding "transformations, etc. (the six types of transformation): First, by internally realizing the principle of equality, one does not perceive external signs of poverty or wealth.

Second, the mind is free from greed and pride, and compassion is impartial and without partiality. Third, one manifests majestic power and is not intimidated by such places as those of rogue elephants, wine-sellers, or prostitutes.
Fourth, it quells the suspicions and resentments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Fifth, it destroys the conceptual discrimination of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
[Commentary] Regarding "the six transformations," etc.: this explains the passage in the Sūtra concerning "having gone for alms in sequence within that city.
Regarding "realizing equality within": because one perceives according to the principle (yathābhūtam). Regarding "the mind being free from greed, pride, and so forth":

not coveting wealth and excellence, nor being disdainful toward poverty and clumsiness; one practices begging with equanimity. Thus it is said that compassion is without partiality. Regarding "manifesting majestic dignity":...

"Virtue and so forth" means that the Buddha established the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna, forbidding entry into the houses of rogue elephants for fear of being harmed, and forbidding entry into the houses of prostitutes or wine-sellers for fear of giving rise to defiled thoughts. That the Buddha enters such places signifies that his majestic virtue is supreme.
"Cessation of ordinary beings and so forth" means that he fears [ordinary beings] might hate this and love that. "Destroying the divisions of the Two Vehicles" [is explained as follows].
As for their differences: Kāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to beg from the poor, intending to generate merit for them;
Subhūti abandoned the poor to beg from the wealthy, not wishing to trouble others, and so forth. Regarding what these two men perceived, each had points of right and wrong.

The Tathāgata differs from these; in his case, right and wrong are unified as one. However, among the five [qualities] mentioned above, the first is Great Wisdom, the second is Great Compassion, and the third...
I. Revealing the Virtue; II. Quelling the Ordinary; III. Refuting the Lesser Vehicle. △ VII.
Explaining the Conclusion of the Transformation, in three parts: First, harmonizing the phrases and meanings; Second, resolving potential objections; Third, clarifying the ritual for the fast.
The first assembly concludes its meaning and returns to its original place. [Commentary]:

The seventh transformation ends. However, the character "已" (yǐ) belongs in meaning to the following phrase, though it is connected in text to the preceding one. As for the characters "飯食" (fànshí), their meaning...
This belongs to the preceding sentence, while its phrasing connects with the following one. If one were to expand the text so that it is complete within the sentence itself, it should read:
"Having completed his alms round in sequence, he returned to his original place to eat; having finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl."

[Commentary] The seven transformations are concluded. Regarding the phrase "yet already," etc., it is a case of harmonizing the characters with their semantic meanings. In reading, one follows the text;

in interpretation, one follows the meaning. Regarding the section beginning "If expanded," several characters have been added provisionally to ensure that both the text and the meaning are fully elucidated.
"Fàn" (飯) means to eat. As the *Lunyu* says: "He ate coarse grain."
△ Second, resolving potential objections.
[Commentary] If the Buddha does not eat, the merit of others will not be fulfilled. [Sub-commentary] Regarding "If the Buddha...
and so forth: this resolves potential objections. One should first raise the objection as follows: The previously cited *Sūryāvatī-sūtra* states that [the Buddha] does not...
Regarding the term "food" (āhāra): why does this sutra speak of food? This is the explanation.
Some say that when the desire to eat reaches the mouth, a majestic deva standing by his side, remaining invisible, intercepts him and carries him to another realm to perform Buddha-work.
This is eating while manifesting in the lower realms; it is not actual eating. For this reason, there is no contradiction between these two perspectives.
△ Third, the manifestation of the ritual for the fast.
[Commentary] The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* states: "Whatever one obtains through begging, divide it into four parts. One part is intended for those who practice the same holy life (*sabrahmacārin*)."
Second, for the purpose of giving to poor and sick beggars; third, for water and land sentient beings; fourth, for one's own consumption.
The *Dvādaśadhotasūtra* speaks of only three portions, excluding that for the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
[Commentary] The passage beginning with "Bao-yun" (Jewel Cloud) below clarifies the ritual for the *śrāddha* feast.

Regarding these four matters, the first two are described as "simulated" (*ni*), while the latter two are not so described because, in the case of those practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) who are poor or ill, one gives to them when they come; if they do not come, one eats it oneself.
This is not the case for the latter two [categories], and thus they are not so described. The *Dvādaśadūta-sūtra* excludes those practicing the holy life because they beg for themselves.

Therefore, they are not divided. △ Second, determining the two [categories]. First, the direct explanation of this passage. Second, reconciling it with the previous symbolic teaching of the Dharma. First, the direct explanation of this passage has two parts:
first, the presentation of the outline; second, the enumeration and explanation. First, the presentation of the outline.
[Commentary] Second, the two meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). This is explained in three sections.
[Record] Regarding "the two concentrations" in the Commentary, there are three sections therein, as stated in the Commentary (etc.).
△ Second, the enumeration and explanation of the three [sections]. First, gathering the necessary requisites; second, purifying the physical actions; third, entering meditative concentration.
First, gathering the necessary requisites:
Having finished eating, he puts away his robes and bowl.

[Commentary]: First, regarding the requisites for practice: when one is about to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must cease all mental clinging to external objects. If the robes and alms bowl are not put away, the mind will be burdened with anxiety;
therefore, the Buddha manifested this practice as a model for future generations. That is to say, one should gather the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and don the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "together with the requisites" (*sārdham upakaraṇaiḥ*): this explains the gathering of robes and bowl mentioned in the sutra. The two characters for "food" (*bhojana*) and "drink" (*pāna*) are as explained previously.
"Finished" (*kṛta*) means completed. One must have the requisites together because, at the time of practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),...
One must possess five conditions. These are: dwelling in a secluded and quiet place; ceasing from worldly affairs and the like.
Although the Buddha is supremely holy and entirely free from all habitual tendencies, he did not harbor even the slightest concern regarding his robes and alms bowl.

If these were not eliminated together [with other distractions], later generations would follow his example, and there would be no way for them to attain meditative concentration. Since the Buddha is the Teacher, all that he does is emulated and studied by others; therefore—
This is shown as a model for future practice.
△ Second, purifying the bodily action:
having washed the feet.

[Commentary: Regarding the second point, the purification of bodily action, the *Āgama* Sūtras state that when the Buddha walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground and lotus flowers receive his feet.
His current manifestation of washing his feet conforms to worldly custom, symbolizes the Dharma, and serves as a model for future generations.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "purifying the bodily karma" and so forth: this explains the three characters "having washed his feet" in the sutra.
○ The section beginning with "Āgama" below restates the objection. Furthermore, among the Buddha’s thirty-two marks, there is the mark of having skin that is not defiled by dust.
"Now, for what purpose is he washing? [The phrase] "Manifesting below" explains and clarifies this; herein there are three meanings. First, because it accords with worldly custom:
when a person returns from outside, they are inevitably feared to be defiled by dust, and thus must wash their feet; the Buddha’s conformity to this is likewise.
○ Second, because it manifests the Dharma: it washes away the defilements of afflictions to reveal the pure Dharmakāya.
○ Third, as a model for those who follow: this is as explained regarding the necessary provisions and conditions.

△ Third, the actual entry into meditative absorption (samāpatti). This has two parts: first, the formal explanation of entering absorption; second, the manifestation of the purpose for entering absorption.

Regarding the first, the formal explanation of entering absorption, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation itself; second, the citation of scriptural evidence. Regarding the first, the formal explanation itself:
He spreads his seat and sits down.

[Commentary] Third, the actual entry into meditative concentration. Regarding "spreading the seat and sitting in meditation": because the body is upright, the mind is free from dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
[Record] The commentary states that "the actual entry into concentration" explains the passage in the sutra concerning "spreading the seat and sitting. ... [Dullness and agitation, etc.]
"Stagnation" (*laya*) refers to torpor (*styāna*), which can induce sleep and increases the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Agitation" (*auddhatya*) refers to restlessness (*auddhatya*), which spontaneously pursues objects and can induce distraction; it likewise hinders the concentrated mind.

Furthermore, among the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), lying down leads to torpor, walking leads to agitation, and standing leads to fatigue; thus, sitting alone is superior, as it avoids both stagnation and agitation.
However, dullness and agitation are the lot of ordinary beings; as for the Tathāgata, he certainly has no such things.
These present rules of conduct are established for the sake of future generations.
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence.
[Commentary]: Therefore, the Wei translation says: "As usual, he spreads his seat, sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), straightens his body, and dwells with unmoving right mindfulness.
The Tang translation says: "Straightening his body and rectifying his intention, he dwells in face-to-face mindfulness."

[Commentary] Some say: "The sūtra merely mentions spreading out a seat; how do we know he enters meditative absorption? Therefore, the subsequent explanation cites the Wei translation and others, from which it is known that he enters absorption.
Regarding the phrase "as usual, spreading out the seat," etc., it means that whenever the Tathāgata preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* in an assembly, he always personally spread out his own seat.
This is because the *Prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Buddhas; it is the Mother of the Buddhas.
To express reverence for the Prajñāpāramitā, he personally prepared his seat. Eight assemblies have already been described; this is the ninth.
Since the ritual protocol does not change, it is said to be "as usual. *Jue* (folding) refers to the tops of the feet. *Jia* (placing) means to press one foot with the other.
*Jie* (binding) means that the two feet are not separated. This symbolizes auspiciousness. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When [Māra] saw him sitting in the *paryaṅka* posture..."
If even ordinary people are thus startled and afraid, how much more so for those who have entered the Way? Therefore, they sit with the body upright and unswaying.

Furthermore, they assume the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) for five reasons of correct contemplation: first, because by restraining the body, one quickly gives rise to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which is the most excellent state;
second, because by sitting calmly in this manner, one can endure for a long duration without causing the body to become quickly exhausted; third...
4. By means of this quiet sitting, it is an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*), for it does not exist among the heterodox or other treatises.
5. By means of this quiet sitting, one’s physical appearance becomes dignified and majestic; when others see it, they develop the utmost reverence and faith. 6. By means of this quiet sitting...
This is that which is universally authorized by all Buddhas and their disciples, and is praised by all worthy sages;
therefore, one should sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) while correctly contemplating five kinds of causal conditions. Regarding "keeping the body upright":

it means neither slouching nor leaning forward, and not tilting to the left or right. Regarding "right mindfulness" (*samyaksmṛti*): to recollect in accordance with reality is called right mindfulness.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). That is to say, it is unmoving, being free from dullness, agitation, existence, non-existence, and so forth;

"unmoving" means not wavering from right mindfulness. (The lower section of the Tang translation also corroborates the same meaning as above. "Right aspiration" (*samyakpraṇidhāna*) is precisely right mindfulness. If explained separately:
"aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) is longing or desire, meaning the longing to abide in face-to-face mindfulness; "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is that which is the object of the aspiration. However...
This must be done prior to entering meditative concentration; otherwise, it is not a correct vow. Regarding "abiding in the presence of the face":

"face" is the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), and "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the dharma (*dārṣṭāntika*). The two characters "abiding" (*sthita*) and "presence" (*sammukha*) apply to both the dharma and the metaphor.

Now, within these [two categories], one element is missing from each: in the dharma, the principle that is illuminated is missing; in the metaphor, the mirror that illuminates is missing. [In the metaphor,] the face abides facing the mirror.

Then [the truth] will manifest of itself. When mindfulness abides in accordance with principle, the principle will manifest of itself. As for the omissions in the dharma-texts and parables, it is because the wording was abbreviated;

or perhaps it is not so. It is sufficient that the contemplation of principle is clear and distinct; just as when one sees a face before one’s eyes, even a small measure of water serves as a metaphor for the principle.
△ Second, revealing the intent of entering meditative absorption. [Commentary] Asuṅga says:
"To reveal that it is solely tranquility" means that one is able to realize and explain this within it.

[Record] Regarding the section beginning with "Asuṅga": this reveals the intent of entering meditative absorption. First, the objection is restated: the intent of entering absorption while taking both as objects lies in...

What? Below this, there is an explanation that provides a comprehensive interpretation. "In this" refers to the *Dharmaparyāya*, as the treatise states. "That which can awaken" is the supernormal power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-abhijñā*);

"that which can explain" is the supernormal power of teaching (*deśanā-abhijñā*). The intended meaning is: one must first attain the supernormal power of concentration before attaining the supernormal power of teaching.

If one preaches the Dharma with a distracted mind, one cannot do so according to reality; however, when speech issues forth from within meditative concentration, it will necessarily be accurate. Therefore, the text below asks: "How is this so?"

He expounded the Dharma for others, yet did not grasp at appearances; he remained as suchness, unmoving. Whenever he wished to preach the Dharma within any of the sutras, he would first enter meditative absorption;
his intention was always thus. (And so forth. This also serves as a manifestation to provide a model for future generations.
If one follows the Tathāgata’s own example, what fault could there be in speaking while in thought? Therefore, the treatise says, "manifesting," and so on.

First, the heading. ○ "The Great Sage" refers to the Buddha. His essence pervades the Dharma-realm, hence he is called "Great"; his wisdom discerns all without obscurity, hence he is called "Sage.
"Manifesting traces" refers to the manifested traces of transformation. "That which is expressed" refers to the deeds performed by the Buddhas, which are never undertaken impulsively;
they always use external phenomena to express the internal body and mind. This is as stated in the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, where the entire body emits light.
Within the light, a flower appears; as the flower withers, one beholds the Buddha. Thereupon Ānanda questions the Buddha, and the Buddha explains it for him.
As described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the heavens, clouds, Mount Sumeru, the great ocean, and so forth are mentioned, each has its symbolic significance.

In all these cases, the phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) serve as the signifiers (*vyañjaka*), while the ultimate reality (*dharma*) serves as the signified (*vyaṅgya*). Since these are not in vain, it is said that they are "inevitable" (*avaśyam*).
...and so forth. △ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, representing the general preface; second, representing the specific preface. First, representing the general preface. [Commentary]:
It represents the Buddha of Original Enlightenment abiding within the totality of the five aggregates; awakening to the fact that the demonic armies are fundamentally empty is called "battle."

Victorious. That which illuminates the mind-consciousness and possesses virtue is the Anāthapiṇḍada (Givaka). Seeking the Dharma to nourish the spirit is called the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* (the assembly of mendicants).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "The Sūtra expresses the Original Enlightenment" (*benjue*) below, there are two interpretations. First, it expresses the general introduction. ○ "Original Enlightenment Buddha" (*benjuefo*) is spoken in contrast to the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"The totality of the five aggregates" (*wuyundou*) is in contrast to the city of Śrāvastī. The Transformation Buddha resides in Śrāvastī; this expresses Original Enlightenment.
The Buddha resides within the city of the five aggregates (*skandha*). Since this city comprises both people and phenomena, the aggregates likewise contain both form and mind.
○ Regarding the "Victory over Mara": *Māra* in Sanskrit is translated here as "the Killer," for he can slay the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) of the practitioner.
There are four types: first, the Heavenly Mara (*deva-māra*), who is the lord of the desire realm; second, the Mara of Afflictions (*kleśa-māra*)...

The Māras: third, the Māra of the aggregates (skandha-māra); fourth, the Māra of death (mṛtyu-māra). What is now called "awakening to emptiness" is as stated in the Heart Sūtra: "To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty;
there is no ignorance, and so on, up to there is no extinction of old age and death. To perceive the emptiness of the five aggregates is to destroy the Māra of the aggregates.
That there is no ignorance and no extinction [of it] is to destroy the Māra of afflictions (kleśa-māra). Up to the point that there is no old age and death, one thereby destroys the Māra of death.
"Māra! Other supramundane dharmas are still empty; how much more so, then, the celestial Māras? ○ Regarding 'the illumination of the mind-consciousness as possessing merit':

this is addressed to Anāthapiṇḍada. The Father, who is deluded regarding the fundamental awakening (pratyag-bodha), is called 'Orphan' (anātha); the Son, who conceals the wondrous function, is called 'Solitary' (piṇḍada).
Now, to illuminate that the nature is inherently endowed with sands-of-the-Ganges virtues, lacking nothing at all—this is precisely Anāthapiṇḍada."
"Seeking the Dharma," etc., refers to the meaning of a bhikṣu as a mendicant. Externally, he begs for food to sustain his life;
internally, he seeks the Dharma to nourish his spirit.
△ Second, the introductory section distinguishing the specific circumstances.
[Commentary: Since the awakened mind has already arisen, how could one abandon worldly toil? Desiring to observe universally, one enters the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

One contemplates the mind and its mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) in successive order; within the false, the true is found, and all attain the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). This joy of the Dharma has no substantial body; it merges with the awakened mind.
Contemplation relies on provisional conditions; when conditions vanish, they accord with the true nature. Contemplative observation is a trace; one brushes away the trace.

Returning to the root and restoring the source. Returning to the root and restoring the source. The Dharma is empty and the mind is tranquil; with the mind tranquil, the true essence is revealed, and Prajñā is brilliantly clear.

[Commentary] Below the phrase "Awakened Mind" (Juexin), these two lines constitute the separate introduction (biexu). Regarding "Awakened Mind" and so forth: this refers to entering the great city of Śrāvastī.
It should be said: Since the awakened mind has already arisen, how could one abandon worldly toil? When the Tathāgata appears in the world, how could he abandon the multitude of beings?

Desiring to observe universally, he enters the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); desiring to teach and transform, he enters the royal city. Apart from cities and towns, whom would he teach and transform?
Apart from mind and consciousness, what matter would he observe? [The various] minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), etc.
This refers to having completed the sequential alms-round within that city. In begging for food, one does not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy;

in observation, how could one choose between the mental factors (*caitta*) and the mind-king (*cittarāja*)? The two lines following "that is, falsely" correspond to having obtained the food through begging.
Externally, he transforms others to obtain food; internally, he contemplates the Dharma to give rise to joy.
(The latter two phrases of "joy in the Dharma" correspond to returning to his original place to eat. Food can sustain the body; the Dharma can benefit the mind.

(The phrase "contemplating the provisional conditions" corresponds to donning the robes and holding the bowl. "The forgetting [of the provisional] accords with the Real" corresponds to putting away the robes and bowl. Having finished begging for food...
"One requires robes and alms-bowl": this reflects the contemplation that one must rely upon causal conditions. Having entered meditative concentration, one unites with the necessary requisites;

yet to accord with the Principle, one must forget discursive thoughts. (The second line of the "Contemplation" section corresponds to washing the feet: if one wishes to sit in peace, one must wash away the dust from the feet; if one wishes to return to the Source, one must sweep away mental conceptions. (The second line of the "Returning to the Root" section:

The second line of the "Returning to the Root" section [corresponds to the phrase "one must forget discursive thoughts"]. To return to the origin, one must eliminate all mental deliberations. Thus, the two lines of the "Returning to the Root" section correspond to the act of sweeping away mental conceptions.

This refers to spreading out the seat and then sitting. The emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*) is the spreading of the seat; the stillness of the mind is the sitting. Only when the seat is spread can one sit;
only when the dharmas are empty does the mind first attain stillness. The two lines following "the mind is still" correspond to the main teaching (*samyak-artha*).
This means that only by sitting peacefully can one preach the sutra, and only when the mind is still can wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) be manifested.
△ Three Conclusions.
[Commentary] Desiring to discuss the main body of the Prajñāpāramitā, he thus manifests this initiation.

△ Second, citing the *Zisheng* (資聖) to briefly clarify two points. First, the formal explanation; second, the citation of proof. First, the formal explanation: [The *Sūtra Commentary*] states:
"Now, there are two kinds of bodies: first, the false; second, the true. The false substance of the five aggregates is nurtured by means of clothing and food.
The formless Dharma-body is realized through the illumination of *prajñā*. Sentient beings preserve the false and neglect the true."
The Buddhas nurture the true and discard the false. Since sentient beings are deluded by the true and grasp at the false, I employ false traces to lead them toward the true;
thus, I rely on the pretext of begging for food to extend the transformation of the joy of the Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding "Zisheng" (資聖) below: this is a brief citation from the commentary of Master Daoyi (道液), which I have now extracted and utilized without taking the full text.
This section contains two parts: first, the formal explanation. Regarding "the body has two": this refers generally to both sentient beings and Buddhas.
The "false" is the form-body (*rūpakāya*); the "true" is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Regarding "the five aggregates," etc.: this refers to clothing.
The external provides covering; food provides internal sustenance. While birth is indeed due to one's parents, once alive, one must rely upon clothing and food.
Regarding "the Dharma-body and so forth": this means it is not produced by productive causes (*janaka-hetu*), but is rather realized through revealing causes (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
Consequently, while the physical body takes food as its life-force, the Dharma-body takes wisdom as its life-force. "Preserving the false" refers to clinging to delusion.

"Uniting with objects" refers to delusion regarding principle and turning one's back on awakening; these are all inversions. "Nurturing the true" means awakening to principle and uniting with awakening;
"discarding the false" means penetrating delusion and turning away from sense-objects. The following section on "the multitude of beings" restates the aforementioned inversions.
"○ 'I then descend' means that he manifests entering the city to beg for food in order to symbolize the Dharma. The intent is to cause the seeking of Prajñā to illuminate and perfect the Dharmakāya;
therefore, it is said that 'he leads forth the Real. ○ 'Therefore, relying on the following' concludes the overall meaning of the symbolic representation of the Dharma."
This means that the manifestation of begging for alms is intended solely for the purpose of preaching the Dharma.

Part Two: The Main Body of the Teaching (Zhengzongfen). This is divided into two: First, the headings and enumeration of the chapters; Second, the detailed explanation according to the chapters. First: The headings and enumeration of the chapters.

[Commentary] The second part, the Main Body (*śarīra*), is analyzed through two gates. First, it provides a preliminary judgment based on the seven types of meaningful phrases (*arthapada*) of Asaṅga;
second, it provides a detailed exposition based on Vasubandhu’s method of answering questions to sever doubts.

[Commentary] Within the main body of the text (*zhengzong*), the sub-commentary (*shu*) has two parts: first, the presentation of the topical headings; second, the interpretation of the one fascicle of sūtra text by means of the two treatises.
In both the *Dayun* and *Qinglong* [commentaries], the two treatises were used concurrently. Now, however, it is not so. Why?

Because Asaṅga assigns [the topics] to eighteen stations (*sthāna*), while Vasubandhu resolves twenty-seven doubts; since their fundamental intents differ, their structural divisions (*keduan*) likewise do.
They differ. Sometimes there are four or five *nivāsas* within a single *vicikitsā*; sometimes there are two or three *vicikitsās* within a single *nivāsa*.

They are occasionally combined and occasionally separated, overlapping what precedes and follows. For this reason, the text appears convoluted, yet the underlying principle is not necessarily profound or abstruse;

it is merely because of this that students find it difficult to understand. Now that I have provided a separate explanation, I hope it will not conflict with others, for the purpose of transmitting and lecturing upon it.
...of this kind. It is merely a case of obtaining much with little effort.

[Commentary] Regarding the "seven meaningful phrases" (*saptārthapada*): after the treatise has set forth the verse of homage, it states, "Once the seven kinds of meaningful phrases have been established, this *prajñāpāramitā* is thereby established.
"Meaningful phrases" (*artha-pada*) distinguishes them from mere "textual phrases" (*vyañjana-pada*).
Since one meaning constitutes a single phrase, this sutra contains seven such meaningful phrases. The names of these seven meaningful phrases are [found] in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
It exists within this [text]. Among these, the first six demonstrate the perfection of the bodhisattva’s activities, while the seventh demonstrates the establishment of this dharma-gate.
Thus, these seven phrases encompass the complete fulfillment of both teaching (śāsana) and principle (nyāya), as well as practice (caryā) and fruit (phala).
Among these, one, two, three, and four refer to practice; five refers to principle; six refers to the fruit; and seven refers to the teaching.
Having thus provisionally determined this section, I have recorded it solely based on the title of Asanga’s work.

△ Second, the enumeration and explanation of the seven [topics]. First, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); second, the arousal [of the thought of enlightenment]; third, the abiding; fourth, the antidotes;

[Commentary] First, the lineage is not severed; this refers to being protected by mindfulness and entrusted [with the teaching].
[Record] Regarding "the lineage is not severed" in the commentary: this does not refer to ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings.
This clarifies that the Buddha-nature (buddhagotra) is never interrupted. ○ The phrase "protecting the lower" refers to the Sūtra; this is the explanation of the meaning.
It means entrusting the small to the great and charging the great to transform the small, continuing in this manner through successive generations. How could there ever be an interruption?

It is like parents entrusting their affairs to their children and grandchildren (and so forth). This is the fundamental intention of Śūnyatā-utpāda (Subhūti); therefore, he praises [the Buddha] on account of this matter.
"Buddha. This introduces the opening of the inquiry.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, "The Characteristics of Initiating Practice": Since one desires that the lineage (gotra) not be interrupted, it is necessary to initiate the characteristics of practice.

△ Third, the places of abiding.

[Commentary]: Third, the places where practice abides; that is, the eighteen abidings (*aṣṭādaśavihāra*). From the Buddha’s correct teaching until the end of the sutra, these constitute the places where signless practice (*animittacaryā*) abides.
[Commentary] Regarding the "places where the three practices abide": since there is that which can give rise [to them], there must necessarily be that which is given rise to.
The names and meanings of the eighteen abodes will be explained extensively in the text below. From "From the Buddha... onwards, this points to the sūtra. From "This is non...
onwards, this explains the names and meanings. Since this is the signlessness of signs, it is not a one-sided signlessness; this is briefly seen in the *Xianxing* (Profound Practice). For...
This accords with our fundamental school; therefore, it is designated as "formless" (*animitta*).
△ Fourth, the Antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

[Commentary]: Fourth, the Antidote. This means that within each and every dwelling place, both wrong practice and right practice are present together. There are two types: [wrong practice and right practice].
Antidote. [Commentary] Among the four antidotes, "wrong conduct" refers to improper conduct; however, anything that does not accord with the Buddha-way is termed wrong conduct.
"Common" means non-uniformity. "Views" refer to the sentiments of discrimination. "Right conduct" refers to the mixed [practice].
"Seeing right practice" does not refer to purely correct practice. Regarding the "two kinds of remedies":
using right practice to remedy wrong practice is the first remedy; using non-conceptual wisdom to remedy conceptual views is the second remedy.
However, the former remedies the entirety of the wrong [practice], whereas the latter remedies only the view within the common [state] and does not remedy the right practice itself. As it says:
It is like sifting sand to find gold: one removes the sand but does not remove the gold. In the present sutra, there are only the remedies (*pratipakṣa*), but no objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*).
For instance, within the first dwelling (*vihāra*), failing to save sentient beings is considered wrong conduct (*mithyācāra*), while saving sentient beings is the remedy.
At the time of saving sentient beings, one perceives that there are sentient beings who are the objects to be saved, and one perceives oneself as the one who saves.

"Transcending" is a view of conceptual discrimination; "transcending while there is no transcending" serves as its antidote (*pratipakṣa*). This principle is actually simultaneous, though in terms of meaning it is divided into prior and subsequent.

Since this is the case for the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the others may be understood by analogy. Therefore, the treatise states: "When practicing in the various stages, there are two kinds of antidotes."
△ Five Non-losses.

[Commentary] "Five" refers to the five non-losses. This means that by means of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), one departs from the two extremes of increase and decrease, thereby not losing the Middle Way.

[Record] In the section on the five non-losses within the Commentary, the phrase "by means of" clarifies the underlying intent. "Departing from increase and decrease" refers to [the abandonment of] clinging...

To increase the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and to diminish the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—to fall into these two extremes previously mentioned is to lose the Middle Way. Now, by departing from both, one does not lose it.
As stated in the Sūtra: "That which is 'not the Buddha-dharma' is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)," which negates the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*).

"That which is called 'the Buddha-dharma' is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)," which negates the extreme of denial (*apavāda*). All other instances of "that which is not" and "that which is called" follow this same principle.

All cases are treated according to this principle. The final conclusion of the treatise states: "Because the Bodhisattva is free from these two extremes, they no longer lose their respective antidotes;
therefore, it is called 'non-loss' (avipraṇāśa)."
△ Six Stages. [Commentary] Sixth, the stages.

This refers to attaining the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*) by not losing the Middle Way. These are: the Stage of Practice through Faith (*śraddhā-pratipatti-bhūmi*), the Stage of the Pure Mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*), and the Stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).
[Commentary] Within the six stages of the *śāstra*, it is explained by way of the "lower" [analysis]. Because the two extremes are deviant and erroneous, they are set aside and not discussed.
The Middle Way is the path to Great Bodhi; therefore, the stages and positions are established therein.
It is like traveling to the imperial capital where there are three different roads: both sides are incorrect, while the middle road is correct. Only upon this correct path can one proceed.
This treatise discusses [the distinctions of] distance, proximity, slowness, and speed; it is the same within the Dharma. Thus, a sutra says:
"All worthy sages (ārya) have their differences based on the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma). ○ Regarding "faith-practice" (*śraddhā-carita*) and below, these are the stages (*avasthā*).

Among the eighteen abodes (*vihāra*), the first sixteen abodes constitute the stage of faith-practice (*śraddhā-caritabhūmi*); this corresponds to the three levels of the worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*). Because one initiates practice based on faith, it is called faith-practice.
It is called the Stage of Practice through Faith (*śraddhā-caryā*), and it is also called the Stage of Resolute Understanding (*adhimukti*), because understanding arises based on faith.

The seventeenth dwelling is the Ground of Pure Mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*); this corresponds to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), for one leaves behind the obstacles of conceptual discrimination and directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness).
The eighteenth dwelling, from the second ground onward up to the stage of Buddhahood, is collectively termed the Ground of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*). Furthermore, by means of all...

Regarding the stages of the Bodhisattva’s realization, they may be presented either extensively or concisely. Extensively, there are fifty-two stages; concisely, they are subsumed such that none remain.
Now, taking a middle path between the extensive and the concise, and avoiding extremes, I shall explain the three stages and five positions.
△ 7. Establishing the Name.

[Commentary]: Seventh, establishing the name. This means that because of the preceding six [aspects], its wisdom is firm and sharp, and its stage and scope are vast; therefore, it is named "Vajra" (Diamond).

[Commentary] Regarding the sevenfold establishment of names in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), it is explained as follows from below: the name "Vajra" is established based upon three types of phenomena.

First, it is named "Vajra" in terms of the essence and function of *prajñā*; this is like the hardness and sharpness of a vajra. Second, it is named "Vajra" in terms of the breadth and narrowness of the stages (*bhūmi*);
this is like the shape of a vajra-pestle (*vajra-ghaṇṭā*), because [the stage of] faith-practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) lasts for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. Third, [it is named so] regarding the purity...
The mind lasts for only a single *kṣaṇa*. The Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) spans two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Like a vajra-pestle, it is broad at the beginning and end, and narrow in the middle.
Thirdly, regarding the name "Vajra" as applied to the written text: this is like a painted image.

It explains the seven folios or more of scripture concerning the stages of faith and practice (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*), the three folios or more of text concerning the Buddha-ground, and the five lines of scripture concerning the stage of pure mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*). It is just like that painting.
The image is likewise broad at the beginning and end, and narrow in the middle. Furthermore, these three—the Dharma, the analogy, and the image—are all successively derived from one another.
Within the analogy, the fundamental substance is a hard and sharp vajra, which is fashioned into a ritual scepter (kīla).
It is through painting that its image is completed. Within the Dharma, the fundamental essence is the Prajñā of both substance and function;

it is through cultivation that its stages and grounds are completed, and it is through verbal expression that its written characters are completed. Furthermore, within these three matters of both the Dharma and the metaphor:
One thing is real, while the other two are both false. In the analogy, the solid and sharp vajra is real, whereas the shape of the mallet and its painted image are both false.
In the Dharma, the essence and function of *prajñā* are real, while the stages, levels, and written characters are all false.
Because these three matters correspond from beginning to end, the name "Vajra" is established. However, the first of these [the vajra] alone represents the Buddha’s fundamental intent.

The remaining two [categories] represent the views of the Bodhisattvas and the ancient masters. Regarding the phrase "due to the preceding six," among them, the first five are firm and sharp, while the sixth is broad and narrow;
within this breadth and narrowness, both the signifier (the means of expression) and the signified (that which is expressed) are contained.

[Commentary] First: The Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). The Sūtra says: “One should subdue the mind in this manner; whatever [afflictions] there may be,” and so forth.
[Record] Regarding the first, “resolving the mind” refers to the generation of the four kinds of minds, such as the vast, the foremost, and so on.
The scriptural text begins from where it says: “The Buddha addressed Subhūti: ‘All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner.’”
The mind. ... Furthermore, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.

△ Second, the dwelling in accordance with the *pāramitās*.
[Commentary] Second: the dwelling in practice in accordance with the *pāramitās*, such as giving without dwelling in form (*rūpa*).
[Record] Second: the sutra continues, "Furthermore, Subhūti, one should dwell in the practice of giving without dwelling on any phenomena (*dharma*)."
"Generosity. ... up to "Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed. Regarding the phrase "not abiding in the [perfections] equally," there are two meanings to "equally":
first, it is equal to the other passages, as cited above; second, it is equal to the other meanings, namely, being equal to the remaining five perfections such as morality and so forth.
This passage, while specifically pointing to the sutra text, simultaneously provides an explanation of its meaning.

Thus, the pāramitās are that which is to be responded to, while morality and the others are that which responds. Because the "capable" (the practitioner) and the "object" (the practice) are united, it is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).

For this reason, merely practicing giving, morality, and so forth without being able to transcend signs, or practicing the transcendence of signs while not practicing giving, morality, and so forth, are both not corresponding practices.
It is only when one transcends signs within the very act of practicing giving, morality, and so forth, and [transcends them] within the state of transcending signs...
By practicing giving, precepts, and so forth, one is then called a practitioner of corresponding conduct.
△ Third, the desire to abide in the form body.
[Commentary]: Third, the desire to abide in the form body can be understood through the characteristics of the body and so forth.
[Commentary] Third: The Sūtra asks, "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks?
and continues until, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Question: The form-body (rūpakāya) is a mark.

"Why seek it by departing from characteristics? The answer is: "The characteristics of the form-body (rūpakāya) are shadows; the dharma-body (dharmakāya), being without characteristics, is the essence.

If one wishes to obtain the form-body with its characteristics, one must first perceive the essence of the dharma-body which is without characteristics. Without having perceived the essence of the dharma-body, one cannot manifest the characteristics.
Therefore, one first causes the perception of the non-existence of characteristics, and only then does one obtain the body of form-characteristics. This is the intended meaning herein.
This lies outside the literal text; therefore, the treatise classifies it according to its underlying intent.
△ Fourth, the desire to abide in the Dharmakāya.
[Commentary]: Fourth, the desire to abide in the Dharmakāya. There are two types of Dharmakāya: first, the Dharmakāya of verbal teaching. Is there not a multitude...?

Regarding "birth" and so forth: because these words reveal the underlying principle, there are two aspects to the realization of the Dharmakāya. First is the aspect of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), as in the passage beginning "The Tathāgata attains Anuttara...
Second is the aspect of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*), as in the passage beginning "If a person fills the three thousand..."
[Commentary] Regarding the "discourse" among the four [kinds of dharmakāya]: the sutra begins with Subhūti addressing the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One...
down to ‘even dharma should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharma. Question: The dharmakāya is not discourse;
for what reason is discourse taken as the dharmakāya? Therefore, the sub-commentary explains: “Because the principle is manifested through discourse. This has two meanings. First, by means of...
Discourse reveals the Dharma-body, yet the Dharma-body is not discourse. The nature of both is free from words and letters;
this is precisely the Dharma-body—there is no separate Dharma-body. Regarding the characteristic of wisdom: the Sūtra asks, "Subhūti, what do you think?"
Does the Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? ... up to all the worthy sages (*ārya*), who all possess distinctions based on the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Thus, the sign of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely the signless and unconditioned dharma.

Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "Because the sign of wisdom cannot be perceived. As for the sign of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*), the Sūtra [says], from Subhūti: "What do you think?"... [text continues]
What do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as alms...
[Subhūti], that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma.

This refers to obtaining a subtle and wondrous physical body through the merit of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*), which is induced by upholding and expounding this sutra; this is what is called the "mark of merit. However, this is the Dharma.
The auspicious marks of the body. These auspicious marks are not the Dharma-body; this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
△ Fifth, dwelling without pride while cultivating the path has three parts: first, the direct presentation of this text; second, a general exposition of the subsequent section;
third, a specific conclusion regarding the antidotes. First, the direct presentation of this text.
[Commentary] Five. Regarding the attainment of excellence on the path of cultivation, there is no pride in abiding as a *srotāpanna* and so forth.
[Record] Regarding "Five," the text has three parts. First, the actual presentation of this passage.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can a *srotāpanna* have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of *srotāpatti*'? and so on, up to...

They delight in the practice of araṇya. Regarding "attaining victory": because the four fruits of the Hīnayāna surpass the four stages of the candidate (*pratipannaka*) and so forth, this highlights their excellence in contrast to what is inferior.
This is an instance of using the small to illustrate the great; even a small person is still without fault.
How could a noble person (ārya) possibly harbor such conceit? It is precisely because they are free from pride that they are able to realize the fruits of the path. Therefore, the sūtras all state:
"I did not have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna),' and so forth."
△ Second, a general summary of the latter section.
[Commentary]: From here up to the sixteenth stage (*vihāra*), twelve types of obstacles are successively countered.

This intends to clarify that those who seek the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) must abandon these obstacles. Because the obstacles are exhausted, one enters the seventeenth stage, the Stage of Realization (*sākṣātkriyā-vihāra*).
[Commentary] From here below, two points generally introduce the latter section. Regarding "The meaning clarifies," etc., this explains the intent of the sequence. First, a question is raised:
"Why was it not stated that the preceding four dwellings involve the 'separation from hindrances'? This is why [the text] says so.

The underlying meaning is that whenever one wishes to practice and advance, one must first resolve the mind (*cittotpāda*); once the mind has been resolved, one then practices. Therefore, there is the first dwelling.
Second, regarding the cultivation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*): one originally seeks the fruit of Buddhahood. Within the fruit of Buddhahood, there are only two bodies;
between the coarse and the subtle, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) comes first and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) follows. Therefore, there are a third and a fourth [stage].

Fearing that the practice of superior deeds (*viśeṣacaryā*) might give rise to pride that obstructs entry into the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), [the Buddha] spoke of the lesser fruits as a metaphor for the Mahāyāna. Now, having abandoned these obstructions, one enters the tenth [stage].
This is the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, it is only from the fifth [stage] onward that the abandonment of obstacles is explained.

However, regarding these twelve obstacles, at each *vihāra* (dwelling), one must trace back to what preceded it to clarify the purpose of their introduction. For example, as it is said: "Although one has attained freedom from pride, one still lacks extensive learning;
therefore, within the sixth dwelling, the obstacle of limited learning is countered. All other cases should be understood by analogy in this manner.
These various hindrances all exist prior to the stages (bhūmi); they are able to obstruct the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) and do not pertain to the stages themselves.

Therefore, it is said that "when the hindrances are exhausted, one enters the Path of Realization. Now, the hindrances are that which is to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*), and their description lies outside the sūtra;
the "abiding" (*vihāra*) is the remedy (*pratipakṣa*), and this is precisely the content of the sūtra. If these are compared with one another, the principle becomes clear.
△ 3. Separate Conclusion on the Antidotes.
[Commentary] Now we shall apply the antidote to the first obstacle, which is pride (*māna*).
[Record] Regarding the phrase "Now we shall," this is the third section: the separate conclusion on the antidotes. ○ However, according to the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, there are seven types of pride.
The nine and the two types differ only in their expansion and contraction; these are explained in terms of those entering the Path. Seventh, the treatise states: First, pride (*māna*):

regarding one who is inferior, one considers oneself superior; regarding one who is equal, one considers oneself equal. Second, excessive pride (*atimāna*): regarding one who is equal, one considers oneself superior;

regarding one who is superior, one considers oneself equal. Third, pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*): regarding one who is superior to oneself, one reckons oneself superior to them. Fourth, false pride (*mithyāmāna*): [one who] is actually...
1. The pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*): to consider oneself superior when one lacks virtue. 2. The pride of equality (*sammānamāna*): to consider oneself equal when one is actually inferior.

3. The pride of superiority (*adhimāna*): to consider oneself superior when one is actually equal. 4. The pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*): to consider oneself superior when one is actually far superior. 5. The pride of self (*asmimāna*): to conceive of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*) with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*). 6. The pride of overweening confidence (*adhimāna*): to claim to have attained what has not been attained regarding the sublime and excellent dharmas.

7. The pride of inferiority (*parāvamāna*): to consider oneself only slightly inferior when one is vastly inferior. That which is abandoned here refers specifically to the fifth and sixth types of pride, as they serve to realize the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Therefore, because he takes up the ultimate fruit.
△ Sixth, not dwelling apart from the time of the Buddha’s presence.
[Commentary]: Sixth, not dwelling apart from the time of the Buddha’s presence. Formerly, when he was with Dīpaṃkara and others, he was free from the second obstacle, that of limited learning.
Not being separated from the Buddha’s presence, one then possesses great learning.
[Commentary] Sixth: The Sūtra proceeds from the Buddha’s address to Subhūti: “What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha...
up to ‘in truth, there was nothing obtained. [Question] How does one leave behind hindrances and achieve abiding? [Exegesis]

Next, it says: "Separated from the lower [level]. This refers to the obstacles being abandoned. "Not separated from the lower" establishes the meaning of *vihāra* (abiding). Within this, the upper phrase establishes the abiding, while the lower phrase refers to the abandonment of obstacles.
If one is separated from the Buddha's world, it cannot be called a place of abiding; for there is no Buddha there to preach the Dharma.
Thus, limited learning becomes an obstacle. If one does not depart from the presence of the Buddha, it becomes a place of dwelling;
by constantly encountering the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, one possesses extensive learning and thereby leaves behind obstacles. However, in all spiritual practice, wisdom is the foundation.
To obtain wisdom, one must necessarily engage in extensive learning; therefore, by relying on the Buddha for one's dwelling, one leaves behind the obstacle of limited learning.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Much hearing increases wisdom; diligent inquiry is the foremost method. Question:
If this is so, according to the present sutra which states that regarding the Dharma there is truly nothing to be attained, how can this constitute "much hearing"? Answer:
This is hearing while there is no hearing, attaining while there is no attaining, attaining through non-attainment—this is true attainment. Hearing while there is no hearing—this is real hearing.
Thus, this dwelling is established. △ Seven:
Dwelling in the Purification of Buddha-lands through Vows.

[Commentary]: Seventh, dwelling in the purification of Buddha-lands through vows. The adornments of the Buddha-lands by Bodhisattvas are not uniform; they are free from the limited objects of perception (*ālambana*) characteristic of the Lesser Vehicle.
To form a conceptual thought is an obstacle to cultivating the path. When conditioned by forms and marks, the land is small; when unconditioned, it is great, for it accords with the dharma-realm.
[Commentary] Seventh: The sutra asks, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-lands?"
...up to "one should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere. ○ Regarding "departing from the small and inferior": that which is to be departed from is the obstacle;
"grasping at objects" (攀緣) is synonymous with "forming mental conceptions" (作念), as they share the same meaning. ○ Regarding "conditioned forms and so forth": the intent is this:
if one takes the characteristics of form, sound, and so on as the land, it will possess limitations; therefore, it is called "small. This is because it does not accord with the Dharma-body. If...
Not grasping at marks, no conceptual discrimination arises; when both mind and objects are forgotten, what limit could there possibly be? Therefore, it is called "Great.

The phrase "In accordance with the Dharma" below explains the reason for this. The intent is to cause one to forget the self in order to adorn the land of the *dharmatā*, rather than causing the mind to arise in order to adorn the land of *dharmalakṣaṇa*.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on form and so forth; one should dwell nowhere."
And thus gives rise to that mind. The verse-commentary explains: "When wisdom practices the penetration of *vijñapti-mātra*, one thus grasps the pure land.
It is not a form; it is the primary essence. It is not an adornment; it is the intention of adornment."
△ 8. Dwelling in the Maturation of Sentient Beings.
[Commentary] Eighth: the dwelling in the maturation of sentient beings. One’s own human body is like Mount Sumeru and so forth; it is to be free from the obstacle of abandoning sentient beings.
If one discriminates between great and small, one will be unable to save all things.

[Commentary] Eighth: The Sūtra says, "Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains," and so on, up to "this is called a 'great body.
Regarding "maturation": it refers to causing sentient beings to plant [the seeds of awakening] through teaching and transformation, so that their faculties ripen and they attain realization.
Regarding "abandoning the inferior" and below: this refers to the obstacles to be abandoned. If one abandons the [inferior] assembly...
If one gives rise to [discrimination], one will be unable to transform others; therefore, one must first leave behind such hindrances before one can achieve abiding.

○ "If one sees greatness or smallness," and so forth, is an exegesis by way of contrast. The intended meaning is that those who are able to rescue sentient beings do so precisely because they do not see greatness or smallness.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The Buddha says it is not a body; it is called the Great Body. How could there be existence of greatness or smallness? If one sees greatness or smallness, then...
If there are distinctions of high and low, close and distant, or feelings of aversion and affection, the mind is already unequal; how can it be called "great compassion"?
Even if one were to transform sentient beings, it would result only in attachment and biased views: those who are disliked would depart, and thus one would abandon sentient beings.
How, then, could they be brought to maturity? By employing the opposite approach, no being will be left behind; whether sooner or later, all can be brought to maturity.
△ Ninth, dwelling in seclusion from external treatises.
[Commentary]: Ninth, dwelling in seclusion from the distractions that follow external treatises, such as the sands found within the Ganges River.
The obstacle of distraction following external treatises that abandon joy: the giving of treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges does not equal upholding this sutra.
How can those of external studies fail to cultivate the True Dharma?
[Commentary] Ninth: From Subhūti in the sutra, "As there are all the sands in the River Ganges," up to "the Tathāgata."
There is nothing to be said. [The phrase] "departing from pleasure" refers to the obstacles to be abandoned. However, to follow external treatises (*bāhyaka-śāstra*) is itself distraction;
merely being able to distance oneself from them constitutes abiding. All things outside of Buddhism—such as Confucianism, Mohism, and literary composition—are considered external treatises.
Since the matters of external treatises are the source of fame and profit, if one seeks fame, how can the mind be free from attachment?
There is distraction. How much more so when one attains it, there is joy; when one loses it, there is suffering; when one suffers, there is anxiety; and when one rejoices, there is excess.
Because of these karmic burdens, one sinks and revolves from lifetime to lifetime. If one traces this back to its root, it all stems from following external treatises.
Below the phrase "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," the text cites the vast merit of upholding this sutra to rebuke those of external studies. The underlying intent is this:

if the merit of one who upholds this sutra is such as this, yet they do not practice accordingly, then [pursuing] fame and profit—which are the source of worldly renown and the very root of the suffering of saṃsāra—is it right to follow them?
On the contrary, one should instead cultivate and study [the Dharma].
△ Ten Contemplations on the Dismantling of the Material Body.
[Commentary]: Tenth, the dwelling in the practice of contemplation that dismantles the grasping of material form and the bodies of sentient beings.

Regarding all the atoms within the three-thousandfold world system, one is free from the obstacle of lack of skillful means regarding the dissolution of the characteristics of reflected images. Since they have already been dispersed...

When distraction is associated with meditative concentration, one employs two skillful means—subtlety and non-recollection—to break the coarse down to the subtle, and dissolve the subtle into emptiness;
thus, the conceptualization of the marks of reflected images is eliminated.
[Commentary] "The ten" refers to the passage in the Sūtra beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms in the trichiliocosm many?
and ending with, "this is called a world. Form (*rūpa*) is the retributive environment, which consists of the external four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The body is the primary retribution, which consists of the internal five aggregates (*skandha*). "Aggregated" (*piṇḍa-grahaṇa*) has the meaning of being combined or harmonized.
The only difference lies in the translations by the Qin and Wei schools. Nevertheless, when summarizing the essential principles, there are two matters that correspond to and encompass all people;

comparing these two matters, there are three pairs in total. First, the internal aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) are both composed solely of the aggregation of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The first is called "lump-grasping" (*kabaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Seeing the physical body and its environment as a basis for grasping at what is self and what belongs to the self, this is "conjunction.

The second consists of the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*); these are formed merely by the conjunction of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), and seeing sensations such as pleasure and pain is "conjunction.
Third, the integration of form and mind to constitute this body is called "lump-grasping."
Grasping. To perceive the existence of mind and form is to be associated with the notion of a self (pudgala). "Activity" (saṃskāra) carries the meaning of flux and volitional construction;
its meaning as something to be observed and dismantled is clarified below. ○ Regarding the characteristic of reflected images:

this refers to phenomena such as form and mind, which are reflections within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and may also be considered reflections of the karmic consciousness (karmavijñāna). As for "separation from dismantling," it refers to that which is to be separated from, as explained below.
Obstruction. For one who lacks skillful means, because they lack such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are unable to break through this image;
this is what is called an obstruction. If one possesses skillful means and breaks through it, then one achieves abiding.

The characteristics of skillful means are manifested in the following text. ○ "Having already departed from below," etc., takes the preceding abiding as the basis for skillful means. Because there is no distraction...
Through disorder, one achieves concentration; from concentration, one is finally able to give rise to wisdom, which observes and breaks [the object] apart.

○ The phrase "by means of the subtle and the coarse" correctly demonstrates the characteristics of the two types of skillful means (*upāya*). However, the breaking of form involves both [subtle and coarse], whereas the breaking of mind involves only one [the subtle], because the subtle and the minute are excluded;
this is because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) cannot be analyzed or broken apart. Coarse form is manifest.

It is difficult to forget grasping attachments; therefore, one must analyze them down to the ultimate atom (paramāṇu). It is easy to dispel deluded thoughts; thus, both methods must be employed, as explained in the following text.
Regarding "characteristics and perceptions": these refer to the mind and its objects. Since both the mind and its objects are forgotten, it is said that they are "removed."
△ 11. Dwelling in Service to the Tathāgata.
[Commentary] The eleventh is the dwelling in service and making offerings to the Tathāgata. One may perceive the Tathāgata through the thirty-two marks, yet this is not equal [to true perception].
It is because one lacks the obstacle-free provisions of merit that one does not perceive Him by means of the marks; rather, constantly perceiving the Dharma-body is what is called [this dwelling].
Attendant: "The merit is boundless.
[Commentary] The eleventh: The sutra asks, "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?
and so on, up to "this is called the thirty-two marks. Regarding the section "free from merit" (*li fu*) below, it refers to the obstacles to be abandoned.
Those who wish to enter the Noble Path must possess the provisions of merit. Just as a person traveling a great distance cannot go empty-handed, so it is with this:
the Buddha is the Most Holy One and is the cause of merit; there is no offering or service that does not yield merit. One should take this very merit as one's provision.
If one obtains merit through making offerings, this constitutes "abiding" rather than an obstacle; conversely, if one does not, it constitutes an obstacle rather than abiding.
[End of section. Regarding the passage beginning with "Not by means of... and so forth: Someone asked, "The text says that one does not see the Tathāgata by means of marks (lakṣaṇa).
Since even the Tathāgata cannot be seen [in this way], how can one serve him? This is the explanation for that.

It means that simply following and corresponding through wisdom is what is called "serving. However, it does not mean abandoning the body of marks (rūpakāya) to separately attend upon a formless Buddha.
To simply realize that appearances are non-appearances and not to give rise to attachment is what is called "correspondence" (*yoga*).
Whatever offerings, services, or acts of reverence one performs are all termed "attending. If attachment arises, one does not accord with principle;
even if one constantly beholds the Buddha, it cannot be called "seeing. As the subsequent passage states: "If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound..."
If a person walks the path of deviance, they cannot see the Tathāgata. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"If a person were to follow the Tathāgata constantly for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet fail to understand the true meaning, they would remain blind and dark, unable to see the Buddha.
Furthermore, when the Buddha formerly ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three months to preach the Dharma for his mother, and later descended to Jambudvīpa, there was the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
Desiring to see the Buddha first, he manifested as the retinue of a Wheel-Turning King and went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha then rebuked him and fully explained the aforementioned matters. At that time, Subhūti, who was in the mountains, also wished to see the Buddha;

however, he immediately reflected: "The principle of emptiness and signlessness is the true Dharma-body. What use is there in seeing physical forms? Having said this, he sat down again and remained there until the end.
He did not go to see him. Thereupon, the Buddha said to Utpalavarṇā: "Subhūti had already seen me before; you came only later.

Thus one knows that clinging to appearances deludes one from the truth: though facing each other, they are a thousand li apart. One who maintains an empty mind and embodies reality perceives heaven and earth as one family.
Therefore, the ancients said: 'Though liver and gall are close, when emotion arises, they are separated; though mountains and rivers are distant, the Way..."
To be in accord is to be a neighbor. Thus we know that only one who penetrates the wondrous principle is a true attendant;
if one serves in such a manner, this is to serve the True Buddha. Therefore, the merit obtained is boundless.
△ Twelve: Abiding in the Renunciation of Regression.

[Commentary]: Twelfth. Because one is far removed from gain and offerings (*lābha-satkāra*) as well as the distress of fatigue and vexation, one does not give rise to indolence or abide in regression.

Even through such acts as giving away bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one remains free from the obstacles of attachment to the flavor of pleasure, laziness, and gain. Constantly...

"O life-giving one, bestow [this teaching]. It is far better to uphold it. How could one, for the sake of a single body, become attached to gain and offerings, becoming weary in body and troubled in mind through indolence?
[Commentary] Twelfth: The sutra continues from Subhūti: "If there be good sons or good daughters who, with the Ganges..."
Giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, up to this point, is called the first *pāramitā*. Regarding the phrase "departing from pleasure" (*li le*) and below:

these are the obstacles to be abandoned. However, the names of these obstacles are somewhat incomplete; if one were to take them in their full extent, they would not exceed the name "abiding" (*zhu*).

However, attachment to the taste of pleasure constitutes an obstacle, while detachment constitutes abiding. For the time being, regarding the arising of faults due to these obstacles, there are five stages:
first, seeking profit for the sake of the body; second, through the pursuit of gain and offerings, causing the body to become exhausted.

This, in turn, has two aspects: first, the exhaustion of the body due to negligence; second, the exhaustion of the body when what is sought is not obtained. Third, [exhaustion] due to physical fatigue...
