if one wishes to seek the flavor of food, one must chew it. The third is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); through practice, delusions are dispelled, just as a disease is cured by taking medicine.
The final phrase is the fruit of these three wisdoms: as bees gather from a hundred flowers to produce honey, so do people accumulate ten thousand practices to realize the Truth.
Once the bees have produced honey, they depend on the honey to live; once a person has realized the Truth, they abide by the Truth. ○ "We...
and below constitute the application of the analogy. ○ The final phrase applies generally to that which is heard.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s correct exposition has two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, following up to sever doubts. First, the direct answer to the question has two parts:
first, citing the general to indicate the specific in order to restate the question; second, employing the specific to reveal the general in order to answer the question.
First, citing the general to indicate the specific in order to restate the question (Commentary): Fourth, first, the direct explanation of the scriptural text; second, the refutation of others.
I. Refuting Erroneous Judgments. II. A Detailed Determination of the Sutra’s Intent. III. A Thorough Ascertainment of the Sutra’s Meaning. IV. Addressing Objections and Providing Explanations.
First, the direct explanation of the sutra text: The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner."

[Commentary: Fourth, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This has two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, [the explanation]. Regarding the first: he initially cites the general heading and specifies the particulars to restate the question.

Here, "subduing" (*parājaya*) serves as the general heading, while "abiding and cultivation" (*vihāra-bhāvanā*) serve as the particulars. That is to say, within abiding and cultivation, there is always subduing;
such is the intent of the Sūtra, which is why it specifically highlights "subduing."

[Commentary] Regarding the four points on the Tathāgata’s correct exposition, there are two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, [the elaboration]. First, he cites the general heading and specifies the particulars to restate the question.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase in the Sūtra, "All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas": Question: Previously, those suited to the teaching were cited as "good sons" (kulaputra). Why is this so?

"O Woman, up until this point in the response, why did you speak of 'Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva'? [She] replied: "When the Great Resolve (mahācitta) has not yet been generated, one is a worldling (pṛthagjana).
Once the resolve has already been generated, one is called a Bodhisattva. Subhūti raised the point by referring to the time when the resolve had not yet been generated;
therefore, he spoke of "sons of good family and daughters of good family. The World-Honored One answered by referring to the period after the resolve has already been generated.
He then said, "O Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. [Commentary:
From this point downward, there are four sections. First is the direct explanation of the sutra text. Since Subhūti’s questions consisted of three types, the Buddha now restates them;
however, he speaks only of "subduing," which is why this explanation is given. The first two phrases constitute the heading. This refers to abiding.

[The commentary] explains: "Below" refers to the subduing [of the mind] while dwelling in the realization that there is no self in the saving of sentient beings; "giving without abiding in signs" refers to the subduing [of the mind] while practicing.
For this reason, "subduing" serves as the general theme. That the intent of the Sūtra lies herein is as follows:
In this practice of abiding through the act of subduing, the text is concise yet its meaning is vast, clearly manifesting the profound and the mysterious.
Although one begins by abiding in cultivation, it culminates in subduing; because the realization of the meaning is so deep, it is simply referred to as "one."
△ Second, refuting the errors of others’ judgments.

[Commentary]: There are those who categorize this heading as "citing the latter to encompass the former. This renders the scriptural text extremely unstable and不畅 (unfluid), resulting in a reversal of logical order.
In the teachings of antiquity, there is only the principle of using the first to encompass the subsequent; I have never heard of using the latter to encompass the former.
[The commentary] "Incorporating the first" [refers to the following]. The section below titled "Two: Refuting the Errors of Others' Judgments" is from the *Dà yún shū* (Great Cloud Commentary).

○ *Qīnglóng* states that this "mentions the end to encompass the beginning," and its meaning is the same. ○ The section beginning with "Thereupon he causes... is the formal refutation of the error; the phrasing is not smooth or elegant.

This [text] should originally have encompassed the later meaning at the outset, using "form" (rūpa) as an illustration for "sound" (śabda) and so forth. Why, then, was that [later category] suddenly raised to include the initial one?
This causes the prose to lack fluency. Such lack of fluency stems from the structural division (ko), and is not the original intent of the scriptural text.
△ 3. Detailed Determination of the Sutra’s Intent.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, when examining the text of the sutra, there is no separate section that answers the question regarding subduing. Thus, one knows that subduing occurs within the context of abiding and cultivation;
causing all things to be free from marks is the answer to the question of subduing.
[Commentary] To elaborate on what follows: the three points clarify the intent of the sutra. Regarding "subduing within abiding and cultivation":

subduing within abiding refers to the fact that, in reality, there is no one who attains [the fruit]; subduing within cultivation refers to giving without abiding. This absence of attainment and absence of abiding is precisely the departure from marks (*animitta*).
Since this departure from marks applies universally to both abiding and cultivation, we know that "subduing" (*parājayati*) is the general principle.
△ Fourth, restating the objection and providing the resolution. [Commentary]:
The reason for not answering separately is that the primary tenet of this sutra is the departure from signs (*lakṣaṇa*). Departing from signs is precisely the subduing of the mind.

Since the fundamental intent is to clarify the subduing of the mind, it must be manifested by way of abiding and cultivation. Abiding, cultivation, and the subduing of the mind are fundamentally inseparable; therefore, [the answer is not given separately].
The eighteen stages of Asaṅga all involve the cultivation of abiding and the subduing of the mind.
[Commentary] The following four sections cite the objection and provide the resolution. First, the initial phrase cites the objection. The objection states:

Since Subhūti asked about the existence of a sequential order, and the cultivation of the stages and the subduing of the mind are clearly differentiated, why does the sutra not provide a specific answer? Rather...
Is it not the case that one cultivates the Middle Way while dwelling in dependence? Below this passage in the sutra, the correct application is shown.

To say that "detachment from characteristics" is for the purpose of subduing the mind—as in the previously cited passages on non-attainment and non-abiding—one must explain this by way of cultivation based on abiding.

If there is the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment and the practice of cultivation, then one may speak of having subdued the mind. If there is no cultivation based on abiding, what could be said of subduing and restraining the mind? This, then, pertains only to...

Abiding in cultivation to subdue discursive and deluded thoughts; therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally inseparable. ○ Regarding "Non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) below, the citation of scriptural evidence can be understood accordingly.

△ Second, revealing the general by means of the specific to answer the question, in two parts: first, answering the question regarding abiding and subduing the mind; second, answering... [the remainder of the text].
The Questions on Cultivating Practice to Subdue the Mind. The first response consists of four sections concerning the questions on abiding in the subduing of the mind:

first, the vast mind; second, the foremost mind; third, the constant mind; and fourth, the non-perverted mind. Regarding the first, the vast mind (the commentary): two parts. First, the explanation of the heading.
Second, the explanation of the enumeration. First, the explanation of the heading.
"All classes of sentient beings whatsoever.

[Commentary] Second, answering the question by manifesting the general through the particular. This has two parts. First, answering the question regarding abiding in the subduing of the mind. This has four parts. First, the vast mind.
The text has two sections. The first sentence is the heading; it refers to universally delivering those within the three realms.

[Commentary] Regarding the section in the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) that answers the question concerning "abiding securely" (*anurūpa*) and so forth: this refers to abiding securely in the four types of mind.
As Maitreya’s verse states: "Vast, foremost, and constant; its mind is not inverted; it dwells in a profound mind of benefit;
thus the merits of this vehicle are fulfilled. Based on this structural analysis, the four minds are enumerated here.
[Commentary] Below the first phrase of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), there are two parts. First, the explanation of the heading. Regarding "universally delivering all within the three realms":
this explains the meaning of "vast. All sentient beings do not transcend the three realms; only by universally delivering those within the three realms can it be called "vast.
If even a single sentient being were not delivered, it would not be vast. Therefore, the Sūtra’s heading states: "All sentient beings whatsoever."
This means "to encompass" or "to include. *Pudgala* (Sanskrit) is translated here as "sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because they arise from the combination of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they are called sentient beings. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"With volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) as the cause and the modes of birth—egg, womb, moisture, and transformation—as the conditions, the initial arising of the five aggregates is termed 'birth'. *Lèi* (class/type) refers to a category or species. That is to say...
The four types, such as those born from a womb or an egg.
△ Second, the explanation of the enumeration has three parts: first, the distinction of birth; second, the distinction of the basis; third, the distinction of the objective sphere.
Regarding the first, the distinction of birth, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the text; second, the resolution of difficulties. First, the explanation of the text.
Whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation.

[Commentary]: From "whether born from an egg" onwards, there are two listings. First, the distinctions in the manner of taking birth: gods and hell-beings are born by transformation; hungry ghosts may be born from a womb or by transformation;
humans and animals each have all four modes of birth. As for all other subtle beings—whether in water, on land, in the air, or elsewhere—it is impossible to categorize their specific types in detail.
[Commentary]: Regarding "if the egg falls," there are two interpretations presented. In the first [interpretation], there are two parts: first, the explanation of the text.

The beginning of receiving a life-force is called "receiving birth" (*upapatti*), which refers to the moment of initial arising. Because there are four distinct types—egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and so forth—it is termed "differentiation. That is to say:
being born from an egg, being born from a womb (*jarāyuja*), being born by depending on moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), and being born through transformation (*upapāduka*); therefore, they are not the same.
Indeed. ○ However, sentient beings of the three realms do not exceed the five destinies (*pañcagati*). By subsuming four [destinies] into five, they are likewise fully accounted for.

Therefore, the Commentary next states: "Transformation-born beings in the heavens and hells. This clarifies the progression from the narrow to the broad. ○ Regarding "transformation-born beings in the heavens and hells":
the heavens and hells consist exclusively of transformation birth; this is the most restricted category. ○ As for ghosts (*preta*), they include both womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*) and...
"Transformation" (huà) refers to the *pūtana* ghosts. This refers to the earth-roaming *rākṣasas* and the Mother of Ghosts (*Hārītī*).
All of these are born from the womb; thus, the Mother of Ghosts said to Maudgalyāyana: "Day and night, I give birth to five hundred sons each time.

As soon as they are born, I eat them myself. Though I exhaust them all, I am not satisfied. From this, we know that there are ghosts born from the womb. All others are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). [Section on] Humans.
Regarding the four types for each category of beings: among humans there are four. The mother Viśākhā gave birth to thirty-two children from eggs; ordinary humans are born from the womb;
the woman Āmrapālī was born from the moisture of an *āmra* tree; and those born by transformation are the humans at the beginning of the eon. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"When the merit of the second dhyāna is about to be exhausted, they descend to be born in Jambudvīpa. Animals likewise possess all four modes of birth.

Regarding this, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "The miraculously born (*aupapāduka*) garuḍa is able to devour dragons of the four modes of birth, even those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*).

Although birds and beasts differ, they are all subsumed within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). Furthermore, other beasts are all born from the womb (*jarāyuja*), while other birds are all born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*).
Regarding "all other minute [beings] and so forth," as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space..."
In the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, there are all manner of sentient beings with various distinctions, namely:
those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation; some who dwell and live depending on earth, water, fire, or wind;
and some who dwell and live depending on space or upon various plants and trees—beings of diverse species and diverse physical forms, and so forth, as it says:
All the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans—including those without feet, with four feet, or with many feet;

those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—since there is no separate passage for them in this present sutra, one must not fabricate empty words.
Therefore, the commentary concludes by stating that their various categories cannot be fully enumerated.
△ Second, resolving the objection. [Commentary]:
Regarding "the egg-born is inferior and placed first," there are two explanations. First, in terms of the object: that which possesses more conditions is primary.
Second, in terms of the mind: they follow the sequence from the root to the end.

[Commentary] "The egg-born is inferior, etc. This addresses two difficulties. One should raise the objection: "The egg-born is the most inferior; why is it placed first? The transformation-born is the most superior;
why does it stand at the end? The second explanation below resolves this. Regarding "in terms of the realm, etc.":

this means that the egg-born necessarily possesses the womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. This is because before birth one must dwell in a womb, and within the womb there is necessarily moisture; [furthermore,] that which did not exist suddenly...

Regarding "transformative birth" (*nirmāṇa*): womb-birth (*jarāyuja*) necessarily includes moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*) and transformative birth; moisture-born necessarily includes transformative birth; but transformative birth does not necessarily include the others.

This is because [the latter] arises suddenly from non-existence. Thus, each preceding category necessarily possesses each subsequent one, whereas each subsequent category does not necessarily possess each preceding one;
therefore, they are arranged in this order. Regarding "according to the mind, from the fundamental," etc.: this refers to the fundamental cause of sentient beings.
The arising of karma (*karma-samutthāna*). The consciousness of karma (*karma-vijñāna*) is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

It is in union with the original nature (*prakṛti*), such that subject and object are not yet differentiated, remaining in a state of chaotic indistinctness like an egg. This "egg" refers to the *aṇḍaja* (egg-born) mode of birth. Thus, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* says: "Break the egg of ignorance and exhaust the river of afflictions. Ignorance initiates karma;
it resides within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as an embryo. Birth occurs through moisture (*saṃsvedaja*). At the time of birth, it emerges from nothingness...
Yet, there are also those who are suddenly transformed through conditioned means; for this reason, they are placed in this sequence.
△ Second, the distinction of the basis:
whether with form or without form.
[Commentary] Second, the distinction of the basis (*āśraya*). There are the four dhyānas of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the four emptinesses (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.

of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). [Record] Regarding the "distinction of the basis": the basis refers to the body of sentient beings. Since the meaning of the basis differs—specifically, as the basis for the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—it is called a "distinction.
Therefore, the Commentary subsequently states "the realm of form and the formless realm," and so forth. "The realm of form" refers to...

Form constitutes the body; for those without form, the four aggregates constitute the body. Furthermore, the realm of form consists of the four dhyānas (and so forth), while the formless realm consists of the four emptinesses (and so forth).
Because such categories differ, it is said that there is a distinction in their bases.
Question: As it is said in a sutra, when the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the gods of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) shed tears like rain.
Since they shed tears, how can they be "formless"? Answer: What is called "formless" means that they lack the form produced by karmic results;
it does not mean they lack the form produced as the result of meditative concentration (dhyāna). Therefore, there is no contradiction.
△ Third, the distinction of objective spheres (*ālambana-viśeṣa*).
[These are: with perception (*saṃjñin*), without perception (*asaṃjñin*), and neither with nor without perception (*naiva-saṃjñin-nāsaṃjñin*).

【Commentary】 Regarding the third, the distinction of objective spheres: Guṇadeva says that "with perception" refers to the two stages of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). "Without perception" refers to...
Then there is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). That which is not equal [to these] is the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
[Commentary: Regarding the distinction of their objects (*viṣaya*): although they are called "objects," the intent clarifies the four spheres beginning with space.
As for the two spheres of space and consciousness, these are the first and second heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The sphere of nothingness is the third heaven.
Furthermore, "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to the fourth dhyāna heaven.

Because it lacks coarse perception yet possesses subtle perception, and because it is the pinnacle of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), it is called the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*). Question:

Since both of the lower realms possess form (*rūpa*), why is only the four dhyānas designated as the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Moreover, within the Form Realm, there is also a heaven named "Non-Perception" (*asaṃjñin*).

Why is it that only the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is designated as "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*)? Answer: When the three realms are considered as a whole, they do not exceed five categories, namely:

desire (*kāma*), form (*rūpa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), non-perception (*asaṃjñā*), and neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*). However, this [sphere of nothingness] is not the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This is restricted solely to the single heaven of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Although a single heaven in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) is named "Non-perception," it is already generally designated as the Form Realm by virtue of its majority;
therefore, only the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is pointed out as "Non-perception.

Regarding the remaining three matters, when compared from the two spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness down to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are differences in the breadth and narrowness of their presence or absence. Namely:
The desire realm possesses all three [characteristics]. The form realm is without desire. The formless realm possesses only perception;

because it lacks both form and desire, it is given the name "possessing perception. Although the form realm does possess perception, it is designated by the term "possessing form" to avoid confusion with the higher [formless] realm.
Although the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) also includes form-perception (*rūpasaṃjñā*), it has already occupied two names [in the classification of realms].

To distinguish it from those [higher realms], it is simply called the "desire realm. In the lowermost level, one must necessarily possess the uppermost; however, the uppermost does not include the lowermost.
Thus, the fundamental basis for establishing these names lies herein. It is like three people: one understands the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras; another understands the Sūtras...
Regarding the Vinaya: one person understands only the Vinaya; thus, they are distinguished by being given a specific title, as can be understood from the various instances [in the texts].

Furthermore: because the objects of the three desires and the five exquisite desires are superior, it is the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); because subtle and exquisite forms are superior, it is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); and because perception and mind are superior, it is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Consequently, "desire" pertains only to the Desire Realm; "form" extends through two realms; "perception" pervades all three realms; and "non-perception" extends to the upper [Formless] realms.
The three realms [of existence] are distinct from the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" realm, which is restricted to the single upper realm;
this differs from the interpretation provided by Gōngdéshī.
△ Second, the first mind (Commentary): This has two parts. First, the explanation of the text; second, resolving difficulties. First, the explanation of the text.
"I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.
[Commentary] Regarding the two [meanings of the term]: "I" in the sutra refers to the Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on *bodhi*; here, the Buddha is speaking of them.

As for *nirvāṇa*, it was translated as "extinction" (*mie-du*) during the Qin dynasty. In this current sutra, the upper character is the Sanskrit term and the lower character is the Chinese (Tang) term; therefore, it says "and [bring them to] extinction."
To translate it: if one were to provide the full Sanskrit phonetics, it should be *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which means "Great Perfect Quiescence.

In the current sūtras and śāstras, it is most commonly referred to as *nirvāṇa*. However, according to the explanation in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), there are four kinds of nirvāṇa:
first, *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), which is possessed equally by both ordinary beings and sages; second, *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).

This is because, due to the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there is a body that serves as the basis for suffering; whereas in the state of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), one transcends birth and death, and suffering no longer has a basis.
However, the Hīnayāna defines "without remainder" as the extinguishing of the physical body and the cessation of consciousness.

There are three types of "remainder": first, the remainder of afflictions; second, the remainder of karma; and third, the remainder of karmic fruition. In the Mahāyāna, however, the ultimate jewel-land (*ratnasthāna*) is taken as [the state of] "without remainder."
There is no remainder. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The exhaustion of the afflictions of the four stages of dwelling is called 'with remainder' (*sopadhiśeṣa*);

the exhaustion of the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling is called 'without remainder' (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). The four [types of] non-abiding consist in the union of compassion and wisdom, because one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] Second, the foremost mind. This is precisely the *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana), which is not shared with the two vehicles; hence it is called "foremost.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "This is precisely," etc.: this refers to the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) of the Mahayana, specifically the *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* among the four types of nirvana.
That is to say, it does not abide in the *parināmika-maraṇa* (death through transformation) of Bodhisattvas, nor does it abide in the *prahāṇa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of extinction) of the two vehicles.
This is precisely the true state of non-abiding, which is termed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

If this were the "without remainder" of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), it would be no different from the mere cessation and diminution of sentient beings; however, the present case is not like that, and is therefore said to be "not shared with the two vehicles.

To say it is "not shared" means it is not the third of those four [types of nirvāṇa]; thus, while the words are the same, the meaning differs. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "If one attains Buddhahood..."
At that time, one will be endowed with the thirty-two marks. Only then can it be said that [defilements] are forever extinguished without remainder;

this means that both obstacles are entirely exhausted and one is forever free from the two deaths. Regarding the first [verse], the intent of the verse’s conclusion returns to the meaning of the title of the section.
The meaning is that if it were not a "remainderless" state of non-abiding, how could Maitreya designate it as the "first"?

Is it the mind? △ Second, resolving two difficulties: first, resolving the difficulty regarding the five natures; second, resolving the difficulty regarding the eight difficulties. First, resolving the difficulty regarding the five natures:
first, the objection; second, the resolution. First, the objection.
[Commentary] Asaṅga asks: "For what reason is this aspiration for the meaning of 'unattainability' [formulated]?

[Record] The first two phrases below [the name of] Asaṅga constitute the objection. The intent is as follows: Since all sentient beings differ in their five natures (*pañca-gotra*), how can they all enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?
Furthermore, three and a half portions of sentient beings cannot attain Buddhahood; therefore, he says "no."
The meaning of "attainable.
△ Second, the comprehensive [explanation].
【Commentary】 Because it is subsumed within birth.
[Commentary] Regarding "those encompassed by birth," this is the answer. This is the formal proof (*pramāṇa*) established by Asanga to demonstrate that all can attain liberation.
The formal proof should be stated as follows: "The three-quarters and a half of sentient beings" is the subject (*dharmin*); "they will certainly all attain Buddhahood" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because it is subsumed under the category of "arising from causes. This is analogous to one portion of sentient beings. The intention is as follows:

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that all who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas; the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says that those with the Buddha-nature and those without it equally achieve the Way of the Buddha.
This is the meaning of "attainability," yet [Huì]’ān claims it is unattainable.
△ Second, the two difficulties regarding the eight obstacles (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). First, the difficulty; second, the resolution. Regarding the first difficulty:

[Commentary] It further states: "If one is born among the egg-born, moisture-born, the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), or at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), how can it be said that one universally enters [the Dharma]?"
[Commentary] It is further stated: "The egg-born and moisture-born [beings]" refers to the difficulty of the birth-states. The egg-born and moisture-born refer to the difficulty of the animal realm;

the Unconscious Heaven and the Peak of Existence refer to the difficulty of the long-lived heavens. Although only two locations are mentioned, the intent encompasses all eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). The eight difficulties are:

the three miserable realms (*durgati*), the northern continent (Uttarakuru), the long-lived heavens, being born before or after a Buddha, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence, and being devoid of sense organs, and so forth. These constitute the difficulties.
The meaning is this: if it were a place of difficulty, one could not be delivered there; how then could all be human? △ Second, the comprehensive explanation.
[Commentary]: There are three causes and conditions: first, those born in places of difficulty await the proper time; second, those born in places that are not difficult have not yet...
Those who are ripened are so for the sake of further ripening; those already ripened are for the sake of liberation.
[Commentary] "There are three causes and conditions," etc., is the answer. Regarding "dwelling in difficult places while awaiting the proper time": this also serves to establish their seeds.
The intention is that sentient beings in difficult places cannot remain permanently fixed there; once they reach a place that is not difficult, they are delivered and liberated.

If one succeeds in establishing the seeds, whether sooner or later, they must necessarily be brought to maturity. Thus, one should give rise to a vast mind so that there is nothing left unaccomplished.
As for those who are not in difficult circumstances, although they have not yet been delivered, one should nonetheless cause them to reach maturity; once they are matured, it can be known.
This is roughly the same as the previous meaning of protecting and entrusting [the teachings].
△ Third, the Mind of Constancy.
"In this way, although immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings are brought to *nirvāṇa*, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary] Third, the Mind of Constancy. First, because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; second, because of the identity of essence. As the Treatise says: "One's own self is *nirvāṇa*; there is no..."
[They are] distinct from sentient beings. (3) Because they are fundamentally quiescent; (4) because they are without mentation;

(5) because they are the Dharma-realm. [Commentary: Regarding the three points, the sub-commentary states: First, regarding "emptiness of nature": sentient beings arise through conditions; that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature, and is therefore emptiness itself.
○ Regarding "identical essence": this is because they share the same single nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "That is to say, according to reality..."
One knows that all sentient beings are, in their suchness (*tathatā*), equal to one's own body, for there is no distinction between them.
The commentary below cites scriptural evidence; this statement is phrased inversely, and it should rather be said: "The liberation of sentient beings is no different from one's own self;

how could one then give rise to the notion of 'other' toward one's own self? As for "primordially quiescent" (*mūla-śānta*), it means that characteristics are inherently exhausted and do not depend upon extinction.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "All sentient beings are the mark of quiescent extinction; they do not undergo further extinction. Question: What is the difference between this and the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)?
Answer: The former merely identifies [beings] with emptiness; this, however, means that they have been Buddha from the very beginning.

To become Buddha is to enter nirvana; therefore, it is called "original quiescence. It should be understood that the former is shallow and the latter is deep. Regarding "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*): if there is thought, then...
There are sentient beings. Just as when there is no cataract, the flowers in the sky do not appear.
Regarding the "Dharmadhātu": it is the one true Dharmadhātu, equal and without differentiation. How could one perceive the marks of self and other within it? Thus the verse says:
"In the equal and true Dharmadhātu, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. These five points above are from the text of the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*; however, among them, the first—
The first [case] refers to the object; the second refers to both the subject and the object; the fourth refers solely to the subject; and the fifth encompasses both the root and the branches.
Generally speaking, the meaning is as follows: if one perceives sentient beings as having something to be saved and consequently gives rise to weariness, one will be unable to save them constantly;
conversely, if one does not do so, then it is constant. Furthermore, regarding saving or not saving, if one’s mind remains non-dual, this is called "constancy. Therefore...

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "If one transforms sentient beings without giving rise to the thought of transformation, nor the thought of non-transformation, nor the thought of neither-transforming-nor-not-transforming, that transformation is truly great.
△ Fourth, the mind free from perversions.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
[Commentary] Regarding the four [sections], as for why the Sūtra asks "Why is this?", the intended inquiry is: even if there were sentient beings to be saved whom one perceives.
"What is this encounter? Next, the general explanation says: "If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, they are not a bodhisattva.
This is an explanation by way of contrapositive negation. Its meaning is: one who is a true bodhisattva must certainly lack a self as the agent of deliverance;
how could they further perceive the existence of sentient beings who attain extinction?

[Commentary] Regarding the fourth, the mind free from perversions: the *Śāstra* states that it is because one is far removed from the characteristics of sentient beings who rely upon the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
[Record] "Far removed from sentient beings who rely upon the view of a self-body": "relying" (*niśraya*) is a synonym for the view of a self-body; it is also called "continuity.

In Sanskrit it is *satkāya*, which here means "view of a self-body. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the notions of a self (*ātman*), a person (*pudgala*), a life-principle (*jīva*), and so on. This...
Regarding the term "view of self" (satkāyadṛṣṭi): because this view arises based upon the body, it is said that sentient beings take the characteristics of the view of self as their basis.
Furthermore, since the view of self is the root from which all other views arise, one now distances oneself from them all;
thus, they are referred to as "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).

[Commentary] Asaṅga says: Having already severed the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), one attains the mark of equality in one's own practice; thus, one gains faith and understanding in the equality of self and others.

[Record] Regarding "having already severed," etc.: internally there is no self, which means there is no self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The absence of self-characteristic is precisely equality. Equality...
"Equality" is precisely the meaning of emptiness. Regarding "faith and understanding," this is comparing oneself to others.

Because there is no intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) within, one attains the absence of extrinsic characteristics (*paralakṣaṇa*) without. The character "zhong" (middle) and the character "gu" (because/therefore) indicate the reason:
since there are neither self- nor other-characteristics, self and other are equal. Master Zhi said: "Because my own body is empty, all dharmas are empty. [This applies to] the thousand varieties.
All myriad species are entirely the same.
[Commentary] This reveals that when the mind is subdued and gathers its scattered thoughts, even the perception of sentient beings does not arise, just like those illusory flames.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "manifesting subjugation, etc.": according to Asaṅga’s treatise, one should abide in the vast and supreme, cultivate the constant mind, and practice non-inversion.
Within this single section, all three meanings are complete; however, the text of this specific section primarily corresponds to the meaning of subjugation.
Therefore, it says, "manifesting subjugation, etc. ○ Regarding "non-reversal" (*avivarta*): "reversal" (*vivarta*) refers to...
The meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) refers to the non-arising of views such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). That "I do not arise" is precisely the meaning of subduing the mind.

*Er-yan* (爾炎) is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Mother of Wisdom. This is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is able to give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
therefore, it is called the Mother of Wisdom. Although fundamental wisdom internally realizes the ultimate truth, it lacks a subject that realizes it.
With such a mind, one attains wisdom hereafter; although one externally delivers sentient beings, there is no thought of a self who delivers them.
Therefore, it is said to be "like a flame. Using the mind in this manner is called the non-perverted mind; to act otherwise is indeed perversion.
△ Second, the response to the five questions concerning the practice for subduing the mind. First, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary;

fourth, the manifestation of benefits; fifth, the exhortation to practice. First, the general heading (Commentary): two parts. First, the explanation of the text; second, the clarification of the intent. First, the explanation of the text.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon (*dharma*). [Commentary:

Second, the answer to the question regarding the cultivation of practice and the subduing of the mind has five parts. First, the general heading: “on phenomena” (*dharmeṣu*) refers to the collective indication of all phenomena.
"There should be no inferiority" correctly clarifies the practice.
[Commentary] The second response regarding the five aspects of practice consists of: first, the general heading.

○ The *Sūtra* states that "the Dharma is universally designated" because the six objects—form, sound, and so forth—are collectively termed "Dharma. Therefore, the Wei translation of the *Sūtra* says: "One does not dwell upon phenomena."
△ Second, the general meaning, which has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. First, the question.
[Sūtra Commentary] Question: Regarding the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva, why is only one mentioned?

[Sub-commentary] "The myriad practices of a Bodhisattva" refers to practices for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others, such as the practice of phenomena (*dharma-caryā*) and the practice of principle (*tattva-caryā*), and so forth.
It is immeasurable and boundless. The mention of "ten thousand" here is merely citing a large number for the sake of illustration.
△ Second, the answer has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the corroborative explanation. First, the direct explanation.
[Commentary] Answer: The myriad practices do not transcend the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The six perfections are collectively termed "giving" (*dāna*).
[Record] Regarding the collective term "giving": the first refers to the giving of material requisites (*āmiṣa-dāna*); the second and third refer to the giving of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*);
and the fourth, fifth, and sixth perfections are all termed the giving of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
△ Second, the proof and explanation has two parts: first, citing verses to prove the inclusion; second, explaining the reason for the inclusion.

First, citing verses to prove the inclusion: [Commentary] Therefore, a verse says: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) includes six: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma; herein, one, two, and three."
This is called the stage of dwelling in practice.
[Commentary] The phrase "The verse says, below" introduces the citation of a verse for explanation. Within this, the first two lines state the heading;
the third line provides the correlation; and the fourth line offers the conclusion. Regarding "one, two, three": this means that one encompasses one, two encompass two, and three encompass three.
Thus, the three types of giving are the means of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), while the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are that which is included.
△ Second, explaining the reason for this inclusion.
[Commentary] As Asaṅga says: "If there is no diligence (*vīrya*), one will become weary and thus unable to preach the Dharma. If there is no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),"
That is to say, one preaches the Dharma with a defiled mind, craving gain, fame, offerings, and respect; or, lacking wisdom, one preaches the Dharma in a distorted manner.

[Commentary] The section beginning with "Wu-zhu" (Asaṅga) summarizes the underlying reasons. While the meanings of the first two types of giving are manifest, the meaning of the gift of Dharma is obscure;

therefore, it is clarified here in the sub-commentary. ○ However, to explain briefly: "Material support" (*āmiṣadāna*) refers to external wealth. "Fearlessness" (*abhayadāna*) arises from maintaining...
Because of precepts and patience, one has no intention to harm living beings; even if one encounters an enemy, one does not seek revenge.
○ Regarding the absence of diligence and so forth, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "In all wholesome matters, the mind does not slacken or regress;
one establishes a firm resolve and remains far removed from cowardice and weakness. ○ Regarding the absence of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth, the following text asks: "What is..."
When a person expounds the teaching, they do not grasp at signs. Suchness is immovable; to be immovable is the meaning of being unstained.

To direct the mind toward it is already a deviation, and this is still termed "staining. How much more so for greed, faith, reverence, fame, profit, and the like—how could these not be transgressions?
Regarding the phrase "if one lacks wisdom," etc.: to describe fire as wet, water as hot, earth as moving, and wind as solid is called perversion (*viparyāsa*).
If one speaks of phenomena as they truly are, and speaks of principles as they truly are, then it is not inverted. By this, the single giving is opened into the three kinds of giving;
the three kinds of giving are opened into the six perfections; and the six perfections are opened into the myriad practices. The myriad practices do not transcend the six perfections;
the six perfections do not transcend the three kinds of giving; and the three kinds of giving do not transcend the single kind of *dāna*. Therefore, this—
In the middle [section], it speaks only of giving.
△ Second, the detailed explanation (according to the *Sūtra Commentary*): three parts. First, the heading; second, the enumeration; third, the explanation. That is to say:
"One gives without dwelling on form; one gives without dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena."
[Commentary] Second, the detailed explanation.
[Record] Second, the detailed explanation.
△ First, the heading.
[Commentary] The root treatise refers only to three matters.
[Record] Regarding the commentary’s reference to the three matters: although the six objects differ, they are collectively comprised of only these three matters.
△ Second, the enumeration.
[Commentary] This refers to one's own person, the repayment of kindness, and the karmic fruit.
[Record] This refers to the following enumeration.
△ Third, the explanation of the two [sections]: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the heading.
[Commentary] The verse says: "One's own person, the repayment of kindness, and the karmic reward—none of these are clung to.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "The verse says" and below: this explains the first two lines as the thesis. As for "none of these are clung to": "these" (si) refers to these three matters;
it means not allowing attachment to these three things.
△ Second, the explanation. [Commentary]:
"Guarding oneself and not giving; preventing others from seeking other matters. [Record]:
The following two phrases provide the explanation. ○ "Guarding oneself and not giving" explains the aforementioned "one's own person. This is because of attachment to self...
Body. Because one does not practice giving. ○ "Seeking extraordinary matters" explains the aforementioned fruit of repaying kindness.
This is not the correct practice of a bodhisattva; therefore, it is called an "extraordinary matter. ○ "Repaying kindness" refers to recompensing past favors.
"Fruit of retribution" refers to looking toward future rewards. Not giving with one's own body pertains to the present. "Guarding" also implies prevention. The meaning is as follows:

To cause one to guard against these three types of worldly phenomena so as to be entirely unattached to them is precisely the practice of non-abiding in form and the other aggregates, which is also giving.
△ Third, the general conclusion (Commentary): Two parts. First, the direct explanation of the sutra text; second, the refutation of erroneous interpretations. First, the direct explanation.
The scriptural text has two parts: first, pointing back to the preceding treatise; second, clarifying the intent of the present sutra.
First, pointing back to the preceding treatise: [Commentary] Third, the summary. Previously, only three matters were pointed out.
[Commentary] Regarding the three [categories] among the four, the intent of the preceding passage is as follows: the first three matters do not exhaustively encompass all cases.

This does not preclude the existence of those who practice giving without being attached to themselves, without being attached to karmic retribution, and without acting out of gratitude; such individuals are nonetheless not "non-abiding."
△ Second, revealing the intent of the present sutra, in two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of evidence. First, the direct explanation:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner: not dwelling upon signs."
[Commentary] Now, the emptiness and existence of both mind and objects are entirely eliminated down to their subtlest levels.
[Record] Regarding the section beginning with "Now": this clarifies the intent of the present sutra. *Heart* (citta) refers to the subjective perceiver; *objects* (viṣaya) refer to the perceived.

*Existence* (bhāva) encompasses both mind and objects, as well as whatever remains uncollected by these categories—all of which are subsumed under the term "existence. As for *emptiness* (śūnyatā): [it refers to that which is devoid of such characteristics].

This refers to being detached from the characteristics of mind, objects, and so forth. Question: While abiding in the principle of objects may involve a contradiction, what further fault is there in detaching from the mind?
Answer: The two dharmas of emptiness and existence are established through mutual dependence. Both existence and emptiness are, in themselves, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
One falls into a single characteristic; this is not the eternal mind. Therefore, all such [notions] must be eliminated. Regarding the "thorough removal of even the subtlest":
regardless of whether the mind or its objects are empty or existent, to give rise to thought or stir a念 (nian) is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma.
For this reason, everything must be entirely removed and discarded. One must simply act with a mind of equanimity when giving, without giving rise to discrimination. Only then...
This constitutes non-abiding. Question: If this is so, then the arising of thought and the movement of mind would not be non-abiding.
Furthermore, the mental activities of sentient beings are spontaneous and impermanent; if one waits for them to correspond [to a state], there will ultimately be no opportunity.

If one does not practice giving at all, it fails to become a cause for Buddhahood. Yet, if one practices giving, one immediately falls into abiding in signs (*nimitta*). Thus, whether one proceeds or retreats, it is impossible. How is this?
What is the matter? The answer is: Those who seek bodhi must necessarily practice giving. When first practicing giving, it is difficult to be immediately in accord with the principle.
One must apply the mind and employ skillful means to follow along, allowing thoughts to arise spontaneously while consciously distancing oneself from [unwholesome] intentions.
By applying the mind for a long time, one will naturally and spontaneously attain accord with the principle. From the subtle to the manifest, one gradually becomes in accord in this manner.
As stated in the *Awakening of Faith* regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*): it transcends words and names, and is beyond the reach of mental objects. Consequently, a question arises:
"If this is the meaning, how can sentient beings accord with it and thereby enter into it? Therefore, the answer is given:
"If one knows that although all phenomena are contemplated, there is neither a contempler nor anything to be contemplated, this is called 'accordance. If..."
To be free from discursive thought is called "attaining entry" (and so forth).
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence.
[Commentary] Thus the verse says: "Far removed from the mind that grasps at signs. The Treatise says: "One does not perceive the gift, the recipient, or the giver."
Asuṅga says: "Do not dwell in the perception of marks.

[Commentary] The verse beginning with "as it says below" cites scriptural evidence for the aforementioned meaning; thus one knows that whether the mind and its objects are empty or existent, they are all without exception nothing but marks (*nimitta*).

The *Śāstra* states below: By means of abandoning the two attachments and the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), it explains the aforementioned "freedom from marks. The object given is the dharma; the giver and the receiver are persons.
Now, since none of these are perceived, one is free from the two attachments, which is termed the "two emptinesses" (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

When both [types of] emptiness are abandoned, this is the essential emptiness of the three wheels. "Wheels" is a metaphor; like the wheels of a cart, it is only when the interior is empty that movement can occur.
Therefore, Laozi said: "When it is empty, it possesses the utility of a chariot. When the three entities are empty in essence, they can bring about the fruit of Buddhahood;
when the three entities are substantial in essence, one falls into the mundane world. This, then, is using the wheel of signlessness to destroy the signs of the three realms of existence.

It transcends both the mundane and the supramundane. ○ Regarding "Non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) below: this merely serves to corroborate the meaning established above. "Marks" (*nimitta*) refers to the objective realm;
"conception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mind.
△ Second, the refutation of erroneous judgments.
[Commentary]: Some take this concluding passage as the answer to the question regarding subduing [the mind]. This is incorrect.

The initial thesis, the subsequent explanation, and the final conclusion all state that there is "no abiding" (*an-āśraya*). These all pertain to the meaning of subduing within the context of cultivation.
Why then do you suddenly and arbitrarily judge this concluding passage to be the answer to a separate question?
[Commentary] "There are some people," and so forth, refers to the refutation of erroneous judgments as found in the text.
△ Fourth, Manifesting the Benefits (Sūtra Commentary): This section has two parts: first, explaining the meaning of the text; second, specifically analyzing the intent of the metaphors.
[Commentary] Fourth, the Sūtra on Manifesting the Benefits: This also separately resolves one doubt. It should be stated that if there is no abiding, then there is no merit or virtue.
This is a doubt. Among the twenty-seven doubts in the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, this is the first. It is called the "doubt regarding the merit of non-abiding.
For now, it is not taken as one of the major categories of doubt. Why? Because within the context of answering questions, it is a doubt that is analyzed in detail.
Thus, the treatise says: "Because one has attained the subduing of the mind, the benefits of giving are explained next."
Because the perfection of giving is achieved by one who does not dwell on signs. Subsequently, the force of the text begins with:
"From this point onward, all the sūtras manifest the severing of the arising of doubt. [The commentary] has two parts: first, the analysis and explanation of the meaning of the text.
△ First section: Explaining the meaning of the text, in two parts. First, explaining the inquiry; second, explaining the response.
First, explaining the inquiry: "For what reason?

[Commentary] Fourth, manifesting the benefits. Regarding the first phrase, "subtle" (*sūkṣma*): the treatise says, "If one is separated from the conceptualization of signs such as giving, how can it be accomplished?"

Regarding the merit of giving. [Commentary: "If one is free from... and so forth explains the subtle meaning. Because the Wei translation says "not dwelling on the perception of signs," a doubt arises:
"If the perception of giving exists, then there is the cause of giving; because there is the cause of giving, there is the fruit of giving. Since [if that were so] there would be no giving...
If one lacks such a thought, there is no cause for giving. When the cause itself is not established, how can the fruit be realized? It is like lending money that must be repaid;
if it is forgotten, who will return it? This doubt is the same as performing an act of giving while in a state of neutral (avyākṛta) mind.

△ Second, the explanation of the explanation has three parts: first, the explanation by way of Dharma; second, the explanation by way of analogy; third, the application of the Dharma. First, the explanation by way of Dharma:
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit and virtue is inconceivable and immeasurable.

[Commentary] From "If a bodhisattva" onwards is the explanation. This section has three parts. First is the explanation by means of the Dharma: for those who doubt that there is no merit, it is used to sever that doubt through the inconceivable.
[Commentary] It is the same within the Dharma. That which cannot be measured is so because it is the merit of this signless giving;
therefore, it cannot be measured.
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the space in the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No, World-Honored One."
[Commentary] "The East" and below are explained through analogy; this is understandable.
[Record] Within the analogy, the east is the foremost of all directions; therefore, it is explained first. The south, west, and north follow in sequence by way of example.
○ Both the Dharma and the analogy are alike and cannot be measured. The meaning is that it does not mean there is no space. This...
The meaning of "mutual correspondence" lies within their union.
△ Third, the Conjunction of Dharmas:
Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without abiding in signs is likewise likewise inconceivable.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "The Bodhisattva has no abiding mark" and below, this is the application to the Dharma.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the meaning of the metaphors.
[Commentary] As for "empty space," Wuzhuo says: "It is like empty space, which has three causes and conditions: first, it pervades everything..."
First, it is the locus because merit arises within the state that is neither abiding nor non-abiding. Second, it is because it is vast, expansive, lofty, and sublime.
Third, it is because it is inexhaustible, ultimate, and without end.

[Commentary] "Below 'empty space'": this is the second section, which specifically explains the purport of the metaphors. "Pervading all places" means that within both the material (*rūpa*) and the immaterial (*arūpa*), there is emptiness.
"Below 'abiding'": this is the application to the Dharma. Within both the abiding and the non-abiding, there is merit.
That is to say, by abiding, one proximately experiences the merit of the ten kings, while distantly summoning the merit of non-abiding toward Bodhi. Furthermore, one proximately attains...

The merit residing in the form-body (rūpakāya) is temporary; the merit of the non-abiding dharma-body (dharmakāya) is far-reaching. Although emptiness is signless, it does not mean that emptiness is non-existent;
although merit is non-abiding, it does not mean that merit is non-existent. Second, "vast and expansive" means that it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions.

"High" means vertically reaching the limits of the three periods of time; "great" means horizontally and vertically encompassing all things. As explained above, both the Dharma and the analogy are "great. Regarding their excellence:
the analogy is that it cannot be destroyed by the three calamities; the Dharma is that it does not shift through the four marks of existence. Third:
"Exhaustless" (*akṣaya*) and "ultimately inexhaustible" (*atyantākṣaya*) are essentially one and the same meaning. However, while worlds have an end, empty space is infinite;

that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) has an end, while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is exhaustless. The meaning of the three kinds of permanence resides therein. Generally speaking, the intent is this:
the merit of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-puṇya*) pervades all things; the merit of non-abiding is lofty, vast, and preeminent.
The merit of abiding in this is ultimately inexhaustible, like empty space, beyond the reach of thought, and commensurate with the Dharma-realm;
thus it attains such a state. Since its benefit is so manifest, what more is there to doubt?
△ V. Summary and Exhortation.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide in accordance with what has been taught.
[Commentary] V. Summary and Exhortation.
[Commentary] Regarding the five [points], the Sūtra states only: "One should abide as instructed. Question: Previously, one was told not to abide; here, one is told to abide.
Between abiding and non-abiding, which is correct and which is incorrect? Answer: The previous instruction to not abide refers to the application of the mind.

This instruction to abide refers to abiding in non-abiding. To abide while not abiding is to abide in true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is like a bird that does not abide in the sky, yet is able to abide there.
Emptiness. If one dwells in emptiness, one does not dwell in emptiness. Therefore, the Wei translation of the Sūtra says: "One should simply practice giving in this manner.

[Commentary] Having answered the three questions according to this, it would be appropriate for the sūtra to conclude here and enter the *parīndanā* (circulation) section. Based on emptiness, [the thought of] giving arises.
In response to the Tathāgata’s answers, doubts arose; thus, he spoke in order to sever them.

Once severed, they arose again, increasing and proliferating until, through the exhaustion of attachments and the removal of doubts, the section concluded at twenty-seven segments. For this reason, there follows further scriptural text below.
Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: A Collated Edition of the Sections and Notes, Fascicle Four;
Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: A Collated Edition of the Sections and Notes, Fascicle Five.
Master Guifeng of the Tang Dynasty: Commentary.
Recorded by the Great Master Changshui of the Song Dynasty;
the junior scholar, the monk Dabin of Yunqi in Guhang, has categorized this.
△ Second, following the traces to sever doubts (the commentary): Part One, dividing the text according to the treatise; Part Two, categorizing and explaining according to the treatise.
First, the text is divided according to the treatise.
[Commentary: Second, following the traces to sever doubts. The treatise states: "From this point onward, it demonstrates the severing of the arising of doubt.
Within this section, there are twenty-seven divisions of severance.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary (shū) has two parts, beginning with "following the traces" (nyaku-seki). This section has two parts: first, the division of the text according to the treatise.
Regarding "following the traces to sever doubts": this means following the traces of the preceding words to sever the sentiments of doubt.

Although the sūtra does not explicitly contain words of doubt, they lie latent within the text; therefore, it simply says "severing" rather than "arising. This is likewise the case in Maitreya’s verses.

Thus, the verse says: "In the matter of disciplining them, one remains far removed from a mind that grasps at signs, severs various doubts, and likewise prevents the arising of conceptualizing thoughts.
Regarding "manifestation," there are two meanings: first, it refers to provisional designations made within emptiness;
second, it refers to pointing out and making manifest.

△ Second, the detailed analysis according to the treatise (the commentary is divided into twenty-seven sections): 1. Resolving doubts regarding the characteristics of abiding while practicing giving with the aspiration for Buddhahood;
2. Resolving doubts concerning lack of faith due to the profundity of both cause and effect; 3. Resolving doubts as to how that which is signless can be explained.
4. To sever the doubt that the Śrāvakas’ attainment of the fruit involves grasping. 5. To sever the doubt that Śākyamuni’s taking up [the teachings] from Dīpaṃkara involves grasping.
6. To sever the doubt that adorning the buddha-field contradicts non-grasping. 7. To sever the doubt that receiving and attaining the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) involves grasping. 8.

To sever the doubt that maintaining and preaching [the teachings] does not liberate one from the fruits of suffering. 9. To sever the doubt that the ability to realize [emptiness] implies a lack of essence and thus is not a cause. 10. To sever the doubt regarding suchness...

10. The doubt that [all things] universally exist, yet there is neither attainment nor non-attainment. 11. The doubt that although one has severed [delusions], one dwells in cultivation and subjugation, leading to the suspicion that this is "self. 12.

The doubt that although one has severed [delusions], there is still a cause for Buddhahood, leading to the suspicion that there is a "Bodhisattva. 13. The doubt that if one severs [delusions], there is no cause, and thus no Buddha-dharma. 14.
The doubt that if one severs [delusions], there is no person to deliver sentient beings or adorn the lands. 15. The doubt that all Buddhas do not perceive all dharmas. 10. (End)
16. To sever the doubt regarding the inversion of the mind concerning merit and virtue; 17. To sever the doubt as to how there can be marks and signs if there is non-existence (*asamskṛta*);
18. To sever the doubt as to how one can preach the Dharma if there is no body; 19. To sever the doubt as to how one can practice and realize it if there are no dharmas; 20.
To sever the doubt that what is taught is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not a cause; 21. To sever the doubt as to how there can be equality.
21. Dispelling the doubt regarding the salvation of sentient beings. 22. Dispelling the doubt that one can know the true Buddha by means of comparison. 23.

Dispelling the doubt that the fruit of Buddhahood is unrelated to meritorious marks. 24. Dispelling the doubt that the appearance of transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) involves the reception of merit. 25.

Dispelling the doubt regarding the identity or difference between the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and the transformation body. 26. Dispelling the doubt that the preaching of the Dharma by the transformation body lacks merit.
Doubt. Twenty-seven: Doubt regarding how one who has severed [delusions] and entered quiescence can preach the Dharma.

First, doubt regarding severing the initial seeking of Buddhahood while abiding in the marks of practicing giving. (Commentary) Two: First, the heading and narration of the doubt; second, the severance of the doubt according to the sūtra.
First, the heading and narration of the doubt, which has three parts: first, the heading; second, pointing out the place where the doubt arises; third, raising an objection.
First, the heading of the section.
[Commentary]: First, resolving doubts regarding the marks of abiding while practicing giving with the aspiration for Buddhahood.
[Record]: The first commentary first presents the heading of the section.
△ Second, the point where doubt arises. [Commentary] The doubt is as follows:
If one practices giving in order to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, this is precisely abiding in the characteristics of the sought-after Buddha; why then is it said that there is no abiding?
[Commentary] "In order to seek," etc., indicates the point where doubt arises. This follows from the teaching on giving without dwelling upon signs.
Having heard that only giving without dwelling upon signs—such as the characteristics of emptiness or existence across the three periods of time—is called true giving, one consequently doubts:
"All acts of giving are surely performed for the sake of seeking Buddhahood; since there is something sought, how can it be said to be 'without dwelling'?"
△ Third, the concessionary objection (*yongnan*). [Commentary:

Furthermore, if non-abiding in marks (*animitta*) is taken as the cause, how could it produce a result characterized by form and marks (*rūpa-nimitta*)? This is because cause and effect would not be of a similar nature.
[Record: Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, non-abiding," etc., this is a concessionary objection. Even if the cause were established as non-abiding, this still would not be...

This is the principle. Therefore, it is stated next that "cause and effect are not of the same category. Now, for something to function as cause and effect, they must necessarily be of a similar nature:
if one exists, both exist; if one is empty, both are empty. This applies equally to the defiled and the pure.

Since the phenomenal form (*rūpa*) is the effect, how can non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhāna*) be its cause? If the cause were empty while the effect were existent, such a principle would likely be untenable. Thus, we shall now examine the cause by means of the effect.
Because of conjunction, there is abiding; yet the Buddha says there is no abiding. Is this deceiving me?
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtra (the sūtra has four parts): First, raising the cause of doubt to ask; second, responding by preventing the grasping of characteristics;
third, explaining that the essence differs from the conditioned; fourth, confirming that the Buddha-body is signless. First, raising the cause of doubt to ask:
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks?
[Commentary] This section on severing doubts consists of four parts. First, the question is posed by citing a cause.
[Commentary] To raise the cause of doubt, the intent of the sūtra says:
"In your view, can one still perceive the Dharma-body Tathāgata by means of a body endowed with the thirty-two marks, or not? These marks are the cause for the arising of this doubt;
therefore, they are raised as the subject of inquiry.
[Commentary]: Originally, it was precisely because they took marks (*lakṣaṇa*) to be the Buddha that doubt arose in contrast to the preceding teaching on not dwelling in marks.
The Buddha raised the cause from which this doubt arose, engaging in question and answer with the desire to eliminate and sever it.

[Commentary] "Below the initial passage" explains the cause for the arising of doubt. Because those of the Two Vehicles take only the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) physical form as the true Buddha, they regard this form as the fruit;
consequently, they do not believe in a cause that is non-abiding, as the cause and fruit would otherwise be dissimilar.
The Buddha now raises the question by citing the fruit, so that they may know the ocean of the fruit is signless (*animitta*), and thus naturally cease to be deluded regarding the cause.
"It is non-abiding.
△ Second, preventing the grasping of characteristics to provide a response:
"No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks."
[Commentary: Second, "preventing characteristics so as to repay [the Buddha’s intent].

[Record: Preventing characteristics serves to repay the meaning of the Sūtra. When Subhūti saw the Buddha raise up a characteristic to question him, he immediately knew that one must not seek it through characteristics;
therefore, he answered "no."
[Commentary: To prevent those who harbor doubts—those who wish to seek the Buddha through physical marks and thereby hope to see him—the text replies that he cannot be seen by means of marks.
As the *Śāstra* states: "This is to prevent the notion that the Tathāgata’s body is established by way of such marks."

[Commentary] Regarding "obstructing and preventing," etc.: the intention is that there is concern lest sentient beings of the final age fail to comprehend this principle and instead grasp at signs as being real.

Therefore, this serves to preemptively obstruct such deluded views. According to the underlying meaning, it correctly cuts off the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of emptiness and obstructs the seeds of the future.

The full significance of this "obstructing and cutting off" is contained in the *Xuántán* (Prolegomena). The section beginning with "The Treatise says, below" cites scriptural evidence. Question: [Regarding] the Sūtra...
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says "view," while the commentary explains it as "accomplishment. How can this be in accord with the Buddha’s intention? Answer:
Since one forms this view, one must necessarily establish this proof; therefore, there is no contradiction.
△ Third, the explanation of the difference in essence has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the sūtra text; second, the specific clarification of the three marks.
First, the direct explanation of the sūtra text:
Why is this? The bodily marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are precisely not bodily marks.
[Commentary] Third, the explanation of the difference in essence from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
[Record] Regarding the sūtra’s statement that the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the thirty-two marks: the intent of the inquiry is to ask, "By what principle is this so?
The intent of the explanation is that it is because the body consisting of the thirty-two marks is that which was taught by the Tathāgata.
"Phenomenal marks. This is because they are not the marks of the Dharma-body. "Ji" (即) means "is indeed"; "fei" (非) means "not. The original text is inverted;
it should correctly be read as "bu shi" (不是), meaning "it is not so."

[Commentary]: "Characteristics" refers to the conditioned states of arising, abiding, change, and cessation. The Buddha-body is distinct from these; therefore, it does not possess physical characteristics. [Record]:
Regarding the phrase "characteristics are," etc., this refers to the thirty-two marks. These are essentially reflections manifested upon the Great Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Since they fall within the category of the conditioned, they are subject to the transitions of the four characteristics. This is all the more so when considering their presence or absence according to the capacities of sentient beings.
It is indeterminate; how could this be taken as the Dharma-body? Therefore, it is said that the marks are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and so forth.
This explains the bodily marks spoken of by the Tathāgata in the sūtras. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-body is different from these":
the essence of the Dharma-body Buddha is different from these conditioned phenomena; therefore, it is taught that the thirty-two marks are not the marks of the Dharma-body. This is the explanation.
"It is precisely not a mark of existence.

[Commentary] Regarding the verse’s statement, "Because the three marks have distinct essences," this means that the essence of the Buddha is distinct from the three marks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
[Recorded Notes] "The verse says... and below provide scriptural evidence. The full text states: "One analyzes the essence of the conditioned to prevent the attainment of its establishment."
Because the three characteristics have distinct natures, the Tathāgata is apart from them. Among these, the first two phrases correspond to the preceding section;
the final phrase corresponds to the next subsection; and the third phrase specifically corresponds to this passage, which is why it is cited as a particular proof.
Regarding the section "The Buddha-body" and below, it further explains the verse, namely what the Sūtra calls "it is not a physical form."
△ Second, the specific explanation of the three characteristics.
[Commentary] The two characteristics of duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*) both belong to the present; therefore, they are combined into one.

[Record] Regarding the section beginning with "duration and change," this explains the meaning of the three characteristics. Since the four characteristics were previously indicated, yet this verse mentions only three, [the reason is as follows:]...
Arising belongs to the past; cessation belongs to the future; and the two characteristics of duration and change both reside together in the present.
Furthermore, these two characteristics are inseparable: it changes while enduring, and it endures while changing. Because they occupy the same time and place, they are combined into one;
however, fearing confusion with the notion of eternal persistence, only "change" is explicitly designated.
[Commentary]: If subdivided, there are four [characteristics]. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Arising indicates that this dharma did not previously exist;
ceasing indicates that this dharma will subsequently be non-existent; change indicates that this dharma is not immutable; and abiding indicates that this dharma temporarily possesses function."

[Commentary] If one subdivides [the characteristics] according to their meaning, there are four: arising (*jāti*), cessation (*nirodha*), alteration (*anyathātva*), and duration (*sthiti*). This cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to explain these characteristics:

that which comes from non-existence to existence is called "arising"; that which goes from existence to non-existence is "cessation"; the transformation before and after is "alteration"; and the brief continuity is "duration.
However, the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is not born at a prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) nor does he cease at a subsequent limit (*aparākoṭi*).
It is without change and cannot be destroyed; therefore, it is different from this.
△ Fourth, the seal that the Buddha’s body is signless has two parts: first, the explanation of the preceding two lines; second, the explanation of the subsequent two lines.
[Commentary] The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "All marks arise from deluded thoughts; therefore, even the marks of a Buddha are illusory.
If discrimination does not arise, marks are naturally markless; one then perceives the non-mark.
When all marks have perished, there remains only the essence of awakening—this is called seeing the Tathāgata. From this, one knows the Buddha.
The body is without marks. ○ Commentary (Sū): Two parts. First, the explanation of the preceding two lines. Second, [the subsequent explanation]. First, the direct explanation.

△ First, the explanation of the preceding two lines: two parts. First, the direct explanation. Second, the citation of evidence. First, the direct explanation: two parts. First, the explanation of the text.
Second, the revelation of the underlying intent. First, the explanation of the text.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory.
[Commentary] The four seals indicate that the Buddha’s body is without marks. It is not only the Buddha’s body that is without marks;
rather, all marks of the conditioned—whether pertaining to ordinary beings or sages, or to the environment or its inhabitants—are entirely false and illusory.
[Commentary] "Not merely" means not alone. "Ordinary beings" refers to those in the six realms; "sages" refers to the worthy and holy ones of the three vehicles.

They are categorized as "pure" or "impure" based on their environment (*āśraya*). "Principal" refers to ordinary beings and sages themselves; it is restated here because it corresponds to the "retributive environment" (*pratyaya-bhoga*).
Although phenomena are numerous, they do not exceed these four categories. Although only four dharmas are mentioned, they encompass all things. This explains the passage from the Sūtra.

All that has marks is entirely empty and illusory. Fearing that people, upon hearing it said that bodily marks are not marks, might think this applies only to the Buddha’s body, [the text] now says "all that" in order to preclude such a limited view.
