△ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.
[Commentary: Because they are manifested from forgetful mindfulness, deluded thought is fundamentally empty; what reality could there be in that which is manifested?
[Record: From "Because" onwards, the reason is explained. Although ordinary beings and sages, defilement and purity, superiority and inferiority differ, all arise from mindfulness.
All that arises is without exception false and illusory. Thought has no inherent characteristic of its own; it does not depart from the nature of awakening.

If thought itself lacks an intrinsic nature, how much less could the appearances it manifests truly exist? Since thought is that which is depended upon (the support) and appearances are what depend upon it (the supported), if the support is already empty, how can that which depends on it exist?
It is just as when the hide no longer exists, where will the hair have anything to attach itself to?
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence, which has two parts: first, positive demonstration; second, negative demonstration.

[Commentary] From "The Awakening of Faith" onwards, there are two citations of evidence. Within these, there is positive demonstration and negative demonstration; they should be examined and understood in full detail.
△ First, the positive demonstration.
[Commentary] Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "All objective realms exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought.
△ Second, the negative demonstration.
[Commentary] If one is separated from mental conceptions, then there are no signs of any objective realms whatsoever.
△ Second, the explanation of the latter two phrases has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the explanation by citing a treatise. First, the direct explanation has two parts:
first, the explanation of the character *xiàng* (signs/appearances); second, the explanation of the character *zhū* (all/various). First, the explanation of the character *xiàng*.
"If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.

[Commentary: The phrase "if one sees all marks" serves to preclude the view that one must abandon form to contemplate emptiness. It is for fear that, upon hearing that marks are illusory and false, one might fall into such an extreme.
Furthermore, one seeks the markless Buddha-body separately; therefore it is said: "Marks are themselves no-marks;
this is the Tathāgata. [Commentary] "If one sees... and below provide two explanations for the latter two phrases. First is the direct explanation.

Regarding the phrase "precluding the seeking apart from [marks]," since form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form, to seek emptiness apart from form is a great error; thus, this precludes it.
...it is so. △ Second, the explanation of the various characters.
[Commentary]: It is not only the physical marks of the Buddha’s transformation body that are the Tathāgata; all marks perceived are, in their very nature, markless.
This is precisely the Tathāgata.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "not merely," etc.: Furthermore, fearing that upon hearing that "characteristics are themselves non-characteristics" they would assume this refers only to the physical marks of the Buddha's body—implying that outside of the Buddha's body, characteristics are not the Tathāgata—it is said that "all characteristics are non-existent."
This explains the various characters within the sutra. ○ For example, when a single human image appears in a mirror, other objects also appear alongside it;
it is not only the empty space occupied by the human image that is the mirror, but the empty space occupied by the other objects is also entirely the mirror.

The application of this analogy to the Dharma can be understood accordingly. ○ One who understands in this way will know that the seeing and the objects of sight appear as if they were present before one, yet they are fundamentally...

I have realized the clarity of awakening. △ Second, citing treatises for explanation, which has four parts: first, citing the *Awakening of Faith*; second, citing Sengzhao’s commentary; third, citing the root treatise; fourth, relying on Asaṅga.
Regarding the first, citing the *Awakening of Faith*, there are two parts: first, proving that all appearances are devoid of meaning; second, proving the non-existence of appearances.
All these are the meanings of "Buddha. First, it is realized that all marks are devoid of meaning.
[Commentary] Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "What is called the meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of mind being free from discursive thought."
[Commentary] Therefore, the following section begins. Second, citing treatises for explanation, there are four parts. First, it cites the *Awakening of Faith*. This has two intentions.
The first is to prove the meaning that all marks are without marks (*animitta*). Since marks arise dependent upon thought, the essence of awakening is already detached from thought;
how much more so, then, regarding marks?
△ Second, the proof that the absence of characteristics is the meaning of Buddhahood.
[Commentary]: That which is free from the characteristics of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
[Commentary] Second, the proof that all characteristics are nowhere and are thus the meaning of the Tathāgata. The characteristic of being free from thought is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since the Dharma-body is equal to empty space, how could empty space ever possess characteristics? This equality of non-characteristic subsumes all characteristics;
this is precisely the Dharma-body. As the text below states: "To be free from all characteristics is what is called the Buddhas. It further says:
The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas; therefore, it is said that he is not merely [the physical form] and so forth.
△ Second, citing Zhaolun’s commentary:
[Commentary] Zhaolun says: When practice accords with reality and understanding is pervasive, one then sees the Buddha.
[Commentary] The section beginning with "Sengzhao says" below cites Sengzhao’s commentary. This clarifies the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the Dharma-body Buddha.

Fearing that people, upon hearing that "all marks are no-marks" and thus perceiving the Tathāgata, might instead long for a formless Buddha as if it were vividly manifest before their eyes—if this were the case, how would it differ from those [conventional] marks?
Therefore, it says "the practice accords with [the principle]," and so forth. Wisdom and Principle...
Profoundly, the mind and the spirit meet; hence it is said that their practice is in accord. Regarding "understanding and penetration":
this refers to the aforementioned understanding that all marks are non-marks. The former is true vision; this is semblance vision. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The Dharma-body has no marks of self or other, nor do they see one another."
△ Third, citing the root treatise.
[Commentary: The verse states, "That which is apart from those is the Tathāgata. Being apart from those three marks refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
[Commentary] "The verse says, 'Below,'" and so forth. Third, citing the root treatise: this refers to the preceding remaining verses. This is an explanation based on Vasubandhu’s commentary.
Fourth, citing Asaṅga.

[Commentary] Non-attachment refers to the form-body (*rūpakāya*). It means merely being free from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and not clinging to the characteristics of form; this is the true form-body.

Thus, that treatise states: "This is to demonstrate the form-body of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, this corresponds to the third [section], which concerns the dwelling place for attaining the form-body.

[Commentary] Below "Asaṅga," four citations from Asaṅga are provided. Regarding "free from parikalpita" (imagined nature): one does not cling to false appearances as real. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (perfected nature) is eternally remote from that former nature. Regarding "the true rūpakāya": [it is so called because it is free from the imagined nature].

There are two perspectives. The first is to regard the illusory as illusory, simply according to the facts, without necessarily taking that which is neither arising nor ceasing to be the ultimate truth.
This is like regarding the moon in water as the moon in water; though it resembles the real, it is not the real.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In the real, one sees the real; in the unreal, one sees the unreal. To understand the Dharma in this way is correct.
These marks are what is called the Buddha. Second, it means that the marks are themselves markless (*animitta*), because they are identical with the *dharmakāya*.
To subsume the derivative into the fundamental is called the true *rūpakāya*, which is precisely the truly excellent and wondrous form. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "This body of mine now..."
This is precisely the eternal body, the Dharma-body, the indestructible Vajra-body. Question: Previously, characteristics were obliterated;
here, characteristics are preserved. How can these not be contradictory? Answer: The previous passage reveals the Dharma-body, and thus it is said that "characteristics are non-characteristics.

The present passage clarifies the Form-body (Rūpakāya), and thus it is said that "non-characteristics are characteristics. This is because a Buddha of the fruition stage must necessarily possess both bodies; these two bodies...
They are identical, like waves and water. Within the two treatises, each reveals a single meaning; while their words appear to be contradictory, their intent is in fact consistent.
The skillful means of the Bodhisattva lies precisely here. Therefore, the two passages that follow both serve to corroborate and clarify the meaning of the form-body (rūpakāya).
[Commentary] Now, within this section on doubt, from the subtle to the manifest, the two bodies—the True and the Responsive—are elucidated in a total of six layers:

first, clarifying that the Buddha’s marks are neither marks nor non-marks; second, clarifying that the Buddha’s marks are not identical to the Tathāgata; third, clarifying that all marks are non-marks;
fourth, clarifying that all marks and non-marks are the Tathāgata; fifth, clarifying that only realization is the mark.
It is so. There is no Buddha to be seen. The sixth point clarifies that the markless mark is the true form-body (rūpakāya).
Now, regarding these six stages, each preceding one is shallow and each succeeding one is increasingly profound; though the text does not repeat itself, the principle is revealed instantaneously.
To those who have attained realization, what is perceived must be simultaneous, without before or after.
△ Second, the doubt regarding the lack of faith in the profound nature of both cause and effect of abandonment. (Commentary) This section has two parts: first, the heading that sets forth the doubt;

second, the resolution of the doubt based on the sūtra. The first part, the heading that sets forth the doubt, has three sections: first, the heading; second, pointing out the source where the doubt arises;
third, concluding the formation of the doubt. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Second: Severing both cause and effect, which are profoundly deep, yet lacking faith and harboring doubt.
[Record] The second commentary first presents the heading.
△ Second, it indicates the point where the doubt arises.
[Commentary]: The Treatise says: "Practicing giving without dwelling is the depth of the cause; seeing the Buddha without signs is the depth of the fruit. [Sub-commentary]:

The phrase "The Treatise says" below points to the place where the doubt arises. Regarding "without dwelling," etc.: this refers to the direct answer that addresses the question concerning dwelling, cultivation, and subduing.
"Seeing the Buddha without signs" is identical to what was stated previously: "If one sees all signs as non-signs, then one sees the Tathāgata."
Come. △ Third, concluding with doubt. [Commentary]:
In the evil world of the future, faith will certainly not arise; what benefit is there in speaking in vain?
[Commentary] "In the future," etc., concludes the expression of doubt. The meaning is as follows: Since both cause and effect are devoid of marks, they are both profoundly deep;
only those like me who have received [the teaching] directly can comprehend and awaken to it. How, then, can those of dull faculties in the final age believe and accept it?
Since they do not believe or accept it, what benefit is there in speaking in vain?
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sutra (the sutra has four parts): First, presenting the doubt by way of a lack of faith; second, manifesting faith through words that rebuke the doubt;
third, clarifying the reason why one is able to have faith; fourth, revealing the profound gateway of the Middle Way. First:
Expressing his doubts based on a lack of faith, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these..."
"Will they give rise to true faith?
[Commentary] There are four sections in the text concerning the severing of doubt. First, raising a doubt based on a lack of faith.
[Sub-commentary] The scripture that raises the doubt poses the question: "In the future, at the end of the age, will there be sentient beings who, upon hearing of this cause and effect..."
Do you generate true faith in these profound chapters and phrases? "Pho" means "to be able. The intent is to distinguish this from mere superficial faith;
therefore, it is called "true faith."

[Commentary] Wei says: "There may be sentient beings in future ages," and so forth. The reason this phrase is omitted here is that its significance is reflected in the [passage concerning] the final five hundred years.
[Commentary] The phrase "The Wei [edition] says, 'below'" introduces the textual alignment with the Wei edition.

Regarding those passages present in the Wei edition but missing from this [Kumārajīva] sūtra, Kumārajīva’s skillful translation lies in its artful omission. Alternatively, this passage may be understood as a question concerning both the present and the future collectively.

Even during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were those who found it difficult to believe in this profound Dharma, such as the followers of the various Hīnayāna schools and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were still Śrāvakas who withdrew from their seats; how much more so now for the *Prajñāpāramitā*? When [the text] speaks of "down to the time of the Buddhas," it refers only to the final age (*paścimakāla*) by way of analogy with the present.
If [this teaching] still exists in the final age, how could it not have existed during the Buddha’s own time? Therefore, [the text says] "now in Qin..."
The root text does not mention the future and so forth.
[Commentary] A phrase (*pada*) denotes differentiation. [Sub-commentary] Regarding "a phrase denotes differentiation":

while a name (*nāman*) merely denotes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena—for instance, the word "form" (*rūpa*) serves to distinguish [it from other things]—a phrase denotes its specific distinctions.

It is not mind and so forth; by saying "mind," it distinguishes [it] from form and so forth. However, since both form and mind each have many varieties, it has not yet been clarified which specific form and mind this refers to.
This phrase is able to distinguish between the true mind and the deluded mind, as well as between form-color (*rūpa*) and manifest-color (*varṇa*), and so on.
Therefore, it is said that [the verse] "expounds the distinctions.
[Commentary: "Chapter" (zhāng) means "explanation of the phrases" (jiě jù).
[Sub-commentary: Regarding "explaining the phrases": although the phrases do expound the distinctions, they have not yet extensively revealed the underlying principles (*yǐlǐ*), because the Truth...
Within the mind, false forms and manifest colors contain manifold meanings; because the "chapters" (*zhāng*) can clarify these, they are called "explanatory phrases" (*jiějù*).
"Chapters" (*zhāng*) means "to manifest. The commentary text follows the sequence of the meanings, and thus first explains the phrases.
[Commentary] Regarding "one who truly believes": The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) states, "To have no belief in any phenomena is to believe in Prajñā.

[Record] This refers to the section on the characteristics of clear faith in the latter part of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. It means that when one perceives phenomena such as form, mind, and the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements, this constitutes believing in all phenomena.
Now, when one illuminates these with Prajñā, all superficial, illusory, and transformative appearances vanish.

They arise in the very place they appear and perish in the very place they cease. These illusory and false manifestations are merely designated as "characteristics," yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.
It is precisely by not believing in any phenomena that one may be said to believe in Prajñā. It is like a clear eye that does not see flowers in the sky;
if one were to cling to those sky-flowers, how could one believe in the clarity of the eye? The application of this principle to the Dharma can be understood accordingly.
△ Second, refuting doubt through words to manifest faith.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as true."
[Commentary] Second, the words of rebuke against doubt serve to manifest faith.
[Sub-commentary] The phrase "Do not speak thus" in the Sutra of Manifesting Faith is a word of rebuke and exhortation. It does not mean that in future generations there will be no faith whatsoever.

For instance, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma-ending period (*mofa*), those who possess the precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*) are able to [realize] the profound meaning in reality.
There is faith; one believes that this is the reality.

[Commentary] Regarding "the final five hundred years," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: In the first five hundred years, liberation is firm; in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration is firm;
in the third, erudition; in the fourth, stūpas and monasteries; and in the fifth, strife and contention—all of which are as described above.
The second section follows this pattern.

[Commentary] In the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, it is explained that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be five periods of five hundred years each; in these periods, each preceding one is superior and each succeeding one is inferior.
○ Liberation (*vimukti*) refers to realization; it is the fruition of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). ○ Meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) refers to practice;

it comprises the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative states of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as their phenomena and principles. ○ Extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) refers to understanding;

it comprises the sudden and gradual, the partial and the complete, and the understandings of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*), and so forth. Regarding these three aforementioned factors, the former must necessarily possess the latter, whereas the latter does not necessarily possess the former.

[The character] "qian" (before). ○ Regarding "stūpas and monasteries": this refers to those who do not seek the ultimate Way but instead take great pleasure in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), using external material resources to cultivate worldly meritorious deeds and the like.
○ Regarding "contention": this clarifies that within the Buddha-dharma there are many disputes and debates.

For instance, in India, the schools of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were like those who divide a river to drink from separate streams; even within the Mahāyāna itself, there are the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Characteristics) schools.
Furthermore, within the Hinayana, the twenty schools differ; each faction champions itself and judges others as wrong.

Even here in this land, one cannot avoid being thus: whether regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or nature (*svabhāva*), the Southern and Northern Schools of Chan and the various expository schools mutually disparage one another.
When factions take sides with one another and refuse to concede to each other, it is called "contention.

Regarding the phrase "all as in the precedent," there must be a period of five hundred years and a firm commitment. As for "firmness," it means that because many people have followed the tradition, they are determined not to abandon it.
However, this is explained merely from the perspective of superior development; it does not mean that other [traditions] do not interconnect. For example, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
Within two hundred years, King Aśoka constructed stūpas; how could this be restricted solely to the fourth five-hundred-year period?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states that during the final five hundred years, immeasurable virtuous people will cultivate meditative concentration, liberation, and extensive learning;

how could there be only one, two, or three such individuals? When this present sūtra speaks of the "final five hundred years," it refers precisely to this time, even though it is an age of strife and contention.
There are also those who possess the virtue of precepts; this refers to the five kinds of firmness, which are spoken of here merely by way of their preeminence.
[Commentary] Originally, there was doubt that there would be no faith in an evil age; therefore, the evil age is cited specifically to sever that doubt.
[Commentary] Regarding the section "Doubts about the following," the Sub-commentary uses the passage on severing doubts to illuminate the preceding point where doubts were presented.
This demonstrates that Subhūti harbored doubts regarding the lack of faith in an evil age. The previous citation from the Wei translation was used to substantiate this meaning:
if such is the case even in an evil age, how much more so in other ages?

[Commentary: "Maintaining precepts and cultivating merit" refers to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Taking this as the reality" means correct understanding free from error.
As Asaṅga states: "The three trainings, beginning with superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), manifest the virtues of practicing few desires and so forth."
[Commentary] "Precepts and concentration" below explains [the practice] in terms of the three trainings. Concentration is the essence of merit; therefore, it is contrasted with concentration.
Regarding "correct understanding is non-erroneous": since there is correct understanding, there is necessarily no erroneous delusion.

To understand the principle that causes and effects are without marks is called "true faith," which is the training in wisdom. "Without attachment" below cites scriptural evidence. The Wei edition of the sutra says:
There are those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, wisdom, and [virtue]. Maitreya’s verse says:

"In the future evil age, one who explains the profound meaning of cause and effect will not be empty of reality; such a person is endowed with the three virtues of a Bodhisattva. These three virtues are precisely the three trainings (*śikṣā*).
In the present text, we simply take these words and phrases as being able to generate faith, regarding them as the reality. This is...
This is wisdom (*prajñā*). If one lacked wisdom, who could take this as reality and give rise to faith? Regarding "few desires" and so forth: by means of few desires one maintains the precepts;
by cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) one stills the mind's turbulence; and by practicing wisdom one severs delusions.

Thus, they are said to be "equal. As for the term "superior" (*adhipati*): because the three trainings, beginning with the precepts, are superior and exalted dharmas, the Sūtras describe them as the "three determinations."
Definition. [Commentary]:
Precepts deliver one from the three miserable realms; concentration delivers one from the six heavens of the desire realm; wisdom delivers one from the triple world. [Sub-commentary]:
"Precepts deliver one from the lower" distinguishes the characteristics of the three benefits. One who possesses precepts does not fall into the hells, the hungry ghosts, or the animals.
Birth. Birth occurs in the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus, the *Śīla-sūtra* says:

"If you wish to be born in the heavens, or if you wish to be born among humans, you must always protect the feet of the precepts (*śīlapāda*) so that they remain free from damage. Regarding "concentration (*samādhi*) transcends the six desires": there is no concentration within the desire realm;

therefore, those who attain concentration are born in the two higher realms. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "Abandoning craving, one delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
It further serves as the basis for the root of craving, whereby there appear the superior fruits of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). As for "wisdom that transcends the three realms":

the root of the three realms consists of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). One who possesses wisdom is able to completely eliminate them; once karma and afflictions are eliminated, [transcendence is achieved].

They naturally transcend [suffering]. Thus, the Heart Sūtra says: "When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby crossed over all suffering and distress.
If those of shallow wisdom can still attain liberation from the three realms, how much more so for the profoundly deep Prajñā of the Mahāyāna!
△ Third, the reasons why one is able to have faith, which consists of two parts. First, clarifying how one accumulates the causes of faith by serving virtuous friends through successive stages.

Second, clarifying how the virtues of faith are accomplished through being taken under the care of virtuous friends. The first part clarifies how one accumulates the causes of faith by serving virtuous friends through successive stages.
It should be known that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;

rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas. Upon hearing these phrases, even if they give rise to pure faith for but a single thought-moment, they shall attain such merit.

[Commentary] The third section clarifies the reasons why one is able to have faith. It has two parts. First, it clarifies how one accumulates the causes of faith by serving virtuous friends through successive stages.
[Record] Regarding the "Sūtra on the Causes of Faith," the distinction between the method of reverse illustration (*pratiloma*) and direct exposition (*anuloma*) can be understood.
[Commentary] Asuṅga states: "To manifest the causes for the accumulation [of merit]: 'having long served virtuous friends under many Buddhas' indicates the excellence of the conditions;
'planting various roots of goodness' indicates the excellence of the causes, as it clarifies that one has long suppressed the three poisons."
[Commentary] Regarding the superiority of the object (*ālambana*): Although one may benefit oneself by taking others as friends, everyone regards them as such;
yet, the ordinary person does not equal the sage, the small does not equal the great, and the cause does not equal the fruit. Even though a single Buddha is a fruit, he does not equal many Buddhas.

Since it is said there are "immeasurable thousands of millions," it is therefore called the superiority of the object. Regarding the superiority of the cause (*hetu*): The three poisons are greed, anger, and delusion. This...

Because clarity (*vidyā*) can harm sentient beings, it is disparagingly termed "poison" (*viṣa*). Since its arising is inherently unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is called a "wholesome root" (*kuśalamūla*) only because it has long been suppressed.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "All the evil karma I have created in the past arises from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Wholesome [roots] refer to faith, shame, and dread; the three roots such as non-greed possess the sense of growth and development."
Therefore, they are called "roots. Both the wholesome and the unwholesome arise from these three; if one can subdue them, this is called "victory over the causes.
Only when both the causes and conditions are victorious does this faith arise. Thus, we know that true faith is indeed not easily obtained.
If it is so even for a single thought-moment, how much more so for perpetual faith, as well as upholding and expounding the teaching?
△ Second, explaining how one is embraced by a virtuous friend to accomplish the virtue of faith. This has two parts:
first, explaining the attainment of merit through being embraced, which reveals the gate of merit; second, explaining the reason for being embraced, which reveals the gate of wisdom.

Regarding the first, explaining the attainment of merit through being embraced to reveal the gate of merit (the *shu*), there are two parts: first, explaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; second, explaining the attainment of merit.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that all these sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable merit.

[Commentary] Second, it clarifies being embraced by virtuous friends and the accomplishment of the virtue of faith. This section has two parts. First, it clarifies the acquisition of merit through being received and sustained, thereby manifesting the gateway of merit.
[Commentary] The *Puṇyamukha-sūtra* states that those who believe in this sūtra obtain immeasurable merit, which the Tathāgata fully knows and perceives.
Regarding such immeasurable merit—referring to the merit of believing in the sūtra—it is like the aforementioned merit of non-abiding giving;
it is as vast as the empty space of the ten directions and cannot be conceived.
△ First, the explanation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
[Commentary] From "Asanga says" below, the text has two parts. First, the explanation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
[Sub-commentary] Asanga says: This means that within all activities of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one knows the mind (the four aggregates) and perceives its...
"By means of reliance [upon the physical body]" refers to the fact that these [actions] demonstrate what is encompassed by a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
[The commentary] states: "Walking, standing, and so forth" refers to the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), each of which possesses its own specific activity.

The note says: "The four aggregates" refers to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). This means [the distinction between] those that are associated (*samprayukta*) and those that are dissociated (*viprayukta*). What is intended? What is recollected? [This concerns the mental factors and their objects.]

Matters such as grasping and rejecting, sorrow and joy, and other such thoughts are all called "mind. ○ The commentary states: "The physical body" is so called because it is that upon which the four aggregates depend.

Here, it is designated according to its functional meaning, hence it is called the "basis," namely for activities such as walking, standing, sitting, lying down, bending, stretching, looking up, and looking down.
○ Thus, in the arising of the mind and the production of thoughts, there is nothing not known; in every movement and action...

There is nothing that is not seen. For the Buddha’s eye of wisdom is vast and boundless; since both the primary and secondary realms (the environment and its inhabitants) are present therein, how could they not be perceived simultaneously?
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "I always know whether sentient beings practice the Way or do not practice it.
Because the mind has no form or appearance, one speaks only of "knowing"; because the physical body has form, one can speak of "seeing. Since this person's virtuous conduct is...

[The Buddha] was fully prepared. If his roots of goodness had been established long ago, yet the Buddha did not take him under his care, how would that accord with principle? Therefore, it is said: "These [passages] demonstrate," and so forth.
Thus, the Buddha’s wisdom is without partiality; he regards all beings as one. When there is a resonance, there is a response. Who could say this is not so?
[Commentary] The treatise states: "If 'seeing' were not mentioned, some might claim that the Tathāgata knows by means of inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
If 'knowing' were not mentioned, some might claim that the Tathāgata sees with the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Therefore, both terms are necessary."
[Commentary] The treatise says "below," etc. Someone may ask: "Since 'seeing' (*darśana*) and 'knowing' (*jñāna*) can be spoken of as one, why are they both mentioned within the Sūtra?

Therefore, it says, "If [it were otherwise], etc. Since ordinary beings also possess knowing and seeing—wherein "seeing" extends to the physical eye and "knowing" includes inference (*anumāna*)—there are instances where they do not know and do not see. The Buddha’s knowing and seeing, however, are not like these.
This is so. It means that one knows at the very place of seeing; it is not a knowledge derived through inference (*anumāna*). One sees at the very place of knowing;
it is not the same as the seeing of the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Thus, there is nothing unknown and nothing unseen. The word "all" (*sarva*) used in the Sūtra finds its significance here.
Therefore, Maitreya’s verse says: "The Buddha does not know by perceiving a result; rather, he perceives directly through the power of his vows and wisdom."
△ Second, the explanation of attaining merit.
[Commentary]: Regarding "attaining merit," the Wei translation says: "One generates such merit; one takes up such merit."
[Commentary] "Obtaining merit" and below: there are two explanations for obtaining merit. First, a scriptural citation is provided. [Sub-commentary] The *Śāstra* states:

"That which gives birth" refers to the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). "That which takes up" refers to the meaning of the fruit of the perfumed self-substance (*vāsita-svabhāva-phala*). As Asaṅga says:
"Producing" refers to the manifestation [of karma] at the very moment merit arises. "Appropriating" refers to the grasping and maintaining of seeds at the moment that [merit] ceases.

[Commentary: The passage beginning with "The treatise says, below" explains the meaning. ○ "The productive cause" refers to the actual cultivation of meritorious deeds—that is, those who possess faith and understanding, uphold [the teachings], and explain them.
○ "The fruit of its own nature" refers to the very essence of the seeds perfumed [by those deeds], which subsequently brings about future results.
Furthermore: "The actual arising" refers to the time when one performs meritorious deeds; it occurs during the manifest activity.
"Its cessation" means that once the manifest activity has ceased and passed away, the seed is finally established, remaining latent within consciousness to bring about the future fruit.

[Commentary]: Regarding the term "attainment" (*de*) used here, it encompasses both the meanings of "arising" (*sheng*) and "grasping" (*qu*). It does not depart from "attainment"; the single character "attainment" subsumes both arising and grasping. [Sub-commentary]:
The phrase "regarding the term 'attainment' used here" correctly aligns with the present text. Because the single character "attainment" contains both arising and grasping, it is said that...
"Born-attained" (*jōtoku*) means "acquired through birth. The subtlety of the Qin translation lies precisely here.
△ Second, clarifying the reason for inclusion to reveal the gate of wisdom (Commentary). This has two parts: first, stating the intent and dividing the sections;
second, providing the formal explanation according to the divisions. First, stating the intent and dividing the sections.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the reason for embracing [the teaching] and revealing the gateway of wisdom. Because one is free from dualistic grasping, one attains this embracing.
The text has two parts; first, it correctly explains that coarse grasping has already been severed.

[Commentary] Regarding the reason for these two [categories], the sub-commentary provides two [explanations]. First, it sets forth the intent and divides the sections. ○ As for "due to the absence of...

and so forth: this means that the absence of the dualistic discrimination of the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) is the reason why they are included [in the category of non-conceptualization].

△ Second, the correct explanation according to the topical outline has two parts: first, the explicit clarification that coarse attachments have already been severed; second, the demonstration through reasoning that subtle attachments have not yet been eliminated.

Regarding the first (the explicit clarification that coarse attachments have already been severed), there are two sections: first, the word-by-word commentary on the sutra text; second, an analytical comparison of the sutra’s intent.
[Commentary] The coarse attachments have already been severed. The meaning of the sutra is as explained in the sub-commentary (*shu*).
△ The first section, which explains the sutra text, has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. First, the inquiry.
Why is this? [Commentary] The first section poses a question: For what reason does one who possesses faith attain the Tathāgata’s complete knowledge and complete vision?
[Record] Regarding the first section below, the text is divided into two parts; the first part explains the scriptural passage. The intent of the inquiry can be understood.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts: first, the absence of the grasping at a self; second, the absence of the grasping at phenomena. First, the absence of the grasping at a self:
These sentient beings no longer have the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.

[Commentary] The subsequent explanation has two parts. First, there is the absence of the grasping at a self (*anātman*). To grasp at one's own essence as a self is [the view of] a person (*pudgala*).

To reckon that this self transmigrates successively through other realms of existence is [the view of] a sentient being (*sattva*). To reckon that this self persists as a continuous succession of various transformations—such as prosperity and decline, or suffering and pleasure—is [the view of] a life-sustainer (*jīva*).
To reckon that this self remains with its vital faculty (*jīvitendriya*) unbroken throughout a single lifetime is [the view of] a life-principle (*poṣa*).

[Commentary] Regarding the "self" (*ātman*) explained herein: it refers to grasping the general characteristics of one's own five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being the self. Regarding the "person" (*pudgala*): it is the reckoning that after one dies as a human, one is born in heaven;

or that after dying as a deity, one becomes an animal, and so forth. Thus, the Sanskrit term *pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes up [a state of existence]" (*shu-qu-zu*), which is precisely what is meant by a "person.
Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*): it is the reckoning that the dharma-characteristics of oneself as a sentient being continue in succession through births.

Therefore. ○ Regarding "the notion of a living being" (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*): it is also called "life-span. It refers to calculating that the life-span of one's existence throughout a lifetime is never severed.

○ However, "self" (*ātman*) is the general subject, while "person" (*pudgala*) and so forth are specific instances. By subsuming the specific into the general, it is termed "clinging to a self" (*ātmagrāha*).

For this reason, all three [of these notions] are described as "calculating a self" (*ātma-kalpanā*). ○ Now, although the above four characteristics are not explicitly present in the sūtra, they are nonetheless implied.
It is not that one cannot understand this.
△ Second, there is no attachment to phenomena,
no characteristic of phenomena, and also no characteristic of non-phenomena.
[Commentary: Second, the attachment to non-existence. The Treatise states: "Regarding the characteristic of non-existence: all dharmas, whether as subject or object, are non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of non-dharmas: the true existence of non-self and empty reality [is affirmed]."
[Commentary] "The grasper, etc. means that both mind and objects have vanished. Although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they are collectively subsumed under mind and objects.
Since mind and objects each possess immeasurable distinctions, it is said "all. "True emptiness, etc.
means that although all dharmas are empty, this does not mean they are entirely devoid of characteristics. It simply means that while one is free from attachment, true emptiness is not severed.
Therefore, it is said that there is also no characteristic of non-dharma.
△ Second, a comparative analysis of the scripture’s purport.

[Commentary]: However, the departure from the two attachments is precisely the foundation for attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and accomplishing pure faith, as well as the root of all wholesome roots.
“Merit and virtue” refers to the combination of the two.

[Commentary] However, setting aside what follows, these two lines weigh the purport of the sutra; they clarify that attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision involves both the auxiliary and the primary.
[Commentary] Therefore, the Treatise says: "Wisdom alone is sufficient. Why, then, does it further speak of the merit of upholding the precepts?

It is for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the distinctions within the arising of the true mark (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). There is also the merit of upholding the precepts, for by relying on faith and reverence, one can give rise to the true mark;
thus, it is not merely *prajñā* that is spoken of."

[Commentary] Therefore, the treatise below cites scriptural evidence. There is an inquiry followed by an explanation, which demonstrates the matter in detail. Regarding the "distinctions of the true mark" (*lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*):
the true mark itself is without distinction; it is only the skillful means that can give rise to the true mark that possesses distinctions.
"The merit of upholding the precepts" refers to the latter section. Regarding "faith and so forth," it is said below:
"When faith is pure, then the true mark arises. Maitreya’s verse states: "That person, relying on faith, gives rise to the true mark through reverence."

Regarding the phrase "not only," the intended meaning is that there are many skillful means capable of producing the true nature (*dharmatā*), and it is not necessary to speak solely of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Although the previous passage spoke of "leaving behind attachments" and this one speaks of "prajñā," it is because prajñā is able to eliminate attachment.
The former refers to that which is to be severed (*praheya*), while the latter refers to that which severs (*prahāṇa*). Although the subject and object differ, their underlying intent does not.

△ Second, revealing through causes that subtle attachments have not yet been eliminated (Sūtra). This has two parts: first, a general explanation of the two characteristics; second, a specific explanation of the two characteristics.
First, the general explanation of the two characteristics.
Why is this? Because if these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they will thereby become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
[Commentary] Second, this reveals that subtle attachments have not yet been eliminated.
[Commentary] "Those who have not yet eliminated subtle grasping" refers to those for whom both types of grasping arise spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*).

Although they have previously abandoned coarse conceptual grasping and are already able to achieve pure faith, their realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision remains shallow; thus, subtle grasping has not been eliminated.
This ultimately obstructs the Noble Path, and therefore it is now revealed so that they may sever it.
[Commentary] The Sūtra poses the question: "For what reason must there be the characteristics of both dharma and non-dharma? The explanation states:
"Because of grasping at characteristics, one becomes attached to the notions of self, person, and so forth. The remaining text is as explained in detail elsewhere.

[Commentary]: "If the mind grasps at [characteristics]," this generally clarifies the two aspects. It comprehensively explains that grasping at both phenomena and non-phenomena is entirely comprised of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it establishes the thesis that if one establishes the grasping of marks, then the marks of self and so forth will arise. This is the fundamental tenet.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has two parts. First, the explanation of the general clarification of the two aspects. Regarding "generally explaining," the Sūtra says: "If the mind grasps at marks.
Within these marks, the meaning includes both the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas; therefore, it is called "general.

Regarding "it is also," this is because the subsequent text separately clarifies that grasping at dharmas and non-dharmas all involves attachment to the marks of self, person, and so forth; thus, this [present section] merely establishes [the premise].
This is its essential tenet.

△ Second, the specific clarification of the two characteristics (Sūtra): [The commentary] has two parts. First, the direct explanation of the two characteristics; second, the separate explanation of the underlying intent of the inquiry.

"If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas, one immediately becomes attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this? If one grasps at the characteristics of non-dharmas..."
This immediately leads to clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
△ First, the correct discernment of the two characteristics has two parts: first, citing Vasubandhu; second, citing Asaṅga. First, citing Vasubandhu.
[Commentary]: If one takes the passage below [the section on] "dharmas," it separately clarifies two characteristics. The *Śāstra* states:
"There is only the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance, but no manifest coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), because it demonstrates the absence of the view of self."

[Commentary] If one takes the latter [explanation], the two interpretations separately clarify the two characteristics. 1. The primary exposition of the two characteristics. ○ Regarding "the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance":
this refers to the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Because it is subsumed under the "ground of abiding in ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), it is termed a "tendency.

○ Regarding "active manifestation (*samudācāra*)" and so forth: this refers to the manifest activity of the discriminative grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). "That which has already been severed" indicates non-self (*anātman*).
"Those who see" establishes the preceding meaning.
△ Second, citing Asaṅga:
[Commentary] Asaṅga says: "It is merely the transformation of the marks of dharma and non-dharma; it is not the notion of 'self' and so forth, because [the notions of] self and so forth..."
"Perception and its basis do not arise.
[Commentary] "Merely grasping," etc., refers to the aforementioned latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*). "That which possesses" means that it arises—that is, it manifests.

○ "The notion of self" (*ātma-saṃjñā*) refers to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the discrimination of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*). ○ "The basis" refers to the seeds of such discrimination. It serves as...

Because it is the basis for their manifestation, the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*) may also be called the "basis," as it serves as the support for that grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*); therefore, none of these arise.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the intent of the inquiry.
[Commentary]: Regarding the inquiry, [the question is]: "Since one grasps phenomena merely as phenomena, for what reason does one then become attached to a self and so forth? The explanation says:
If grasping at what is not the Dharma (*adharma*) also leads to attachment to a self (*ātman*), how much more so for grasping at the Dharma?

This explains the latter [the subtle] by means of the former [the coarse]. [Commentary: The section beginning with "In between" consists of two parts that separately explain the meaning of the inquiry; this can be understood.

Regarding "explaining the latter by means of the former," it would not be as appropriate to say "explaining the coarse by means of the subtle," for in that case the meaning would be easier to perceive.

[Commentary] Question: Since those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) also possess attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha), why do they not give rise to the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi)? Answer:

Because from the very beginning of their practice, those of the two vehicles focus exclusively on severing attachment to a self; thus, by the time they reach the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), both coarse and subtle [attachments] are entirely eliminated.
Therefore, although there may still be attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*) does not arise.

Now, regarding practitioners of the Mahāyāna, both types of conceptual attachment are severed and simultaneously dispelled, yet the two innate forms (*sahaja*) remain; it is from these that the two attachments arise spontaneously.
Therefore, Asaṅga said: "Because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the mark of self (*ātman*) have not been severed, there is grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*).
△ Fourth, showing the profound gateway of the Middle Way (Sūtra), in two parts: first, the formal conclusion returning to the Middle; second, citing scriptural statements as proof.

[Commentary] The Sūtra of the Profound Gate states: "For this reason" means that because one previously grasped at both phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*), clinging to them as a self (*ātman*) and so forth, it is therefore exhorted that one should not do so;
this is precisely entering the Middle Way. "By virtue of this meaning" means that because one does not grasp at either phenomena or non-phenomena for this reason.
△ First, the formal conclusion that returns to the Middle Way.
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
[Commentary] Fourth: This demonstrates the profound gateway of the Middle Way. First, the formal conclusion that returns to the Middle Way.

[Commentary] Regarding the summary in the sub-commentary: "One should not grasp at dharmas," which means departing from existence; "one should not grasp at non-dharmas," which means departing from non-existence.
Since one has departed from both existence and non-existence, one returns to the Middle Way.
△ Second, citing scriptural authority as proof:
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma to be like the simile of the raft."
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone that which is not the Dharma.

[Commentary] The subsequent citation of this teaching serves as proof. Regarding the analogy of the raft: it is through provisional words that the meaning is revealed; one should not grasp at the meaning according to the literal words.
"Not grasping" means not taking up; it does not mean total abandonment.

[Commentary] "Using provisional words to reveal the meaning" means that what is spoken is not the Dharma itself, but rather reveals that the essence of the Dharma is free from conceptual attachments to its nature.
If there were no words that are not in accordance with the Dharma, one would have no means of knowing their meaning; all other cases are to be understood by this analogy.

One should know that meaning does not manifest of itself, but must rely upon words. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "There is no departure from words to explain liberation. Regarding the phrase "should not," etc.:
it means that although one hears what is not in accordance with the Dharma, one must not grasp at the meaning of emptiness according to the literal expression. This precludes the first [extreme].

This refers to those who cling to words. Regarding "not clinging to [words]," etc.: it means that if one were to completely discard words that are not in accordance with the Dharma, how could one understand the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena?
One should know that this merely removes the illness, not the phenomenon itself;
this negates those who seek to depart entirely from words. Thus, both total clinging and total discarding are untenable; therefore, the *Avataṃsaka*...
The Commentary states: Now, phenomena are without words or images, yet they are not separate from words and images. Because of delusion, one fails to see that they are without words and images;
because of attachment, one becomes confused regarding words and images and loses sight of the Truth. [Commentary] The verse says: That non-abiding compliance is the realized wisdom within phenomena.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "and so forth" in the verse, the remaining two lines state: "Just as a person abandons a boat or raft, so it is with the meaning within the Dharma.

[Sub-commentary] The treatise explains: "Non-abiding" means that having attained realized wisdom (*prāptajñāna*), one abandons the teaching (*śāsana*), like reaching the other shore. "Conformity" means...
The teaching that accords with that realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*) is like not yet having reached the shore.

[Commentary] The treatise states below that this further explains the verse. Regarding "attaining realized wisdom" and so forth: one uses words to express wisdom, but upon attaining wisdom, one forgets the words;
forgetting the words is precisely non-abiding. It is like boarding a raft to cross a river and discarding the raft once the shore is reached.

Regarding "conforming," etc.: as long as one has not yet attained realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*), one must not entirely forget the words [of the teachings]. As long as one has not reached the other shore, one should not discard the raft.
[The Commentary] states that Vasubandhu said: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, because they arise as real characteristics; how much more so non-dharmas? This is the principle.
Because it should not [be grasped]. [Commentary:
Regarding the arising of the true nature (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*): "true nature" refers to the Dharma. Having attained the wisdom of true nature, there is neither sign (*nimitta*) nor attainment;

therefore, it is said that one should relinquish it. Because the true nature is signless, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom is entirely absent..."
Regarding "that which is obtained": as for what is logically untenable, even this dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended;
how much less so all dharmas apart from the true mark? Since everything other than the true mark of all dharmas is the work of Māra, it is called "not the Dharma."
This does not accord with reason; therefore, it is inconsistent. Since it is incorrect by this analogy, the text says, "How much more so?
△ Third, resolving the doubt regarding the absence of characteristics (*animitta*). (Commentary) Two parts: first, the heading and the statement of the doubt;

second, resolving the doubt according to the sūtra. First, the heading and the statement of the doubt has three parts: first, the heading; second, pointing out the source where the doubt arises; third, the conclusion.
The doubt is established. First, the chapter heading is presented.
[Commentary] Third: Regarding the section on severing non-characteristics, how can doubt be spoken of?
[Sub-commentary] Within the third section, the chapter heading is first presented.
△ Second, pointing out the source where doubt arises. [Commentary] The *Śāstra* says:
"As previously stated, one cannot see the Buddha through marks; the Buddha is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
[Record] Regarding "As previously stated" and so forth: this points to the source where doubt arises. This follows from the first section, for that text says: "No..."
One may perceive the Tathāgata through his physical marks. ○ The Buddha is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*). This refers to the verse which says:
"By discerning the nature of the conditioned, one prevents its attainment; because its three characteristics are distinct in essence, that which is apart from them is the Tathāgata."
Therefore, it is said that they are not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This is also a definitive establishment of the principle.
△ Third, the conclusion of the doubt.
[Commentary] How did Śākyamuni attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? How did he preach the Dharma?
[Commentary] "How so? and below, he concludes by forming a doubt. If the Buddha is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then it would be inconsistent for him to have attainment or to preach the Dharma.
Why, then, did Śākyamuni attain enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and preach the Dharma in various assemblies before and after that?

Since there is both attainment and preaching, he would fall into the category of the conditioned. How can one then say, as was previously stated, that one does not see [the Buddha] by means of his marks?
Is it unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sutra (the sutra has two parts). First, resolving doubts through question and answer; second, comparing to reveal superiority.

Regarding the first, resolving doubts through question and answer, there are four sections: first, raising the cause of doubt to ask the question; second, responding in accordance with the true principle; third, explaining...
Regarding the statement that there is no fixed dharma, there are four explanations for the reason why it is said that nothing is to be grasped. First, he raises the cause of doubt to pose a question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?

[Commentary] This section on severing doubts consists of two parts. First, the question and answer that sever doubts. Within this, there are four sections; first, the raising of the doubt through four questions.
[Commentary] This raises the cause [of the doubt]. The intent of the sutra asks: "In your mind, what do you think?
Do I attain bodhi or not? Do I preach the Dharma or not? He originally harbored this doubt, and therefore [the Buddha] raised it as a question.
[Commentary] The Buddha’s question as to whether [it was attained] intends to show that it was not attained; thus, Asaṅga says: "It is shown by reversing the grasping at perfect enlightenment.

[Record] Regarding "The Buddha’s question, etc.": Subhūti harbored doubts regarding attainment and doubts regarding the teaching. The Buddha then questioned him in accordance with those doubts; although the phrasing...

"Attaining" is said to manifest "non-attainment. To test his response, one examines whether he understands or does not understand. Below the section on "Non-attachment," a scriptural citation is introduced as proof.
He [the interlocutor] suspects there is grasping; the Buddha reveals there is no grasping. By using non-existence to refute existence, it is called a "reversal.
This principle is applied by analogy to the teaching of the Dharma.
△ Second, responding in accordance with the true principle:
Subhūti said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
there is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach."
[Commentary]: Second, repaying [the debt] by conforming to the true principle. [Record]:

It can be understood that conforming to the principle is the repayment of the intent of the Sūtra. "Certainty" (niyata) means the ultimate reality; that is to say, the absence of real dharmas is termed bodhi.
"The Tathāgata speaks of dharmas that have no reality. This is a response strictly from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
[The Commentary] states in verse: "The emanation-body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma."

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "and so forth" in the verse, the subsequent lines state: "The teaching of the Dharma is non-dual and without grasping; it is without speech and free from the characteristics of words.
The intended meaning is that Śākyamuni Tathāgata is an emanation (nirmāṇakāya). As for the characteristics of such an emanation, they exist conventionally but are ultimately non-existent.

Therefore, in all the answers, it is stated that there is no fixed [nature]. According to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there is no distinction within the fruit of Buddhahood.
The qualities of form and sound exist only as suchness (tathatā) and the wisdom of suchness; this alone is the true Buddha.
Since the present [manifestations] differ from this, how can they be called true? Therefore, it is said that "the responsive and transformational [bodies] are not the true," and so forth.
△ Third, the explanation of the statement that there is no fixed dharma (the Commentary). This has two parts: first, citing Asaṅga; second, citing Vasubandhu. Why is this?
Because all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
[Commentary] Third, the explanation of the phrase "no fixed dharma.
[Record] Regarding the *Aniyata-dharma-sūtra*, the intent of the inquiry is: for what reason can no fixed dharma be spoken of? The intent of the explanation is:
if one wishes to say it exists, it is formless and nameless; if one wishes to say it does not exist, the Sages take it as their spiritual reality (*satya*).
If the principle is such as this, what could possibly be said? Even "saying" cannot be attained; what, then, could be grasped? To grasp is precisely to attain.
Therefore, it was stated above: "There is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak," and so forth.
△ First, citing Asaṅga.
[Commentary]: Asaṅga says: "That which cannot be grasped" refers to the time of correct hearing; "that which cannot be expressed" refers to the time of correct teaching.
"Not the dharma" is because of its nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); "not non-dharma" is because of the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has two parts. First, it cites Asaṅga. Regarding "hearing and so forth": this means hearing without hearing and speaking without speaking;
it does not mean that there is no hearing or speaking at all. As the *Fuming* (Floating Name) says: "Now, as for those who preach the Dharma..."
There is no speaking and no showing; for those who hear the Dharma, there is neither hearing nor attainment—this is the meaning of this principle.

Regarding the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): all dharmas exist with their distinctions based solely upon deluded thought. Since even thought is ultimately non-thought, how could dharmas be truly dharmas?
Therefore, they are said to be "non-dharmas. Regarding the selflessness of dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*): it is simply that when the nature of discrimination ceases, this is [it].
The principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is not non-existent; therefore, it is said that it is "not non-dharma.
△ Second, citing Vasubandhu [has two parts]: first, the explanation of the text; second, resolving difficulties. First, the explanation of the text.
[Commentary] The Treatise states: "Those dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. This is spoken according to the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).

They are "not dharmas" because all dharmas lack intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). They are "not non-dharmas" because that *tathatā* exists as the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of selflessness (*anātman*).

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "The treatise says" below has two parts: first, citing Vasubandhu; second, explaining the text. Regarding the phrase "relying on the truth," etc., this merely establishes the fundamental basis upon which one relies.
Furthermore, it is said that above this basis, one transcends both existence and non-existence. Regarding the phrase "all," etc.:
The dharmas that arise through conditions have, from the beginning, no real substance and no real characteristics; therefore, it is said they are "not.

As for the existence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): since all dharmas are non-existent, this is precisely the true mark. Because the true mark is not non-existent, it is said they are "not non-dharmas.
This means that [the negation] negates even the non-dharma.
△ Second, resolving the objection.
[Commentary]: Why is it that only "discourse" (yanshuo) is mentioned and not "realization" (zheng)? Because if there were discourse, it would already constitute the meaning of realization.
If one does not realize, then one cannot speak.

[Commentary] "Why? and below constitute two responses to an objection. The intent of the objection is as follows: Originally, both the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) and the teaching (*deśanā*) were doubted;

thus, the questions and answers have hitherto encompassed both. Now, within the explanation of the underlying reason, why is it that one speaks only of "that which is taught" and not of "realization"?
The passage beginning with "There is a saying... provides the explanation. This uses the teaching to conversely verify the realization. Furthermore, there is a river... [text ends].
A pearl does not wither; a mountain possessing jade increases in luster. If there is no root of virtue within, how could one speak of it without?
Thus, mere words serve only to manifest one's own realization. Furthermore, these words themselves constitute the realization.
△ Fourth, the explanation for why it is said that there is no grasping.
Why is this so? Because all noble ones and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
[Commentary] Fourth, the explanation of the reason why it is said there is no grasping and no teaching.
[Record] Regarding the *Anupādāna-sūtra*, the intent of the inquiry is: Why is it said that there is no grasping and no teaching, and that it is neither dharma nor non-dharma?
[Explanation] The intent of the response is: The Sage is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the unconditioned is precisely non-discrimination (*avikalpa*).
If there is grasping at the teaching that "this is Dharma" or "this is non-Dharma," all such instances belong to conceptual discrimination and are not termed unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

How, then, could one be a noble one (*ārya*)? Therefore, there is no grasping at such teachings and so forth. Regarding the term "worthy and noble" (*xiánshèng*): "worthy" (*xián*) is itself "noble" (*shèng*); this is an etymological explanation based on proximity.
[Commentary] Wei states: "All sages are named after the unconditioned dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*).

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "Wei states," etc.: Question: Since the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) apply to both ordinary practitioners (*śaikṣa*) and sages (*ārya*), why does [the text] refer only to sages? Answer:

If discussed in general terms, this includes those at the stage of the worthy (*śaikṣa*). Since this clarifies the depth and shallowness of the realization of the fruit, it refers exclusively to the "sages" (*ārya*).

Regarding the "attainment of names," this refers to their differentiation; for all sages establish their names based on the meaning of their differentiated realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For example, by realizing the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness), one receives the name "Bodhisattva of the Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and so forth.
This is merely a distinction in nomenclature; it refers to one and the same meaning.
[Commentary] The intent of the treatise is that the Sage derives his name solely based on the purity of True Suchness (tathatā), and does not obtain any separate dharma.
Therefore, there is no grasping or verbalization.
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of the treatise and so forth: this refers to those from the first bhūmi (ground) upward.

As they realize each portion of *tathatā* (suchness), they sever one hindrance and two delusions; this is precisely "one-portion purity. Based on this principle, a single name is established for each stage, continuing in this manner up to the Buddha-ground.
○ "Not attaining a separate dharma" means attaining through non-attainment; this is itself the Truth (*bhūta*).
One attains Bodhi. If one says there is attainment, that is precisely non-attainment. One should know that beneath the Bodhi tree there is no substantial reality at all;
thus the verse says, "The manifested and transformed are not the true Buddha," and so forth. Therefore, there is no grasping for a speaker;
this concludes by returning to the meaning of non-discrimination in the scriptural text.
[Commentary] Regarding the existence of distinctions: the *Śāstra* states that True Suchness possesses both "complete purity" (*pariśuddhi*) and "partial purity.
[Record] "Complete purity" refers to the Buddha. This means that all afflictions and habitual tendencies have been entirely severed and eliminated;

being utterly free from even the slightest speck of defilement, it is pure, singular, and unmixed. "Partial purity" refers to the Bodhisattva. This means they have partially severed the various obstacles.
One partially realizes True Suchness (*tathatā*), yet because defilements have not been entirely removed, it is termed "partial. Thus, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* (Foding jing) states:

"When remaining traces of dust still persist, one is among those in training; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata. This is explained in detail in the section of the Preface concerning the one who has fully perfected pure awakening.
[Commentary] Asaṅga says: "The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has the meaning of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

For this reason, Bodhisattvas receive the designation 'those in training' (*śaikṣa*), while Tathāgatas receive the designation 'those beyond training' (*aśaikṣa*). The initial unconditioned is manifested at the time of subduing distraction."
Regarding the "subsequent unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): it refers exclusively to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because it is the unsurpassed training.

[Commentary] Below the section on Non-attachment (*Asaṅga*), the noble and holy ones (*ārya*) are elucidated by way of the distinctions among the unconditioned. ○ "Non-discrimination" (*avikalpa*) is precisely the meaning of the unconditioned.
Because there is no purposeful activity (*abhisamskāra*), it is called "unconditioned. Unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) is, in essence, a single dharma.

Regarding "Bodhisattvas and so forth": because they possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and because they have something to be accomplished. Regarding "Tathāgatas and so forth": because they are without conceptual discrimination and because they have no further activity to perform.
Regarding "the first unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): this refers to the Bodhisattva. Regarding "subduing" (*vinaya*) and so forth: [this refers to the Tathāgata].
This refers to the state of contemplation. Because conceptualization does not arise and one attains partial correspondence with reality, it is called "manifest" (*abhivyakta*).

Regarding the subsequent "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): this refers to the Tathāgata. Being free from further conceptualization, it is the true unconditioned, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to the Buddha; thus, the word "furthermore" is used. Since there is nothing superior to it, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). "Awakening" (*bodhi*) is itself the Buddha.
[Commentary]: The worthy and sages of the three vehicles all cultivate and realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, they are collectively described as having distinctions. [Record]:
From "The three vehicles" onwards, this concludes by encompassing all vehicles. Since those of the two vehicles also partially realize the true principle, they are included here.

Thus, one knows that the worthy and sages of the three vehicles all cultivate and realize the unconditioned; although what they realize— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the nature of the realization.)

There is no difference in depth; rather, there is a distinction in the capacity for realization, just as three animals crossing the same river differ in their ability to cross while the distance crossed remains the same.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Those who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
those who seek the Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, or the unsurpassed Buddha vehicle—all are told they should study the Prajñā."
Pāramitās. Therefore, the sūtra says, "all worthy sages.
△ Second, the comparative evaluation to manifest superiority (the sūtra) has four parts: first, raising inferior merit as a question; second, answering by explaining the abundance of merit;
third, judging that the merit of the sūtra surpasses it; fourth, explaining the reason for this surpassing.
[Commentary] Second: Comparing and weighing to manifest superiority.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "comparing and weighing," etc.: Question: Originally, Subhūti gave rise to doubt, which is why the World-Honored One acted to sever it.
Now that the doubt has been severed, what is the use of comparing and weighing? Answer: The Treatise says: Although the Dharma cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed, yet...

"Because it is not empty. The intention is this: fearing that some, upon hearing that this Dharma cannot be grasped or described, might wish to utterly reject and discard the verbal teachings, he thus employs this comparative evaluation to manifest its excellence, so as to cause them to expound and uphold it.
At this point, the *Mahāmegha* establishes a fifth doubt regarding "not-empty merit," because the treatise does not explicitly state that it resolves doubts.
Therefore, it is not established here.
△ First, he raises the question by citing inferior merit:
"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and use them..."
[The Buddha said: "If this person were to practice giving, would the merit they obtain be great?
[Commentary] This first raises a lesser form of merit to pose the question.

[Recorded Notes] Regarding the meaning of the question concerning "little merit": the seven treasures are the most precious, and the three-thousandfold world system is the greatest; yet one uses these to practice giving.
Whether one's merit is great or small.

[Commentary] A verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—each set of one thousand is called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. One thousand times this..."
The Great Trichiliocosm all undergoes formation and destruction simultaneously.

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 12, explains the three thousandfold world system. Regarding the four great continents: they are the continent of Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body), and so forth.
Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānīdvīpa in the west, and Uttarakurudvīpa in the north. Regarding the sun and moon: these illuminate a single caturmahādvīpaka (four-continent world system) as one.
Sumeru is also called Sumerulū; this is merely a difference between the colloquial and literary registers of the Sanskrit language.
It is translated here as "Mount Wondrous High" (Mt. Meru). It is composed of four precious substances and is eighty thousand yojanas in height.
The "Desire Heavens" (*kāmadeva*) refer to the six heavens of the desire realm:

namely, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. The "Brahma World" refers to the first heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within it, there are further three heavens: namely, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven. [Each...]
"Regarding 'one thousand' and so forth: when each of the aforementioned [worlds] reaches one thousand, it constitutes a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).

Regarding "this small chiliocosm" and so forth: when one thousand small chiliocosms reach one thousand, they constitute a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*). Regarding "this thousand" and so forth:
furthermore, when one thousand medium chiliocosms reach one thousand, they constitute a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). All are identical in this manner."
The term "etc. refers to the fact that from the fourth dhyāna upward, the three calamities do not reach; therefore, their formation and destruction are not mentioned.

From the third dhyāna downward, all are encompassed by the three calamities; hence it is said that they share the same formation and destruction. Within this, from the first dhyāna downward, there is the calamity of fire;
from the second dhyāna downward, the calamity of water; and from the third dhyāna downward, the calamity of wind.
[Commentary] The seven treasures are: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, red pearls, and crystal.
[Record] The seven treasures and so forth may be understood as they are commonly known.
△ Second, the explanation of the abundance of merit as a response.
Subhūti said: "Very much, World-Honored One. Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit;
therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great."
[Commentary] Second: Explaining the abundance of merit as a recompense.
[Record] The text for the answer regarding the abundance of merit as a recompense for the sutra is evident. ○ The inquiry asks: For what reason is it said to be "abundant"?
