○ The intent of the explanation is: It is not in terms of ultimate emptiness that it is called abundant; rather, it is in terms of conventional existence that it is called abundant.
[Commentary] Asuṅga says: "This merit" is the introductory designation; "it is not" refers to ultimate emptiness;
"therefore" refers to conventional existence.
[Commentary] Regarding "ultimate emptiness" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): this gate is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) beyond all characteristics; it cannot be described as either merit or non-merit.
Since merit does not exist, there is nothing by which it could be called "much. Regarding "conventional existence" (*saṃvṛti-sat*):
this gate possesses characteristics and is conditioned; it can be described as merit. Because merit exists, it can also be described as "much."

△ Third, the judgment that the merit of this sutra surpasses all others (*śū*). This has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the sutra text; second, the specific indication of the characteristics of the phrases.
"If, moreover, there should be a person who receives and maintains even as little as a four-line verse from within this sutra and explains it for others..."
The merit of this [latter] surpasses that [former].
[Commentary on the Sub-commentary (Sū): Third, judging that the merit of the sūtra exceeds [that of other practices].
[Record (Jì): Judging the merit of the sūtra—the intent of the sūtra can be understood. However, if even these four lines are thus, how much more so the entire text?
△ First, the formal explanation of the sūtra text.
[Commentary] The verse says: "Upholding the Dharma and expounding it are not in vain regarding merit; yet merit alone does not lead to Bodhi, whereas these two can lead to Bodhi."
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the sutra text. The verse explains the practice of upholding and preaching, clarifying the reasons for its excellence.

Compared with the subsequent sutra text, this section appears somewhat abrupt; however, it should be understood that this is because the verses form a continuous chain that cannot be divided. Thus it is known.
"Those who uphold and explain" indicates two dharma-gates.

"Not in vain," and so forth, means that upholding and explaining this sutra is not like the empty attainment of merit through the gift of jewels. "What further thing is obtained? refers to the subsequent passage.
"Merit does not lead to Bodhi" means that although the gift of jewels may be great, it only accomplishes mundane, out-flowing (sāsrava) merit.
In the end, they will be unable to achieve unexcelled bodhi. Second, those who can proceed toward bodhi are those who uphold and expound this sutra;
by doing so, they sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and since the state where afflictions are exhausted is itself bodhi.
△ Second, the specific indication of the characteristics of the verses, in two parts: first, the direct exposition; second, the resolution of objections. First, the direct exposition. [Commentary]:
Regarding the "four lines" (catuṣpāda), when the expression of the meaning is complete within four lines, it constitutes a four-line verse (gāthā).
[Commentary] Following the four lines [of the verse], there is a second section that specifically demonstrates the characteristics of the lines. Regarding "expressing meanings, etc.":

this means that one line expresses one meaning, one meaning constitutes one line, and four meanings together constitute one stanza (*gāthā*). Whether it be identity or difference, existence or emptiness, permanence or impermanence, and so forth—each of these possesses its own set of four lines.
[Commentary]: As it is said: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
This is most wondrous.

[Commentary] However, regarding these four lines of the present sutra, there are differing explanations. Some say that taking "no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span" constitutes the four lines.
Others say that taking "if one sees me by means of form," and so forth, constitutes the four lines.

Some say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and so forth constitute the four phrases (*catuṣpāda*). Others say that one simply takes any four phrases from within a single sutra to form the four phrases.
Still others say that they only constitute the four phrases when beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and ending with "and practiced accordingly" (*yathānuśiṣṭam pratipatsye*).
However, none of these aforementioned views represent the correct meaning. [The section] beginning with "As for ordinary people... clarifies the correct [meaning].
This refers to the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) based on existence, non-existence, and so forth. That is to say: the first is the proposition of existence;
the second is the proposition of non-existence; the third is the proposition of both existence and non-existence; and the fourth is the proposition of neither existence nor non-existence.
It is both complete in its phrasing and its meaning; therefore, it is called "most wondrous. By means of these four meanings, one can penetrate the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*);
these are the four gates.
△ Second, resolving objections.

[Commentary: However, in terms of meaning, these are fully contained within four propositions. Upholding and reciting them leads directly to Bodhi. As for the wording, it may be expanded or abbreviated; it need not consist of exactly four.
If the meaning is deficient, then one will mutually commit slander [against the Dharma].
[Commentary] However, from "But only... onwards, it addresses a general objection. First, the question is raised:

if the first two lines each consist of four characters, while the third line alone consists of six characters, how can these constitute verses (gāthā) given the discrepancy in the number of syllables?

This passage provides the explanation for this. Regarding "upholding, reciting," etc.: these four meanings are the gateway to all dharmas; if one understands these four meanings, one attains universal penetration.
The myriad dharmas. Since the myriad dharmas are thus penetrated, how could one fail to realize Bodhi? Regarding "the texts may be equal," this refers only to their meaning;
the meaning does not reside in the text. While the meaning must be complete and perfect, the text may increase or decrease accordingly.

Regarding "if the meanings were equal," it means that to omit [a part] constitutes slander, whereas to include it constitutes a gateway. "Constituting slander" means that to omit [a necessary element] results in [the teaching being perceived as] non-existent.

To exaggerate [existence] constitutes the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*). To deny existence constitutes the slander of deprecation (*apavāda*). To deny both existence and non-existence constitutes the slander of contradiction (*virodha*).

To deny both existence and non-existence simultaneously constitutes the slander of frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is because what exists must definitely exist, and what does not exist must definitely not exist;
the other two cases follow this pattern. Thus, four types of slander are established. Why is this so? Because phenomena are not like that, and because one views them as not being like that.
This is the Prajñāpāramitā; it is like a great mass of fire that cannot be grasped from any of its four sides.
To "possess the four phrases" means that the meaning is complete and lacks nothing. There is existence that is not fixed as existing; this is the existence of non-existence.
"Non-uncertainty does not exist" means that this is precisely the non-existence of existence. The other [phrases] are to be understood by analogy.
Within each single phrase, one fully perceives the meaning of all four phrases, thereby avoiding the fallacies of exaggeration or diminution. Thus, it constitutes a "gate. Why is this so?
Because the Dharma is thus, and because one perceives it according to the Dharma, this is the Prajñāpāramitā;
it is like a cool pond into which one may enter from all four sides. ○ However, while people rely upon the Dharma, the Dharma differs from people and they diverge.
If the meaning of the Dharma is fully realized, how could one fail to realize Bodhi? Therefore, it is said that receiving and upholding this sutra is superior to...
The Merit of Giving.
△ Fourth, explaining the reason for the transcendence (Sūtra), in two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the further explanation. First, the direct explanation: Why is this so?
Subhūti, all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas...
"The dharmas of bodhi all issue from this sutra. [Commentary:
To correctly explain the intent of the scriptural inquiry, it says: For what reason is the upholding and preaching of this sutra superior to the gift of jewels?
The meaning of this commentary can be understood [as follows].
[The *Śāstra*] provides four explanations for the reason why [the two accumulations] transcend [the bodhisattva stages]. Regarding the first, the direct explanation:

"The dharma of the Bodhi of all Buddhas" refers to what the *Treatise* calls the *Dharmakāya*. With respect to that *Dharmakāya*, these two [accumulations] function as the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) for its realization. As for "all Buddhas": [text continues]
This refers to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya). The *Śāstra* says: "In this regard, it can act as the cause of production. [Commentary:
"The bodhi-dharmas of all Buddhas" distinguishes these from the bodhi-dharmas of other vehicles. However, other forms of bodhi do not fail to emerge from this;
rather, the most excellent ones are cited here by way of illustration. These two refer to upholding and expounding.
Regarding the "revealing cause" (了因): the Dharma-body is the fundamental principle of true reality, neither arising nor ceasing.
It is merely obscured when shrouded by afflictions and revealed when realized through wisdom. By upholding and expounding this Dharma, wondrous wisdom manifests of itself.

When one contemplates and shatters the afflictions (*kleśa*), the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) manifests. Regarding the "causes of birth": the bodies of recompense (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) do not exist inherently;
they are brought about by myriad practices (*pāramitā*) and are therefore termed "birth. Thus, Maitreya’s verse states: "With respect to reality, it is the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*);
it is also the cause of birth for the others. The Wei translation of the sutra says: "All the *bodhi*-dharmas of all Buddhas arise from this."
The Sūtra says:
△ Second, the interpretive explanation.
Subhūti, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is precisely not Buddha-dharma.
[Commentary] This further explains the Sūtra. That which is called "Buddha-dharma" exists from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
that which is "not Buddha-dharma" does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
[Commentary] Second, the explanation by way of turning [the perspective]. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are no Buddha-dharmas that emerge from the sūtras.

[Record] Regarding "the ultimate" and so forth: this means that within the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there exist the distinctions between delusion and awakening, defilement and purity, and ordinary beings and sages.

Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-dharma emerges from the sūtras. The principle of ultimate truth transcends the characteristics of delusion and enlightenment, defilement and purity, and ordinary person and sage;
thus, the meaning of the Buddha-dharma cannot be expressed in words. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:
"The wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas is fundamentally without bodhi or nirvāṇa, and likewise without the attainment of Buddhahood."
One does not become a Buddha. There is neither deluded saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra. ○ Thus, this fundamental treatise differs from this [view], so as not to cause further confusion.

[Commentary] The fourth section of the commentary introduces the chapter: "The doubt that the Śrāvakas' attainment of the fruit is grasping.
[Record] The fourth section of the commentary first introduces the chapter.

[Commentary] The *Śāstra* says: "As previously stated, the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) of the sages cannot be grasped or described.
[Record] "As previously stated" and below point to the locus where the doubt arises; this follows from the third section. ○ "Cannot be grasped or described."
As the preceding text states: "All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible.
△ Third, the conclusion of the doubt.
[Commentary]: Why is it that the śrāvakas each take their own fruit and speak according to what they have realized?
[Commentary] "How so? and below conclude the doubt. Previously it was said that "all worthy sages" (āryas) encompass those of the three vehicles;

therefore, there is a doubt as to whether the attainment of the fruit by a śrāvaka constitutes grasping (*upādāna*). For example, when a person who has attained the first fruit realizes their own first fruit, they likewise say of themselves, "I have realized the first fruit," and so forth.
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtras (the sūtra has four parts): 1. the fruit of stream-entry; 2. the fruit of once-returning;
3. the fruit of non-returning; 4. the fruit of no-more-birth.
[Commentary] There are four sections in the text that resolve doubts. First, entering the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna). △ First, entering the fruit of stream-entry (Commentary):
three parts. First, the direct explanation of the scriptural text; second, a comparative analysis of the realization of the fruit; third, the conclusion resolving the state of doubt.
First, the direct explanation of the scriptural text (Sūtra): four parts. First, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation.
The first question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna'?"
△ 2. The response.
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One.
△ 3. The inquiry.
Why is this? △ Fourth, the explanation:
A srotāpanna is called "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nothing entered. He does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is...
He is named *srotāpanna*. [Commentary:
The *Sūtra on the Fruit of Entering the Stream* asks: "In your view, how is it?
Do you think that a person who is a *srotāpanna* forms the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*'? He answers: "No. The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
If this is so, for what reason is one named a *srotāpanna*? The explanation states:
it is simply by virtue of not entering the realms of form and so forth that one is named a *srotāpanna*.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has three parts. First, the direct explanation of the sūtra text. [Sub-commentary]:

*Srotāpanna*. This is translated as "entering the stream," because one enters the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is also called "pre-stream" (*yùliú*), because one joins the stream of the noble ones.

[Commentary] Regarding "one who has entered the stream" (*srotāpanna*): the four fruits [of the path] are termed "noble ones" (*ārya*). Because one now first enters the category of the noble from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is so called.
"Stream" (*srotas*) means "category" (*jāti*). "Entry" (*prati*) means "to join" or "to be included in."

[Commentary] It is precisely because one does not enter the six sense-objects that one is said to "enter the stream of the sages. This is not because there is some other separate object to be entered.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "Precisely because," this explains the reason for receiving this name. As for "entering" (入), it carries the meaning of grasping or attachment. If one were to grasp the six sense-objects...

To remain stagnant within the stream of ordinary beings is to not grasp at the six sense objects; this is called entering the stream of the sages. Thus, one knows that merit and fault reside in the person and not in the realms of the six sense objects.
Based on this, how could there be any separate dharma to be taken up as an object of entry?
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* states: "The Sage, having attained the fruit, does not grasp at a single dharma, nor does he grasp at the objects of the six sense-fields;

therefore, he is called one who flows against the current. [Record] The passage beginning with "The *Śāstra* states" cites evidence for the aforementioned meaning. Regarding "not grasping at a single dharma": this does not refer merely to the six sense-fields.
Regarding the term "逆流" (niùliú), it means to go against the flow of the ordinary person. This is to say that if one grasps at the six sense objects, one enters the flow of the ordinary;
to go against the flow of the sages is to not grasp or be attached to them, thereby entering the flow of the sages and going against the flow of the ordinary.
[Commentary] Up to and including the Arhat, not a single dharma is grasped. For this reason, they are called Arhats.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "up to and including" (*naitai*): this serves as an illustration for the remaining fruits. If even the first fruit is thus, how much more so the others?
△ Second, the comparative examination of the realization of the fruit.
[Commentary] However, it is not that they do not take the unconditioned as their own fruit.

[Record] Regarding the section "However, it is not... and below: this is the second, the comparative examination of the realization of the fruit. Someone may ask: "If neither of them takes [the fruit], then they should likewise not [realize it]."
This is the explanation for the realization.

this is fundamentally different from what was previously doubted. [Commentary: If one follows the sequence for severing doubts, this section is already concluded. This is because the four fruits represent the stages of cultivation, realization, and practice of the worthy and noble ones (*ārya*) of the Hīnayāna;
therefore, they are explained in detail within the Sūtra.

[Commentary] Furthermore, these four fruits have four corresponding paths of approach (*pratipannaka*), so called because they are directed toward the fruits; namely, the path of approach to *srotāpanna* and so forth.

[Commentary] Among the four fruits, the first constitutes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the next two constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the last one constitutes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
[Commentary] First, regarding the initial practice: one attains entry into the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which consists of sixteen moments of mind.
By severing the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of conceptual delusion belonging to the four truths of the three realms, one realizes the fruit of the first stage (*srotāpanna*).
[Commentary] This means that each of the three realms possesses its own four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). Beneath each truth there are specific afflictions (*kleśa*), namely:

greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Depending on whether these are fully present or absent beneath each of the four truths, they constitute the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Beneath [the truth of] suffering, all are fully present; beneath [the truth of] origin..."
The path eliminates three views; in the higher realms, it does not function as anger. (This refers to the first phrase.
That is to say, under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are fully present. (This refers to the second phrase.

That is to say, under the two truths of Origin (*samudayasatya*) and Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), three views are each eliminated—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). The reason these three are excluded is as follows:

The body is the root of suffering; having contemplated suffering, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is severed. Since the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arises based on the body, it likewise perishes along with it.

There is no grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) because, regarding the Truth of Origination, one does not reckon what is not the path to be the path, and the Truth of Cessation is not yet the stage of cultivation;
therefore, in both cases, there is no grasping at precepts and observances. As for the Truth of the Path, it is precisely the stage of cultivation, yet [some] might...
They exist; therefore, they are not eliminated. Thus it is said that the Path eliminates the two views, but does not eliminate the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Consequently, there are ten under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), seven each under the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*); totaling these with the preceding, there are twenty-four.
Under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are eight; together they total thirty-two.
Regarding the subsequent statement that "in the upper realms, anger (*vyāpāda*) does not operate," this means that from each of the two sets of four truths, one instance of hatred is excluded.
Thus, each realm has twenty-eight, totaling fifty-six. Combined with the thirty-two of the lower Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), they altogether constitute eighty-eight.

[Commentary] What are the sixteen moments of mind? This refers to the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), each consisting of one patience (*kṣānti*) and one knowledge (*jñāna*), thus forming eight moments of mind.

Furthermore, the two upper realms are combined into a single set of four truths; by analogy with the contemplation that abandons [defilements] in the lower desire realm, these also each consist of one patience and one knowledge, thus forming eight moments of mind.
These two sets of eight constitute the sixteen moments of mind. Regarding "patience" (*kṣānti*): it is...

The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is the moment when one is correctly severing the afflictions; the knowledge (*jñāna*) at that time is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which is the moment when the severance is finalized.

These are: the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*);

and so on, up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*). This process of severance continues until the fifteenth moment of mind, which is the path of uninterrupted transition.
The patience regarding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) is called "the candidate for the first fruit.

Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one is said to have realized the first fruit and entered the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), becoming a *srotāpanna*. The coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are distinguished and abandoned all at once.
It is like splitting a bamboo stalk; all three joints open simultaneously. Thus, the eight knowledges of the realization of the truths (dṛṣṭi-jñāna) constitute the essence of the first fruit.
[Commentary] The characteristics of the first fruit have been briefly explained in this manner. As for the remaining three fruits, they shall be seen in the subsequent text.
△ Second, the fruit of the Once-returner (Sūtra), in four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation. First, the question:

Why is this? △ Fourth, the explanation:
A *sakṛdāgāmin* is named "one who comes and goes once," yet in reality there is no coming or going; this is what is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
[Commentary] Second: the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*). "Sakṛdāgāmin" is translated here as "once-returner.

although they go back and forth between the human realm and the heavenly realms only once, despite this coming and going, in reality there is no going.
Those who come [to this stage] are designated as *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner) based solely on this meaning.
[Commentary: Regarding the severance of the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm: [Sub-commentary:

As for "severing afflictions," there are four types of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, namely: greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*). These are the [afflictions] common to all.

The subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*) that arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) obstruct the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); because they are difficult to sever, they are divided into nine grades, namely from the "superior-superior" (*adhimātrādhimātra*) down to the "inferior-inferior" (*mṛdumṛdu*).

These nine grades of afflictions are severed by those who have attained the second and third fruits. When one has severed up to five grades, one is called a "candidate for the second fruit" (*dvitīyaphalapratipannaka*).
When one has completely severed six grades, one is called the "second fruit" (*dvitīyaphala*). Thus, it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
It is said: "Having abandoned [the first five fetters], one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one is a once-returner.
[Commentary]: Having passed away from here, one goes once to the heavens and returns once more to the human realm.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "at first glance" (*yiwǎng*): the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can moisten seven births within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Specifically, the highest-of-the-high grade (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) moistens two births; the next three grades each moisten one birth; and the next two grades together moisten one birth. Now, six grades have been severed.
Six births have already been eliminated; only the lower three grades remain. These moisten one more birth in the desire realm;
therefore, after going once to the heavens, one must return once more to the human world to take birth in order to sever the remaining afflictions.
[Commentary] "He immediately attains the fruit of Arhatship.

[Recorded Notes] Regarding the phrase "immediately attains," etc.: Question. According to this sequence, he ought to be at the third stage. Why do you presumptuously say that he "immediately attains Arhatship"?
Answer. As for the statement that he "immediately attains Arhatship," it does not mean that he bypasses [the intermediate stages] and fails to realize the second.
Third: This refers only to the exhaustion of afflictions within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is described as "going and not returning" from the perspective of a single departure;

thus it says, "one immediately attains," and so forth. Why would one change "immediately attains" to "goes directly"? although he could drive them back and forth, they truly possessed no feelings or thoughts by which to deliberate.

[Commentary] Three: The Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala).
[Record] Regarding the Sūtra on the Fruit of Non-returning, the questions and answers are intended in the same manner as above. The explanation of the meaning states:
One who is an Anāgāmin goes once to the heavens and does not return again. Although they do not return, there is nonetheless no such thing as a "non-returner."
Based solely on this meaning, one is called an Anāgāmin.
[Commentary] *Anāgāmin* is translated here as "not coming" (*bù lái*) and also as "not returning" (*bù huán*).
[Record] "Not coming" and "not returning" are essentially one and the same meaning.
[Commentary] Having severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, they are completely exhausted.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "severing afflictions" and so forth: this refers to the remaining three lower grades among the aforementioned nine grades; it means having severed up to the eighth grade.
This is called the candidate for the third fruit. When the nine grades [of afflictions] are completely severed, it is called the third fruit. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"When seven or eight grades of afflictions are severed, one is called a candidate for the third fruit; when all nine grades are completely severed, one immediately attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*)."
[Commentary] At the end of his life, he goes once and for all to the heavens and does not return again to the lower realms.

[Record] Regarding "not returning again": there remain only three grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm. These three grades of afflictions together moisten a single lifetime;
now that they have been severed, there are no longer any afflictions to provide moisture. Since the entanglements are completely cut off, there is no further rebirth.
[Commentary] Therefore, it is said: "he does not come.

[Sub-commentary] The phrase "therefore, it is said" below concludes the third fruit. It consists precisely of the eight classes of non-conditioned dharmas (*asamskṛta*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, the nine grades of the path of cultivation and the unconditioned [attainments] constitute the essence of these fruits.
One should know that for those who have attained these second and third fruits, the severing of afflictions is like cutting wood: it is merely a horizontal severance.
[Commentary] In reality, there is no one who does not come. This meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
[Record] "The same as before" refers to what should be stated: having already realized non-self, who would be able not to come?

First, being without thieves. [Commentary]: 1. Being without thieves, because the afflictions of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation have been exhausted.
[Commentary] Regarding "those who are not thieves": the intent is that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are regarded as thieves.

This is because they sever the life-force of wisdom and plunder the wealth of merit, causing practitioners to lose the Noble Path and be cast adrift in the wilderness of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), failing to reach the precious site of Nirvāṇa.
Since their harm is so profound, they are called "thieves. Regarding "the paths of seeing and cultivation, etc.": this refers to each of the two upper realms.

There are three types of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation: namely, greed, delusion, and pride. Because these afflictions are subtle and difficult to eliminate, they are divided according to the eight stages (*bhūmi*).

Each stage is further divided into nine grades (*prakāra*), totaling seventy-two grades. Each grade consists of one path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
When one has eliminated up to seventy-one grades, one is called a candidate for Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*). Upon eliminating the seventieth...

When the two categories of afflictions are exhausted, one becomes an Arhat. This fruit of the abandonment of delusions is like ascending a multi-storied tower; one climbs higher and higher step by step.

When the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are discussed together, including the single stage of the desire realm, the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) states totaling eighty-nine in number constitute the essence of this fruit.

[Commentary] If one defines the substance [of the fruits] in terms of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), then for the first fruit, it takes only the single path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) as its substance.

For the second, it takes only the single path of liberation of the sixth grade among the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm as its substance.
For the third, it takes only the single path of liberation of the ninth grade as its substance.

As for its essence: the Arhat takes as its essence only the single path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) within the ninth category of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
That which is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*); that which is "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
△ Second, non-arising.
[Commentary] Second, non-arising: because one does not undergo further existence.
[Record] Regarding "non-arising" and so forth: it means "my births are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished," and so on.

One undergoes future existence. However, the first three phrases constitute the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the final phrase constitutes the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*.

This means that one no longer undergoes a body of suffering within the three realms. This is because worldly causes have perished and their fruits are lost, while supramundane causes have been fulfilled and their fruits realized.
△ Third, the Worthy of Offerings (*Arhat*). [Commentary:

△ Third, the explanation has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the indirect explanation. First, the direct explanation:

Second, explaining through non-appropriation as the answer.

An *arhat* is one who is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), does not undergo further birth, and is worthy of offerings. For these reasons, he is named an *arhat*.

Third, citing one's own realization to inspire faith in others. This has three parts.

Upāli upheld the Vinaya, while Subhūti understood emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That he is now called "One Without Strife" (*araṇāvihārin*) is precisely because, by understanding emptiness, he attained the state of being without strife.
This is also like the ten eminent disciples of the Master (Confucius), each of whom had his own particular capability:
Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, and Zhong Gong were noted for their virtuous conduct; Zai Wo and Zi Gong for their eloquence in speech; and Ran You and Ji Lu for their administrative affairs.
[The disciples] Yu and Xia were experts in literature.

[Commentary: As for "those who have abandoned desire," the afflictions of the three realms—wherever there is a mind of craving—are all termed "desire"; it does not refer exclusively to the Desire Realm.
[Commentary] Regarding "detachment from desire" (*vairāgya*) and so forth: this refers to the underlying tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*), which pervades all three realms (*traidhātuka*).

Only when this greed is completely severed is one truly detached from desire. Question: If that is so, then since all Arhats have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, why is Subhūti praised as the foremost?

This does not refer to being free from desire (*vairāgya*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "I have attained the *araṇā-samādhi*, and am foremost among men.
Furthermore, the Wei translation of the Sūtra states: "If I were to harbor such a thought, the World-Honored One would not have declared me foremost in the practice of *araṇā*.

Among these, he is called the foremost.

[Commentary] The *Buddhābhiprāya-sūtra* states: "If, at this time, I were to think, 'I have attained the fruit of Arhatship,' the Buddha would not say of me that I am one who delights in tranquility (*śamatha*).

It is precisely because I do not form such a thought that the Buddha praises me. Regarding "non-action" (*apracāra*), it refers to the absence of such thinking; thus, the sūtra speaks of it conversely.
Regarding the statement, "If one forms this thought, it is explained accordingly that, in reality, there is nothing practiced," the *Śāstra* says:
One is free from two kinds of obstructions. First, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is abandoned through attaining the state of an Arhat;
second, the obstruction to meditative concentration (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*), which is abandoned through attaining the state of being without contention (*araṇa*). Therefore, there is nothing practiced.

[Commentary] "Free from the obstacle of afflictions" means that the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), such as greed and so forth, have been completely eliminated in both their coarse and subtle forms.

Regarding "free from the obstacle to *samādhi*": *Samādhi* refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while "obstacle" refers to delusion (*kleśa*). Thus, "the obstacle to *samādhi*" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

This differs from the case where "affliction" itself is the "obstacle," which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound. Furthermore, there are distinct reasons for being free from each of these two obstacles. As for being free from...
The obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*): because one has attained arhatship. The obstacle to samādhi:
because one has attained the state of being without strife (*araṇa*). [Commentary: *Araṇa* means "quiescence" (*śānti*) here.

[Commentary] "One who is tranquil" (*śānta*). Tranquility here refers to the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-contention). The meaning is that Subhūti is one who delights in tranquility. △ Fifth:
Resolving the Doubt Regarding Śākyamuni’s Attainment of Enlightenment under Dīpaṃkara. (Sub-commentary) Two parts: First, the heading and the narration of the doubt; second, based on...

The Sūtra resolves doubts. Part One: The Presentation of the Chapter and the Narration of Doubts (three sections). First, the presentation of the chapter. Second, the narration of the intent of the doubt.
Third, the indication of the source from which the doubt arises and the subsequent formation of the doubt. First, the presentation of the chapter.
[Commentary] Five: Resolving the doubt regarding Śākyamuni’s and Dīpaṃkara’s taking up and expounding [the teaching].
[Record] The fifth commentary: First, the heading of the section.
△ Second, the statement of the intent of the doubt.
[Commentary] The Treatise says: "In the past, Śākyamuni received the Dharma from Dīpaṃkara Buddha; that Buddha preached the Dharma for this Buddha.
[Record] From "Śākyamuni" onwards, the intent of the doubt is first stated. This refers to Śākyamuni during his causal stage as the Seer (ṛṣi) Kalyāṇabuddhi.
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon him this prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.

Because he advanced from this point and entered the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), it is said that he "received the Dharma. There are extensive causes and conditions for this, as explained in the twelfth [chapter].
△ Pointing to the place where doubt arises, one immediately forms the doubt.
[Commentary] It asks: "Why is it said that it cannot be grasped and cannot be described?
[Record] From the phrase "Why" onwards, he points to the place where doubt arises and thereby forms the doubt. ○ This also follows from the third [section] above.
[The passage] comes from the middle [section]. For that text states: "All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible.
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtra (the sūtra has two parts): first, the question; second, the answer. [Commentary]:
Resolving doubts based on the sūtra.
△ First Question:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain anything in terms of dharmas?"
[Commentary] The intent of the question in the Sūtra is as follows: "In your opinion, what is the case?
That is to say, when I was formerly in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, regarding the words of his bestowal of prophecy, was there any dharma that was attained, or was there nothing attained?"
△ Second, the answer:
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.

[Commentary] The meaning of the answer is that when the Tathāgata was formerly in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, amidst the verbal discourse of the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he attained nothing at all.
In reality, there is no dharma to be attained.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "in reality there is nothing to be attained regarding dharmas," this refers to the words spoken by Dīpaṃkara Buddha. Śākyamuni heard these words;
he heard only the sounds of the speech. Since the speech itself is not the reality, it is because he realized the Dharma through wisdom.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "these words and so forth": because these are words, nothing is attained. As for "words are not real," it means that words arise from conditions;
since conditions lack intrinsic nature, they are entirely empty in their very substance. Because they are empty, there is no attainment.
This is what is meant by "hearing yet not hearing" and "speaking yet not speaking. "The wisdom that realizes the Dharma" explains the receipt of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
This is the reason for it. The intent is to clarify that one merely uses non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to realize the principle of self-identity and non-differentiation.
When wisdom merges with the principle and the object unites with the spirit, how could there be anything said or anything attained?
[Commentary] The Treatise states: When Śākyamuni was with Dīpaṃkara, he did not grasp the realized Dharma through the words spoken.
For this reason, it is shown that that realized wisdom is ineffable and ungraspable.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "The treatise says" below cites evidence for the preceding meaning. Because the realized Dharma is free from the characteristic of verbal expression, it cannot be spoken;
because the realized Dharma is free from the characteristic of being an object of mental cognition, it cannot be grasped.
△ 6. Severing the Doubt that Adorning the Land Contradicts Non-Appropriation (Sūtra Commentary). Part Two: First, the heading and the statement of the doubt;
second, severing the doubt based on the sūtra. First, the heading and the statement of the doubt. Part Three: First, the heading; second, indicating the source where the doubt arises;
third, concluding the doubt. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Six: Severing the doubt that contradicts non-attachment regarding the adornment of the land.
[Record] The sixth commentary: First, the heading of the section.
Second, pointing to the place where the doubt arises.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* says: "If a dharma cannot be grasped.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "If a dharma," this indicates the point where doubt arises. This also follows from the third section of the preceding [text].
△ Third, the formation of doubt.
[Commentary] It asks: "How is it that the various Bodhisattvas take up the adornment of the pure land? How is it that they personally receive the body of a Dharma King?
[Record] From "How" onwards, the doubt is established. Since they have initiated their meritorious practice and cultivated the six perfections in unison, [they must now turn...]
Regarding the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and the adornment and purification of the Buddha-lands: if these are not grasped, then what is it that grasps?
The doubt concerning the Buddha-body is likewise intended in this same way; because these two retributions are inseparable, the treatise presents both doubts together.
However, in this current section, only one type is resolved.

△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtra (the sūtra has three parts): First, raising the question regarding the adornment of grasping at signs; second, providing the answer regarding the adornment of being free from signs;
third, exhorting based on the adornment of the pure mind. First, raising the question regarding the adornment of grasping at signs.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields?
[Commentary] This section on severing doubts consists of three parts. First, he raises the question regarding the adornment of fields through the grasping of marks.
[Commentary] The intent of the question in the sutra is stated as follows: "Does a bodhisattva take up the characteristics of form to adorn the Buddha-land?
[Sub-commentary] The Buddha’s intention was to clarify that the true land is the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature); therefore, he asked whether one takes up the characteristics of form to adorn the land.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s intention," etc.: Subhūti originally harbored doubts concerning grasping (*upādāna*). The Buddha intended to reveal that there is no grasping.

Since grasping and non-grasping pertain to both the land of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabhūmi*) and the land of nature (*dharmatābhūmi*), he provisionally raised a question regarding characteristics to test whether [Subhūti] understood.
△ Second, the explanation of the answer regarding the adornment of being free from marks (sūtra), in three parts: first, the answer; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation. First, the answer:
"No, World-Honored One."
[Commentary] The explanation clarifies the intended meaning: one does not grasp at signs while adorning the Buddha-lands.
△ Second, the inquiry: Why is this so?
[Commentary] The intent of the inquiry is as follows: For what reason does one not take up the marks [of form] to adorn the Buddha-lands?
△ Third, the explanation:
That which is called "adorned Buddha-lands" is precisely non-adornment; it is given the name "adornment."
[Commentary] The explanation of the meaning states: "Not adorning with marks" is true adornment.
[Sub-commentary] Second, the explanation of the answer regarding adornment free from marks.
[Commentary: The verse says: "When wisdom practices the penetration of consciousness-only, one thus grasps the pure land. It is not a form; it is the primary essence.
It is not an adornment; it is the intention of adornment."

[Commentary] Regarding the passage beginning with "The verse says, below": therein, the first three lines provide a direct explanation of the Sūtra, while the final line serves as a counter-explanation for the third line of the verse.
Furthermore, the first two lines explain the phrase from the Sūtra, "adorning the Buddha-lands," as being non-material;
this explains that it is "not adornment" (the primary essence), and explains that it is "called adornment" yet is not adornment, thereby clarifying the meaning within the verse.

It is not a formal shape; it adorns the mind and reveals the first essence within the verses. This merely points to and assigns the text, while the underlying meaning is revealed gradually and sequentially.
[Commentary] The treatise explains: The Buddhas have no concern for the adornment of buddha-fields; they possess only the thorough penetration of true wisdom and habitual consciousness.
Therefore, these [adornments] cannot be grasped.
[Commentary] The section from "The Buddhas" downwards to "ungraspable" explains the first half of the verse.
It means that by cultivating non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and penetrating the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), one accords with suchness through wisdom;
this is termed "adornment," which is precisely the meaning of being without grasping. As for the doubt regarding the existence of grasping:
From here on, the explanation is concluded.
[Commentary] There are two kinds of adornment: first, the aspect of form; second, the aspect of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "There are two kinds of adornment" and below, this explains the latter half [of the verse]. First, the two lands are listed. The "aspect of form" refers to the Dharma...
The land of characteristics refers to such things as golden ground and jewel ponds; in short, whatever is seen or heard belongs to the realm of form and appearance.

The primary meaning (*paramārtha*) is the land of dharma-nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*); this means being free from all characteristics, where there is nothing seen or heard—this is precisely the principle of *tathatā*.

[Commentary]: "Not adorned" means that it lacks formal characteristics (*nimitta*). The sense of "adornment" refers to the foremost adornment, because it is adorned by the accomplishment of all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).
[Commentary] "Not adorned" (*aśobhana*) and below is the formal explanation. The third phrase [of the verse] provides the reason for this:
because of this, it is both "not adorned" and yet "adorned. "Not adorned" serves to distinguish this from the *dharmalakṣaṇa* lands, which are not what is being adorned here;
in terms of the sūtra, these would not be considered "adorned. As for the meaning of "adornment," it reveals...
The Dharma-nature realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*) is that which is adorned by this; in the sūtras, this is termed "adornment" (*vyūha*).
That is to say, it is adorned by manifesting merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges. It is like gold fashioned into a vessel:
the vessel does not come from outside, yet by means of this very vessel, the gold itself is, in turn, adorned. Therefore, the treatise cited previously states: "The Buddhas have no..."
Regarding matters such as the adornment of the land, among all forms of adornment, there is nothing that surpasses this; therefore, it is called the "supreme adornment" and so forth.
As for the meaning of the term "intention" (yi), it refers to the fact that the non-form, supreme essence is neither adorned nor embellished.
"Intention" (yi) here signifies the underlying reason or cause.
[Commentary] Question: The bodies and lands of the Buddhas must possess both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to be considered definitive (*nītārtha*).
Now, since this [teaching] emphasizes only the essence, does it not lack the characteristics? Answer: The characteristics of the bodies and lands are but reflections of the mind;
they can only manifest when the mind is pure. If one is able to purify the mind, the bodies and lands will naturally appear. It is just like...
Polishing a mirror: when the dust is cleared away, the image appears; this occurs spontaneously and is not the result of deliberate fabrication.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) can manifest and give rise to reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdoms. Moreover, this involves the disappearance of characteristics within the very midst of characteristics;

it does not mean abandoning characteristics to grasp at their nature. If one is simply free from clinging attachment, what obstacle could characteristics pose? Nevertheless, because the central tenet of the sutras is formlessness (*animitta*), this—
The meaning increases slightly; it is thus from beginning to end. ○ Regarding the characteristics of the application of the mind, they are as explained in sequence.
△ Third, the exhortation based on the adornment of the pure mind:
"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to such a pure mind; they should not..."
One should not dwell on form when generating the mind; one should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas when generating the mind. One should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere.
[Commentary] Third: Exhortation based on the adornment of the pure mind.
[Commentary] The *Jingxin quanjing* (Sutra on Exhorting Pure Mind) states: "For this reason, you bodhisattvas should give rise to a pure mind that is non-abiding.
[Sub-commentary] The *Śāstra* says: "If a person discriminates that a buddha-field possesses conditioned forms and characteristics, saying 'I shall accomplish it'..."
This refers to those who dwell within the objects of form and so forth.
[Commentary: From the words "If a person" onwards, the mind that is to be refuted is first described. The intention is that they take formal characteristics (*nimitta*) to be the true Buddha-land.
Because of this perception, one then desires to adorn their physical form; hence it says, "I shall achieve [perfection]," and so forth.
[Commentary] The passage beginning with "He dwells below" reveals the fault. The intent clarifies that while the original desire was to purify and adorn, how is it that instead a defiled mind arises?
For dwelling upon forms and such is precisely the mind of birth-and-death; how, then, can it be called pure?
[Commentary] To preclude this, it says: "One should give rise to a pure mind in this manner; one should not dwell on form and so forth.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "To preclude...": this refers back to what was previously excluded, thereby introducing the intent of the sutra. Since one does not dwell on form and so forth...
To purify the mind, one should know that dwelling upon form and other sense objects is truly defiled.
[Commentary] That which gives rise to this mind is correct wisdom; this is the true mind. If there were no mind at all, it would be identical to the view of emptiness (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi).

[Commentary: Regarding "right wisdom" (samyag-jñāna): since the mind that is non-abiding is right wisdom, one should know that the mind produced by abiding is likewise deluded consciousness (vikalpa-vijñāna).
Herein, when it is said that right wisdom "arises," this refers to its manifestation; it does not mean that it arises anew from nothing.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The non-arising of all dharmas is the Prajñāpāramitā."
It is born from honey. Because this prajñā is neither arising nor ceasing, it is called the true mind (zhēnxīn).
If one were to dwell in the lower [realms], it would manifest its intent to block errors. Fearing that one might fall into the view of emptiness (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi), it causes this true mind to arise.

The true mind of heaven is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; however, if one dwells upon objects due to conditions, one becomes disassociated from it, yet it is not something that is annihilated. This is the mind.
If one does not abide [in form, etc.], then Prajñā is luminously clear and likewise not something that arises. Fearing that people might be deluded by this, it is therefore manifested and negated.
[Commentary: Thus, the previous instruction to "not abide in form, etc. was the negation of existence; the subsequent instruction to "give rise to the mind" was the negation of non-existence.
Having already departed from existence and non-existence, this is precisely what is called the Middle Way. To realize and penetrate it in this manner is true adornment.
How could there be any buddha-field that is not pure? Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If you wish to purify a buddha-field, you should purify your own mind.
According to the purity of the mind, the buddha-field is purified. To purify the mind is precisely to depart from existence and non-existence.
△ Seven: Resolving Doubts Regarding the Attainment of the Reward Body through the Severing of Feelings (Sūtra Commentary). Part Two: First, the heading and the statement of the doubt;

second, the resolution of the doubt according to the sūtra. Part One: The heading and the statement of the doubt. Subdivision One: The heading; Subdivision Two: The statement of the doubt. Subdivision One: The heading.
[Commentary] Seven. There is doubt regarding the attainment of the *saṃbhogakāya* through the severance of sensation.
[Record] The seventh commentary: first, the heading;
second, the narration of the doubt.
[Commentary] The intent of the doubt is as previously stated.
[Record] The reason for the arising of this doubt has already been set forth in the preceding chapter. Question: What is the difference between this and the third [chapter]? Answer:

The former is a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), whereas this is a retribution-body (vipākakāya); therefore, they are not the same. Because in the preceding [chapter] one heard that the response-body is not real, there was no grasping [at it]. Thus...
It is said: "The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) is real; therefore, there must be a mind that grasps it. This doubt arises based on that third [point].
△ Second, resolving the doubt according to the sutra. (The Sutra) has two parts: first, resolving the doubt through question and answer; second, comparing and manifesting its superiority.
[Commentary] There are two sections to the text on resolving doubts. First, the resolution of doubts through question and answer.
△ First: Question and Answer Resolving Doubts (Sūtra). Four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation. First, the question.
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be considered large?
△ Second, the answer.
Subhūti said: "It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One.
[Note: The questions and answers regarding the severing of doubt may be understood from the *Juedi jing* (Sutra on the Severing of Doubt).
△ Third, the inquiry.
For what reason?
[Commentary] The intent of this inquiry is to ask: by what meaning is it called "Great"?
△ Fourth, the explanation.
The Buddha said that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.

[Commentary] The meaning of this explanation is that it is not a contaminated (*sāsrava*) or conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) body, but rather an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) body.
If one follows Asaṅga, however, it differs entirely from this. Generally, both the beginning and the end are explained according to the two truths (*satyadvaya*). Now...
Within this commentary, some parts rely on Vasubandhu and some rely on Asaṅga; thus, this particular section relies upon Vasubandhu.
△ First, the question-and-answer resolving doubts (Commentary): Part two. First, a general explanation of the meaning of the metaphor; second, a detailed explanation of "not being the body."
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has two parts. First: a general explanation of the purport of the metaphors.
△ First, the general explanation of the purport of the metaphors further has three parts: first, clarifying the similes; second, correctly clarifying that which is illustrated by the metaphors;
third, concluding with verses. First, clarifying the similes.

[Commentary] The treatise states: Just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is called "Great" because its power and majesty are lofty and far-reaching, yet it does not conceive the thought "I am the King of Mountains," for it is free from discrimination.

[Commentary] Regarding "lofty and distant," etc.: this refers to Mount Sumeru, which rests upon the Golden Wheel at a height of eighty thousand *yojanas* and has sixty thousand mountains as its retinue;
therefore, it is called "great. Thus, the *Huayan shu* (Avataṃsaka Commentary) states: "Sumeru spans the ocean, casting down the heights of the myriad peaks.
Regarding "yet not taking [it as an analogy]," although that mountain is great—being composed of the four jewels and possessing five stages—it is not taken [as a model].
Within the dharmas, it is subsumed under the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*); within the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), it is included in the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
How could there be any conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) such that it is taken as the king? △ Second, the explicit explanation of the analogy.
[Commentary: The Buddha of Retribution is also like this. He is called "Great" because he has attained the essence of the unsurpassed Dharma King;
yet he does not grasp at the thought, "I am this Dharma King," because he is free from discrimination.

[Commentary] "The Reward Buddha" below correctly clarifies the metaphor being illustrated. It means that through cultivation over many kalpas, his merit and wisdom are perfectly luminous, pure and stainless, with nothing surpassing this;
hence it is called "unsurpassed. He alone reigns as sovereign over the Dharma-realm, and is thus titled "Dharma King.
There are two meanings to "Great": first, regarding essence, because his body and wisdom are vast and all-pervading; second, regarding rank, [he is superior] to all sages.
Because it is beyond reach. ○ As for "non-discrimination": it is not like material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) by nature;
rather, because one has cultivated [the path] throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* until all myriad thoughts are utterly forgotten, and wisdom is thus tranquil, it is called non-discrimination.
△ Third, the conclusion by means of verses.
[Commentary] Therefore, the verse says: "As the King of Mountains has no grasping, so it is with the receiving of retribution.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "the verse says" and below: this concludes the section by means of verses.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the non-body has two parts: first, citing the sutra to provide a brief indication; second, quoting the śāstra for a detailed explanation.
First, citing the sutra to provide a brief indication:
[Commentary] "The non-body is called 'body' because it is not a body of outflows or conditioned phenomena; it is a body that is outflow-free and unconditioned."

[Commentary] Regarding the section "Not the Body" (*na-kāya*) below: there are two parts to the detailed explanation of "not the body. First, the brief citation and indication of the sūtra. Regarding "untainted and unconditioned" (*anāsrava-asamskrta*):
"untainted" (*anāsrava*) distinguishes it from the mundane; "unconditioned" (*asamskrta*) indicates that it is not subject to arising and ceasing. Question:
Since this passage clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), it ought to be conditioned and untainted. Why, then, is it described here as unconditioned? Answer: This is based on...
The teaching of ultimate reality does not rely on provisional doctrines; therefore, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states:
"The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. The Buddha-body is without outflows (*anāsrava*), for all outflows have been exhausted."
△ Second, the extensive explanation by citing treatises, which has two parts: first, the root verses; second, the citation of the treatise. First, the citation of the root verses:
[Commentary] Therefore, the verse says: "Because it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)."
[Commentary] Therefore, the verse says [as follows]. Second, the extensive explanation by citing the treatise has two parts. First, the citation of the root verse.
This verse indicates the distancing from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the outflowing (*āsrava*). Its intent is to reveal that only outflowing phenomena possess a substantial nature (*svabhāva*).
△ Second, citing the treatise, which has two parts: first, the dual heading; second, the dual explanation; third, the dual conclusion. First, the dual heading.
[Commentary]: The treatise says: "If it is thus, then there is no entity; if it is thus, then it is called an entity."

[Commentary] The section beginning with "The treatise says" below consists of three parts: first, citing the treatise; second, [the main body]; third, the initial dual heading. Regarding "If it were thus," this indicates the heading by pointing to the scriptural passage that raises the inquiry.
△ Second, the dual explanation. [Sūtra Commentary]:
Because there is only the pure body; because it is far removed from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). [Record]:
Regarding "Because there is only" and so forth, these two provide a dual explanation. ○ The "pure body" is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This explains that there is a substantial reality.
This phrase refers to what is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*) in the sutra. Question: This explains the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); why then is it called the Dharma [Body]? Answer:

Because the Dharma Body and the Reward Body are spoken of in combination; the two bodies are not distinct. Since this is the teaching of ultimate reality, principle and wisdom are non-dual; therefore, it may be so described.
[Commentary] "By being far removed from the lower [realms]" explains the phrase "the absence of things. This refers to what the Buddha said in the sutra regarding "non-body.
Since the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is free from the arising and ceasing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Since the conditioned is thus transcended...
How much more so for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*)? Therefore, this commentary on the text does not mention "all outflows.
△ Third, the double conclusion.
[Commentary]: For this reason, there truly exists a self-substance (*ātman*), because it abides without depending on other conditions.

[Commentary] "By this" and below concludes the three pairs. This means that because it is both "detached from" and "only," one realizes the true self of the Dharmakāya—untainted, unconditioned, neither arising nor ceasing, and profoundly pure—and thus it possesses a substantial reality, which is termed "an existing thing.
It is not like the self of the ordinary person’s pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), which is tainted and conditioned. That is to say...
That which arises is immediately extinguished; like a dream or an illusion, it possesses no substantial reality.
[Commentary] By stating "because it does not depend" and below, the text concludes that there is no such thing as a substance; this is also a further clarification of the reason.

Because it does not abide by depending on the conditions of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) or conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), only *tathatā* (suchness) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain alone.
Therefore, there is a real self. One should know that ordinary beings all dwell in dependence upon the conditioned five aggregates as their conditions.
If even the five aggregates are merely provisional, how much more so the self they imagine? Since these conditioned phenomena are not themselves, it is said that they "depend on others."
△ Second, the comparative evaluation that reveals superiority (Sūtra), in two parts. First, a broad demonstration of the superiority of the sūtra by comparing it with external wealth.

Second, a further demonstration of the superiority of the sūtra by comparing it with internal wealth. Regarding the first—broadly demonstrating the superiority of the sūtra by comparing it with external wealth—there are two sections:

first, the comparison of their relative excellence; second, the explanation of the reason for its superiority. Regarding the first—comparing their relative excellence—there are three parts. First, regarding...
1. Distinguishing the sand by means of many rivers; 2. Manifesting merit by means of much sand; 3. Revealing excellence by means of great merit.
Regarding the first—distinguishing the sand by means of many rivers—there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. First, the question:
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
What do you think? Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?
△ Second, the response. Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One. Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands.

[Commentary] Second, the comparison that reveals superiority. This has two parts: first, a comparison based on external wealth to extensively reveal the superiority of the sutra. This has one part: 1. [The comparison itself].
Comparing their relative superiority and inferiority, there are three [points]. First, using many rivers to distinguish the sand.
[Commentary] The meaning of the *Bian sha jing* (Sūtra on Distinguishing Sand) can be seen [therein].
[Sub-commentary] The Ganges River flows out from the eastern side of Lake Anavatapta; it is forty *li* in circumference, and its sand is as fine as...
Wheat flour. Gold sand flows mixed [with it].
[Commentary] As for Lake Anavatapta: from the center of this Jambudvīpa toward the north, there are nine Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇa-parvata*).
Next is the Great Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*). Next is Mount Gandhamādana. Between the north of the Snowy Mountain and the south of the Fragrant Mountain lies Lake Anavatapta. This is translated as...
The Lake Anavatapta is fifty yojanas in length and breadth. It is filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
From its four sides, four great rivers each issue forth: the eastern one is named the Gaṅgā River; it circles the lake once and flows into the eastern ocean.
The southern is the Sindhu River; the western is the Vakṣu; and the northern is the Sītā. Each of these circles the lake once and flows into [the respective oceans] in succession.
Regarding the southern, western, and northern seas: the Ganges mentioned in the present sutra is the Gaṅgā. The term "Heng" (恒) is a corruption introduced by the translators.
As for its circumference of forty *li*, this refers to the location where it first emerges from the mouth of the lake.
[Commentary] The Buddha frequently approached this [state] when teaching the Dharma; therefore, it is taken as a metaphor.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the passage "The Buddha frequently," etc., this explains the reason for taking it as a metaphor. However, at the time he preached this sutra, it was solely in the Jeta Grove.
When he preached the Dharma at other times, [the assembly] was mostly similar to that [occasion]; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.

Though [the text] is weighty, its underlying meaning is not so.

[Commentary] It is for the purpose of gradually transforming sentient beings and causing them to believe in the supreme and subtle meaning.

refers to the general application according to the Dharma. This means that prior to the parable, it had not yet been stated that the four fruits are without mind.
Śākyamuni has no attainment; he adorns and purifies the land, yet it is adorned without being adorned. He cultivates and realizes the Buddha-body, yet it is realized without being realized.
Therefore, even the analogy of comparison cannot surpass this. Later, having clarified this meaning, the Dharma-principle is doubly profound.
Consequently, the analogy of comparison is likewise exceptionally superior. Alternatively, it may give birth to Buddhas.

First, the praise of the excellence of the person at the site of the Honored One has three parts: first, clarifying that the site is worthy of veneration; second, manifesting the benefits obtained by the person;
