including its devas, humans, and asuras— as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the reasons for its superiority. This has five parts. First, praising the person’s superiority by way of their exalted station. This has three parts. First, clarifying that the location is worthy of reverence.
[Record] That the location is worthy of reverence can be understood from the sutra.
[Commentary]: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that Śakra, Lord of Devas, was not present. Whenever the various devas arrived, they saw only empty seats;
they would all pay homage, make offerings, and then depart.
[Commentary] In the lower section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, this passage is cited as scriptural evidence.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, regularly preaches the Dharma of the *Prajñāpāramitā* to the assembly of devas within the Sudharmā Hall. At times he may not be present;
yet whenever the devas arrive, they all pay homage with reverence toward his seat. This is because they hold the Dharma in high esteem and, by extension, revere the place where it is taught.
[Commentary]: *Stūpa* is translated here as "high and manifest. *Tā* is a corrupted term from a frontier region.

[Record]: It is called "high and manifest" because, since it honors a person of distinction, it is placed in a prominent location so that those both far and near may see it, thereby generating merit through reverence.
[Commentary] "Temple" (miào) means appearance. One installs the physical appearance of the Buddha within the stūpa.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "physical appearance" and so forth: within the stūpa there is the physical appearance of the Buddha; when people see it, they will inevitably give rise to a heart of reverence.
Seeing the place where he preached the Dharma is also like seeing the physical appearance of the Buddha. ○ If the Sanskrit term is *caitya*, this is translated here as "numinous" (líng).
A shrine (miao). Some say it refers to a place where offerings may be made; this is largely the same as the present case.
△ Second, revealing the benefits obtained by persons:
"How much more so for those who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety. Subhūti, you should know that such persons achieve the most [supreme merit]."
The foremost, most rare Dharma.
[Commentary] Second, revealing the benefits obtained by people.

[Record] The intent of the sūtra regarding the benefits obtained is as follows: even at a place where the four lines [of verse] are proclaimed, one still receives the offerings of devas and humans; how much more so [in this case]?
How much more so for one who can receive and uphold this entire sutra text? As the sutra describes it:
[Commentary] The previous four lines were already superior; how much more so for one who can receive and uphold this in its entirety. Therefore, this is the most supreme and highest.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the first four lines, etc.," according to the intent of this sutra, there are two degrees of superiority and inferiority when compared to the preceding section.

What constitutes the "preceding" refers to the description of the location; this [present section] describes the person. The former clarifies the four-line verse, while this clarifies its complete upholding.
For this reason, the former is the lowest of the low, whereas this is the highest of the high. This is stated by way of contrast.
Therefore, it is said, "How much more so! The "Supreme" refers to the Dharmakāya; because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it transcends all that is higher.
The "Foremost" refers to the Saṃbhogakāya; as the most honored among all sages, there is nothing superior to it.

The "Rare" refers to the Nirmāṇakāya; this is due to the four matters previously mentioned. The intent is to clarify that by receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [this teaching], one fully attains these three [bodies].
The body is the perfection of merit. ○ Some say: because it can lead one toward Bodhi, it is called "supreme" (*parama*);
because it excels all vehicles (*yāna*), it is called "foremost" (*agrya*); and because it is peerless in the world, it is called "rare" (*āścarya*).
△ Third, manifesting that the Buddha is present in the location.
Wherever this sutra may be, there is the Buddha or his honored disciples.
[Commentary] Third, manifesting that the Buddha is present in the location.
[Commentary] There is a Buddhist scripture which states: "Wherever this sutra text exists, there is a Buddha and his disciples.
[Sub-commentary] This sutra reveals the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; based upon the Dharma, there exist the Reward-body and the Transformation-body.

[Commentary] The Sūtra reveals the reason why there is a Buddha and why he exists. That is to say, the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* must rely upon the *dharmakāya*, and the *dharmakāya* is in turn revealed by the Sūtra.
Since there exists the teaching that reveals [the truth], there must necessarily be the Buddha who is revealed.
Furthermore, the sutras are the Dharma of teaching, while the Buddha is the Dharma of fruition. Fruition is manifested through principle, and principle is attained through practice.
Thus, the three Buddhas are fully present and the four Dharmas are perfectly complete; in whatever place this occurs, how could one give rise to thoughts of inferiority?

[Commentary]: Furthermore, all worthy sages (ārya) derive their names from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since the Sūtra reveals the unconditioned, there must necessarily be worthy sages and honored disciples [who realize it].

[Commentary] Furthermore, the phrase "all those below" clarifies the reason why there are disciples. The noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles have as their essence the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because the sutras manifest the unconditioned, there are noble ones. "Those who are respected" refers to those who have realized Suchness (*tathatā*);
they are all sages who have entered into principle, and are thus worthy of honor and respect. If one follows the Wei translation, it simply states that they "exist."
The Buddha causes others to respect him; he does not say that there are disciples distinct from himself. Therefore, the text says:
"He is thus respected as a Buddha, resembling a Buddha. II.
Distinguishing the Names according to Meaning (Sūtra), Part Four: 1. Question 2. Answer 3. Interrogation 4. Explanation I. Question:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sūtra be named? How should we uphold it? [Commentary:
Regarding the question of its name, the intent of the inquiry is: "I do not yet know what title this sūtra possesses; if it has no title," [how shall we proceed?]
"How should it be upheld?
△ Second, the answer:
The Buddha told Subhūti, "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name..."
"You should uphold this. [Commentary:
The meaning of the answer can be understood from the text.
△ Third, the inquiry.
Why is this so? [Commentary] The intent of the inquiry is as follows: The Tathāgata has constantly taught that the names and characteristics of all dharmas are empty.
What is the reason for now specifically establishing these names?
△ Fourth, the explanation:
"Subhūti, that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not [in fact] the *prajñāpāramitā*.
[Commentary] The intent of this explanation is as follows: That which I have established is that names are themselves nameless. How could a name that is nameless contradict emptiness?
Meaning. ○ It is for the sake of upholding [the teaching] that names are established by force within the nameless.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding meaning, the distinction of names is clarified. When the Buddha establishes the title of a sutra, he does so based on its ability to sever delusions; it is "superior" because it severs delusions.
[Commentary] The Buddha establishes the name below. He explains the cause for its designation. "Cause" (hetu) has the meaning of that upon which something depends.

That is to say, "Vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt) possesses the sense of being able to destroy; "Prajñā" (wisdom) possesses the merit of contemplative observation. Because both the metaphor and the reality are manifested together, it is called *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* (Diamond Wisdom).
In truth, it is also established based on the sense of being "firm," but for now, I shall explain it according to its functional application.
[This is] as explained in the title and within the sevenfold exposition of the meanings. Regarding "it is superior because it severs delusions":

sentient beings undergo the cycle of transmigration because they encounter the defilement of delusions. If one severs these delusional defilements, there is no doubt that one will attain Buddhahood; how could this not be superior?
[Commentary: "That which is not Prajñā" refers to the antidote for the attachment to words, as Asaṅga states.

[Recorded Notes: Regarding the phrase "antidote," etc., this explains the meaning by means of the name. While the meaning is real, the name is empty. If one were to cling to these empty names, how could one attain the real meaning?
Anticipating such an attachment, this antidote is established.
△ Section Three: The Superiority of the Buddha’s Non-differentiated Teaching (Sūtra, Part 2). First, the question; second, the answer.
First, the question: "Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?"

[Commentary] This refers to a superior sūtra that presents a different teaching. The intent of the question is as follows: Do you maintain that, apart from the dharmas realized by the Tathāgata, there exists some other distinct teaching?
△ Second, the response.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to speak.
[Commentary] The meaning of the response is that, apart from the Dharma he has realized, the Tathāgata has no other distinct teaching.

[Commentary] This section follows from the preceding passage concerning the establishment of names. Its intent is to say: it is not only the case that this sutra’s name is established as being "nameless";
rather, all that is spoken is likewise so. Furthermore, it is not only I who am thus; all Buddhas are the same.
△ 3. The Superiority of the Buddha’s Lack of Contradictory Teachings (Commentary): First, the outline; second, the formal explanation; third, the citation of evidence.
First, the outline: 【Commentary】 3.
The superiority of the Buddha’s lack of contradictory teachings.
△ Second, the correct explanation of the four [points]. First, the explanation of "no teaching. Second, the presentation of the reason. Third, the general application to all Buddhas.
Fourth, the conclusion establishing the aforementioned meaning. First, the explanation of "no teaching."
[Commentary] "There is nothing taught" means there is no teaching that involves differentiation, addition, or subtraction.

[Recorded Notes] "No differentiation," etc., refers to the fact that throughout the beginning, middle, and end of Śākyamuni Buddha’s teachings, there is ultimately no difference, addition, or subtraction.
This is based solely on the reality that is without discrepancy; it does not concern any differences in the verbal expressions.
△ Second, the reason for this.
[Commentary] It is simply spoken according to what has been realized. Since it is according to what has been realized, there is nothing to be said.
[Record] "Simply as below" provides the reason. Generally, whenever there is speaking, it is all in accordance with what has been realized; within that realization...
There is no teaching; how could there be any difference?
△ Third, the conclusion that this applies to all Buddhas.
[Commentary]: All Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise thus.
[Commentary] "The three periods of time," etc., concludes by extending [this principle] to all Buddhas. Since all Buddhas have realized the same truth, there is ultimately no second source;

if they do not realize it, that is one matter, but once realized, there is no difference. If one has not yet reached the ultimate stage and remains on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), then according to what is taught, each case is distinct.
Why? Because that which is realized differs, as is the case for those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The ten stages above differ in their respective levels. Since these are persons who have attained the fruit, there can certainly be no divergent explanations.
△ Fourth, concluding the preceding meaning.
[Commentary]: Therefore, it is said that there are no divergent explanations.

[Commentary] Therefore, it says "below," concluding the preceding meaning. Since there is but one Buddha and yet many Buddhas, and what is taught regarding the past and future is entirely the same, all being in accord with their realization—how supreme is this teaching that accords with such realization!
△ Third, citing scriptural evidence, which has two parts: first, citing the root treatise; second, citing Asaṅga. First, citing the root treatise:
[Commentary] Therefore, the treatise says: "There is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata alone has taught while other Buddhas have not."
[Commentary] Therefore, the treatise says "below," citing scriptural evidence. Regarding the phrase "only and alone" and so forth:
it states that *prajñā* can sever afflictions, and there is not a single Buddha who does not say this. All others are likewise.
△ Second, citing Asaṅga.
[Commentary] Asaṅga says: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is ineffable. [Record] Regarding "the ultimate," etc.:
because the principle of the truths (*satya-tattva*) is free from the characteristic of verbal expression and free from the characteristic of names and words, it cannot be expressed.
[The text] says: "This proves that since it is as it is realized, there is nothing to be taught.
However, although the words of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu appear to differ, their meaning is actually the same. Since it is as it is realized, is this not the ultimate truth (paramārtha)?

△ Third, the explanation:
Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata speaks of, the Tathāgata says they are not atoms; they are called "atoms.

[Commentary] The explanation of the meaning is as follows: that which is called "dust" (rajas) is not the dust of afflictions, but rather the dust of the earth.
That which is called the "world" (loka) is not the realm of the causes of defilement, but rather the realm of the dust of the earth.
[Commentary] Four: The merit of giving is inferior;
the object [of the teaching] is superior. [Record] This follows from the previous comparison.

Because those who heard that the gift of jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges does not equal the upholding of this sutra were unable to believe it with sincerity, the Tathāgata specifically explained this meaning so that they might...
One clearly perceives the superior and the inferior, thereby washing away all doubts; this is fully present in the commentary (*śū*), where it can be seen with clarity.
[Commentary] The treatise states: "The merit of giving precious things is a cause of affliction (*kleśa*), because it is capable of accomplishing the affairs of affliction."
Earth-dust is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is not a cause for afflictions; therefore, dust is superior while giving is inferior.
[Commentary] The treatise says "below," which explains this to its full intent. The meaning is as follows: when the elements are crushed into dust, afflictions do not arise regarding that dust.
Yet, by giving jewels one obtains merit, whereas indulging in the five desires brings about greed and anger, leading one to commit every kind of evil. Therefore, dust is superior.
It is traditionally said that giving material wealth is the third type of "enmity born of generosity. Therefore, even the gift of a mere speck of dust surpasses the gift of jewels.

For even a speck of dust is superior simply because it does not give rise to transgression; how much more so when one upholds this sutra, which will certainly bring about the fruit of Buddhahood—how could it ever be considered inferior?
By comparing them in this way, there are thus three levels of superiority and inferiority, namely:

The gift of jewels does not equal the merit of the realm of atoms; the realm of atoms does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra. Since upholding this sutra is superior even to the realm of atoms, how could it not be superior to the gift of jewels?
It is like the common people being inferior to a prime minister, and the prime minister being inferior to the Son of Heaven.
If a celestial king is superior even to a prime minister, how could he not be superior to the common people? In this analogy, the celestial king is the most eminent;
in the Dharma, upholding this sutra is the most eminent. How could the reason why the sutra is superior not be manifestly clear?
[Commentary]: "Great Cloud" and so forth. Therefore, the "dusts of the stages" (*bhūmi-rajas*) are not the dusts of afflictions such as greed; they are called the "indeterminate dusts of the stages.

When the Tathāgata speaks of the "three thousandfold world-system," he means it is not a realm that serves as a cause for the defilement of afflictions; this is called the "indeterminate realm of the dusts of the stages."

[Commentary] From "Great Cloud" downwards, this merely uses the sūtra text to distinguish between the dharma and its metaphor; there is no further meaning. However, the underlying intent is as follows:
it speaks of "dust" (*rajas*) to refer to minute particles, and likewise to refer to greed and other afflictions, because both possess the quality of defilement.
It speaks of the "trichiliocosm" as a realm (*dhātu*), and likewise speaks of the causes of afflictive defilement as a realm, because both serve as causes for conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
Because of this meaning, the three thousandfold world system may also be understood as the realm of the vessel (the physical environment), while afflictions constitute the realm of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that what is being excluded here are not the objects of greed and other such defiled causes, but rather the dust of the earth and the three thousandfold world system itself.

[Commentary: This means that while the sense-spheres (*dhātu*) serve as the cause for objects (*viṣaya*), the objects do not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*); whereas giving serves as the cause for merit (*puṇya*), merit gives rise to afflictions.

constitutes the inquiry. The intended meaning is: since he has already attained the thirty-two marks, why does he not attain Bodhi?

[Commentary] Furthermore, within these, the Dharma-body is superior and the form-body is inferior. Why is this? Because the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) due to its being the true nature (*dharmatā*);

because the cause consisting of the gift of jewels is inferior, one attains the form-body among the results. Therefore, it is said above:
The heading states: "To uphold and expound this sutra is superior to that merit.

[Commentary] The merit of the sūtra is able to surpass the merit of giving, whereby one attains the thirty-two marks.

[Record] Regarding the section "The merit of the sūtra" and below, this serves to overturn and refute erroneous interpretations. [He continues: Fearing that those who give precious treasures, upon hearing what has been said above, might say:

Although one knows that the physical body (rūpakāya) is inferior to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and that the gift of jewels is not equal to upholding and expounding [the Dharma], I—being unable to uphold and expound it—do not seek the Dharma-body, but constantly practice the gift of jewels to accomplish the physical body. Once its marks and signs (lakṣaṇavyañjana) are perfected, is that not also wonderful?
It is for the sake of refuting this view that the following is said. ○ This means that previously, for the time being, we distinguished [the two bodies] according to their specific meanings.

Regarding cause and effect, it is said that giving brings about a body of marks (*lakṣaṇakāya*). However, if discussed according to the ultimate meaning, empty giving does not produce the fruit of marks.
Why? Because, due to a lack of wisdom, one gives rise to conceptual attachments to signs; thus, although what is given may be much, it results only in outflowing (*sāsrava*) merit.

Even if one were to attain the thirty-two marks, such a person would merely be a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); though their physical appearance may be identical, they are not called a Buddha.
If one can uphold and expound this sutra, then wisdom will arise in its full perfection; acting with generosity based on that wisdom, one dwells neither in existence nor in emptiness.
By means of untainted causes, one attains untainted fruits; it is through such thirty-two marks that one is first named a Buddha.

[Commentary] The intent clarifies that the merit of the sutra descends upon the donor, whereby one attains the physical marks of a Buddha-body. If it were merely the gift of jewels, it would simply be a cause for affliction.

At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this.
Since the past, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."

[Commentary] Regarding the purport of the *Kṣāntivarga-sūtra* (The Sutra of Lamentation): This means that when Śūnyatā-janman heard what was said above, his extreme joy turned into grief, and he wept incessantly.
He then expressed the depths of his heart: "I have long been an Arhat; though my eye of wisdom has heard [the Dharma], I have never before heard such a teaching."
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the reason for its superiority. This has five parts. First, the superiority of weeping and lamenting over not having heard the profound Dharma.
[Commentary]: The suffering of sacrificing one’s body has already moved the hearts of people; how much more so when one hears that one cannot uphold or explain it?
For this reason, he wept with grief.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "giving up the body" and below: this is the reason for his weeping with grief. There are three points to this. First, it is because he laments that the Bodhisattva’s sacrifice of his own body was rendered in vain; the intention is that although he has given up his life as many times as the sands of the Ganges, it is inferior to upholding and expounding [this teaching]. Failing to reach its profound meaning, his labor was without merit. Second, it is because he mourns not having encountered [the teaching] in past kalpas; the intention is that while still an ordinary being, he did not hear it. Third, it is because he rejoices in having now finally attained it; the intention is that he has now, at last, been able to encounter the profound principle. Thus, he weeps with sorrow for the past and rejoices with joy for the present. That he should attain the stages of sagehood by his own merit was something unheard of; thirdly, it is because rejoicing at having now heard [the teaching] reaches such an extreme of joy that it becomes sorrow.

In this present commentary, we shall clarify only the former of these two points.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* says: "Recalling the suffering of that body, one sheds tears of compassion because of reverence for the Dharma.
[Record] The section beginning with "The *Śāstra* says" below cites scriptural evidence.
[Commentary] "Wisdom-eye" refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); "not yet having heard" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
[Commentary] Regarding "the wisdom-eye and so forth": this refers to those such as Śāriputra, who blended their tracks with the world and provisionally occupied the stages of the Hīnayāna.

Since the realization of the emptiness of persons had already been attained, they had not yet heard the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), because the emptiness of phenomena is the object realized by the Mahāyāna.

[Commentary] However, there are two layers of meaning regarding why this is considered the superior basis for the sūtra. First, it means that if the teaching were coarse and shallow, its hearing would be commonplace;
yet, because it evoked such lamentation and weeping, one knows it to be profound and subtle.
Second, it means that while the weeping of ordinary people is not remarkable, the sorrow of Subhūti should be known as supreme. Is the reason for its superiority not thus made clear?

△ Second, the section on purifying the mind to accord with reality and possess supreme merit (*sūtra*). This has two parts: first, the direct clarification; second, the clearing away of traces. First, the direct clarification:
"World-Honored One, if there are further people who hear this sutra and their minds of faith become pure, they will give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It should be known that..."
This person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
[Commentary] To clarify the meaning of the sutra: if a person hears this and is able to give rise to faith, once this faith arises, they will no longer cling to the various dharmas.
Thus it is said that when all dharmas have been extinguished, the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) manifests; this is the merit of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
From this point on, the exposition is complete; is it not superior? Regarding the first grade, as clarified previously, the scriptural text is abbreviated;
therefore, only two [grades] are indicated.

[Commentary]: Second, the purity of mind accords with reality and possesses superior qualities compared to the other two. First, the direct explanation: The treatise states, "Within this [wisdom] there is the true mark (lakṣaṇa);
the others are not the true mark."
[Commentary] Herein, "this" refers to the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā; "the others" refers to the teachings for the two vehicles and for devas and humans prior to the exposition of Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding what is called "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is the characteristic of the absence of characteristics (*animittalakṣaṇa*). That is to say, it is the absence of the characteristics of self and dharmas.
To state the essential point: being free from all characteristics is, each and every one, true reality. Therefore, the text below says: "Free from..."
All marks are precisely what are called the Buddhas. ○ Regarding the phrase "that which is not found in other teachings":

this means that within the teachings for humans and devas, the two attachments are fully present; within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) still persist. One cannot take the marks of these two attachments to be the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
therefore, it is said that "others" are not the true mark. "Non-" (fei) is equivalent to "non-existent" (wu). ○ Regarding the phrase "this exists":

This means that the two attachments are suddenly eliminated and the two emptinesses are simultaneously revealed. When even the sickness of emptiness is empty, both extremes are abandoned and the Middle Way is manifested;
this is called the "true mark" (dharmatā). Therefore, it is said: "In this there is existence."

[Commentary] Question: The principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is something that the teachings can only express; how, then, can the arising of faith in it immediately produce the true mark itself? Answer:
It is said that one who can believe in this sutra will necessarily be free from the two attachments (dvaya-grāha). That state of being free from the two attachments is itself the true mark;
it does not mean that a separate true mark arises.
△ Second, Erasing the Traces.
"World-Honored One, this true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is actually no-mark. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true mark.

[Commentary] The intent of the passage on erasing traces is that this true mark, in its essence, corresponds to the ultimate truth (paramārtha); it is simply and solely without marks (animitta). This is the name.
"Based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is therefore called 'true reality' (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
[Commentary] Second, the wiping away of traces. Wuzhuo says: "This is for the purpose of abandoning conceptualizations regarding true reality.

[Record] Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of abandoning," etc.: it is feared that upon hearing the name "true reality," one will immediately give rise to a conceptualization of true reality; such a conceptualization is precisely...

This is a matter of discrimination. It is because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is profoundly subtle that it transcends both speech and thought. Although one must resort to speech and thought, only through direct realization is there true correspondence.
If one allows it to arise according to one's own subjective emotions, it remains merely a mental image. Fearing that one might mistake this for the reality itself, it is said: "it is not."
△ Third: The Superiority of Resolving Faith and Understanding the Three Emptinesses, Equal to that of the Buddha (Sūtra). Three parts: First, a general statement of resolving faith and understanding;
second, a detailed exposition of the three emptinesses; third, the Tathāgata’s seal of confirmation. First, the general statement of resolving faith and understanding.
“World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.
But if, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it,
those people would be the most rare and extraordinary of all.”

[Commentary] The meaning of the sūtra’s intent is explained as follows: For me to be an Arhat who has personally received the Buddha’s words, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold them, is not a difficult matter.

However, if in a future age—a turbid and evil world when the time is far removed from the Sage—one does not hear the Buddha’s teaching, but instead surveys these bequeathed instructions and believes and understands the emptiness of all phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), receiving, maintaining, and relying upon that understanding to give rise to practice—such a thing is indeed difficult.
Is it not likewise difficult for those of similar class?

[Commentary] Third, the superiority of the three types of faith-and-understanding (śraddhādhimukti) which equally realize the three emptinesses (trīṇi śūnyatāni), identical to that of the Buddha. Part one: a general statement on faith-and-understanding.
[Commentary] Vasubandhu says: "When dharmas of the future cease, there are still bodhisattvas who uphold them; therefore, there is no self (ātman) or person (pudgala)."

[The term] "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes [future beings]. Why is it that you, during the time of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), distance yourselves from practice and fail to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse?
[Commentary]: Regarding "the future and so forth," this refers to the appearance of the Unattached One (*Asaṅga*) in the world during the period of the True Dharma.

Thus, by citing superior persons of future generations, he admonishes the inferior persons of the present time. From this, one knows that whether in small or great men, there have been neither superior nor inferior individuals in any era.
This refers to those mentioned in the second section on doubt who, during the final five hundred years, uphold the precepts and cultivate merit.

△ Second, the specific elucidation of the three emptinesses (sūtra), in three parts: first, the emptiness of self; second, the emptiness of phenomena; third, the emptiness of both. First, the emptiness of self:
The Emptiness [of the Threefold Purity] has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. First, the inquiry:
"For what reason? [Commentary:

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Threefold Emptiness*, the intent of the inquiry is: even if there were one who could believe, understand, accept, and uphold [this teaching], by what principle would they obtain [the result]?
This is rare.
△ Second, the explanation:
This person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span.
[Commentary] The meaning of the explanation is as follows: Because it possesses characteristics such as selflessness (*anātman*), etc. This refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
II. Emptiness of Phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. First, the inquiry.
Why is this so? [Commentary] The intent of this inquiry is: what is meant by causing the absence of marks such as "self" and so forth?
△ Second, the explanation.
The mark of self is precisely no-mark. The mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life-span are precisely no-marks.
[Commentary] The meaning of the explanation is as follows: because the marks of self and so forth are precisely no-marks. The essence of the mark of self consists of the mind and mental factors;
since this essence does not exist, it is the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
△ Three: Both are empty. First, the inquiry; second, the explanation.
First, the inquiry: "For what reason?
[Commentary] Furthermore, the intent of the inquiry is: by what principle does one cause the characteristics of the self and dharmas to be non-existent?
△ Second, the explanation.
To be free from all marks is precisely what is called "all Buddhas.
[Commentary] The intent of the subsequent explanation is that because being free from all marks is named "Buddha," although there are many marks, they do not [constitute it].
Transcending my Dharma, this [teaching] now subsumes all; therefore, it is called "all-encompassing. These characteristics are all abandoned, which constitutes universal emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The principle of universal emptiness is what is named the Buddha. Since the Buddha is realized from this, it is called "supreme."
[Commentary]: Second, the specific exposition of the three emptinesses.

[Commentary]: As Asaṅga says: "The absence of self and so forth" refers to the non-apprehension of persons; "the absence of signs such as self and so forth" refers to the non-apprehension of phenomena.
[Commentary] The two types of grasping—grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena—their meaning can be understood.
[Sub-commentary] "Free from all" reveals the characteristics of the training followed by the bodhisattvas.
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are free from all marks, we should train ourselves in this manner.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "to manifest, etc.": This is for the sake of the two kinds of emptiness—of self and phenomena—which constitute the portion of the Bodhisattva.

Only by being free from all marks does one become a Tathāgata. Now, this meaning is manifested so that all Bodhisattvas may follow it through skillful means, study and practice it, and seeing the worthy, strive to equal them, thereby swiftly attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, it says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones," and so forth, up to "Tathā."
This is the training.
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s seal of confirmation:
The Buddha told Subhūti, "So it is, so it is."
[Commentary] Three: The Tathāgata’s Seal of Confirmation.
[Record] The meaning of the sutra as confirmed by this seal can be understood from the text.
[Record] However, based on what preceded—starting from "At that time, Subhūti heard this sutra being preached" up until "detached from even one..."—it is evident.
"All characteristics are named the Buddhas"—these are entirely the words of Śūnyatā-utpanna. Within this, there are six successive stages: namely, weeping with grief upon hearing the Dharma;
the arising of faith in the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa); the mutual manifestation of the difficult and the easy;

and the clarification that the attachments to self, person, and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, whereby all become Buddhas. Such as these explanations are all truly sincere and authentic words. Therefore...
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, sealed it thus. (Symbol: ○) To speak it twice is to express that the words have reached their ultimate limit.
△ Fourth, the supreme rarity of remaining unmoved at the time of hearing.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear it, one should know that such a person is truly rare.
[Commentary] Fourth: The excellence of being rare and unshakable at the time of hearing.
[Commentary] The purport of the *Acalaprabhā-sūtra* states: This sūtra is profound and subtle; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
When some hear it, they often give rise to alarm and fear. If one can avoid such alarm and fear, would that not be truly rare?
It is indeed difficult to find such a person, for it is because the sūtra is so superior. The meaning of the sūtra’s superiority is clearly evident.
[Commentary] The treatise states: "Startled" (*jing*) refers to the fear that one is not capable of delivering sentient beings. "Terrified" (*bu*) refers to being unable to sever the mind of doubt.
"Apprehensive" (*wei*) refers to being consistently afraid; thus, the mind ultimately falls into a state of alarm and terror.

[Commentary] Regarding "startled fear" (*samtrāsa*): these three aspects are distinct. "Startled" (*sam*) refers to being suddenly struck with wonder or strangeness; "frightened" (*bhīta*) refers to being agitated and bewildered whether advancing or retreating;
"afraid" (*bhaya*) refers to being consistently terrified. It is like a person wishing to go to the capital who travels along the main highway;
because they have not previously experienced it, they are suddenly startled and think to themselves, "How is it that I have come to this? Or...
Whether advancing or retreating, they waver between doubt and certainty, ultimately lacking a resolute mind.

Thinking that this path was originally not the right one, they may turn back and fail to proceed, or they may become so terrified as to go mad, falling into ravines or leaping from cliffs, thus failing to fulfill their natural lifespan.
The Dharma is likewise in this regard. Within the teachings for humans, devas, and those of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha spoke of emptiness and spoke of existence.

Those who did not grasp his underlying intent adhered to the literal words. When he taught this sutra, which reveals the principle of the Middle Way—neither empty nor existent—those previously attached were all struck with alarm and fear;
they instead regarded it as false and were unable to advance toward it. Or...
They fall among the ordinary worldlings or descend into the Lesser Vehicle; from this point on, they will forever lose the true emptiness of Bodhi.

The intent of the present sutra, however, states: if a person hears this dharma that is neither existent nor non-empty—a teaching difficult to believe—and does not give rise to a heart of alarm or fear, then they will be able to not abandon Bodhi and advance toward the Great Way. Its underlying purpose is profound and subtle; those who possess it are rare indeed.
If there should be such a person, it would be truly rare. △ Section Five:
The First Supreme Purity of the Five Great Causes (Sūtra). Part Two. First, the inquiry; second, the explanation. First, the inquiry.
Why is this? [Commentary:
The *Mahānidāna-sūtra* poses the following inquiry: "By what meaning is it that hearing [this] and not being startled, etc., constitutes something rare?"
△ Second, the explanation:
Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the "foremost pāramitā" is not a foremost pāramitā; it is designated as the "foremost pāramitā."
[Commentary] The explanation of the meaning is as follows: Because this Dharma-gate is the foremost among all the pāramitās, it is called the "first pāramitā.
However, if this pāramitā is considered from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), it cannot be described; therefore, it is said to be "not first," and so forth.
Is it not likewise the case that what is being taught here is spoken of according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti) for the sake of the sense of superiority? Therefore...
"It is called 'name' and so forth.
[Commentary] Five. The great cause is pure and foremost supreme.

[Commentary] Why is this? There are two reasons: first, it refers back to the preceding [section on] not being startled and so forth; second, it refers back to the entirety of the preceding excellence.
[This is] for the purpose of inquiry.

[Commentary: Regarding the two sections below, in order to provide the reasons why the Sūtra is superior—having already set forth nine gates in the preceding two layers of comparison, each of which represents a distinct meaning—it is not yet known by what fundamental principle it is called superior.
Ah! This is why it is superior; let us further investigate the reasons for its superiority.
[Commentary] The Treatise states: "This Dharma-gate is called the 'Great Cause,' for it surpasses all other sūtras."
[Commentary] "The great cause" refers to the sixth *pāramitā*, that of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since the Buddha possesses three bodies and the *dharmakāya* is the greatest among them, and because this [perfection] is able to attain it, it is called the "great cause. As it is the most excellent among the six, it is designated as the "first."
Regarding the phrase "surpassing others" and so forth: it means that within the teachings of humans, devas, and the two vehicles, this Dharma was not expounded; it is only now that it is expounded.

Because their objects of expression (the *vācya*) were inferior, their means of expression (*vācaka*) were also inferior; because the objects of expression here are superior, the means of expression are also superior.
[Commentary] It is named "Pure. It is taught identically by immeasurable Buddhas.
[Record] Regarding "pure" and so forth: phenomena that follow characteristics necessarily differ when expressed in words;

however, the principle that transcends characteristics is without discrepancy when explained, because it is of equal and single flavor. This equal and single flavor is precisely the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Because...
This is the ultimate truth; therefore, it is pure.
[Commentary] Thus, precious substances such as sandalwood do not possess such merit. For this reason, among all forms of merit, this merit is supreme.
[Commentary] "Therefore, in the passage below... serves as a general explanation of the overall purport of the inquiry. ○ *Dāna* (generosity) is equivalent to giving;
it encompasses both internal and external wealth, which is why the term "etc. (*ādi*) is used.

○ "Lacking such merit" means that, in the causal stage, there is no efficacy for destroying delusions, and in the resultant stage, there is no virtue of the Dharma-body. ○ "This merit" refers to receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the scripture].
However, while the preceding sections all manifest the excellence of the sutra, none surpass this section as the very foundation of that excellence;
for it is capable of accomplishing the pure *dharmakāya*. Therefore, it is designated as "excellent. How could internal and external material gifts possibly be compared to it?
