Since the Dharma is free from all names, marks, and conceptual discrimination, to speak in accord with this is to preach in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore, the subsequent passage asks: "How does one expound the teaching for others?
Without grasping at marks, remaining as the Suchness (tathatā) without movement."
[Commentary] However, regarding the third, fifth, seventh, and this [present] passage—these four locations all clarify that there is no speaker, yet their underlying intentions differ.

This is because the third [passage] doubts whether the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) speaks; the fifth doubts whether realized wisdom (*jñāna*) can be spoken; the seventh clarifies that the Buddha has no divergent speech;
and this text doubts how one could speak if there were no body. It is by virtue of these differences that they are distinguished.
△ Third, regarding the fact that what has been taught is profound and thus met with neither faith nor doubt: (1) questioning due to doubt over its profundity and lack of faith;
(2) responding by distinguishing those who possess the nature of a noble one; and (3) resolving the matter by inquiring into right and wrong to engender faith.
[Commentary] However, among the various commentaries, between the eighteenth and nineteenth [sections], based on the text of the Wei translation of the sutra, all raise a single doubt.
They state that, outside the Dragon [translation], it is said: "Who can believe? Who doubts? and so forth. This refers to the ability to believe in the profound Dharma while harboring doubt.

Now, since this passage does not exist in the Qin translation, the commentaries likewise did not record or explain it. Yet, upon examining recent editions of the Qin text, this [passage] is present in all of them.
Duan then provides a brief essential explanation within his commentary, titled "Since What Is Taught Is Profound, There Is Neither Belief Nor Doubt.
The treatise states: "If one speaks of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma, there is nothing preached; this non-preaching is not separate from the Dharmakāya."
The Dharma-body is without marks. What kind of person could believe in such a profound realm of reality? [This is] to sever [doubt].
△ First, the doubt regarding the profundity and lack of faith is raised as a question.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?"
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being preached, will give rise to faith?"
[Commentary] This doubt is profound; it is asked because of a lack of faith. ○ He is foremost in the understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). His wisdom is perfectly penetrating;
since he takes wisdom as his life, he is called "one whose life is wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*). ○ "To give rise to faith" means to give rise to the correct Mahāyāna faith.
Not believing in any phenomena (*dharma*) is precisely what constitutes correct faith. Because this faith accords with the nature of the sages (*ārya-gotra*), it arises.
Xin-yun said: "Those who, having accomplished such faith, give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, enter the stage of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again regress;
this is called abiding within the lineage of the Tathāgata, in accord with the primary cause."
△ Second, the selection of those of noble nature, with someone responding.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
[Commentary] Next is the selection of those of noble nature, with someone responding.
[Commentary] The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
[Commentary] Following Subhūti’s statement, it should be said: "In reality, there are sentient beings who are able to believe this Dharma. Those who are able to believe..."
They are not ordinary sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings who lack the nature of the sages.

The *Śāstra* states: "Not sentient beings" means they do not possess the body of an ordinary person; "not non-sentient beings" means they possess the body of a sage. Thus, they are not non-sentient beings who lack the body of a sage.
The verse says: They are neither sentient beings nor [merely] sentient beings; they are neither sages nor non-sages.
In this context, "the holy body" refers to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Because this is the root of faith, [the text] next investigates right and wrong in order to explain how faith arises.
△ Third, the investigation of right and wrong to explain the arising of faith.
Why is this? Subhūti, those who are called "sentient beings" by the Tathāgata are not sentient beings; they are merely named "sentient beings.
[Commentary: Next, he raises the question of whether they are or are not sentient beings to provide an explanation.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "For what reason, Subhūti? 'Sentient beings, sentient beings,' as the Tathāgata has said, are not sentient beings;
they are merely named 'sentient beings.'"
[Commentary] "Why is this? is an interrogative inquiry. For what reason is it said that they are not sentient beings, yet are also called sentient beings?

"Subhūti, 'sentient beings, sentient beings'"—this is a restatement. That which is spoken of as sentient beings among those who are not sentient beings—"The Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings;
they are called sentient beings. As for "not sentient beings": [it refers to those who have realized the non-arising of dharmas].

This is not the case for ignorant, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The phrase "this is called a sentient being" establishes that the person capable of faith possesses the essence of a noble one (*ārya*).
As the verse says: "The teaching and the teacher are profound; it is not that there are none capable of faith."

[Commentary] This preceding scriptural passage exists in the Wei translation but is absent from the Qin edition. Since both treatises comment upon this text, it must have been added by later generations;
yet there is no loss in doing so. Moreover, as there are instances of karmic retribution in the unseen realm, it is indeed appropriate to believe in it.
△ Nineteen: Resolving Doubts Regarding the Cultivation and Realization of Non-existent Dharmas (Commentary). Part two: First, the heading and the statement of doubt;

second, resolving the doubt according to the sūtra. Regarding the first, the heading and the statement of doubt, there are four sections: first, the heading; second, indicating the source where the doubt arises; third, forming the doubt;
fourth, pre-indicating the intent of resolving the doubt. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Nineteen: Resolving doubts regarding how to practice and realize when there is no dharma to be severed.
[Record] The nineteenth section of the Commentary. First, the heading of the chapter.
Second, pointing to the place where the doubt arises.
[Commentary] The Treatise says: "The Tathāgata does not obtain a single dharma.
[Sub-commentary] "Does not obtain a single dharma" points to the locus where doubt arises.
This follows from the third, twelfth, and thirteenth sections, for in those passages it is stated that there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi.
△ Third, the formation of doubt.
[Commentary] It asks: "How does one, having departed from the higher and higher realizations, progressively attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

[Record] The phrase "How" and so forth constitutes the formation of the doubt. ○ Regarding "departing from the higher and higher": this refers, for example, to the first stage (*bhūmi*), which is equal to all other stages.

The preceding is called "superior. Even those who have not yet transcended the two stages, up to and including Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), have not yet escaped being "above" the Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmabodhi*).
Only the Buddha’s ultimate realization is "above" all superior stages; there is no stage higher than this. Therefore, it is said that he has "transcended the superior and the most superior.

Thus, ordinary beings transcend the "lowest of the low," while the Buddhas transcend the "highest of the high"; those in the intermediate flow between them do not transcend both the upper and lower extremes.
Regarding the term "successive transformation" (*parāvṛtti-parāvṛtti*): it refers to the successive relinquishing of the two obstacles and the successive attainment of the two fruits.

Because there is both successive relinquishing and successive attainment, it is called "successive transformation. The underlying intention is this: if one has already successively attained bodhi, why would one not attain even a single dharma?
Thus, a doubt arises.
△ Fourth, the meaning of pre-indicating the severance of doubt.
[Commentary] To sever this doubt, it is demonstrated that that which is not a realized dharma is called *anuttara-bodhi*.
[Record] "To sever" and below indicates the intent of pre-indicating the severance of doubt. Because it points out and makes manifest, it is termed "demonstration" (*shixian*).
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtra (Commentary). This section has two parts: first, the outline; second, the detailed explanation. First, the outline [Commentary]:
The text for resolving doubts consists of three parts.
△ The Exegesis in Two Parts (of the Sūtra), Part Three. First, awakening through the non-existence of dharmas; second, awakening through equality;
third, awakening through the cultivation of the primary and auxiliary practices. First, awakening through the non-existence of dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, is it as one who has attained nothing?
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Regarding my anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...”
"Up to and including the point where not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended—this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] Initially, it takes the non-existence of dharmas to be right awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
[Commentary] There is no dharma that constitutes the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment. Even if one were to ask about it, it can be understood that non-attainment is itself attainment.
[Sub-commentary] The verse says: "In that state, there is not even a slight dharma; thus one knows enlightenment to be unsurpassed."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "In that place," etc.: this clarifies that there is not a single dharma that can be called "superior.

Whether it be Mount Sumeru, which is the greatest, or a minute atom, which is the smallest, none escape being "superior" because they all exist. It is like space, which, because it does not exist [as a substantial entity], cannot be so designated.
It is named "Unsurpassed.
[The Commentary] states: At that locus of awakening, there is not a single dharma that can be realized; this is called *anuttara-bodhi* (unsurpassed awakening).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the locus of bodhi": *bodhi* is the locus that is realized. As for the phrase "not a single dharma, etc.":
it is simply the exhaustion of delusion and the fulfillment of awakening that is termed *bodhi*. Apart from this, how could there be any *bodhi* to be attained?
△ Second, attaining perfect enlightenment through equality.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] Second, [the verse] states that equality is perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
[Sub-commentary] It can also be understood from the *Sūtra on Equality as Perfect Enlightenment*.
[Commentary] The verse says: "The Dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases."

[Commentary] "Neither increasing nor decreasing" explains the passage in the Sūtra stating that there is no high or low. This means that because it does not increase when one is among the noble ones (ārya), there is no "high";
and because it does not decrease when one dwells as an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), there is no "low. This is the meaning of equality.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* says: "This Dharma is equal; therefore it is called 'unsurpassed' (*anuttara*), for there is nothing further above it.
[Recorded Notes] Regarding the term "equal" being named "unsurpassed": Generally, the "superior" receives its name in dependence upon the "inferior.
Since the inferior is not established, how could the superior exist? "There is nothing further below" further explains the meaning of "unsurpassed."

[Commentary]: Within this dialogue, there are three kinds of meanings for "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). In the first question, the phrase "the unsurpassed above the head" refers to cultivation and realization.
Next, it is called "unsurpassed" because no dharma can surpass it; this refers to emptiness and quiescence.
Finally, it is called "unsurpassed" because there is nothing below it that can oppose it; this refers to the identity of the essence of ordinary beings and sages.
The latter two points represent the intended meaning of the response.
△ Third, cultivating perfect enlightenment through the primary and auxiliary practices:
by practicing all wholesome dharmas while being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span, one then attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as for what are called 'wholesome dharmas,' the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as 'wholesome dharmas.'"
[Commentary] Third, using the primary and auxiliary practices to cultivate perfect enlightenment.

[Record] The intent of the *Sūtra on Cultivating Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Although there is no dharma, and although all is equal, this does not mean that one can achieve perfect enlightenment without cultivation.
One should cultivate all wholesome dharmas with a mind of non-self and so forth; only then will one achieve it. 〇

However, these wholesome dharmas do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), yet they do exist from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Devaśarman differs from this; examine it in detail.
[Commentary]:
Non-self and so forth are the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), which is the Right Path. Cultivating all wholesome dharmas is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).
This is precisely the path of assistance (*upāya-mārga*). This is the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

[Commentary] Regarding the "cause of realization" (*vyañjana-hetu*): "realization" has two meanings. First, the meaning of "thoroughly severing": because *prajñā* can thoroughly realize that afflictions (*kleśa*) are empty.
Second, the meaning of "manifesting": because it can manifest the *dharmakāya*. Here, [the statement] "non-self and so forth" refers to this latter meaning.

It is also called the "direct cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*). It is precisely because of this wisdom that one eliminates delusion and attains the Dharma-body; thus, it is now termed the "right path. Here, "path" (*mārga*) carries the meaning of "cause.
As for the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), it refers to the five practices such as giving and precepts, which serve as supporting conditions for that *prajñā* (wisdom).
"Assisting" (*jù*) means "providing support. By providing support for the power of the direct cause, one severs afflictions and realizes *bodhi*. It is just like...
A lamp can dispel darkness and reveal emptiness, but it must rely upon the oil of the mind as a supporting condition. This "Perfect Enlightenment" (Sanskrit:
*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is here translated as "Right Awakening," which refers to the fruit that has been realized.
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), this serves as the heading and pointer. As for the phrase "it is not [a wholesome dharma]," the *Śāstra* states:

"Because those dharmas lack any outflowing dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*), they are called 'non-wholesome dharmas'; because they possess outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are called 'wholesome dharmas.'"

[Commentary] Regarding "untainted (anāsrava) wholesome [dharmas]": Question: Since there are also wholesome dharmas within the tainted (sāsrava), why is this term restricted exclusively to the untainted?
Answer: Because they are cultivated through characteristics such as non-self (anātman), they are exclusively untainted.
Furthermore, because tainted wholesome dharmas are not causes for bodhi, and since the present aim is bodhi, they must be untainted.

[Commentary] Question: Among the three preceding sections, the first two involve no attainment, while the last one involves realization; since these meanings appear contradictory, how can both be maintained?
Answer: What is called "cultivation" merely refers to the elimination of the self and phenomena to manifest one's own true reality, such that ultimately not a single dharma can be attained.
For this reason, the two meanings are perfectly consistent with one another.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the third, twelfth, and thirteenth [chapters], as well as this present section—these four locations, both preceding and following, all state that one cannot attain *bodhi*.
How are these differences to be distinguished? Answer: Although the preceding and following passages are similar in form, their underlying meanings differ.

This is because the doubt in the third chapter concerns Śākyamuni’s attainment of the fruit, whereas the doubt in the twelfth chapter concerns the formation of the cause by Sudhana. The tenth... [text fragment].

The third [doubt] is that there is neither Dharma nor Buddha; the nineteenth [doubt] is that there is cultivation and realization. These meanings are far apart; please do not confuse them. △ Twentieth:
Severing the doubt that what is taught as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not a cause. (Commentary) Two parts: first, the heading and narration of the doubt; second...

Resolving doubts by relying on the sūtras. Part One: Setting forth the chapter and recounting the doubt (in four sections): First, setting forth the chapter; second, indicating the source from which the doubt arises;
third, concluding the formation of the doubt; fourth, establishing the reasoning. First, setting forth the chapter.
[Commentary] Twenty: Severing the doubt regarding what was explained as being non-causal and indeterminate.
[Record] The twentieth section of the commentary. First, the heading of the chapter.
Second, pointing to the place where the doubt arises.
[Commentary] The Treatise says: "If one cultivates all wholesome dharmas, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Record] The section beginning with "If one cultivates" points to the place where doubt arises; this follows from the nineteenth [section].
△ Third, the conclusion of the doubt.
[Commentary] "Then the Dharma taught" refers to the inability to attain Bodhi.
[Record] Regarding the phrase "Then the Dharma taught" and below: this forms a conclusion of doubt by contrasting it with the preceding several sections. The meaning is: since it has been said...
"One attains Bodhi by cultivating all wholesome dharmas. Why, then, has it been repeatedly stated previously that one attains Bodhi by upholding and expounding [this teaching]?
△ Fourth, establishing the principle.
[Commentary] Because these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.

[Sub-commentary] From "Because these" onwards, the principle that upholding and reciting [the teachings] does not lead to the attainment of *bodhi* is established. This is because [the teachings consist of] the three: name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and phoneme (*vyañjana*).
It is subsumed under the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature. Since there is no cause-and-effect within phenomena of the indeterminate nature, how could it possibly bring about Bodhi?
△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtras.
[Commentary: Resolving doubts based on the sūtras.
Subhūti, if there were someone who took all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm,
and likewise heaps of the seven treasures, and used them as a gift for others;
If a person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
the former merit would not equal one-hundredth part of it; nor one-hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor even any part expressible by calculation or analogy.
[That which] cannot be equaled.
[Commentary] The comparison in the sutra can be understood from the text as it stands.
[Sub-commentary] The verse says: "Although it is said to be an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma, it is taught to be the cause of that; therefore, this single Jewel of the Dharma is supreme."
"Immeasurable treasures. [Commentary]:
Although it says "equal," this is permitted as being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); yet when it says "and so forth," non-causality is not permitted.
Therefore, [the text] below explains the intent of the sutra: because it can serve as the cause for Buddhahood, it surpasses the gift of jewels.
[The *Śāstra*] states: "Because one cannot attain Great Bodhi apart from the Dharma that is taught, this Dharma can serve as the cause of Bodhi."
[Commentary] The treatise states below: This further explains the reason for [the teaching] being the cause. Since the Sūtra elucidates the ultimate truth, one attains awakening through that cause;

based on this understanding, one initiates practice, and only then does one attain Bodhi. If there were no gateway of the teaching, how could one know where to enter? Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"By means of the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, one emerges from the suffering of the triple world."

[Commentary] Furthermore, it says: "Your dharma is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas my dharma is determinate (*vyākṛta*); therefore, [my dharma] excels [yours], which merely abandons immeasurable seven treasures.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, it says" and below: this is a specific intention of the treatise. "Your dharma is indeterminate" refers to the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.

Thesis: It is said that sound (*śabda*) permeates both the wholesome and the unwholesome, whereas the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding "The Dharma of our school is determinate": this refers to the Mahāyāna school. The names and so forth manifested within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) by Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are exclusively wholesome in nature;
they are not indeterminate. "Is therefore" and so forth means: even with respect to the indeterminate alone, it is still...
If even that [neutral state] can serve as a cause, how much more so this [state], which is subsumed under the nature of untainted goodness—how could it not result in bodhi?

[Commentary] Question: What is the difference between this and the ninth doubt? Answer: The former concerns the difficulty regarding the lack of substantiality in conditioned phenomena; the present concerns the difficulty regarding the neutral being not a cause.

Furthermore, the former is based solely on the difficulty regarding the maintenance and explanation [of the teaching]; the present, however, addresses the difficulty in relation to wholesome dharmas as well.
They are vastly different. △ Twenty-one:
Severing Doubts Regarding Equality. (Commentary) Two parts: First, the heading and the narration of the doubt; second, severing the doubt according to the sutra.
First, the heading and the narration of the doubt has three parts: first, the heading; second, pointing to the source where the doubt arises.
The third section concludes the doubt. First, the heading is presented.
[Commentary] Twenty-one: Resolving the Doubt Regarding the Equality of Severance.
[Record] The twenty-first commentary; first, the heading is presented.
△ Second, pointing out the place where the doubt arises.
[Commentary] The *Lun* (Treatise) says: "If dharmas are equal and without high or low.
[Record] "If dharmas" and below points to the place where the doubt arises; this follows from the nineteenth [section].
△ Third, the formation of doubt.
[Commentary] "How can the Tathāgata deliver sentient beings?

[Record] From "How" onwards, the doubt is established. Since he delivers sentient beings, there must be distinctions of high and low; and where there are distinctions of high and low, [there is inequality].
This is unequal; therefore, doubt arises.

△ Second, resolving doubts based on the sūtra (Sūtra Commentary). This has two parts: first, the outline of the sections; second, the detailed explanation. First, the outline of the sections [Sūtra Commentary]:
The text for resolving doubts consists of four parts.
△ The Exegesis in Two Parts (of the Sūtra) has four sections. First, the refutation of erroneous interpretations; second, the demonstration of the correct view;
third, the counter-explanation of the underlying reason; fourth, the successive clearing away of traces. First, the refutation of erroneous interpretations.
[Commentary]: First, he refutes erroneous interpretations.
"Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: 'I shall deliver sentient beings.'"
Subhūti, do not conceive such a thought.
[Commentary] This is a mistaken interpretation of the sutra text. First, there is the direct negation; second, it can be understood as a further exhortation.
△ Second, showing the correct view.
[Commentary] Second, showing the right view. Why is this?
[Sub-commentary] The intent of the inquiry in the Sūtra is: for what reason does it cause one not to form such a thought?
"In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
[Commentary] The meaning of this explanation is that, in truth, there are no sentient beings who are delivered by the Tathāgata. [Sub-commentary] The verse says:

"In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings; for their names are identical to those of the aggregates (skandhas). This is because [the name "sentient being"] is not distinct from the aggregates.
"Detached from the dharma-realm.
[Commentary] The two lines following "equality" establish the fundamental tenet of the doctrine. The two lines following "by means of the name" explain the reason why this is so.
[Commentary]: The treatise states: "The provisional designation of 'sentient beings' coexists with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and is not separate from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
[Record]: The section beginning with "The treatise states" below provides a further explanation of the latter two phrases. Regarding "provisional designation":
there is only the name "sentient being," but no substantial entity of a sentient being; therefore, it is called "provisional. Regarding "coexisting with the five aggregates": this means that...
The place where the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are harmoniously combined is called a "sentient being" (sattva). It is neither identical to nor separate from [the aggregates];

therefore, it is said to be "shared. Regarding "not separate from the dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu): the Buddha is one who has attained ultimate realization and is already entirely identical with the dharma-realm.

Although sentient beings have not yet realized this, because that which arises through conditions (pratītyasamutpāda) lacks intrinsic substance, they too are identical to the dharma-realm. How could one use the dharma-realm to deliver the dharma-realm?
Therefore, the verse says, "equal and impartial.
△ Third, the reverse explanation of the reason.
[Commentary]: Third, the reverse explanation of the reason.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, the Tathāgata would then possess the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
[Commentary] Therefore, the scriptural text employs a reductio ad absurdum to clarify this point. If it were stated directly, it should say:
"Because the Buddha is devoid of the marks of a self, a person, and so forth, he does not perceive any sentient beings as objects to be delivered."

[Commentary] The Treatise says: "If the Tathāgata were to have such a mind as to think that there are sentient beings to be saved within the five aggregates, this would be the fault of grasping at signs.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "the fault of grasping at signs" and so forth:
it is because he asserts what does not exist to be existent; because it does not accord with the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); and because he fails to understand conditions (pratyaya).
Because it arises, it consequently becomes possessed of recollection.
[Commentary] Asaṅga says: "The Tathāgata knows according to the *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, if there is the notion of a sentient being, this constitutes the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*)."
[Commentary] *Er-yan* (爾炎) is a Sanskrit term that has two meanings. First, it means "mother of wisdom," as previously explained.

Second, it means "objective realm" (*viṣaya*), specifically the objective realm within meditative concentration; here, this latter meaning is adopted. The intent is as follows: Buddha-wisdom knows in accordance with the objective realm.
Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) exists, it knows it as existing; since sentient beings do not [ultimately] exist, it knows them as non-existent. If...
Regarding the commentary on the Mother of Wisdom: it is the fundamental wisdom that realizes the principle of equality, which is free from conceptual discrimination.
Now, observing sentient beings is likewise thus.
△ 4. Successively Erasing the Traces.
[Commentary]: Fourth, successively erasing the traces.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," it is not that there is a self; yet ordinary people take it to be so.
"There is a self, Subhūti.
Those who are called 'ordinary persons' by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not ordinary persons. [Commentary:

The purport of this passage from the *Fojijing* (Sutra on Erasing Traces) is that although the Buddha speaks of a "self," fundamentally there is no self. Those who cling to the existence of a self are merely...
These are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Although it is said they are ordinary beings, there are no such things as ordinary beings. It is like a person in a dream who sees a tiger;
both the tiger and the person in the dream are unobtainable. It is the same within the Dharma. Because ordinary beings cling to a self, it is said that there is "no-self.
Fearing that they might cling to the notion of being ordinary beings, it is said that they are "not ordinary beings. In this way, one gradually eliminates all clinging attachments.
Therefore, it is said that "traces are successively wiped away.

As for Vasubandhu’s remark that "one does not speak of the annihilation of dharmas," it means that one penetrates the nature of dharmas exactly as they abide.
Without severing the phenomena that are reflections of all birth and death, one attains mastery over nirvāṇa and carries out activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

[Commentary: The verse says: "This merit and its retribution are for the sake of transforming all sentient beings; through such spontaneous karma, the Buddhas manifest throughout the ten directions."
[Commentary]: "This merit and so forth" refers to the corresponding retribution for that untainted (*anāsrava*) merit; it is the stainless fruit (*vimala-phala*).

Within this fruit, there are no characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the treatise states: "In the fruit of Buddhahood, there are no characteristics of form, because they do not see one another.
Furthermore, the treatise states: "In the fruit of Buddhahood, there are no distinct forms or sounds; only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain alone. Thus.
There is no coming or going, and so forth. ○ Regarding the phrase "for the sake of transforming those below":

Someone may ask, "Since the Buddha-fruit has no distinct forms, sounds, coming, going, and so forth, how is it that he appears and receives blessings for the sake of sentient beings' enjoyment? Therefore, the meaning of this explanation is stated as follows:

when the faculties of sentient beings have matured, they serve as the conditioning cause capable of eliciting a response; through the Buddha’s objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), accumulated over immeasurable eons...

The roots of goodness for benefiting others permeate the pure *dharmadhātu* to form wholesome habits; thus, there is a spontaneous and effortless response whenever a stimulus arises, without deliberate thought.

This is like the single moon that does not descend [to the water], yet appears in a hundred waters without them rising up. Such is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the power of the roots of goodness in compassion.
This is precisely the intent of severing doubt. If there were a mind that experiences enjoyment within the fruit, then there would likewise be one within the cause.

Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata. [Commentary] This is the *Sūtra on Right View*.

This is not something different that appears as different. [Commentary] It is said: "If the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, they see the Buddha come. He comes from nowhere."
When turbid, one sees the Buddha manifest extinction at the Twin Śāla Trees and says, "The Buddha has departed. Yet, as for departing, there is nowhere to which he goes.
[Commentary] From "Great Cloud" downwards, this explains that according to the defilement or purity of the sentient being's mind, one consequently perceives the Buddha as having coming and going;
this is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). That he comes from nowhere and departs to nowhere is precisely immobility; this is called the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). This...

Thus, from the perspective of the perceiving faculty (*indriya*), there appears the coming and going of a Buddha; yet the Buddha is truly unmoving. All such phenomena arise from the self; what do they do for that [Buddha]?
In this context, the analogy of water briefly illustrates the mind of sentient beings.

One should understand that the moon represents the *dharmakāya*, the reflection represents the *nirmāṇakāya*, and clarity or turbidity represents defilement and purity. When the water is clear, the moon appears; yet the moon does not come. When the water is turbid, the moon...
It is hidden. It is not that the moon has departed; rather, it is simply that the water has clarity or turbidity, not that the moon rises or sinks. It is the same with the Dharma:
when the mind is pure, one sees the Buddha, yet it is not that the Buddha has come; when the mind is defiled, one does not see him, yet it is not that the Buddha has gone.
However, it is the defilement and purity of sentient beings that is meant, not the concealment or manifestation of the Buddhas.

[Commentary] Sengzhao says: When understanding reaches its ultimate limit, one accords with Suchness; in essence, there is no fixed location. When conditions arise, the Buddha appears; yet his coming has no point of origin.

[Commentary] Regarding "the resolution reaches its limit," etc.: when the resolution reaches its limit, the mind ceases; when the mind ceases, one accords with Suchness (*tathatā*). Since the essence of Suchness is fundamentally pervasive, it has no spatial location.
This clarifies the reality that is identical to the response. Regarding "when conditions arrive," etc., this clarifies the response that is identical to reality.
It is so. The meaning is the same as that of the great cloud appearing and disappearing.
[Commentary] Regarding the intent of severing doubt: the Buddhas fundamentally have no coming or going; it is only through the deluded perceptions of sentient beings that they see coming and going.
Since there is not even a Buddha who appears, how could there be the matter of receiving blessings?

[Commentary]: This term "atom" (paramāṇu) is according to the Mahāyāna school. Within a single mass of form, one performs a conceptual analysis until reaching the most subtle form, which constitutes an atom;

[Commentary] The following statement distinguishes this from the Great and Small Vehicles.

In the Mahāyāna, one employs contemplation and conceptual analysis to give rise to the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), thereby breaking down and analyzing that form until it reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). This is something that cannot be seen even by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of the followers of the Two Vehicles;
it is the ultimate limit of subtle reduction, beyond further breakdown or analysis, and is thus called "extremely reduced form" (*paramāṇurūpa*). It is not [the form] of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "those who rely on [such views]": because their school is deluded regarding the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and fails to realize that all phenomena are empty, they reckon these subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be substantially existent.
Therefore, they assert that the world is formed by the accumulation of these subtle atoms. As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

Whether extensive or concise, these are scattered throughout the various sūtras and śāstras.

Regardless of which specific sūtra or śāstra one follows, although their specific thematic aims (*abhiprāya*) may differ, their general intent is always to refute the pervasive conceptual constructions and emotional attachments of sentient beings, or their emotional attachments themselves.

Regarding "the many": those who do not penetrate the Dharma give rise to doubt based on metaphors. Since the illness is chronic, the medicine must be administered gradually, taking awakening as the limit;

thus, the Dharma and its metaphors are layered upon one another. Now, relying on the commentary to the "Ten Patiences" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, while also incorporating the essential thrust of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, I shall clarify the intent of these various metaphors so that they are not confused or conflated.
[Commentary] The Buddha taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty.
[Record] That "all phenomena are empty" is the fundamental tenet of this doctrine. Those of superior faculties understand it immediately upon hearing it;
those of middling faculties gain clarity through a single analogy; while those of inferior faculties give rise to successive delusions, and thus further analogies are employed.
As analyzed below:
[The Commentary] raises a doubt, asking: "Since all objective realms are directly perceived, why are they said to be like illusions? For although illusory phenomena do not exist..."
[This] is clearly visible. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "presently seen," etc., the objection is raised: "If all phenomena were not perceived, one might indeed say that they are all empty.
Yet they are presently seen with vivid clarity; on what basis can they be said to be empty? Therefore, the passage beginning with "like an illusion" uses a metaphor to explain the metaphor.
The following sections are all to be understood according to this principle.
[Commentary] Furthermore, a doubt arises: "If illusory phenomena are non-existent, why is there attachment to them? Therefore, it is said that they are like a mirage;
just as a thirsty deer perceives it as water and rushes toward it out of craving and attachment.
[Commentary]: Regarding "attachment and so forth," an objection is raised: "If sentient beings were not attached, it would be appropriate to teach that they are like illusions.
But since they have already given rise to a mind of attachment, how can they be like illusions? The passage beginning with "Therefore, it is said they are like a mirage" provides the explanation.
[Commentary] Furthermore, a doubt arises: if the thirsty deer ultimately never obtains water, how can those who are greedy all come to enjoy it?
Therefore, it is said that it is like a dream; even what is seen within a dream can be enjoyed.
[Commentary] Regarding "not obtaining water": an objection is raised: "If one seeks with greed but does not obtain [the object], then it is appropriate to say that all teachings are like a mirage.
But since those who seek have their hearts' desires fulfilled, how can they be said to be like a mirage? Therefore, the passage beginning with "like a dream" follows, which serves as the explanation.

[Commentary] Furthermore, one may doubt: "If one performs good or evil deeds in a dream, there is no karmic retribution upon waking; if one strikes one's elders in a dream, there is no grief or fear upon waking.
Therefore, it is said that [the dream] is like a shadow or an echo, lacking any substantial reality whatsoever. It is like a form reflected in a clear mirror, or a sound echoed in a hollow valley."

Whether beautiful or ugly, high or low, each and every thing corresponds exactly; there is never any confusion, and there is never any discrepancy. [Commentary] Regarding "dream-creation" and so forth:
An objection states, "If good and evil have no retribution, one may indeed say that phenomena are like dreams. But since the facts of cause and effect are so manifest, how can they be like dreams?
Therefore, the passage beginning with "hence they are said to be like shadows" provides the explanation. *Yán* (妍) means beautiful and excellent.
"Ugly" (*chī*) means hideous. This refers to the reflection in a mirror. "High and low" refers to the echo in a valley.
"Each responding individually" means there is not a single image that does not respond to its color, nor a single resonance that does not respond to its sound.
"Without confusion" means that it never manifests ugliness in response to beauty; for what is high must respond to what is low.

[Commentary] Furthermore, a doubt arises: "If there is no reality whatsoever, why does the Bodhisattva perform acts of benefit and happiness? Therefore, it is said that [the world] is like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
This means that although a transformed being knows it is unreal, it nonetheless performs the work of a transformation.

[Commentary] Regarding "benefit and happiness," etc.: An objection is raised: "If Bodhisattvas do not undergo birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), it may be said that they are like echoes or shadows;

but since Bodhisattvas do indeed undergo birth by transformation, how can they be like echoes or shadows? Therefore, the passage beginning with "hence, they are like transformations" provides the explanation.

One who performs transformative deeds cannot be said to perform transformative deeds and yet claim them to be real. One cannot be said to deliver sentient beings and yet [claim that they truly exist].
Sentient beings truly exist; it is precisely because sentient beings are empty that they do not realize this due to delusion. Therefore, [the Buddha] teaches them so that they may awaken.
If they possessed a real, substantial essence, what benefit would there be in transforming them? Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"One should contemplate sentient beings as being like illusions and transformations, like the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror, and like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Mañjuśrī asked: "If that is so, how does a bodhisattva..."
"What is the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? Vimalakīrti replied, "To preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—this is true loving-kindness.

[Commentary] The five successive rounds of inquiry and explanation above all reveal the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). This was because confusion arose due to metaphors; thus, through a series of instructions and clarifications, we have reached this final stage.
When the metaphors are exhausted, the Dharma is fully manifest, and the ice of doubt naturally melts away. However, in various sūtras, sometimes...

The mention of the city of Gandharvas, the moon in water, a stump, a ghost, a rope-snake, cataracts, flowers in the sky, tortoise hair, and rabbit horns is all spoken according to the capacity and circumstances of the listener, intended to lead them toward liberation.
It certainly does not imply that these five stages exist in a fixed, sequential order.

△ Second, a comparative analysis of the three assemblies regarding the Qin translation of the sutra, in two parts: first, pointing to the metaphor to reveal the Dharma; second, the actual comparison of the extensive and abbreviated versions.
First, pointing to the metaphor to reveal the Dharma, in three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, revealing the benefits; third, the concluding praise. First, the direct explanation.
[Commentary] The third assembly reconciles this with the version of the sutra translated during the Qin dynasty.

[Commentary] Through the metaphors of dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, the principle of emptiness is fully revealed; through the two similes of lightning and dew, impermanence is thoroughly manifested.
[Commentary] Regarding the "dreams, illusions, and so forth" in the Qin translation:

because these four things—dreams and the rest—all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being like dreams and such, the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) becomes easy to understand. As for the two things, dew and lightning:
they exist for a moment and then vanish. If one contemplates all phenomena as being like dew and lightning, impermanence (*anityatā*) is spontaneously revealed.
△ Second, the manifestation of benefits.
[Commentary] To realize true emptiness is to not dwell in any marks; to contemplate arising and ceasing is to exhort and stimulate one’s practice.

[Record] Regarding "To realize true emptiness" and below: this manifests the benefits. ○ As for "not dwelling in marks": ordinary beings, being deluded regarding true emptiness, already dwell [in them].
Regarding "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*): one should know that awakening to true emptiness is precisely not abiding in marks. To "abide" means the sense of grasping and defiled attachment.
Furthermore, ordinary beings are deluded and inverted; failing to understand impermanence, they cling to the world and do not apply themselves to cultivation and progress.
One should know that all things are entirely of the nature of impermanence, shifting and passing away from moment to moment, neither abiding nor lasting long. For this reason...
Fearing birth and death, they aspire to nirvana with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire, vying with every passing moment.

For this reason, within the assembly at the time of the Nirvana Sutra, the Buddha specifically praised this contemplation as the foremost. However, within each of these two phrases, there are both understanding (*jñāna*) and practice (*caryā*);
their respective correlations can be understood through interpretation.
△ Third, the concluding praise.
[Commentary] "Exquisitely conforming to the school that destroys marks; skillfully demonstrating the contemplation that transcends emotional attachment.
[Record] Regarding "Exquisitely conforming... and below: this is the concluding praise. ○ "Conforming to the school that destroys marks" praises the preceding four metaphors. However, the Buddha...

Within the teachings of this one lifetime, there are three schools of tenet within the Mahāyāna: first, the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school, which refers to scriptures such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*;
second, the Dharma-destruction (Poxiang) school, which refers to various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*;

and third, the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school, which refers to scriptures such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, as well as treatises such as the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.

The *Śālistamba-sūtra* and other treatises, as the Prajñāpāramitā school fundamentally deconstructs all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), now describe conditioned phenomena using metaphors such as dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
this clearly accords with the essential tenets of the school. Regarding the phrase "demonstrating the extinction of emotional attachments" and so forth: this praises the latter two metaphors.

If one contemplates all worldly phenomena as being like lightning or dew, one will naturally cease to bind one's emotions to body, life, or wealth, thereby giving rise to the understanding of impermanence.

Furthermore, by means of the first four metaphors, wisdom brings about the cessation of emotional attachment; by means of the latter two metaphors, the practice of meditative concentration brings about the cessation of emotional attachment.
Moreover, the former involves the cessation of the emotion that clings to existence, while the latter involves the cessation of the emotion that calculates permanence.

If one does not realize emptiness and impermanence, one remains bound by emotional attachment to the body, life, and material requisites; now that one has awakened to this principle of emptiness and impermanence, then [emotional attachment]—
Contemplating disintegration and transformation, true wisdom manifests before one. This is "wondrous" because it accords with the essence of the Sūtra above;
it is "skillful" because it accords with the sentiments of sentient beings below. II.

The actual reconciliation of the extensive and abbreviated versions has three parts: first, restating the question; second, explaining and resolving it; third, concluding with praise. First, restating the question:
[Commentary] Regarding the nine similes in the Wei translation and the three omissions in the Qin edition:
[Sub-commentary] "Regarding the Wei translation" below introduces the question. Someone may ask: Why are there nine similes in the Wei translation, while the Qin scripture omits three?
Why is this? It is set forth here in this document.
△ Second, the Explanatory Elucidation.

[Commentary]: Because stars and lamps possess substantiality, and clouds and seeds contain living beings, one fears it will be difficult to accord with the empty mind, as latent growth will instead foster the perception of phenomena.

[Commentary] “By means of the stars” below explains the general principle. ○ Regarding “having substance”: although the stars are not like the sun, and a lamp relies upon oil, they are not entirely empty;
therefore, it is said that they have substance. ○ Regarding “clouds and seeds”: both the phenomenon (dharma) and the metaphor (upamāna) are presented together.
Clouds can contain rain, and seeds inevitably produce sprouts; hence, it is called “containing life. ○ Regarding “difficult to conform to,” etc.: this is because one's habitual attachments are firm.

Indeed, they do not realize that things are empty from the outset; for this reason, metaphors are employed to sweep away their conceptual discrimination. If one contemplates objects as having substantial existence, it is equivalent to analyzing matter (into atoms);
thus, it is difficult to awaken to their immediate emptiness, and the contemplation of emptiness fails to be established—hence it is said that they find it difficult to accord with [the truth].
Regarding "secretly nourishing" and so forth: since they do not understand impermanence, they give rise to the notion of permanence regarding objective phenomena and are unable to relinquish them.
"Even if not intentional, the emotion arises spontaneously and is triggered without awareness; therefore, it is called 'latent' (qian).
△ Third, the concluding praise.
[Commentary]: The excellence of this translation lies in its capturing of the intended meaning.

[Commentary] Regarding "capturing the meaning" (*qùyì*) and so forth, former masters have all said: when it comes to a word-for-word correspondence between Chinese and Sanskrit, Xuanzang is preeminent;
however, when it comes to translating scriptures by capturing the intended meaning, Kumārajīva is supreme.

[Commentary] However, regarding the three metaphors beginning with clouds, they are directly excised. Among the remaining six, one metaphor is further replaced—namely, the shadow (*chāyā*) replaces the cataract (*timira*).
The reason for this replacement is that, like the cataract, the shadow equally serves to manifest the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

△ Third, the Section on Dissemination (Sūtra Commentary). This has two parts: first, an individual explanation following the text of the sūtra; second, an explanatory praise by citing treatises and commentaries.
[Commentary]: The third is the section on dissemination.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy.
Believing, accepting, and practicing accordingly.

[Commentary] The text regarding the circulation of the scripture is evident. ○ Regarding the phrase "When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra": since the original purpose was for Śāriputra (Kōshō) to pose a question, the Buddha answered by explaining the stages of descending, abiding, and practicing.
Once the answers to the questions were concluded, it would have been appropriate for the scripture to end; however, he proceeded to continue [the discourse].
Traces give rise to doubt; there were twenty-seven linked sections [of uncertainty]. Upon reaching this text, those doubts were dissolved like ice.

Since Subhūti had no questions to ask, Śākyamuni ceased his proclamation. Although this single fascicle of the sutra includes both teacher and disciple, it is designated as "Spoken by the Buddha" because it emphasizes the superior [authority].
The meanings of terms such as "Elder" (sthavira) are as explained previously.
△ First, a detailed explanation according to the text of the sūtra.
[Commentary] *Ni* (尼) means "woman" (*strī*). ○ *Upāsaka* (優婆塞) means "male lay follower" (*upāsaka*). *Upāsikā* (優婆夷) means "female lay follower" (*upāsikā*).
They are so called because they draw near to the *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* to attend to their needs. ○ *Asura* (阿修)...
*Rākṣasa*. This is translated here as "Non-God" (*asura*).
[Commentary] The sub-commentary has two parts; first, a detailed explanation following the text of the sutra.

[Commentary] Regarding "male and female lay followers" (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*): the headings and explanations are clear. They are also called "male near-dwellers" (*upavāsaka*), "male pure-faithers" (*śraddhāmanas-kārin*), and so forth.
This may be understood accordingly. ○ "Not a deva" means it is also not a human; that is to say, it is not subsumed under the destinies of devas or humans.
It is also called "without wine.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "all are great," etc., the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are three meanings for which one should joyfully practice.
First, the purity of the speaker: they are not defiled by attachment to gain or offerings. Second, the purity of what is spoken:
because they know the essence of phenomena as it truly is. Third, the purity of the attainment of the fruit.
[Commentary]: "According to reality" and so forth means that principles are explained according to principle, and phenomena are explained according to phenomenon. Regarding "purity of the fruit":
because one gives rise to practice based on understanding and attains the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is pure.

△ Second, citing the treatise and the commentary to praise and explain the exposition, in two parts: first, citing the treatise; second, citing the commentary. First, citing the treatise: [Commentary] As Asaṅga said:
"If one hears such a meaning and yet has no realization regarding the Mahāyāna, I consider them to be more [insentient] than a stone."
Because they are ultimately without cause.

[Commentary] Below the section on Asaṅga, there are two parts: citing the treatise and providing a commentary and explanation. ○ "Lacking awakening" means not giving rise to the wisdom of the two emptinesses.
○ "The two attachments are firm and solid, like the hardness of stone. Even stone can be ground or carved; however, when hearing the sutras... [text ends].
One can understand through non-self; this is not merely like a stone. Therefore, it is said to "exceed" [the stone]. A poem says:
"My heart is not a stone, which cannot be turned. "Turned" (*zhuan*) implies movement; "grinding" and "polishing" both carry the sense of movement. Furthermore, the *Treatise* states:
"Ordinary people, regarding the profound Dharma, are unable to awaken to or believe in it. Most people in the world are like this; for this reason, the Dharma falls into ruin."
"Regarding 'without cause': it means that because one lacks the true cause of the Mahāyāna, one cannot attain Bodhi.
[Commentary] Vasubandhu says: "The dharmas of all phenomena are rare and constitute the Dharani; their profound phrases and meanings are immeasurable.
Having heard these from the Venerable One and having explained them extensively, I dedicate this merit to all living beings."
[Commentary] "The Dharma of *dhāraṇī*" refers to the secret Prajñāpāramitā. "What is the meaning of 'profound'? refers to the manifest Prajñāpāramitā.
Alternatively, "the Dharma of *dhāraṇī*" refers to the text of the sūtra, while "the profound phrases and meanings" refers to the root verses.
"From the Venerable One" refers to Maitreya and Asaṅga. "Extensive exposition" refers to the treatise itself.
△ Second, citing the Commentary.

[Commentary]: The Great Cloud states: "The Great Sage has finished expounding the sutra; its wondrous principles are now complete. The two emptinesses are perfectly consummated, and the fourfold assembly shall practice accordingly."

[Commentary] Zhaò says: "Listening together and awakening in unison, the joy of the Dharma cleanses the mind; donning the robes and following the rites, one eternally honors that which is imperishable.

[Commentary] Zishèng says: "The profound Prajñā sūtras are the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods. Hearing even a single four-line verse of the sūtra already transcends the causes for rebirth in the evil realms;
maintaining it with purity for a single thought-moment will surely secure the prediction of Bodhi. Therefore, among humans, devas, and other species, there is none who..."
I have received and shall reverently practice it with devotion.
[Commentary] As for "Mother of Buddhas," it is so called because she can give birth to all Buddhas and the dharmas of enlightenment. The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
